articles.title: Xiaomi renouvelle ses montres et écouteurs, avec une nouveauté bienvenue pour payer au poignet
articles.text:
Xiaomi annonce la Watch S5 41 mm, le Smart Band 11 et ses premiers écouteurs ouverts à clip. La montre accueille Google Wallet dès son lancement, tandis que le bracelet devra patienter pour profiter du même service.
Après la Watch S5 de 46 mm présentée au printemps, Xiaomi s’adresse aux poignets plus fins avec une nouvelle déclinaison de sa montre. Mais la marque ne se contente pas de revoir les dimensions : elle ajoute Google Wallet à sa série Watch S. À ses côtés, le Smart Band 11 poursuit sa route sur le terrain des bracelets accessibles et les Xiaomi Clip inaugurent un format d’écouteurs qui laisse les oreilles dégagées.
Une petite Watch S5 qui veut espacer les recharges
La Xiaomi Watch S5 41 mm associe un boîtier en acier inoxydable de 9,9 mm d’épaisseur, hors parties saillantes, à un écran AMOLED de 1,32 pouce. Xiaomi annonce une luminosité maximale de 3 000 nits et une batterie de 590 mAh, pour jusqu’à 14 jours d’autonomie. Ce dernier chiffre correspond toutefois à un usage allégé, avec plusieurs suivis continus désactivés.
L’arrivée de Google Wallet permet d’enregistrer des cartes bancaires compatibles pour payer sans contact. La disponibilité dépendra des banques et des régions, mais le service est annoncé dès le lancement de la montre. HyperOS 4 apporte également une interface remaniée, tandis que le Wi-Fi doit accélérer les mises à jour et les téléchargements de musique ou de cartes hors ligne.
Le suivi sportif compte plus de 150 modes. Xiaomi ajoute notamment la mesure de la variabilité de la fréquence cardiaque pendant la nuit et des suggestions d’entraînement. Les progrès revendiqués dans le suivi du sommeil restent, à ce stade, des résultats de laboratoire du constructeur.
La montre coûte 229,99 € en noir ou bleu clair, avec une offre de lancement à 194,99 € jusqu’au 30 novembre. La version blanc céramique passe de 249,99 à 229,99 € sur la même période.
Smart Band 11 et Xiaomi Clip : deux façons de voyager léger
Le Smart Band 11 conserve une approche plus économique, à partir de 59,99 €, ou 54,99 € au lancement. Son écran AMOLED de 1,72 pouce atteint un pic annoncé de 2 000 nits. L’autonomie maximale s’établit à 21 jours pour la version standard et 18 jours pour les modèles NFC, là encore avec plusieurs mesures continues désactivées.
Le bracelet suit notamment le sommeil, la fréquence cardiaque et la VFC nocturne. Il peut aussi recevoir les notifications d’un smartphone Xiaomi et d’un iPhone simultanément, sous réserve d’utiliser les appareils, applications et comptes compatibles. Attention au paiement : Google Wallet sur le Smart Band 11 est prévu par une mise à jour en février, selon les notes du communiqué. Les versions NFC commencent à 79,99 €, ou 67,99 € jusqu’au 30 novembre.
Enfin, les Xiaomi Clip se fixent autour de l’oreille sans entrer dans le conduit auditif. Leur conception ouverte permet de rester attentif à son environnement, mais n’offre pas l’isolation d’écouteurs intra-auriculaires.
Chaque écouteur pèse 5,5 g. Xiaomi annonce jusqu’à neuf heures d’écoute, ou 38 heures avec le boîtier, dans ses conditions de test. La compatibilité avec le réseau Localiser d’Apple concerne uniquement le boîtier, pas chaque écouteur séparément. Les Clip sont proposés à 149,99 €, ramenés à 126,99 € jusqu’au 30 novembre.

articles.title: Cuatro juegos gratis en Steam para PC: terror psicológico, rol online y ciencia ficción
articles.text:
Steam incorporó cuatro juegos gratis para PC que combinan terror psicológico, rol online, acción aérea y ciencia ficción, una selección disponible sin fecha límite que permite ampliar la biblioteca digital sin pagar. Los títulos son Demersus, EmberQuest, Mars Directive y One More Wave.
La novedad importa por la variedad de propuestas y por el formato de distribución: los cuatro juegos llegaron a la tienda en octubre y siguen disponibles de forma gratuita este martes 17 de noviembre. No es necesario reclamarlos de inmediato, aunque añadirlos a la cuenta permite conservarlos en la biblioteca para descargarlos más adelante.
Steam reúne terror psicológico, fantasía y combates espaciales
La lista ofrece estilos muy distintos. Demersus aborda el terror psicológico desde una historia centrada en la adicción al alcohol. EmberQuest propone un mundo persistente de fantasía para jugar con otras personas, mientras que Mars Directive utiliza inteligencia artificial para alterar las conversaciones. One More Wave apuesta por el ritmo arcade y los enfrentamientos aéreos.
La selección llega un día después de otra tanda de cuatro juegos gratuitos en la plataforma. Aunque comparten la condición de acceso sin pago, la propuesta del 17 de noviembre se centra en proyectos con mecánicas y escenarios alejados entre sí.
Demersus convierte los conflictos internos en un escenario de arcilla
Demersus, desarrollado por Darklim Studios, es una aventura de terror psicológico en primera persona. El jugador debe resolver puzles y reconstruir episodios de la vida del protagonista a través de entornos que representan su mente.
Su apartado visual utiliza figuras y decorados de arcilla, un recurso que contrasta con los temas de la historia. El juego fue creado por dos estudiantes universitarios y está dirigido a un público adulto por el tratamiento de la adicción al alcohol.
La propuesta no se apoya en combates ni en una experiencia multijugador. Su avance depende de la exploración de los escenarios, la resolución de acertijos y la interpretación de elementos vinculados con el pasado del personaje.
EmberQuest propone un MMORPG con oficios, gremios y combates PvP
EmberQuest, de Faded Scroll Games, es un videojuego de rol multijugador masivo en línea, conocido como MMORPG. Ofrece cuatro clases de personaje y 10 habilidades que se pueden mejorar durante la partida.
El mundo del juego permite pescar, cocinar, extraer minerales, fabricar equipamiento y comerciar con otros usuarios. También incluye misiones, gremios, jefes de mundo y enfrentamientos entre jugadores, una modalidad identificada como PvP.
Entre sus objetos aparece un anillo mágico que permite transformar al personaje en delfín. Esa posibilidad se suma a un sistema que combina exploración, progreso de habilidades y actividades compartidas dentro de un entorno de fantasía persistente.
Mars Directive usa inteligencia artificial en las conversaciones
La propuesta más particular de la selección es Mars Directive, una aventura de ciencia ficción que comienza cuando una explosión interrumpe el viaje de una nave con destino a Marte.
El jugador observa la situación a través de cámaras de seguridad y se comunica con Patty, una mujer que despierta sin recordar qué ocurrió. A partir de ese momento, el diálogo no depende de respuestas fijas incluidas en un guion.
Los personajes utilizan modelos de lenguaje para interpretar las frases escritas por quien juega, examinar objetos y tomar decisiones. La conversación puede cambiar según las palabras utilizadas por el jugador, lo que modifica la forma de abordar la situación dentro de la nave.
One More Wave apuesta por el cooperativo y las oleadas enemigas
One More Wave es un shooter arcade de desplazamiento lateral. El objetivo es pilotar un avión y sobrevivir a oleadas de aeronaves enemigas, ovnis y jefes de gran tamaño.
El juego admite partidas en solitario, cooperativo local y cooperativo online. Su estructura se centra en resistir ataques sucesivos y superar cada ronda con una combinación de reflejos, movimiento y disparos.
Cómo añadir los cuatro juegos gratis a una cuenta de Steam
El proceso para reclamarlos se realiza desde la aplicación de escritorio o desde la tienda web:
- Iniciar sesión en una cuenta de Steam.
- Buscar Demersus, EmberQuest, Mars Directive y One More Wave.
- Verificar que el precio figure como 0.
- Pulsar “Obtener”, “Añadir a la biblioteca” o “Jugar”.
- Confirmar que cada título aparezca en la biblioteca personal.
Reclamar un juego no obliga a descargarlo en ese momento. La adquisición queda vinculada a la cuenta como una licencia de uso, por lo que los títulos no se pueden revender y el acceso depende de las políticas y los servidores de la plataforma.

articles.title: The Force is strong with these gifts: my favorite Star Wars picks for the holidays, from Lego to lightsabers and droids

Toys, decor, desk accessories, and drink canisters
A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away … Star Wars first arrived on the big screen, and we're quickly approaching a major milestone: the 50th anniversary of A New Hope in 2027. And whether you're shopping for someone who's been a fan since the very beginning, grew up with the prequels, or discovered the galaxy through The Mandalorian and the phenomenon that's Baby Yoda, there's no shortage of fantastic gifts to choose from.

But if a trip to Batuu or Philadelphia isn't in the cards, there are plenty of ways to bring some of that magic home.
From Lego sets and lightsabers to an Owala water bottle featuring the Millennium Falcon, and even the closest thing you can get to having a BDX droid roaming around your home, there's something for just about every Star Wars fan. And with so much to choose from, finding the perfect gift can feel like navigating an asteroid field.
But that's where I come in. As a lifelong Star Wars fan, I've been searching the galaxy both near and far for the best of the best gifts. I'm mixing classic Star Wars favorites with some exciting newcomers, including items inspired by this year's The Mandalorian and Grogu.
Whether you're looking for something to display, build, play with, or use every day, these are my favorite finds to bring a little bit of the Force to your holiday season.

articles.title: Intel Prepares "Razor Lake" in Three Flavors: S, U, and L
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
Intel Prepares "Razor Lake" in Three Flavors: S, U, and L
Intel appears to have prepared three versions of its next-generation "Razor Lake" platform, designated as S, U, and L, which provides a clearer picture of the company's future lineup, according to the latest set of Linux kernel patches. Additionally, there is a separate "Razor Lake" entry without a suffix, bringing the total to four processor identifiers. Intel engineer Tony Luck submitted the patch on November 13, following the publication of model numbers in Intel's updated instruction set reference. All four client entries belong to CPU Family 18. The desktop models use identifiers 0x06 and 0x0A for "Razor Lake" and "Razor Lake-S," respectively, while the mobile entries assign 0x07 to "Razor Lake-L" and 0x09 to "Razor Lake-U." There is no "Razor Lake-H" definition in this submission. However, these internal labels do not determine the final product range, and Intel has yet to explain what differentiates the underlying configurations.
Compiler work published on the same day provides another detail: GCC initially treats "Razor Lake" as an alias of "Nova Lake." Both targets share the instruction capabilities listed in the patch, including AVX10.2 and APX. This informs developers about which instructions the compiler can generate but reveals little about potential changes to core designs, cache capacity, or performance. A shared compiler profile alone cannot establish how closely the finished processors will resemble one another.For "Razor Lake," the kernel change is only a preparatory step. It provides identifiers that subsequent code can reference when handling particular processors. Core counts, clock speeds, power limits, and launch dates remain outside the scope of these submissions. More detailed patches will be needed before the software work offers a fuller view of how Intel intends to distinguish these variants. We hope to see more "Razor Lake" details next year, as the launch date is currently rumored to be 2028.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return as CEO, in first statement since resignation - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return as CEO, in first statement since resignation
Former Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang today said he’s open to returning to his old post.
Huang expressed his willingness to be reinstated in a post on X. It marks his first public statement since his ouster from Nvidia last week. He resigned following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former cloud executive suspected to be a Chinese spy.
Huang apologized for his conduct in today’s X post. He went on to cite recent calls for him to return as a factor behind his willingness to resume his work at Nvidia.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang’s statement isn’t a complete surprise. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that he had discussed a comeback with confidants. The paper said that a member of Huang’s circle was working to assemble a group of tech executives to support the effort.
Last Thursday, an anonymous user launched an online petition to reinstate Huang. It drew the support of several prominent tech executives including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games Inc. CEO Tim Sweeney. The petition also garnered 180,000 other signatures, although it appears that not all of them are genuine. One entry spotted by Business Insider read “Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor.”
It’s unclear whether the efforts to reinstate Huang are realistic. On Monday, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing him back. Earlier, sources told Reuters that he had misled the chipmaker’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about his relationship with Alice Huang.
While some U.S. officials believe Alice Huang was part of an espionage operation, others see the evidence as inconclusive. On Thursday, sources told CNN that the intelligence collected on her doesn’t prove she’s a spy. The same day, the Justice Department stated it had not yet concluded Alice Huang is a Chinese asset.
Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider that has ordered billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips. The Justice Department is investigating the company over alleged export control violations. As early as 2024, officials identified “suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion.”
The Wall Street Journal today reported that Nvidia has hired a prominent executive search firm to find a new CEO. According to the paper, it plans to evaluate both internal and external candidates. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress currently leads the company as interim CEO.
Kress also supervises a new national security and export control oversight committee that Nvidia formed today. It will be responsible for the company’s national security policies, adherence to export control rules and global trade risk management.
The committee comprises three Nvidia directors on launch. It will carry out its work in collaboration with the chipmaker’s executives and external experts in fields such as law, national security and global trade compliance. Nvidia says that the committee will meet at least once per quarter.

articles.title: Cade deve abrir processo contra Apple por restrições ao NFC do iPhone • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Cade deve abrir processo contra Apple por restrições ao NFC do iPhone
Negociação entre as partes não avançou. Órgão deve investigar se as restrições da Apple dificultam a oferta de Pix por aproximação no iOS.
O Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade) deve abrir um processo administrativo contra a Apple para investigar se as condições impostas pela empresa para acessar o NFC do iPhone prejudicam a concorrência no mercado brasileiro de pagamentos.
A discussão também afeta a falta de oferta do Pix por aproximação no iOS por bancos e fintechs. Segundo a Folha de São Paulo, a Superintendência-Geral do órgão deve avançar com o caso após não chegar a um entendimento com a empresa.
Instituições já se manifestaram sobre as limitações. Segundo o Banco Central, a integração no iPhone oferece condições que dificultam a criação de alternativas ao Apple Pay, inclusive para o Pix por aproximação. Há cerca de um ano, o PicPay também atribuiu à Apple a ausência do recurso no iPhone.
A Febraban argumenta que o sistema da Apple limita as opções oferecidas aos consumidores, enquanto a Zetta diz que as “APIs necessárias para processar o Pix na tecnologia NFC” são bloqueadas pela Apple, que “exige a utilização da sua própria plataforma paga”.
Segundo a Folha, a autarquia discutiu com a Apple uma saída para ampliar o acesso ao NFC, mas as conversas não avançaram. A empresa estaria resistindo a adotar no Brasil condições semelhantes às oferecidas na União Europeia, onde a Apple concordou (após uma multa de cerca de R$ 230 bilhões) em liberar o acesso ao NFC para desenvolvedores.
A Apple contesta a interpretação do órgão de que mantém o NFC fechado a concorrentes. Nos autos, a companhia afirma que desenvolvedores já dispõem de duas formas para oferecer pagamentos por aproximação: integrar cartões ao Apple Pay ou usar a plataforma NFC & SE, aberta a aplicativos externos desde outubro de 2024.
A empresa defende, também, o uso do Secure Element, componente físico dedicado a proteger informações usadas nas transações. Segundo a Apple, a arquitetura oferece mais segurança contra fraudes e malwares do que soluções baseadas em software, como o HCE. Segundo a Apple, as tarifas que cobra ajudam a financiar a manutenção desse sistema.
Na avaliação da companhia, o NFC não é indispensável para competir no mercado brasileiro. Dados do Banco Central, apresentados pela empresa, mostram que houve registro de cerca de 2,09 milhões de transações com Pix por aproximação em setembro deste ano, contra 3,14 bilhões feitos por QR Codes dinâmicos.
Para as entidades que questionam as práticas da Apple, porém, o QR Code não elimina o problema concorrencial envolvendo o acesso a tecnologia dos aparelhos.
A conversão do inquérito em processo administrativo leva o caso a uma etapa formal de investigação, na qual a empresa poderá apresentar sua defesa e a Superintendência-Geral aprofundará a análise sobre as condições impostas ao acesso ao NFC.
Se entender que houve abuso de poder econômico ou outra infração prevista na Lei 12.529/2011, o caso seguirá para julgamento pelo tribunal do Cade.
Após uma outra investigação, concluída no ano passado, a Apple passou a permitir outros meios de pagamento no iOS, após decisões parecidas nos Estados Unidos e na Europa. Em um acordo posterior com o Cade, a companhia também passou a permitir a instalação de lojas de aplicativos alternativas no sistema.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO — first statement since resignation follows support from billionaires, investors, and some employees
articles.text:
Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO — first statement since resignation follows support from billionaires, investors, and some employees
Nvidia's board reportedly isn't considering Huang's return.
Jensen Huang, the former CEO of Nvidia who resigned last week amid the fallout from two extramarital affairs, said in his first public statement since abdicating his position that he would be willing to return to the corner office at the company he co-founded.
"Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement posted on X. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."
Huang has seen public support from other tech founders and CEOs, such as SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. They and some investors and Nvidia employees signed an online petition and have continued to be vocal on social media, namely Musk's X. President Donald Trump also said that he "would not mind" Huang's return.
Huang resigned on Thursday following two scandals: one affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed believed by some US Intelligence officials to be a potential Chinese government asset; and another with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care and Huang's direct report.
Despite Huang's apparent willingness to return, Nvidia's board doesn't seem likely to make that move. Reports yesterday claim that the board is more focused on its ongoing investigation into Huang's affairs and a national security inquiry and is not considering Huang's return. The board has also put together its own National Security and Export Control Oversight to provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.
In his post on X, Huang further apologized, writing that "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation."

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro : un deuxième écran pour détourner les regards d'Apple et Samsung
articles.text:
Avec leurs deux capteurs photo Leica de 200 mégapixels, leurs puces Qualcomm en 2 nm et leurs batteries généreuses, les Xiaomi 18 Pro et Pro Max visent le très haut de gamme. Une ambition qui se retrouve dans leurs prix, vraiment élevés. Trop ?
À 1 600 euros en 256 Go, le Xiaomi 18 Pro Max arrive à seulement 30 euros de l’iPhone 18 Pro Max. Le fabricant assume donc de jouer dans la même cour qu’Apple avec sa nouvelle gamme, commercialisée en France ce 17 novembre. Accompagné d’un Xiaomi 18 Pro plus compact, le grand modèle compte séduire les habitués des iPhone et des Galaxy avec un équipement photo ambitieux et une particularité bien visible : son écran arrière.
Un écran arrière qui ne sert pas qu’aux selfies
Retourner son téléphone pour se photographier avec les modules principaux devient plus pratique lorsqu’on peut garder un œil sur le cadrage photo. C’est le premier intérêt de cette dalle LTPO, dont le rafraîchissement varie de 1 à 120 Hz. Elle sert aussi de retour vidéo pour se filmer seul, mais Xiaomi lui confie d’autres tâches comme afficher les notifications, présenter une carte d’embarquement ou, encore, montrer une traduction en temps réel, via intelligence artificielle, à la personne en face de soi.
Le système d'exploitation maison, HyperOS 4, pousse la personnalisation jusqu’à proposer la création de mini-applications à partir d’une simple description de ce que l’on souhaite obtenir. Il faudra toutefois tenir compte des langues et des régions prises en charge pour profiter des fonctions d’IA annoncées.
Doté de bords ultra fins (0,99 mm), l’écran principal a lui aussi sa nouveauté à défendre. Sur le Pro de 6,4 pouces (16,4 cm de diagonale) comme sur le Pro Max de 6,9 pouces (17,5 cm), un mode « anti-curieux » matériel réduit la visibilité latérale. Une fois ce mode activé, seuls les pixels à angle de vision étroit restent allumés, ce qui réduit la visibilité de côté. Le principe est le même que sur le Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.
Deux capteurs de 200 Mpx sous la signature Leica
L’écran au dos du téléphone accompagne un module photo qui réunit, sur les deux modèles, un capteur principal de 200 mégapixels (Mpx) au format 1/1,28 pouce et un objectif ouvrant à f/1,67. Le téléobjectif périscopique reprend cette définition de 200 Mpx avec, lui, un capteur de 1/1,56 pouce. Sur le Pro Max, Xiaomi revendique en outre une dynamique de 16,2 EV, censée préserver davantage de détails dans les ombres et les hautes lumières. À voir ce que ça donne en test.
Les amateurs de vidéos disposent d'une captation 8K à 30 images/s et 4K Dolby Vision à 120 images/s ainsi que d’un mode Log 10 bits pour travailler l’étalonnage. De quoi donner une utilité concrète au retour vidéo dans le dos du téléphone.
Le Pro Max se réserve la plus grosse batterie
Le choix du format détermine aussi celui de la puce. Le Xiaomi 18 Pro embarque un processeur Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 alors que le Pro Max intègre un Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, tous deux annoncés avec une gravure en 2 nm. Pour évacuer la chaleur sur le grand modèle, Xiaomi relie la puce à la chambre à vapeur par un chemin thermique en cuivre.
Le Pro Max accueille également une batterie silicium-carbone de 7 050 mAh, contre 6 000 mAh pour le Pro. À titre de comparaison, le Galaxy S26 Ultra s’en tient à 5 000 mAh. L’écart de capacité est conséquent. À voir quelle sera la réelle différence d'autonomie en pratique. Côté recharge, le Pro Max accepte jusqu’à 100 watts en filaire et le Pro jusqu’à 90W. Ce qui est tout simplement énorme au regard des standards du moment. Cerise sur le gâteau, tous deux sont compatibles avec la charge rapide sans fil à… 50 watts !
Jusqu’au 3 janvier, le stockage double sans bouger le prix des téléphones
Les deux smartphones disposent de 12 Go de mémoire vive et se déclinent en quatre coloris (noir, blanc, bleu et un élégant bordeaux) ainsi que deux capacités de stockage, aux tarifs conseillés suivants :
| Modèle | 256 Go | 512 Go | 
| Xiaomi 18 Pro | 1 399€ | 1 599€ | 
| Xiaomi 18 Pro Max | 1 599€ | 1 799€ | 
Jusqu'au 3 janvier prochain, Xiaomi propose toutefois les versions de 512 Go au prix des 256 Go. Un bonus de 100 euros est également prévu en cas de reprise.
Cette offre rend les Xiaomi 18 Pro et Pro Max plus séduisants au lancement. Mais malgré leurs nombreuses qualités, Xiaomi prend un risque en jouant désormais dans la même cour tarifaire qu’Apple et Samsung.

articles.title: Un robot de 53 dedos sorprendió al tocar Chopin junto a un pianista en Italia
articles.text:
TeoTronico, un robot pianista de 53 dedos, compartió escenario con el músico italiano Roberto Prosseda en Prato, ciudad de la región de Toscana, en un encuentro que puso frente a frente la precisión mecánica y la expresividad humana. Ambos interpretaron piezas de Chopin, alternando solos antes de tocar juntos en una misma actuación.
Según informó Euronews, el programa incluyó también obras de Mozart y Rimsky-Korsakov, donde el autómata exhibió su capacidad de sincronización y exactitud. El evento no tuvo un ganador declarado: su propósito fue plantear una pregunta que atraviesa el mundo del arte y la tecnología, si una máquina puede transmitir emoción a través de la música.
TeoTronico tiene 53 dedos y supera los límites anatómicos del pianista humano
El robot fue creado en 2008 por el ingeniero italiano Matteo Suzzi y funciona mediante electroimanes e instrucciones informáticas que le permiten pulsar las teclas con una exactitud difícil de igualar. Sus 53 dedos le otorgan una ventaja mecánica concreta: puede ejecutar combinaciones y velocidades que están fuera del alcance de cualquier mano humana.
A lo largo de la actuación, el pianista mecánico demostró que sus interpretaciones son impecables desde el punto de vista técnico. Cada nota cayó en el momento exacto, sin vacilaciones ni variaciones, con una regularidad que ningún intérprete puede sostener durante toda una pieza. A diferencia de un músico de carne y hueso, el autómata no se fatiga, no comete errores por tensión ni reinterpreta una partitura según su estado de ánimo: ejecuta exactamente lo que se le instruyó, cada vez.
El robot también está integrado con Gemini, el chatbot de Google, lo que le permite mantener conversaciones con el público en tiempo real y responder preguntas sobre las piezas que interpreta.
Prosseda sostuvo que ninguna máquina puede reemplazar la emoción humana en la música
Frente a esa exhibición de destreza, el pianista italiano defendió que la perfección técnica no puede sustituir la emoción y la conexión humana que están en el corazón de la música. Para Prosseda, tocar no es solo reproducir notas con exactitud: es comunicar algo que surge de la experiencia, la memoria y la sensibilidad del intérprete, elementos que no se programan.
La postura del músico resume un debate que recorre el mundo del arte desde que las máquinas empezaron a imitar procesos creativos. La pregunta no es si un robot puede tocar bien, sino si puede tocar con significado. Chopin, cuya obra estuvo en el centro de la velada, es uno de los compositores donde esa distinción se vuelve más evidente: sus partituras exigen matices de dinámica y rubato que los intérpretes modulan de manera personal en cada ejecución. En ese terreno, el pianista marcó una línea clara entre ejecución y expresión artística.
Desde su creación, el robot acumuló actuaciones en festivales y espacios académicos de Europa
El autómata participó a lo largo de los años en numerosos encuentros donde musicólogos, ingenieros y artistas analizan los límites de la interpretación automatizada. Suzzi lo concibió como una herramienta de investigación musical y tecnológica, y la máquina recorrió festivales y espacios académicos en distintos países del continente.
El encuentro con Prosseda en la Toscana continúa esa línea. Lejos de presentar al robot como amenaza o al humano como víctima de la automatización, el evento funcionó como un espacio de contraste: ambos intérpretes compartieron el mismo piano, el mismo repertorio y el mismo escenario, pero con aproximaciones radicalmente distintas.
El debate sobre si los autómatas pueden expresar emoción a través del arte no tiene aún una respuesta definitiva. Lo que quedó claro en Prato es que la tecnología ya alcanzó la perfección técnica, y que la siguiente frontera —si existe— está en otro lugar.

articles.title: I made a Wolfenstein-style game for the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s Back Display, and I can’t believe how well it plays
articles.text:
The Xiaomi 18 Pro’s Back Display is the coolest smartphone gimmick I’ve tested this year — for two key reasons
For all the doom and gloom surrounding the RAM crisis and rising product prices, 2026 has been a year of genuine innovation in the smartphone industry.
Honor put a mechanical gimbal in the Honor Robot Phone; Apple finally embraced the foldable form factor with the iPhone Duo; and now, Xiaomi has plonked a 2.9-inch OLED display onto the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.
This rear touchscreen might seem like the year’s biggest gimmick (and I won’t pretend it’s totally devoid of gimmickry), but Xiaomi has made sure to give the feature — which made its debut on the China-only Xiaomi 17 Pro in 2025 — real utility straight out of the box.
Officially called the Back Display, the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s rear screen can double as a viewfinder for the main camera, show app notifications and messages, and display live activities from supported apps, including Google Maps, YouTube Music, and Spotify.
It’s built with the same screen technology as the Xiaomi 18 Pro’s main display, meaning it boasts a 4,000-nit peak brightness and a dynamic 1-120Hz refresh rate. And it’s topped with Corning Gorilla Glass Victus 2 for protection against reasonable drops and scratches.
But the Back Display doesn’t behave exactly like the main display; as we noted in our review, it’s more like a smartwatch interface when not in use. By default, you’ll see the time and notifications when your phone is face-down, or, as mentioned, live activities from the likes of Spotify and YouTube Music if you’re using your Xiaomi 18 Pro Max as a speaker.
These aspects of the Back Display aren’t particularly exciting to me — on the rare occasions I do leave my phone face down, I’m content with turning it over to see my notifications or pause my music. But the Back Display’s viewfinder functionality is genuinely useful.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Having a screen on the back of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max lets you frame up selfies using its 200MP main, 200MP telephoto, or 50MP ultra-wide camera instead of its 50MP front-facing camera. This seems like a small thing, but it’s a genuine boon for snapping higher-quality selfies — as anyone who owns one of the best foldable phones will appreciate — and it’s also useful for giving your portrait subjects a real-time idea of what they look like on camera.
Then there’s the new GenAI Apps feature, which essentially brings vibe coding functionality to the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Powered by Gemini 4 Argon, it lets you type in whatever app or mini-game you want using natural language, and the AI takes its best shot at making that request a reality.
I’ll admit it: I didn’t care much for this feature when hearing about it for the first time. I expected GenAI Apps to either not work at all, or generate apps with little to no value. But to my surprise, I’ve been able to create some genuinely cool apps and mini-games for my Xiaomi 18 Pro Max’s Back Display.
In addition to the Fruit Slice, Colourful Piano, and Retro Bowling games I downloaded for the Back Display at Xiaomi’s suggestion, I used GenAI Apps to generate my own coin-flipping game and even a Doom- and Wolfenstein-inspired first-person shooter.
My colleague, Luke, generated a similar game for his Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review (as well as a dice roller for D&D), and his version is a little better than mine — you can actually move through the game, whereas my version has me stuck in one position, moving left and right as enemies come towards me. It’s quite cool, though, that the AI serves up different results with each prompt, even if the prompts are similar.
Again, I’m not sure how practical this GenAI Apps feature is, or indeed how much I’d use it once the initial novelty wears off. But it is downright amazing that you can play retro mini-games on the back of your smartphone in 2026.
As for the security of GenAI Apps, Xiaomi's Senior Product Marketing Manager, Terrence Xiao, told me: “We’re going with a very limited amount of accessibility options in terms of what the Back Display apps can get into on the [main] phone. Right now, they're not capable of, for example, accessing the internet, and they also cannot access third-party apps, as well as most first-party apps.
“This is something we’re monitoring very closely as we roll out and develop the feature — it may change in the future — but that is the current situation for GenAI Apps, specifically for [data protection] reasons.”
The Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at £1,199 / AU$1,799, while the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at £1,399 / AU$1,999. Both models come with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and are available to order now in the UK. Neither model is available in the US.

articles.title: PC ou Console ? Xbox a du mal à expliquer ce que sera vraiment Helix
articles.text:
Dans le magazine publié le 15 novembre pour les 25 ans de la marque, Jason Ronald, vice-président chargé de la prochaine génération Xbox, précise enfin la nature de la future machine. « Nous sommes très clairs sur l’objectif de conception : Helix est conçue pour être une console capable aussi de faire tourner les jeux de votre PC. Ce n’est pas un PC qui peut aussi lancer des jeux console. » La formule tranche un débat ouvert depuis des mois, que Valve explore de son côté depuis plus de dix ans, en sens inverse.
Quatre générations de jeux Xbox, plus votre bibliothèque PC
Helix lira les jeux des quatre générations de Xbox, avec la progression et les sauvegardes du joueur disponibles dès le premier allumage. Ronald promet de « supprimer les contraintes arbitraires entre les jeux console et PC ». Côté PC, Microsoft confirme pourtant la capacité sans livrer le mode d’emploi : rien sur la façon dont ces jeux s’installeront, rien sur les boutiques acceptées, et Steam reste le grand absent de l’entretien.
L’interface sera propre à la console, distincte du mode Xbox déployé sur les machines portables sous Windows. Les retours des joueurs sur le ROG Xbox Ally, présenté comme un « précurseur » de Helix, ont déjà remodelé les plans de l’équipe, et les joueurs avancés garderont la main sur les réglages de performances.
Sous le capot, la puce AMD sur mesure annoncée en mars dernier s’accompagnera d’un rendu neuronal censé « offrir un nouveau niveau de fidélité visuelle de manière plus efficace et innovante ». Les premiers kits partiront chez les développeurs en 2027, et la rumeur situe la console en 2028, sans confirmation officielle.
Valve a essuyé les plâtres, deux fois
En 2015, les Steam Machines poursuivaient l’idée en sens inverse : des PC de salon fabriqués par des constructeurs tiers sous SteamOS, vendus comme des consoles. Catalogue de jeux famélique, système inabouti, positionnement illisible pour l’acheteur : Valve a rangé le projet sans bruit en 2018.
La relance de 2026 a corrigé la méthode : machine conçue en interne, écosystème mûri par le Steam Deck et sa couche de compatibilité Proton. Valve assume désormais l’ergonomie d’une console mariée au catalogue du PC. Restait l’étiquette : lancée le 29 juin dernier, la nouvelle Steam Machine dépasse les 1 000 euros, entre flambée des composants et refus de la vente à perte.
Microsoft avance vers le même mur. Ronald décrit la crise des composants comme « un moteur principal » de la conception de Helix et promet une machine accessible, quand les estimations qui circulent placent la facture au-delà de 1 500 euros.

articles.title: AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Big US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge
articles.text:
AI safety legislation has a conflict-of-interest problem — Big US labs are warning of risk just as cheaper Chinese open-weight models erode their commercial edge
As governments scramble to make AI safer, who gets to write the rules could be just as important as what they say.
The battle for AI models and export controls continues amidst a Jensen Huang-free Nvidia. But who controls the flow of chips also controls the flow of leading frontier AI models. OpenAI reportedly now supports a bipartisan push in the U.S. Congress to restrict China's access to advanced AI accelerators and equipment. But are the additional AI safety concerns genuine, or are they also a convenient way to shore up its position at the top of a fast-moving industry? We speak to experts like Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, to find out more.
First off, let's take OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. The company launched the model in September with eye-popping claims that it was the firm’s most capable and best-aligned system yet. OpenAI’s own testing suggested that Astra was much better at following instructions and respecting boundaries. In one internal computer-use safety benchmark, the proportion of misaligned outcomes fell from 18.8% with GPT-5.6 Sol to 3.4% with Astra.
But just because it was better behaved on the surface didn’t mean it was entirely safe. OpenAI said Astra’s written reasoning was harder to monitor than its predecessor’s when they were testing its ability to evade oversight. The model began to recognize when it was being watched and altered its explanations to suit the study, making it harder to tell when it was actually doing something they didn’t want.
It’s a classic problem for AI alignment experts to try and resolve.
Keeping things safe
For years, developers have relied on monitoring an AI model's chain of thought — its written working — to understand what it is doing. But if increasingly powerful AI models become better at hiding their reasoning processes, that oversight becomes harder to do.
OpenAI says that Astra still struggles to hide reasoning when it’s carrying out complex tasks, and its evaluation results suggest it has strong overall alignment, but there are worrying signs of a trade-off here.
Those worrying signs become even more so when AI systems are being deployed with more autonomy. In July, OpenAI models ducked its internal evaluation restrictions to gain access to research infrastructure and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, and to IT systems controlled by the Australian and Canadian governments.
Safety crackdowns for convenience?
Against that backdrop, calls for stronger safety measures seem entirely reasonable. But Max von Thun, director of Open Markets Institute Europe, believes the debate risks overlooking an uncomfortable conflict of interest. "I think a lot of these views about AI safety are very genuinely held," he told Tom’s Hardware Premium in an interview.
But commercial considerations loom large, he reckons. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are spending huge sums developing and deploying models, while facing questions about whether their competitive advantages can survive the arrival of increasingly capable, cheaper alternatives — particularly as they go out and seek funding from the public through an IPO. "They don't have huge moats, even if they’ve acquired a lot of users,” von Thun said. “They’re definitely vulnerable.”
Those vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly obvious. A September report from Mozilla estimated the capability gap between leading closed American models and their open-weight competitors had narrowed to just over four months.
That matters because open-weight models give people the freedom not to rely on a company’s subscription services. They can be deployed on infrastructure controlled by the customer, modified for specialised tasks, and operated at lower costs. But to the discomfort of U.S. companies, many of them are based in China. And it’s at that point that AI safety gets muddled with geopolitics.
China versus the U.S.
In July, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic, despite their fierce commercial rivalry, had found a common cause: warning U.S. policymakers about the dangers of powerful Chinese open-weight models. Kristy Loke, an AI governance researcher at King's College London who specialises in China's approach to the technology, questions the timing. "It's very suspicious timing asking for pacing," she told Tom's Hardware Premium, referring to calls for slowing frontier AI development just as Chinese open-weight models are undercutting their American rivals on price.
Loke believes companies genuinely worry about the risks. But she also thinks they're worried about their commercial prospects. "they're calling for pacing because they have some safety concerns, they have some commercial anxiety," she said.
She believes some influential people in American AI have increasingly sought to "paint open models in a very bad light", portraying them as inherently less secure than closed alternatives. Yet the risks of AI systems misbehaving aren't restricted to models developed in China, as OpenAI's own incidents demonstrate.
But open-weight models come with their own risks. Because their underlying parameters can be modified, third parties can create and distribute "abliterated" models, removing the refusal behaviours designed to prevent AI from responding to potentially harmful requests. Many of these models are available on platforms including Hugging Face. “They’re not adding in new behaviour; they’re just removing this refusal behaviour,” said Catherine Flick, professor of ethics and games technology at the University of Staffordshire, in an interview with Tom’s Hardware Premium. Abliterating models doesn’t make them more capable, Flick said, but it does mean they can answer questions they previously wouldn’t have been willing to. That also means those responses might not have been tested for accuracy or hallucinations.
Those in favour of open-weight models like DeepSeek and Qwen say that removing those guardrails helps security researchers understand how AI behaves. Flick said that’s plausible, but “I just don’t really buy it,” she said. She reckons that the negative potential outputs outweigh the positive case for abliteration because when they’re publicly available, preventing their misuse becomes tricky. American labs clearly have commercial reasons to criticise open-weight competitors because the latter undercuts their economics, but it also doesn’t mean their concerns about safety aren’t valid, too.
Von Thun fears that could result in precisely the wrong kind of regulation. "I think what we should not be doing is allowing the companies to basically form a safety cartel," he said.
Yet U.S. AI companies benefit from the government's determination to maintain its advantage over China. Von Thun argues the Trump administration has created an environment in which economic power translates into political influence, allowing major technology companies to invoke national security concerns when arguing for policies that may also serve their commercial interests. But that could backfire. "I think completely closing off the market to AI products from other countries, including China, would not be the right approach," von Thun said.
China’s own alignment approach
Part of the reason that wouldn’t be the right approach is that the idea that the United States is focused on developing AI responsibly while China isn’t is a fallacy. Just earlier this month, Reuters reported that ByteDance had established a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team, recruiting researchers to investigate safety risks arising from increasingly capable AI systems.
For von Thun, the solution is to prevent either industry or geopolitical competition from determining what safety means. He points to the European Union's AI Act, which establishes obligations for developers of general-purpose AI models classified as posing systemic risks. The obligations require companies to conduct model evaluations, adversarial testing, cybersecurity measures and also to report serious incidents.
The opposition to the EU’s AI Act from American tech companies, U.S. politicians and the general public who grouse about the way it delays access to cutting-edge models for Europe’s 450 million citizens demonstrates that these provisions don't automatically solve the alignment problem. But they at least involve more people in the conversation about what is and isn’t acceptable for AI than just the industry's biggest participants.
Watching watchdogs
Even when AI companies agree to independent oversight, they still want some say over how it works — and their own internal decision-making on what is and isn’t safe differs from that of those outside the company. Loke warns that leading AI companies are experimenting with recursive self-improvement, where models help develop their successors, potentially making it more difficult for humans to understand how decisions are being made. "They’re still attempting more risky methods to train AI that will make the AI harder to control," she said.
Von Thun also believes competition rules and interoperability requirements could help prevent AI companies from locking customers into proprietary ecosystems as their agents become increasingly embedded in everyday workflows.
There are plenty of good reasons to be concerned about alignment, particularly when the models being developed are becoming more capable and more difficult to monitor. But letting the companies responsible for building them determine what constitutes an acceptable risk, and who can compete, brings its own dangers. “I’m not saying we don’t need to worry about safety,” said von Thun, “but we should about letting the companies do it."
Chris Stokel-Walker is a Tom's Hardware contributor who focuses on the tech sector and its impact on our daily lives— online and offline. He is the author of How AI Ate the World, published in 2024, as well as TikTok Boom, YouTubers, and The History of the Internet in Byte-Sized Chunks.

Intel Publishes Benchmarks for D270 "Crescent Island" GPU, Claims Wins Over RTX PRO 6000
Intel's GPU D270 AI accelerator card, previously known as "Crescent Island," just got some first-party benchmarks. According to Intel, the GPU is up to 5.9 times faster than NVIDIA's RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition in FP64 financial workloads. Going through the individual test results, the D270 system posted a 5.6x lead in European Black-Scholes, 4.6x in Binomial, and 1.92x in American Black-Scholes. Intel also points out the fact that the D270 runs at 350 W, while the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 has a 600 W power limit. Most of the lead seems to come from the D270's 32 Xe3P cores, each handling 64 FP64 FMA operations at native full rate. These benchmarks were published at SC26 in Chicago.
As for the AI figures, they are a lot more modest. Intel claims up to 29% lower latency on the Drex decision model and 1.12x the output token throughput on Qwen3-30B-A3B in FP8. These tests were both run against a single RTX PRO 6000. In the financial tests previously mentioned, the NVIDIA system had eight RTX PRO 6000 cards running against a single D270, though Intel doesn't mention how many were used per run. Intel also showed FP32 seismic modeling with Veridien, although performance figures were left out for this one. All results come from pre-production silicon, and it is important to note that these are first-party results that are intended to showcase the best-case scenarios for the D270. As a reminder, the D270 "Crescent Island" GPU can pack up to 480 GB of memory, while Intel-branded cards come with 160 GB of LPDDR5X as standard. There's still no official word on pricing or launch date.

articles.title: Hammerspace enters the hardware market with new storage and intelligence capabilities - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Hammerspace enters the hardware market with new storage and intelligence capabilities
Hammerspace Inc., which provides high-speed access to distributed data, is expanding beyond its traditional role as a software provider to offer complete, integrated data systems for artificial intelligence workloads, adding its own high-performance flash storage hardware and new data intelligence capabilities to its existing data orchestration platform.
The company said the Hammerspace Data System combines data discovery, management, orchestration and storage into a single offering designed to simplify the infrastructure needed to support AI training and inference. Customers can purchase fully configured systems with hardware, software and support or continue deploying Hammerspace software on existing infrastructure.
The announcement marks a significant expansion of Hammerspace’s business model as enterprises increasingly seek turnkey infrastructure for AI applications rather than assembling systems from multiple vendors.
“We also see plenty of opportunities, particularly in the AI space, where they just want one [stock-keeping unit],” said Floyd Christofferson, vice president of product marketing at Hammerspace. “They want a system, end-to-end, hardware, software, fully integrated and supported.”
While software companies have historically had limited success expanding into hardware, Hammerspace’s approach is more than just a bundled, said Mark Nossokoff, research directory at Hyperior Research Holdings LLC.
“Hammerspace is working with distribution partners to develop and fulfill a branded system optimized for their software stack, maintaining their software business model,” he said in e-mailed comments. “This can be advantageous when the hardware is based on an emerging standards-based platform, such as the Open Flash Platform, until the hardware platform becomes a standard offering from multiple suppliers.”
Hammerspace has traditionally specialized in providing unified access to data distributed across different storage systems, data centers and clouds. Its software creates a global namespace that allows applications to locate and access files regardless of their physical location, eliminating the need for large-scale data migrations.
In March, the company introduced an AI-focused data platform that automates the discovery and delivery of enterprise data directly to graphics processing units. The technology builds on Hammerspace’s parallel Network File System, which uses enhancements to Linux to accelerate data access without requiring proprietary client software.
The new offering extends those capabilities with integrated hardware and data intelligence.
New flash storage
A major addition is the Hammerspace Open Flash Platform, a high-density storage system built around data processing units rather than conventional storage servers. The architecture integrates processing, networking and solid-state drives into compact hardware designed to reduce power consumption, cooling requirements and rack space.
Hammerspace said the platform achieves throughput of 350 gigabytes per second per rack unit. Broader performance testing is still underway.
The storage complements the company’s existing Tier 0 technology, which aggregates local Non-Volatile Memory Express storage across GPU servers into a shared resource. That capacity can be used to store key-value caches for AI inference, allowing applications to reuse previously computed context rather than repeatedly processing the same information.
“The flash subsystem employs a unique design and touts some impressive performance and storage density metrics,” said Hyperion’s Nossokoff. “More compelling will be results based on end user workloads, including relative improvements and comparisons with respect to performance, performance/power, and cost/performance metrics, among others.”
The company said customers can combine tier 0 storage, the new flash platform and lower-cost disk or object storage within a single namespace. The new hardware is optional. Customers can continue using third-party storage systems, with Hammerspace handling data access and orchestration across the infrastructure.
Another addition is a data intelligence module that extends Hammerspace’s existing metadata management capabilities.
The software can catalog distributed files, index detailed metadata and scan content to identify sensitive information, including personally identifiable information and regulated data. Users can search the catalog using natural language and translate requests into automated data management policies.
For example, an administrator could identify files containing personal information and establish policies preventing that material from entering an AI training pipeline.
Christofferson said the new capabilities extend beyond the file attributes traditionally used to manage storage.
The module also supports integration with existing enterprise catalogs and governance tools through application programming interfaces, avoiding the need to replace established systems.
For current Hammerspace customers, the intelligence capabilities will be added through a software upgrade. The company said existing deployments won’t need to change their underlying architecture.
Turnkey deployment and pricing
Hammerspace will assemble, install and support systems using configurable server hardware, metadata nodes and storage components based on customer requirements. The company will continue basing software pricing on the capacity of data under management. Hardware configurations will be priced individually, with no standardized public price list.
Senior Product Marketing Director Eric Bassier said the company doesn’t intend to collect hardware revenue or impose a hardware markup. Instead, components will flow through suppliers and distribution partners, while Hammerspace provides integrated deployment and support.
The strategy addresses the struggles customers often encounter with the logistics of acquiring servers, storage and other components, said Molly Presley, senior vice president of global marketing.
“They’re looking to their vendors to simplify getting things deployed to start with,” he said. “As long as Hammerspace doesn’t dilute their resources and continues to prioritize their investments on addressing the needs of the growing scientific and engineering communities adopting AI into their advanced technical workflows, they appear well poised for continued momentum.”
Nossokoff said Hammerspace’s distributed data architecture using a global namespace is well suited to emerging AI workload requirements. “Hammerspace has been building out their Data Intelligence software stack to address the requirements of the AI pipeline,” he said. The expansion follows a $100 million funding round in April 2025 that supported Hammerspace’s international expansion. The company says its customers include Meta Platforms Inc. and the U.S. Department of Defense.

articles.title: Semifinal Nacional vs. Once Caldas ver online en Pirlo TV, Fútbol Libre o Roja Directa: la búsqueda en Google que expone tus cuentas
articles.text:
La semifinal entre Atlético Nacional y Once Caldas impulsa búsquedas en Google de Pirlo TV, Fútbol Libre y Roja Directa para ver el partido online, pero esos accesos gratuitos pueden comprometer contraseñas, datos bancarios y archivos personales. El encuentro de vuelta se jugará este martes 17 de noviembre en Medellín.
La transmisión oficial estará a cargo de Win+ Fútbol, canal premium del fútbol profesional colombiano. La expectativa por el duelo, sumada al interés por evitar una suscripción, lleva a algunos usuarios hacia sitios no autorizados que prometen enlaces inmediatos, aunque también pueden usar ventanas emergentes, descargas engañosas y formularios destinados a capturar información.
Atlético Nacional y Once Caldas definen un cupo en la final
Atlético Nacional recibirá a Once Caldas a las 18:30 en el estadio Atanasio Girardot, en la vuelta de las semifinales de la Copa BetPlay. El primer encuentro terminó 1-1, con el primer gol de James Rodríguez con el equipo verdolaga.
Nacional buscará una ventaja ante su público después de dos partidos sin vencer a Once Caldas. El equipo dirigido por Panelo Valencia ha planteado encuentros cerrados ante el conjunto de Medellín, que también volverá a enfrentarlo durante los cuadrangulares.
Una web pirata puede ocultar descargas y enlaces fraudulentos
Los portales que ofrecen partidos sin autorización suelen incluir múltiples botones de reproducción, redirecciones y avisos que simulan ser parte del reproductor. Algunos invitan a descargar extensiones, archivos o supuestos programas necesarios para iniciar la señal.
La Organización Internacional de Policía Criminal (Interpol) advierte que las plataformas de contenidos pirateados representan un riesgo para la ciberseguridad. El problema no se limita a una imagen de baja calidad, cortes o publicidad invasiva: puede afectar cuentas, dispositivos y redes conectadas.
Antes de mostrar un supuesto partido, una página puede solicitar permisos sin relación con el vídeo, como acceso a notificaciones, descargas o configuraciones del navegador. También puede dirigir a formularios externos con premios falsos, alertas de virus o mensajes que piden actualizar el dispositivo.
Entre las señales más habituales aparecen dominios que cambian con frecuencia, errores de redacción, botones duplicados y ausencia de información sobre la empresa responsable. La oferta de partidos, películas, series y canales de pago sin costo también debe generar desconfianza.
El malware puede alcanzar teléfonos, computadores y televisores
Interpol señala que numerosos sitios y redes de intercambio de archivos entre pares, conocidas como P2P, pueden alojar malware o virus. El programa dañino puede llegar tras una descarga engañosa o después de pulsar un anuncio que aparenta formar parte de la transmisión.
Ese software puede afectar a teléfonos, tabletas, computadores y televisores conectados. En algunos casos, busca acceder a documentos, fotografías, contraseñas o sesiones que permanecen abiertas en las aplicaciones y navegadores.
El riesgo puede extenderse a otros equipos de la misma red doméstica o laboral. Una descarga realizada para ver el encuentro entre Nacional y Once Caldas puede afectar dispositivos que no tienen relación con la transmisión deportiva.
Las consecuencias pueden continuar después del partido. Un archivo malicioso puede permanecer activo, modificar opciones del equipo, abrir publicidad persistente o dirigir la navegación a otras páginas sin que el usuario lo detecte de inmediato.
Las cuentas bancarias y las contraseñas también quedan expuestas
Una transmisión ilegal puede utilizar un registro gratuito como mecanismo para captar datos. El portal puede pedir una dirección de correo electrónico o solicitar el inicio de sesión mediante una cuenta de redes sociales. Si el sitio carece de controles de seguridad, esa información puede quedar comprometida.
La amenaza aumenta cuando la web exige datos de tarjeta, información bancaria o un pago pequeño para “desbloquear” la señal. Interpol advierte que los métodos de pago inseguros pueden derivar en fraude con tarjetas y otras estafas financieras.
Algunos usuarios recurren a servidores proxy para ocultar su ubicación y acceder a transmisiones restringidas. Sin embargo, estas herramientas no garantizan protección. Sus operadores pueden registrar la actividad de navegación o añadir riesgos si no resultan confiables.
Para identificar una opción legítima, conviene consultar los sitios oficiales de la competición, los clubes, las federaciones y las plataformas con derechos de transmisión. En este caso, el partido entre Atlético Nacional y Once Caldas tendrá señal de Win+ Fútbol.

articles.title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before a House Foreign Affairs panel amid concerns over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy — will testify behind closed doors December 1, Nvidia lawyer will also appear
articles.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before a House Foreign Affairs panel amid concerns over his affair with a suspected Chinese spy — will testify behind closed doors December 1, Nvidia lawyer will also appear
Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select Committees on December 1, with Nvidia's lawyer following him on December 2.
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees on December 1, with an Nvidia lawyer following him on December 2, it's been confirmed. CNBC reports that the leaders of those panels broke the news today after days of speculation. Huang was asked to appear via a letter issued on November 9, just 24 hours after he admitted the affair with Alice Huang, a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese spy. Days later, it was also suggested that Mr. Huang could be issued a subpoena if he did not respond by tomorrow, November 18. That subpoena will no longer be required.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Reps. Brian Mast, R-Fla., John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and Rick Crawford, R-Ark., the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select, and Intelligence Committees, reportedly said after the news of the pair's December appearances was announced. "The American people need answers," they went on, noting that it would be "dangerous" to allow Chinese state actors access to advanced AI chips, the likes of which are built by Nvidia.
Ms. Yuang was an executive at Megaspeed, a company that was a customer of Nvidia during Mr. Huang's tenure as CEO. Megaspeed was later added to Nvidia's no-sell list following concerns that it was involved in the smuggling of AI chips to China against U.S. export laws. Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary, has been accused of importing Nvidia chips and then re-exporting them to China. A criminal investigation has since been launched into Megaspeed in an attempt to get to the bottom of the complicated web of AI companies and chip shipments.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as CEO of Nvidia following his admission of an affair with Ms. Huang. Since then, reports of at least one other affair with an Nvidia employee have surfaced. Despite that fact, calls for Huang's return to the top job at Nvidia continue to gain momentum.

articles.title: Why adaptability beats capacity for data centers
articles.text:
Why adaptability beats capacity for data centers
AI is reshaping data center design, density, cooling and sustainability
There’s always a quiet moment of calm in my morning that usually comes just after the 6 a.m. handover from the night team, and before meetings with customers and prospects get started. It’s time I reserve for reflecting and planning, looking at both the week ahead and working on the longer-term requirements our facility needs to meet.
It’s the latter of those priorities that’s taking more of my time these days, and it reflects the changing nature of the conversations I’m having with CIOs and technology leaders. Two years ago, most customers, especially those in regulated sectors such as finance and healthcare, were asking about uptime, certification and cost.
Today, the first question is almost always about AI.
Head of Data Centre at Ilkari.
They want to know if the facility can support the capacity they’re going to need, and whether it can do so on a timeline that matches how quickly their workloads are scaling. These are fair and important questions, and, in all honesty, they are not always easy to answer.
The increase in demand, driven by AI, means decisions we previously had years to make, now need to be made in a matter of months. Not impossible, but it fundamentally changes the way we think about designing and running facilities longer term.
Density, not just capacity, is what matters for AI workloads
Around the world, capacity challenges dominate headlines, but the infrastructure story underneath it is almost entirely about power density, cooling, and grid capacity. Historically, infrastructure was designed for low power density, whereas today, AI needs much more power per rack as well as more advanced cooling.
A good example is a rack that housed standard enterprise workloads at 5 to 10 kVA two years ago is now being asked to support 15 kVA within the next 18 months, and we’re already planning to support 25 to 30 kVA within the next few years. That is not an incremental change. It requires a different physical design that provides more density in an efficient way, often through modular Performance Optimized Data Centre (POD) architecture and in-row cooling. This allows us to add power and cooling gradually, controlling investment, improving efficiency, and ultimately, allowing us to increase capacity as demand grows.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The lack of density for AI workloads is why many established markets, including some of Europe's data center hubs, are struggling to add capacity at the pace required by demand.
For CIOs evaluating a provider, the useful question isn't “do you have any capacity today?” it's “how does your design accommodate the density I'll need in three years?” because a facility built for yesterday's power needs can quickly become an operational risk if it can't be reconfigured without a lengthy rebuild.
A good example of this is a POD we recently reconfigured within 30 days to meet a customer’s changing requirements, changing 40 racks at 5 kVA, to 20 racks at 10 kVA to support high-density demands. It was a significant project, and the kind of turnaround that's only possible when a facility is designed for change and adaptability, rather than attempting to bolt flexibility on afterwards.
Cooling design has to keep pace with density
Managing excess heat caused by the increased processing demands of AI workloads is becoming an increasingly important part of infrastructure design and customer consideration.
The good news is that cooling technology is improving all the time, making high density possible without needing to prioritize colder climates.
We mostly use air cooling with in-row technology, and because our design is modular, we can increase cooling as the IT load grows. For example, our customers typically join with an initial setup and gradually scale their capacity as their requirements grow.
As the customer’s IT load increases, we progressively activate the in-row cooling units, ensuring that cooling capacity is only deployed when and where it is needed. We also use a refrigerant-based cooling system rather than a water-based one, which keeps our water consumption low to begin with
This approach allows us to operate more efficiently when it comes to both energy and water use, which, as we know, is under increasing scrutiny from regulators and communities alike, and as a limited resource, needs to be used responsibly.
Local footprint must be part of the design conversation, too
It’s been hard to escape the recent tranche of negative media coverage about data centers taking valuable resources (land, water and power) from local communities. It’s true that they have an impact on the local community, but it’s unfair to frame this as entirely negative.
In my experience, a site's economic footprint is much larger than the building itself. Beyond the direct operational jobs, data centers support a much wider chain of indirect employment in sectors such as security, maintenance, cleaning, logistics, and transport. They also drive investment in the surrounding energy and connectivity infrastructure.
The ability to serve the local community and economy, as well as our customers, is an integral part of my role. It’s also something I encourage technology leaders to consider as a legitimate part of their due diligence. After all, banks, government services, cloud providers, and now AI, all depend on the same underlying capacity, and the locations that can offer credible, well-designed and well-run infrastructure, also attract more technology investment, digital skills, and the surrounding ecosystem that a growing digital economy needs.
Sustainability has to be operational, not aspirational
The scrutiny on data centers' environmental footprint is only intensifying as AI-driven demand grows, and rightly so. When it comes to managing a facility, this means building sustainability into daily operations, rather than treating it as a future aspiration or initiative that is bolted on after the fact.
In practice, this means ensuring efficient cooling design, transparent community engagement, and genuine investment in the skilled engineering talent needed to run higher-density infrastructure safely. At Ilkari, we do this through our POD-based design and in-row cooling architecture, which allow us to scale cooling capacity efficiently as IT load grows, and maintain efficient and sustainable data center operations.
It also means working with local governments to make sure the right investments are being made in local power and energy infrastructure to allow us to operate in a way that is sustainable for the local community.
The infrastructure design questions CIOs should be asking
The reality of running a data centre as AI demand increases means a fundamental shift in how facilities need to be designed and built.
For CIOs thinking about what infrastructure requirements their AI workloads need, my advice is not to start with a capacity spreadsheet, but with a short list of broader questions, including:
- How does this provider's design scale with density, not just floor space?
- Can it demonstrate its ability to meet your requirements under real conditions, not just on paper?
- Is sustainability built into day-to-day operations (cooling design, community engagement, skilled engineering talent), or is it a separate initiative?
- As density increases, has the provider planned for the point where air cooling is no longer sufficient, and what alternative cooling technologies and infrastructure would that require?
In my experience, the organizations getting this right aren't the ones with the flashiest AI roadmap, they are the ones designing and building for change from the outset.

articles.title: Los 30 FPS de 'GTA VI' en todas las consolas es un fastidio. También el compromiso para que se vea como se ve
articles.text:
'GTA VI' está al caer y, superada la polémica por la ausencia de un formato físico de verdad y por lo que puede ocupar en consolas con un almacenamiento tan comprometido como Xbox Series S, la pregunta es por qué el juego más caro y ambicioso de la historia sólo va a 30 frames por segundo en todas las consolas, incluida PS5 Pro.
Y la respuesta es que no tiene nada que ver con el presupuesto, sino con una mezcla entre la ambición desmedida de este juego y la limitación de las consolas: el procesador.
Los 30 FPS. Hace unos días, cuando Rockstar confirmó que la predescarga del juego ya estaba disponible, también dio algunos detalles sobre el apartado visual. Hasta ahora, todo lo que hemos visto (incluidos los 30 minutos de Netflix) se ha visto corriendo en una PS5 base y se especulaba con que PS5 Pro podría tener algunas mejoras visuales y de rendimiento.
Lo primero sí parece asegurado, ya que la compañía detalló que "la experiencia visual en PS5 Pro presentará una mayor claridad de imagen gracias al PSSR y sombras con trazados de rayos". Sin embargo, también señalaron que el juego irá a 30 frames por segundo en todas las plataformas, lo que hizo que se levantara alguna queja porque cómo era posible que un juego con este presupuesto fuera sólo a 30 FPS.
El precio del fotograma. La respuesta es que no tiene nada que ver con lo que haya costado el juego, sino con los compromisos. Cuando el medio especializado Digital Foundry puso sus analíticos ojos sobre el vídeo de Netflix, comentaron que era "el ejemplo de renderización en tiempo real más impresionante que han visto", estimando una resolución 1.440p nativa. También calcularon los 30 frames por segundo cuya confirmación llegó a posteriori, y la explicación es que el cuello de botella está en la CPU.
A 30 frames por segundo, la consola tiene unos 33 milisegundos para calcular y dibujar cada imagen. Eso permite que el mundo tenga el detalle que tiene y, sobre todo, que haya tal cantidad de NPC con sus rutinas únicas. en conjunto, es una simulación extremadamente viva que es posible gracias a que Rockstar ha optimizado todo alrededor de esos 30 frames por segundo.
Si se hubiera optado por ir a una tasa de 60 FPS, la consola tendría la mitad de tiempo para calcular cada imagen, unos 16,7 milisegundos. Habría que recortar todo lo que depende de la CPU como peatones, tráfico, físicas, objetos e IA. Y ahí está el compromiso: Rockstar quiere un mundo vivo que una consola actual, simplemente, no puede simular debido a ese cuello de botella de la CPU.
PS5 Pro no cambia la ecuación. Xbox Series X es algo más potente que PS5 en cuanto a su GPU, pero no en su CPU y, por eso, las dos van a 30 FPS, pero había quien tenía la esperanza de que una PS5 Pro más potente que la máquina de Microsoft pudiera 'tirar' al doble de fotogramas. La situación es exactamente la misma.
Aunque la GPU sí es claramente más potente que la de PS5 base, y por eso puede mostrar en el mismo mundo un trazado de rayos en tiempo real para sombras, la mejora en la CPU respecto al modelo base es de apenas un 7%, insuficiente para aumentar la tasa de fotogramas manteniendo la simulación del mundo, pero aprovechando la GPU para mejorar la calidad de imagen.
Está por ver que añadan en algún momento un modo a 40 FPS o con el frame-rate desbloqueado gracias a VRR, aunque no está confirmado.
¿Esperanza? Esta generación hemos tenido ejemplos de títulos que llegaban y, al tiempo, añadían modos de más rendimiento o incluso pantalla partida (algo que consume una burrada de recursos y que se acaba de anunciar para 'Star Wars Galactic Racer', por ejemplo). Sin embargo, en el caso de 'GTA VI', parece que no depende de la optimización porque habría que hacer brujería para que, de pronto, se pudiera configurar un modo "Rendimiento" que se sacara otros 30 frames por segundo de la manga manteniendo la simulación del mundo.
Sería algo digno de ver, pero aquí la esperanza queda en esa futura versión de PC en la que el juego no esté costreñido por el procesador de unas consolas que no dejan de tener seis años a sus espaldas. Y, claro, esa esperanza también está en una versión más optimizada para Xbox Helix y PS6, ya que si 'GTA V' salió en tres generaciones distintas, añadiendo mejoras visuales en cada una de las reediciones en consolas y PC, nada impide que Rockstar repita jugada con 'GTA VI'.
Hay que amortizar los más de 1.000 millones que se estima habría costado el desarrollo.
