articles.title: Phison Pascari X201P 15.36TB SSD Review: Fast PCIe 5.0 write performance for AI and ingest servers
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
Phison’s Pascari X201P meets its rated specs and pairs 12 GB/s sequential writes with a steady 600K random write IOPS, making short work of AI checkpoints. It gives ground at low and moderate queue depths, where QD1 writes and mixed workloads lag, and it ran warm on our bench.
Reasons to buy
- + Fast sequential and random writes
- + Tight write latency under load
- + Quick AI checkpoint saves
Reasons to avoid
- - Slower low-queue-depth writes
- - Mixed-workload performance trails at middle QDs
- - Runs warm
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event. The drive is part of the Performance X-Series, which handles intensive workloads where consistency is the name of the game. We were nevertheless pleasantly surprised by its write performance, with a steady 12 GB/s for sequential and over 600,000 random write IOPS, considering it’s marketed at the 1 drive write per day (DWPD) endurance point.
Part of that surprise comes from the fact that this is Phison’s read-intensive PCIe 5.0 data center drive, a successor to the X200P. It comes in the U.2 form factor — which can be more convenient in many cases — from 1.92TB to 30.72TB, and an E3.S version from 3.84TB, in both single- and dual-port models. It stands next to its mixed-use sibling, the X201E, which is the one rated for 3 DWPD. What makes the X201P exciting, in part, is its own 16-channel X2 controller and the flash that’s inside.
This drive is aimed at AI, analytics, and database servers, with its case made in the 4K 70/30 mix at higher queue depths. It passed Phison’s one-million-IOPS mark at QD128 in our testing of the 15.36TB model, and the drive met all of its rated specs, though its random read rating required polled I/O to reach on our bench. It faced challenges with QD1 writes, log commits, and the middle range of our mixed sweeps. Given its blend of performance, capacity, and endurance, we consider it a very competent entry from the company that was perhaps better known in the consumer SSD market until recently.
Phison Pascari X201P Specifications
| Product | 1.92TB | 3.84TB | 7.68TB | 15.36TB | 30.72TB | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pricing | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | N/A | 
| Form Factor | U.2 (15 mm) | U.2 (15 mm) | U.2 (15 mm) | U.2 (15 mm) | U.2 (15 mm) | 
| Interface / Protocol | PCIe 5.0 x4 / NVMe 2.0d | PCIe 5.0 x4 / NVMe 2.0d | PCIe 5.0 x4 / NVMe 2.0d | PCIe 5.0 x4 / NVMe 2.0d | PCIe 5.0 x4 / NVMe 2.0d | 
| Controller | Phison X2 | Phison X2 | Phison X2 | Phison X2 | Phison X2 | 
| DRAM | Yes (size not published) | Yes (size not published) | Yes (size not published) | Yes (size not published) | Yes (size not published) | 
| Memory | 3D TLC | 3D TLC | 3D TLC | 321-layer 3D TLC | 3D TLC | 
| Sequential Read | 14,800 MB/s | 14,800 MB/s | 14,800 MB/s | 14,800 MB/s | 14,800 MB/s | 
| Sequential Write | 2,300 MB/s | 4,600 MB/s | 9,200 MB/s | 11,800 MB/s | 10,000 MB/s | 
| Random Read | 1,400K | 2,700K | 3,300K | 3,250K | 2,800K | 
| Random Write | 75K | 230K | 480K | 600K | 490K | 
| Security | ISE or SED (TCG Opal 2.02) | ISE or SED (TCG Opal 2.02) | ISE or SED (TCG Opal 2.02) | ISE or SED (TCG Opal 2.02) | ISE or SED (TCG Opal 2.02) | 
| Power-Loss Protection | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Endurance | 1 DWPD | 1 DWPD | 1 DWPD | 1 DWPD | 1 DWPD | 
| Power (Active / Idle) | ≤25 W / ≤5 W | ≤25 W / ≤5 W | ≤25 W / ≤5 W | ≤25 W / ≤5 W | ≤25 W / ≤5 W | 
| Part Number (ISE) | XP208H081T92P322T0410 | XP208H083T84P324T0910 | XP208H087T68P328T1910 | XP208H0815T3P3216T310 | XP208H0830T7P3232T710 | 
| Part Number (SED) | XP208H081T92P222T0410 | XP208H083T84P224T0910 | XP208H087T68P228T1910 | XP208H0815T3P2216T310 | XP208H0830T7P2232T710 | 
| Height | 15 mm | 15 mm | 15 mm | 15 mm | 15 mm | 
| Warranty | 5-Year | 5-Year | 5-Year | 5-Year | 5-Year | 
The drive met or beat every rated performance figure that we can test, which should be the target of any enterprise SSD released today. If there’s an exception, it’s due to how we test; Phison lists a ceiling of 3,250K IOPS for 4K random read, which is higher than our bench allows with our interrupt-driven I/O, which we use rather than a polled approach. We also run a polled test on every drive for cases like this, and our result was 3,283K IOPS at the same queue depth Phison specifies, which shows the drive does exceed its specification.
Phison Pascari X201P Features and Management
| Feature | Phison Pascari X201P | 
|---|---|
| NVMe Specification | NVMe 2.0d | 
| OCP Specification | Datacenter NVMe SSD v2.0, with v2.6 telemetry features | 
| Host Link | PCIe 5.0 x4, single port (2x2 dual-port models offered) | 
| Power-Loss Protection | Yes | 
| End-to-End Data Protection | Yes | 
| Security Options | ISE, SED (TCG Opal 2.02) or non-SED; AES-XTS 256-bit | 
| Sanitize | Cryptographic erase and block erase | 
| LBA Formats | 512-byte and 4,096-byte, each with optional metadata | 
| Namespaces | Up to 128 | 
| Power States | Six: 25 W, 22 W, 20 W, 18 W, 15 W and 12 W maximum | 
| Temperature Thresholds | 77°C warning, 85°C critical | 
| Thermal Management | Host-controlled thermal management supported | 
| Firmware Slots | Seven; activation without reset | 
| Out-of-Band Management | NVMe-MI 1.2 over SMBus and PCIe | 
| Flexible Data Placement | Not supported | 
| Tested Firmware | X2WM6026 | 
Phison Pascari X201P: A Closer Look
Our sample is in the U.2 form factor, 15mm thick. We have the single-port SKU, ISE model XP208H0815T3P3216T310, with firmware X2WM6026. Some data we previously saw from the drive was reportedly on X2WM6025, but we confirmed X2WM6026 for all relevant results. We mounted the drive on a PCIe 5.0 x4 add-in card adapter for U.2, standing upright in the slot.
Phison did not provide firm hardware details, but we were able to discover some things on our own. The flash was probably the easiest, as the company claimed it was a 321-layer part. That can only be SK hynix’s V9 TLC, which is not flash we’ve tested before in any product. It’s exceptionally fast and uses a three-deck design, which is relatively new for TLC flash. The flash could be credited with some of the exceptional performance measurements we see on the drive.
As for the proprietary controller, we’ve heard that it’s using a combination of the standard Arm Cortex-R5 — these would be the main cores — with AndesCore RISC-V on the side. We’ve seen the latter before on the Phison E28 consumer SSD controller, which did have some enterprise-like aspects to it. The E28 is the newer design, built on a 6nm process with Andes’ newer N45 cores alongside the N25F, while the X2 is a 12nm part that, as far as we can tell, sticks with N25F-class co-processors.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
In this case, the X2 has twice the flash channels, which enables a superior level of performance out of TLC flash, as in enterprise you do not rely on pSLC. That mix of cores sets the X2 apart from other 16-channel PCIe 5.0 enterprise controllers: Marvell’s Bravera SC5 and Silicon Motion’s SM8366 rely on Arm cores throughout, whereas Phison pairs its Cortex-R5 cores with small RISC-V co-processors.

articles.title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a rear display, a built-in privacy screen, and a very large price tag
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is an excellent all-rounder with great performance and very impressive cameras. The star of the show is the extra screen on the back, which is really handy for filming yourself or taking extremely high-quality selfies. The drawbacks are a weaker ultra-wide camera, a privacy display feature that feels somewhat half-baked, and some minor software quirks.
Reasons to buy
- + Useful rear screen
- + Great cameras
- + Powerful performance
- + Excellent speakers
Reasons to avoid
- - Ultra-wide camera isn't the best
- - Privacy Display is weaker than Samsung's
- - It's expensive
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Two-minute review
Towards the end of 2025, Xiaomi introduced the 17 Pro series — two phones with an iPhone 17 Pro-like design and an extra screen on their rear camera modules. As a content creator who often films himself, I was immediately intrigued by this novel feature, but there was a big problem: the Xiaomi 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max only launched in mainland China.
Now, the Xiaomi 18 Pro series has launched globally (well, everywhere except the US), meaning Xiaomi fans across the world can finally experience this rear screen.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max take a similar approach to their predecessors, but bring improved camera specifications, newer SoCs, and larger batteries to the table. They also add a new privacy display feature, just like the one on the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Xiaomi is the first brand other than Samsung to adopt this kind of tech.
I tested the larger Pro Max model for this review, and like most high-end flagship phones, the cameras on the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are one of its main attractions. Both the main and telephoto cameras get a super-high 200MP resolution, and they can capture images with stunning clarity in almost any lighting conditions.
The telephoto is especially good for macro photography, as it can focus very close up. Meanwhile, the phone's image processing, developed in partnership with Leica, produces some fantastic colors, and you get plenty of different picture styles and film simulations to experiment with.
The weak point of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera setup is the ultra-wide lens, which isn't particularly wide, at 17mm equivalent, and has a fairly small sensor, which means it isn't great in the dark.
The phone's rear screen makes it really easy to film yourself or take high-quality selfies, but I was surprised by how much else you can do with it. There are lots of fun apps to play with, and you can even create your own with AI, which means you might use this screen more often than you expect.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's main front screen is equally great, and its speakers are even better. The built-in subwoofer adds some much-needed bass to the equation.
The phone's Privacy Display feature, though, feels a little undercooked. It doesn't work from the top and the bottom of the screen, only from the sides, and it isn't quite as effective as Samsung's overall.
Overall performance is fantastic. Qualcomm's latest flagship chip lets you run the most demanding games with relative ease on the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, while a big battery and fast charging mean you can do so all day long.
Xiaomi's software is also looking nicer than ever, and it's absolutely packed with handy features. That said, there are still a few small niggles that could use ironing out, like advertisements in the Themes app and pre-installed bloatware that comes pre-installed.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is an excellent device, and I don't feel it falls short in any particular area. The main attraction is that rear display. If you have a use for it (like I do), you won't find that anywhere else. For the right person, it's a game-changer.
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Price and availability
- 12GB of RAM + 256GB of storage costs £1,399 / AU$1,999
- 12GB of RAM + 512GB of storage costs £1,599 / AU$2,299
- Not sold in the US
At the time of writing, I only have UK pricing information for the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, but the phone will be available to order in most regions across the world, excluding the US. The bad news is that it doesn't come cheap.
The model with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage costs £1,399 / AU$1,999, while the model with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage costs £1,599 / AU$2,299. The smaller Xiaomi 18 Pro (in the same configurations) costs £1,199 / AU$1,799 and £1,399 / $2,099, respectively.
It's to be expected, really; global component shortages have increased prices across the industry, but the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max now costs more than both the equivalent iPhone 18 Pro Max and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, which is a tough pill to swallow.
In its defence, the Xiaomi offers more impressive cameras, a rear screen, and a larger battery — so there's certainly an argument to be made that it should cost more than those rival flagship handsets. As for whether it's worth the extra outlay, that's for you to decide.
- Value score: 3 / 5
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Specs
Here’s a look at the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max’s key specs:
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Xiaomi 18 Pro Max | 
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 163.4 x 77.6 x 8.4 mm | 
| Weight | 229g | 
| OS | HyperOS 4, based on Android 17 | 
| Display | 6.9-inch LTPO AMOLED, 120Hz (plus 2.9-inch rear screen) | 
| Resolution | 1208 x 2624 pixels | 
| Chipset | Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 (2 nm) | 
| RAM | 12GB / 16GB | 
| Storage | 256GB / 512GB / 1TB | 
| Battery | 7,050mAh | 
| Rear cameras | 200MP (f/1.7) main, 50MP (f/2.4) ultra-wide, 200MP 3.2x periscope telephoto (f/2.4) | 
| Front camera | 50MP (f/2.2) | 
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Design
- Aluminum frame and glass back
- Black, White, Velvet Red, Cosmic Blue color options
- IP68 dust and water-resistant
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max looks a lot like last year's China-only 17 Pro Max, and in turn, that means it also looks a lot like the iPhone 17 Pro Max and iPhone 18 Pro Max. It has the same raised "plateau" surrounding the camera lenses, but the big difference is that this camera bump has a screen on it.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is a very big and weighty phone, tipping the scales at about 229g. As a guy with big hands who's used to using ultra-flagship phones, I didn't have any trouble with the size and weight. If you're used to something more compact, though, this might be a tough adjustment.
On the other hand, it is still lighter than the equivalent iPhone, despite having a bigger battery and an extra screen.
My review sample came in the Velvet Red colorway, which is quite clearly inspired by the iPhone 18 Pro's Burgundy finish. Xiaomi's take on it is a bit more vibrant, leaning less toward the brown tones, and personally, I prefer it.
The 18 Pro Max has an aluminum frame, a glass rear panel, and it's IP68-rated for dust and water resistance. You get a basic TPU clear case included in the box, and there are factory-applied screen protectors on both screens, so you're well protected without needing to shell out on accessories.
Xiaomi has added a new button similar to Apple's Action Button on the left-hand side of the phone. Xiaomi calls it the AI Button, but I'm not really sure why, as at the moment, the only AI-related thing you can do with it is open the AI Translate mode.
I was initially excited to try this extra button. I normally set them to activate the torch or quickly access Google Wallet. Sadly, you can't do either of those things here. The functionality is really locked down, and you can only use it to switch between silent and ring, activate the new Privacy Display, open voice notes, or use the aforementioned AI Translate feature.
I really hope Xiaomi unlocks more functionality for this button with a future update, because at the minute, it's more limited than the equivalent buttons offered by every other brand I've tried.
Otherwise, the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a typical flagship smartphone feel. The front and rear are flat, the edges are squared off, and it feels premium throughout.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Display
- 6.9-inch 120Hz LTPO OLED with Privacy Display
- 2.9-inch OLED rear display
- 4,000 nits peak brightness and 2160Hz PWM dimming
The most novel thing about the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is the fact that there's a screen on the back. So let's start this section by talking about that. It's a 2.9-inch OLED panel with large circular cutouts for the main and telephoto cameras.
The rear screen doesn't behave like the main display. For instance, you can't just run any app you like on this back screen. It feels a bit more like a smartwatch. By default, it will display the time, and with a swipe to the right, you can quickly open your camera to take a photo or a video with the rear cameras. You can also quickly access your calendar to see if you have any upcoming events.
In the system settings, you can choose from a wide variety of animated wallpapers and themes, many of which have cute 3D animated animal mascots. You can also set any photo you like as the wallpaper, which makes it really easy to show off your personality through the back of your phone.
There's a small selection of apps that can run on the rear screen, but the most interesting feature is the ability to create your own. Xiaomi has added a generative AI app builder, and by typing a simple sentence, the AI can build almost anything and have it run on the back panel.
I started out with the simple task of asking it to build a dice roller for D&D, which it did, and then I got more ambitious. I asked it to build a fully playable (albeit unofficial) version of Doom, and I was shocked that it worked within a couple of tries.
You can do almost anything with this feature, so long as you can think it up. It's a really cool use of generative AI, and it makes this rear panel a lot more useful than it would have been otherwise.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
As for the main display, it essentially gives you what you would expect from a high-end flagship phone. It has slim, symmetrical bezels on every side, a bright 4000-nit output, and a 120Hz adaptive refresh rate. However, this panel also has a trick up its sleeve.
This is the first phone, other than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, to have a Privacy Display mode. By toggling a setting, you can make it much more challenging for other people to see what's on your screen, as it restricts the viewing angle and dims the screen when viewed off-center.
Some aspects of Xiaomi's Privacy Display are better than Samsung's. For instance, when it's turned on, the resolution doesn't drop quite so much, and it feels like the screen doesn't dim as much either.
The big drawback is that this Privacy Display only works from the left and right sides of the phone (when held vertically), and it has no impact when viewed from above or below. This means when you're holding your phone in landscape mode to watch a YouTube video or play a game, the privacy effect doesn't really work.
It's also not as effective as Samsung's overall. When the S26 Ultra is set to its maximum privacy mode, you can barely tell that the phone screen is on. With the Xiaomi, you can still see the screen; it's just very, very dim when viewed off-axis.
I set the Privacy Display to automatically activate when I opened things like my banking app. Then, for the most part, I forgot it was doing anything. Hopefully, it made it harder for strangers to see my screen, but I'm certain they'd have a harder time if I were using my Samsung.
- Display score: 4 / 5
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Cameras
- 200MP main (f/1.67)
- 50MP ultra-wide (f/2.4)
- 200MP 3.2x periscope telephoto (f/2.4)
- 50MP selfie camera (f/2.2)
You can tell from the design of the 18 Pro Max that Xiaomi is prioritizing the main and telephoto cameras over the ultra-wide. The latter camera is positioned in a small separate pill next to the flash unit, rather than prominently featured on the camera island like the other two lenses.
That's not necessarily a problem. Most people use the ultra-wide less than the other two cameras, and it normally has the weakest specs on a flagship phone. But with the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max giving the ultra-wide a huge bump in quality, I was hoping to see a bit more here.
Honestly, this ultra-wide camera isn't bad, but it's a massive step down compared to the main and telephoto cameras. Both have a higher 200MP resolution and significantly larger sensors, too. This means that when the light gets low, the other cameras are in a completely different league from this one.
The real issue is that the ultra-wide just isn't very wide. It's a 17mm-equivalent lens, which is a lot more zoomed in than the 13mm-equivalent ultra-wides on rival phones. In most scenarios, it makes more sense to just jump to the main camera, which isn't really that much more zoomed in.
As for the main and telephoto cameras, they're both excellent. They're incredibly sharp and detailed, and they perform well in all lighting conditions. Since this phone has a screen on the rear, I found that I was using the main camera a lot more often, as it was the obvious choice for selfies and group photos rather than relying on the selfie camera.
My favorite thing about the telephoto is how close it can focus. It's a 75mm-equivalent lens, and it can focus from just 10cm away, which makes for stunning macro shots. The lens provides a good amount of compression and soft, natural bokeh that looks closer to the results you'd get from a professional camera than from a smartphone.
The Xiaomi's selfie camera is perfectly adequate, but it's nothing special. I like that it has autofocus, and it has a decently wide field of view, too. The thing is, this phone makes it so easy to use the main rear camera or ultra-wide instead, and in most scenarios, you'll get better results with those. For me, that meant the selfie camera was resigned to video calls and face unlock duties, and it's overkill for either task.
Xiaomi is still partnered with Leica for its image processing, and there are loads of impressive filters and film simulations that you can access in the camera app. My favorite feature is a new mode called Essential Moment, which seems like Xiaomi's answer to Oppo's Master Mode.
Essential Moment removes some of the HDR effect and sharpening that you get from the standard photo mode, giving your photos a more naturalistic look. Somewhat counterintuitively, it's actually powered by an on-device AI Model, trained on photos from classic cameras. So while it looks more natural, behind the scenes, it's anything but.
Essential Moment is not the right choice for every situation; at night, I found I preferred the more aggressive processing from the regular photo mode, but during the day, it can give really stunning results, and I used it a lot.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is also an impressive video camera. It can shoot at up to 8K/30fps or 4K/120fps on the main and telephoto cameras, while all the other lenses will let you shoot at up to 4K/60fps.
There's a very impressive Log profile, too. You can apply LUTs directly in the app, and the stabilization and microphones are both solid.
- Cameras score: 4 / 5

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Performance
- Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset
- 12GB or 16GB RAM options
- 256GB / 512GB / 1TB UFS 4.1 storage options
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is powered by Qualcomm's most powerful chip, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. My sample came with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. This powerful new chip, combined with a redesigned vapor chamber cooling system, means that the phone is ready for whatever you can throw at it.
In normal daily use, the 18 Pro Max is an absolute rocket. Apps open in an instant, multitasking is no trouble at all, and you can run some seriously demanding games, too. I played a few hours of NTE on maximum graphics settings, and the 18 Pro Max handled it without issue.
The frame of the phone does get very warm when playing challenging games for extended periods, but that's probably a good thing. It just means the vapor chamber is doing its job, moving the heat away from the processor and dissipating it through the frame of the phone. The best way to get around this is to use a case or gaming grip to keep the heat away from your hands.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a triple speaker system. There's a speaker on the base of the phone, one that doubles as the earpiece, and a dedicated subwoofer as well.
These speakers sound really good. They might not be the loudest around, but there's better low-end response than most competitors, which makes for a more well-rounded sound with better balance.
They're still no match for headphones or a Bluetooth speaker, but I think they sound better than 90% of the phones on the market. They do the job nicely for playing games at home or watching Netflix in bed.
- Performance score: 5 / 5
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Software
- HyperOS 4, based on Android 17
- Refined design
- Speed and smoothness improvements
The 18 Pro Max runs Hyper OS 4, which is Xiaomi's custom version of Android 17. Much like the design of the hardware, there's a distinct Apple flavor to the software, too.
If you've tried any phone from Redmi, Poco, or Xiaomi in recent years, this operating system will feel quite familiar. The main changes this generation are just aesthetic tweaks; there's a refined Liquid Glass style effect, and extra capabilities for Xiaomi's Dynamic Island clone.
It's not the most original approach, but I don't necessarily think that's a bad thing. HyperOS is looking more visually pleasing than ever. It runs really smoothly, and tweaks to the underlying architecture mean apps open more quickly than before.
Where HyperOS excels, compared to iOS, is with its customization options. If you don't like the way things look by default, or if you don't like the way things behave, you can almost certainly change them. Xiaomi lets you tweak everything from the animations to the icon style to the home grid layout. You can really make this phone feel like your own.
The downsides to HyperOS are unfortunately still unaddressed. There are still advertisements in the theme and wallpaper apps, which really cheapen the way this phone feels. You'll also find a little bit of bloatware when you first set it up.
My review unit had things like AliExpress and WPS Office installed by default, and while it only takes a few moments to delete these apps, they shouldn't really be there in the first place, especially when a phone costs this much.
- Software score: 4 / 5
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Battery
- 7,050mAh battery
- 100W wired charging
- 50W wireless charging
As we've seen from most Chinese smartphone manufacturers recently, the global version of the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max has a smaller battery than the domestic version. In this case, we get a 7,050mAh battery compared to an 8,500mAh battery in the Chinese model.
The discrepancy is all due to shipping regulations, and I don't think there's much that Xiaomi can do about it, but it still stings, especially when cheaper phones, like the Poco F9 Ultra, get a larger battery.
That said, 7,050mAh is still a high capacity, and I found it was enough to get me through at least a day and a half on a single charge. I moved into this phone from the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max, and I was definitely getting longer battery life with that device, but I had the 8,000mAh version of that phone, so that's to be expected.
Thankfully, the charging speeds are unchanged from the Chinese model, which means you get a whopping 100W charging speed with a wire and 50W wireless charging. There's no charger included in the box, at least not for the UK version, just a USB-A to USB-C cable.
One of my favorite things about Xiaomi phones is how well they work with third-party chargers. Most brands will require you to buy their official wall adapter to get the maximum charging speed, but with this phone, I could use my Sharge power bank and still get the full 100W speed.
While 100W sounds very fast on paper, the reality isn't quite so impressive. 30 minutes on the charger will take you from fully flat to about 60% charged, which isn't bad, but it's not much faster than something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. In fairness, though, this phone does have a much larger battery.
- Battery score: 4 / 5
Should you buy the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | Rising component costs mean that the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max costs more than its mainstream rivals. In some ways, that's justified, but it's certainly not a bargain. | 3 / 5 | 
| Design | While there's some Apple-influence to the styling, the rear screen sets it apart. It's a unique offering in the space, and personally I think Xiaomi's Velvet Red looks a lot nicer than Apple's burgundy. | 4 / 5 | 
| Display | The screen is well-specced and looks great in use, but I'm not as convinced by Xiaomi's version of the Privacy Display. | 4 / 5 | 
| Cameras | The main and telephoto cameras are both superb, and the software features are great, too. Unfortunately, the ultra-wide lets the team down a little. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | With Qualcomm's fastest chip inside and a redeveloped vapor chamber calling system, this phone can do it all with relative ease. | 5 / 5 | 
| Software | HyperOS 4 is feature-packed and looks nicer than ever, but there are a few lingering niggles that should be addressed. | 4 / 5 | 
| Battery | Battery life is very good and charging speeds are decent. It's just a shame that the global version doesn't get the same mammoth battery pack as the Chinese model. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You're a vlogger or a selfie addict
If you often take photos or videos of yourself, then having a screen on the rear of your phone is an absolute game-changer.
You're bored of iPhones
In many ways, the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max reminds me of the iPhone 18 Pro Max. But with novel features like a rear screen and Privacy Display, this device is so much more fun than Apple's latest.
Don't buy it if...
You love ultra-wide shots
The ultra-wide camera on this phone is fine, but it's not especially wide, and it struggles in low-light conditions. If you love ultra-wide shots, you should definitely look elsewhere.
You're keen on the Privacy Display
It's great to see other brands adopting this innovative display tech, but Xiaomi's implementation is nowhere near as effective as Samsung's. If it's this feature that piqued your interest, you will have a better time with the Galaxy S26 Ultra.
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max review: Also consider
The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max is a very compelling flagship phone, but it's important to consider the competition, too. Here are a couple of competitors that are worth looking at.
iPhone 18 Pro Max
From the naming to the design and the software, it's clear that Xiaomi took a lot of inspiration from Apple's latest phone. Personally, I had more fun with Xiaomi's version, but if you're already in the Apple ecosystem, you might have a better time with the original.
Read our iPhone 18 Pro Max review
Oppo Find X10 Pro Max
If you like the sound of the Xiaomi, but the weaker ultra-wide camera turned you off, then you'll want to look at the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. It has easily the best ultra-wide specifications of any phone in this class, which makes it way more versatile. There's no screen on the back, though.
Read our Oppo Find X10 Pro Max review

I put my SIM card into the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max and used it as my main phone for a week. I used it exactly as I would use any other phone, taking photos and videos, playing games, messaging, working, streaming video, and navigating with Google Maps.
I also compared the experience of playing graphically challenging games like NTE to my experience on other flagships like the iPhone 18 Pro and Oppo Find X10 Pro Max. I ran benchmarks on the handset, including Geekbench 7, to confirm my performance findings.

articles.title: Receita Federal publica códigos no GitHub pela primeira vez • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Receita Federal publica códigos no GitHub pela primeira vez
Três projetos de software incluem calculadoras de CBS e IBS e poderão ser usados, modificados e distribuídos por desenvolvedores.
A Receita Federal publicou pela primeira vez projetos de software em repositórios públicos no GitHub. A iniciativa envolve a Calculadora de Tributos, ferramenta que aplica as regras da reforma tributária sobre o consumo e pode ser incorporada aos sistemas utilizados por empresas.
Segundo comunicado divulgado pelo órgão nessa segunda-feira (16/11), os projetos adotam a licença MIT, que permite utilizar, modificar e distribuir o código, inclusive em aplicações comerciais. A medida foi publicada no Diário Oficial da União.
A Calculadora de Tributos integra as regras de cálculo da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS), do Imposto sobre Bens e Serviços (IBS) e de outros tributos previstos na reforma. O objetivo é permitir que desenvolvedores utilizem a mesma lógica da Receita em programas de faturamento, gestão e emissão de documentos fiscais.
O órgão disponibilizou três projetos no GitHub:
A expectativa da Receita é reduzir diferenças de cálculo, custos de desenvolvimento e dificuldades na adaptação às novas regras.
Com a publicação no GitHub, desenvolvedores poderão consultar as versões dos projetos, acompanhar alterações e analisar como os tributos são calculados. A licença MIT também permite adaptar os códigos para diferentes aplicações.
A Receita afirma que a iniciativa pretende aumentar a transparência e a segurança jurídica na implementação da reforma tributária. Vale destacar que o uso de softwares de código aberto não significa ausência de regras. Mesmo licenças permissivas, como a MIT, estabelecem condições para a redistribuição e reutilização dos projetos.
A calculadora já estava disponível para download na Plataforma CBS desde 2025. A novidade é sua publicação no GitHub, ambiente que facilita o acompanhamento de versões e a análise do código pela comunidade de desenvolvedores.
Desenvolvidos em parceria com o Serpro, os projetos não substituem os programas utilizados pelas empresas. A proposta é oferecer componentes oficiais que possam ser incorporados às soluções existentes durante a transição para o novo sistema tributário.

articles.title: The best of AI is yet to come, say experts at Bengaluru Tech Summit
articles.text:
The best of AI is yet to come, say experts at Bengaluru Tech Summit
During a panel discussion, Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge, Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan, Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw, and Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash stressed the potential of AI to create solutions with population-scale impact.
The potential of artificial intelligence (AI) still remains unexplored, and there is much more to come from this technology, in the form of solutions that will have a population scale impact, said panellists during a discussion at Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) 2026.
During a panel discussion on the topic 'AI & Beyond: Emerging India', Karnataka Home and IT Minister Priyank Kharge highlighted how the state government is integrating AI in various departments, be it for cybersecurity or building solutions with participation from startups to improve governance.
“We ensure that we have the first mover advantage when it comes to using technology across all our departments,” the minister said.
AI has had a significant impact on the software sector and the IT industry at large, especially with the automation of the coding processes.
Infosys Co-founder S Gopalakrishnan said AI has given the opportunity to create newer kinds of products and services. While IT outsourcing will continue in its present form, AI is giving the opportunity to reimagine the entire technology stack, he said.
The technology has made deep inroads into several areas, giving rise to newer opportunities. It is also solving many unresolved problems in areas such as mathematics and biology.
Biocon Group Chairperson Kiran Mazumdar Shaw said AI is really about accelerating intelligence, and the technology will help simplify even a complex subject like biology, leading to many discoveries in medicines, diseases and diagnostics. She remarked that AI can help connect the dots to develop the next generation of drugs.
“Biology is the most important frontier for AI to be deployed. Because if you know how to deploy AI to unravel the mysteries of biology, you can unravel so many other things,” Shaw said, adding, “The real opportunity from AI is taking molecules faster from lab to clinic to patients."
Accel India Founding Partner Prashanth Prakash said the bigger opportunity in AI is not in making what is existing more efficient and more usable, but it lies in the ability to serve hundreds of millions of people by making services more affordable.
However, the biggest challenge with AI in India is availability and use of data.
Kharge felt this is an opportunity to understand the value of this technology and build solutions that are scalable and applicable for a wider section of the population.
Prakash said delivering value through AI to the rural population will be the last frontier as it still remains an unsolved sector. “It is a multi-dimensional problem as it is about the right technology from where to go, what to do, and how to grow.”
The panellists were of the view that as AI delivers value, especially through automation, one must also review the whole process and ensure a governance structure for this technology.

articles.title: L’immense marche en avant de la Chine : après Mars, elle veut se poser sur Callisto, une lune de Jupiter
articles.text:
Aucun engin spatial ne s’est posé sur l’une des nombreuses lunes de Jupiter. Mais la Chine entend bien devenir la première à réussir cet exploit. Cap sur la mission Tianwen-4.
Depuis 2021, le programme Tianwen contribue à placer la Chine à l’avant-garde de la conquête spatiale. À commencer par Tianwen-1, qui a placé un orbiteur autour de Mars et posé le rover Zhurong sur la planète rouge dès sa première tentative. Lancée en 2025, Tianwen-2 a atteint en juillet dernier l’astéroïde Kamoʻoalewa, d’où elle doit rapporter des échantillons fin 2027.
Pékin prépare déjà la suite avec Tianwen-3, qui doit repartir vers Mars à la fin de 2028. Cette fois, il s’agira de ramener sur Terre au moins 500 grammes de roche pour y débusquer quête de traces de vie passée. Une prouesse qu’elle pourrait accomplir avec les États-Unis. Mais l’Empire du Milieu n’est pas rassasié et vise encore plus loin.
La Chine accélère
Dans les tuyaux depuis 2022, Tianwen-4 entre enfin dans une phase concrète avec un appel à propositions formulé par l’agence spatiale chinoise (CNSA), rapporte Space News. Celui-ci invite des équipes de recherche, chinoises comme étrangères, à proposer des instruments scientifiques qui viendraient compléter les douze dispositifs déjà prévus.
La mission transportera deux vaisseaux. Un orbiteur d’abord, qui survolera plusieurs lunes de Jupiter avant de se placer autour de Callisto, puis un atterrisseur qui viendra se poser à la surface de la lune. Au programme : l’étude de la plus grande planète du Système solaire, notamment de son champ magnétique, des particules qui l’entourent et de ses aurores.
Concernant Callisto, des caméras ainsi qu’un altimètre laser doivent cartographier son relief. De même, des spectromètres se chargeront d’analyser la composition de sa surface. L’atterrisseur, lui, embarquera un instrument doté d’un laser pour identifier les matériaux au sol, en plus d’un magnétomètre. Associé aux mesures de l’orbiteur, ce dernier doit aider à savoir si un océan d’eau salée se cache sous la croûte de glace.
La lune galiléenne la plus éloignée de Jupiter
Le choix de Callisto pour Tianwen-4 n’a évidemment rien d’un hasard. Plus éloignée de Jupiter que les autres lunes galiléennes, Io, Europe ou Ganymède, elle reste en grande partie à l’écart des puissantes ceintures de radiations de la planète qui mettent l’électronique à rude épreuve. C’est, en outre, celle qui exige le moins de carburant pour freiner, se mettre en orbite et se poser. Enfin, sa surface, l’une des plus anciennes et des plus criblées de cratères du Système solaire, conserve une archive intacte de l’histoire géologique de la région.
Si aucune date fixe n’a pour l’instant été fixée, le lancement devrait avoir lieu aux alentours de 2030 à bord d’une fusée Longue Marche 5. La sonde enchaînera ensuite des survols de Vénus et de la Terre pour gagner en vitesse sans épuiser son carburant. Elle devrait atteindre le système jovien en 2035, avant de se placer en orbite autour de Callisto, à environ 300 kilomètres d’altitude, vers 2038.
Pour rappel, la sonde américaine Juno s’y promène depuis 2016. Elle sera rejointe par l’européenne JUICE en 2031, quelque temps après Europa Clipper de la NASA, déjà en route et consacrée à Europe. Mais aucune de ces missions ne prévoit de se poser. Si Tianwen-4 y parvient, la Chine signerait le premier atterrissage de l’histoire sur une lune de Jupiter.
Une mission de retour d’échantillons doit non seulement collecter de la matière sur un corps céleste, mais aussi la conditionner, la faire décoller, puis la ramener sur Terre pour une rentrée atmosphérique contrôlée. Cela implique généralement plusieurs véhicules (atterrisseur, module d’ascension, orbiteur) et des opérations de rendez-vous et d’amarrage automatisés en espace lointain. Les contraintes de masse et d’énergie sont plus strictes, car chaque gramme ramené coûte cher en propulsion. La protection planétaire complique aussi le design : il faut éviter de contaminer l’échantillon et, inversement, limiter tout risque biologique lors du retour. Enfin, la chaîne de responsabilité est longue : chaque étape est un point de défaillance potentiel.
Un appel à propositions sert à sélectionner des instruments capables de répondre à des objectifs scientifiques précis, tout en respectant des contraintes d’ingénierie (masse, consommation électrique, volume, résistance aux radiations). Les équipes candidates doivent détailler les performances attendues (résolution, sensibilité, cadence de mesure), mais aussi les besoins opérationnels (température, pointage, débit de données). Ce processus permet aussi de définir l’architecture de la charge utile : quels capteurs travaillent ensemble et comment leurs données se complètent. Ouvrir l’appel à des équipes étrangères peut accélérer la maturité technologique et diversifier les expertises, mais suppose des règles claires sur l’export, la propriété intellectuelle et le partage des données. À la fin, l’agence spatiale arbitre entre ambition scientifique et faisabilité industrielle.
Le système jovien baigne dans des ceintures de radiations intenses alimentées par le champ magnétique de Jupiter, ce qui peut endommager l’électronique et dégrader les capteurs si la conception n’est pas fortement durcie. La distance à la Terre impose des communications à faible débit relatif et avec un délai de plusieurs dizaines de minutes, ce qui limite le pilotage en temps réel et exige beaucoup d’autonomie à bord. Les conditions locales sont difficiles : températures très basses, faible lumière solaire et, selon la lune visée, surface glacée potentiellement instable pour l’atterrissage. La navigation et l’atterrissage demandent des capteurs précis (altimétrie, imagerie) et des algorithmes capables d’éviter les zones à risque. Enfin, les contraintes énergétiques poussent souvent à utiliser des générateurs nucléaires ou des batteries dimensionnées pour des phases critiques, car les panneaux solaires deviennent moins efficaces aussi loin du Soleil.

articles.title: La Voyager 1 llegará mañana a un día luz de la Tierra: sus señales tardarán 24 horas en llegar hasta nosotros
articles.text:
La NASA está a punto de recibir por primera vez un mensaje enviado desde un día luz de distancia. Tanto esta como otras agencias espaciales están más que familiarizadas con recibir señales mucho más lejanas que esa, gracias a los avances de la tecnología espacial. Sin embargo, será la primera vez que alguien recibe un mensaje tan lejano emitido por un objeto creado por el ser humano. Dicho objeto es la sonda Voyager 1, lanzada en 1977.
Los datos. El 18 de noviembre, 10:16 UTC (11:16, hora peninsular española), la Voyager 1 enviará señales de telemetría a los científicos de la NASA como lleva haciendo casi 50 años. Sin embargo, en esta ocasión el mensaje tardará justo 24 horas en llegar, ya que la sonda estará a 1 día luz de nuestro planeta. Esto no supone nada a nivel práctico, pero es un gran hito que está siendo muy celebrado tanto por la comunidad científica como por toda la sociedad.
Un saludo simbólico. Aunque la Voyager 1 no nos enviará ningún mensaje especial, nosotros sí podemos hacerlo. La NASA ha preparado para la ocasión una web con la que los móviles y tablets pueden parpadear simbólicamente en “VGR”, la señal de llamada de la sonda en código Morse. Esperan que muchas personas se unan a la iniciativa para que haya un anillo de luces saludando a Voyager 1 a lo largo de todo el mundo.
Medio siglo de viaje. En 1965, un estudiante de posgrado de Caltech llamado Gary Flandro estaba estudiando una rara alineación que se da entre Júpiter, Saturno, Urano y Neptuno cada 175 años cuando se dio cuenta de algo interesante. Si se aprovechaba la alineación que tendría lugar en 1977, se podría impulsar una nave hacia todos esos planetas en un tiempo récord, ya que la gravedad de cada uno de ellos le daría un impulso hacia el siguiente. Esta fue la semilla de la que nacieron las misiones Voyager, con las que se enviaron 2 sondas al espacio en 1977. La Voyager 2 se lanzó primero, el 20 de agosto de 1977, y la Voyager 1 despegó 16 días después, el 5 de septiembre. La Voyager 2 visitó los cuatro planetas, mientras que la Voyager 1 pudo observar de cerca tanto Júpiter como Saturno.
Ambas cumplieron sus cometidos y continuaron vagando por el espacio, más allá del Sistema Solar. Actualmente siguen funcionando, con la Voyager 1 más adelantada. De hecho, se calcula que la Voyager 2 alcanzaría el día luz en 2035, aunque posiblemente deje de funcionar antes.
Apagado de instrumentos. Poco a poco, las dos sondas se van quedando sin energía. Tanto la Voyager 1 como la Voyager 2 funcionan con un generador nuclear de plutonio, y la energía disponible baja unos cuatro vatios al año en cada sonda. Para aprovechar esa energía al máximo, se han ido apagando instrumentos poco a poco. De los diez instrumentos que llevaban inicialmente, la Voyager 1 ha apagado ocho y la Voyager 2 siete, así que trabajan bajo mínimos. En este tiempo, la NASA ha exprimido a la perfección la energía de las sondas, pero llegará un momento en el que esta se acabará. Mientras tanto, siguen batiendo récords como el que le espera a la Voyager 1 mañana mismo.

articles.title: Red Hat and Microsoft bring OpenShift virtual machines to Azure - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Red Hat and Microsoft bring OpenShift virtual machines to Azure
IBM Corp. subsidiary Red Hat and Microsoft Corp. are expanding their longtime engineering partnership to enable enterprises to run virtual machines on Microsoft Azure using Red Hat’s OpenShift Virtualization platform, providing an alternative to traditional hypervisors and what Red Hat called a path to modernizing legacy applications.
The collaboration, announced today, involves changes to Azure’s underlying computing architecture to connect it natively with Linux through Microsoft direct virtualization. That’s an Azure feature that gives performance-sensitive workloads near-bare-metal access to underlying hardware components.
Red Hat said this provides a direct pipeline between key hardware such as graphics processing units and isolated workloads. The companies are also working to give Linux-based workloads more direct access to Azure’s hardware resources, including graphics processing units.
Separately, Red Hat said it’s making its Lightwell Network vulnerability remediation service available through Microsoft’s Azure Marketplace.
The virtualization initiative addresses growing enterprise concerns about hypervisor licensing costs, hardware availability and the complexity of managing virtual machines alongside newer containerized applications. Red Hat said those pressures have intensified as organizations seek to accommodate AI workloads without abandoning existing applications.
Virtualization market leader Broadcom Inc. recently took aim at the same issue by open-sourcing its software for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same protocols that the Kubernetes container orchestrator uses. At the center of the effort is Microsoft’s direct virtualization, which lets Linux-based and cloud-native platforms running on Azure virtual machines access the same virtualization and hardware capabilities available to Azure-native services.
Red Hat said it will be the first commercial Microsoft partner to support the technology through OpenShift Virtualization on Azure Red Hat OpenShift, the jointly engineered and managed Kubernetes service offered by the two companies.
The agreement includes collaboration on several upstream open-source projects, including KubeVirt, LibVirt, QEMU and the Linux kernel. KubeVirt enables organizations to manage virtual machines and containers using Kubernetes tools.
Microsoft has extended KubeVirt beyond the Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine hypervisor by adding support for its own hypervisor. That allows OpenShift Virtualization to run on Azure virtual machines using Microsoft’s direct virtualization technology.
Simpler migration
The approach is designed to let organizations consolidate traditional virtual machines, containerized applications and AI workloads on a common platform. Red Hat said its migration toolkit for virtualization will help customers move workloads from existing hypervisors.
The companies said the architecture will also improve resource utilization by supporting CPU and memory overcommitment, enabling more workloads to share available infrastructure. Kernel-level isolation is intended to protect sensitive workloads without compromising performance.
“Enterprises shouldn’t have to choose between managing rising hypervisor costs and accelerating their IT roadmaps,” Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer, said in a statement. He said the collaboration would provide a common foundation for modernizing existing virtual machines and running AI workloads.
The companies did not announce a general availability date for the new virtualization capabilities.
Red Hat also said Lightwell Network is immediately available through private offers on Azure Marketplace, allowing customers to obtain remediated versions of vulnerable open-source software dependencies.
Lightwell addresses a persistent application security problem: correcting vulnerabilities in third-party software without forcing upgrades that could disrupt production applications.
The service provides version-specific fixes through secured repositories, accompanied by signed software artifacts and supporting provenance, software bills of materials and vulnerability information where applicable.
Customers can incorporate those fixes into existing development and deployment pipelines without replacing their vulnerability scanners, artifact repositories or build systems. Findings can surface in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, while Azure Policy provides governance controls.
Customers can purchase Lightwell subscriptions through Azure Marketplace and apply eligible spending toward their Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitments.

articles.title: Cohetes reutilizables: la tecnología de Elon Musk que apunta a reducir el costo de ir al espacio
articles.text:
La nave Starship de SpaceX volvió a la Tierra y fue capturada por la torre de lanzamiento en Texas. La operación ocurrió el 14 de noviembre de 2026, al término de un vuelo de más de 22 horas y 14 vueltas alrededor del planeta. La prueba puso a la vista la apuesta de Elon Musk para abaratar los viajes espaciales: recuperar los vehículos y volver a utilizarlos, en vez de desecharlos después de cada misión.
El resultado tuvo un matiz importante. SpaceX no logró recuperar en ese mismo vuelo las dos partes del sistema: el propulsor Super Heavy cayó en el golfo de México tras abortarse su intento de retorno, mientras que la nave Starship sí regresó y fue atrapada por la torre.
Cabe precisar que la captura del propulsor ya se había conseguido antes, en octubre de 2024. Sin embargo, esta es la primera vez que SpaceX logra recuperar la nave superior después de un vuelo orbital.
Cómo funciona la recuperación de Starship
El sistema está compuesto por dos vehículos: el propulsor Super Heavy, que impulsa el despegue, y la nave Starship, que continúa el viaje y puede transportar carga o tripulación. Ambos están diseñados para regresar a la plataforma. En vez de aterrizar sobre patas, el propulsor y la nave pueden ser atrapados por los brazos mecánicos de una torre que SpaceX llama Mechazilla. La maniobra exige que los vehículos reduzcan su velocidad y se coloquen con precisión frente a los brazos.
Recuperar las partes es solo una etapa. Para que la reutilización reduzca los costos de manera sostenida, SpaceX debe demostrar que puede inspeccionar, reparar y preparar cada vehículo para otro lanzamiento en menos tiempo y con menos trabajo que fabricar uno nuevo.
La empresa describe Starship como un sistema totalmente reutilizable y plantea que sus componentes puedan regresar a la plataforma para volar otra vez.
El contraste con los cohetes de un solo uso ayuda a entender el interés económico. Si el vehículo principal puede volar repetidamente, los gastos de construcción se reparten entre más misiones. También podría aumentar la frecuencia de los lanzamientos y facilitar el transporte de satélites, equipos y suministros.
Sin embargo, el precio final dependerá de factores como el mantenimiento, la vida útil de cada nave, el combustible y la infraestructura necesaria en tierra. La recuperación exitosa todavía no revela cuánto costará un lanzamiento comercial de Starship.
La prueba pendiente para llegar a la Luna
Starship también tiene un papel dentro del programa Artemis de la NASA. La agencia contrató a SpaceX para desarrollar una versión de la nave que pueda llevar astronautas desde la órbita lunar hasta la superficie.
Para una misión de ese tipo, la empresa necesita demostrar, entre otros aspectos, que puede transferir propelentes —combustible y oxígeno líquidos— entre vehículos en el espacio. El plan requiere varios vuelos de naves cisterna para abastecer a la versión lunar antes de su viaje.
Ese desafío muestra por qué reutilizar el cohete no basta para habilitar viajes frecuentes a destinos lejanos. SpaceX también tendrá que completar pruebas de reabastecimiento orbital, validar el desempeño de la nave y resolver los requisitos de seguridad para misiones tripuladas. La captura de la nave tras su vuelo orbital ofrece datos y demuestra una maniobra clave, pero el sistema aún debe probar que puede repetirla con regularidad y volver a volar.
La recuperación de noviembre marca así un avance relevante en el desarrollo de Starship y en la apuesta por cohetes reutilizables. El objetivo de Musk es que el sistema pueda realizar vuelos frecuentes y reducir el costo de acceso al espacio.

articles.title: India has 300,000 startups; farmers open to using technologies, says Union minister Jayant Chaudhary
articles.text:
India has 300,000 startups; farmers open to using technologies, says Union minister Jayant Chaudhary
The conference was held alongside the Singapore-India Hackathon at the Singapore Management University (SMU) here.
India has around 300,000 registered startups, many of which are led by women, Union minister Jayant Chaudhary told global tech leaders on Tuesday, and underlined that farmers across the country are also enthusiastic about using technology.
"Farmers are not going to be developers of any tech solutions for the future, but they are users (and) they are very open to using technologies," he told over 300 delegates at the TIECON 2026 conference organised by The Indus Entrepreneurs (TiEcon) in Singapore.
"With the farmers, there is great enthusiasm," the minister of state for skill development and entrepreneurship said.
The conference was held alongside the Singapore-India Hackathon at the Singapore Management University (SMU) here.
Highlighting the success of startups in India, the minister said that the country has nearly 300,000 registered startups today, which are from Tier-II and Tier-III cities. A lot of these startups are led by women.
"Our seeds are sown throughout the country," he said, adding that it is not just Bengaluru, Mumbai or Hyderabad -- the traditional power centres where the startups have grown and established a global footprint.
"So, that is the great potential," Chaudhury said as he described the Indian startup ecosystem. "India's startup story today is very, very robust."
"A great depth is in the fact that our academia is also contributing today to the research. Our universities are no longer closed. They are contributing to research innovation. Our professors are part of some of these boards (of the startups)," said the minister.
He further shared that the Indian Institutes of Technologies are now launching deep tech funds. "They (the IITs) are working with some of the fund management companies, and trying to get even small ticket investors to come (to India) and work for the future."
"So, that gives me great confidence that the Indian story is (scaling) with such a young population," he underlined.
TiE Singapore President Prantik Mazumdar welcomed Minister Chaudhary's update on the startup ecosystem in India.
"We are grateful to Shri Jayant Chaudhary for his presence and support of our ambitions, and share his belief in the importance of investing in human capital.
"With TiEcon SG 2026, we want to explore how we can harness the complementary strengths of Singapore and India to build the next generation of global technology giants from Asia. By deepening our collaboration with institutions such as Singapore Management University, we hope to nurture entrepreneurial talent and facilitate greater talent mobility between the two countries," said Mazumdar.
Themed 'Frontier Tech Reshaping The Coming Decade', the one-day conference brought together a distinguished community of founders, investors, policymakers, business leaders, and technology and innovation leaders to explore trends, technologies, and opportunities shaping the next decade of venture building.
The TIECON SG 2026 conference celebrated 25 years of TiE in Singapore.

articles.title: Xiaomi dévoile la Watch S5 et la Smart Band 11 : prix, autonomie, nouveautés… tout ce qu’il faut savoir
articles.text:
Xiaomi vient de dévoiler une nouvelle montre connectée : la Xiaomi Watch S5 – 41mm. Celle-ci a tout d’une montre connectée, mais ressemble davantage à une montre classique. Le constructeur chinois a également dévoilé le Xiaomi Smart Band 11, un bracelet connecté à l’écran ovale. Ces deux produits sont dès à présent disponibles sur les canaux officiels de Xiaomi et auprès des revendeurs agréés. Spécificités et prix : voici tout ce qu’il faut savoir.
La Xiaomi Watch S5 – 41mm
Avec la Watch S5 – 41mm, Xiaomi propose une montre connectée qui ressemble à une montre traditionnelle. On retrouve un écran Amoled de 1,32 pouce placé sur un boîtier en acier inoxydable de 9,9 mm d’épaisseur. La luminosité de l’écran peut quant à elle atteindre 3 000 nits. La montre propose par ailleurs quatre cadrans animés qui mettent en scène des animaux qui réagissent au toucher, à la progression de l’activité physique, à l’heure et à la météo. L’atteinte d’objectifs sportifs permet de débloquer de nouvelles postures pour ces animaux.
En parlant de sport, cette montre connectée propose 150 modes sportifs, ainsi que des indicateurs de suivi. La fonction « Sélection d’entraînements », par exemple, propose des types et des durées d’exercices en fonction de la météo, de la condition physique, des habitudes sportives et du niveau de forme. La fonction « Aperçu de la santé » analyse quant à elle plus de 50 indicateurs de forme, de sommeil et de santé afin de mettre en évidence les évolutions notables. Les bilans sont consultables aussi bien sur la montre que sur un smartphone connecté.
Côté suivi du sommeil, l’algorithme de nouvelle génération promet d’améliorer de 11 % la précision de détection de l’endormissement et du réveil, et de 14 % celle des phases de sommeil, par rapport à celui de la génération précédente. À noter également que la montre propose un suivi de la variabilité de la fréquence cardiaque (VFC) pour apporter davantage d’informations sur la récupération. Côté connectivité et applications, la montre offre une connexion Wi-Fi (pour télécharger plus rapidement les mises à jour, des musiques, des cartes hors ligne, etc.), et intègre Google Wallet, Google Pay et les paiements NFC.
La Xiaomi Watch S5 41 mm promet par ailleurs un suivi précis du cycle menstruel grâce à un capteur de température amélioré, capable de prédire les règles et l’ovulation. Attention toutefois, l’accès à certaines analyses approfondies requiert un abonnement à Clue Plus (trois mois gratuits sont offerts à l’achat de la montre). Enfin, précisons que Xiaomi annonce jusqu’à 14 jours d’autonomie grâce à une batterie de 590 mAh.
La Xiaomi Watch S5 41mm est déclinée en Noir et Bleu Clair. Ces deux modèles sont équipés d’un bracelet en sport souple et sont vendus au prix de 229,99 €. Un troisième modèle, Blanc Céramique, bénéficie quant à lui d’un bracelet en cuir et est vendu au prix de 249,99 €. Du 17 au 30 novembre 2026, dans le cadre d’une offre de lancement, les modèles Noir et Bleu Clair sont vendus au prix de 194,99 € (soit 35 € de remise), tandis que le modèle Blanc Céramique est proposé au prix de 229,99 € (soit 20 € de remise).
Le Xiaomi Smart Band 11
Ce bracelet connecté présente un écran Amoled ovale de 1,72 pouce, dont la luminosité maximale peut atteindre 2 000 nits. Il intègre par ailleurs 150 modes sportifs et la reconnaissance automatique de six activités. Notons également la présence d’un capteur PPG à double LED et double photodiode, fonctionnant simultanément avec l’algorithme propriétaire de Xiaomi, qui permettrait d’atteindre une précision globale de la fréquence cardiaque allant jusqu’à 98,2 %.
Il est possible de nager avec ce bracelet connecté puisqu’il est étanche jusqu’à 5 ATM, tandis que le suivi de la fréquence cardiaque continue de fonctionner sous l’eau. Bien entendu, on retrouve un suivi du sommeil avec une détection de l’endormissement et des cycles de sommeil. À noter que ce bracelet peut être connecté aussi bien à un smartphone Xiaomi qu’à un iPhone, afin de recevoir des alertes d’appel, des messages ou encore des rappels. Enfin, notons que Xiaomi annonce jusqu’à 21 jours d’autonomie pour la version standard et 18 jours pour les modèles NFC.
Le Xiaomi Smart Band 11 se décline en plusieurs versions. Le modèle standard, dont le cadre en aluminium est proposé en noir, argent ou rose, est vendu au prix de 59,99 € (ou 54,99 € du 17 au 30 novembre 2026, soit une remise de 5 €). Un modèle dont le cadre est couleur or est quant à lui proposé à 64,99 € (ou 59,99 € du 17 au 30 novembre 2026, soit une remise de 5 €).
Les modèles NFC (paiement sans contact) se déclinent également en deux éditions spéciales : une version Céramique blanche et une version Unibody entièrement métallique, proposée dans un coloris lavande. Côté tarifs, la version NFC classique est affichée à 79,99 €, mais bénéficie d’une offre de lancement à 67,99 € du 17 au 30 novembre 2026. Les éditions Céramique et Unibody sont quant à elles proposées à 89,99 €, avec des prix de lancement respectifs de 75,99 € et 79,99 €, soit 14 € et 10 € de réduction.

Tuesday, November 17th 2026
Kensington Launches the Expert Mouse Pro TB900 EQ Trackball
Kensington, a worldwide leader in desktop computing and mobility solutions for IT, business, and home office professionals, today announced the launch of Expert Mouse Pro TB900 EQ Trackball, a wired and wireless trackball designed for engineers, editors, and creative professionals who need precise cursor control and customizable navigation.The TB900 combines Kensington's DIAMONDEYE dual-sensor optical tracking system with a large 55 mm trackball and polling rates up to 1 kHz for smooth, accurate cursor movement with less hand and wrist motion compared to traditional mice. Designed for precision-intensive applications including CAD, video editing, audio production, graphic design, and professional computing, the advanced dual-sensor system maximizes tracking coverage and enables highly accurate cursor control from nearly the entire surface of the ball.
Users can connect up to four devices at once using two Bluetooth channels, one 2.4 GHz wireless connection, or wired USB-C. The TB900 supports quick switching between connected computers and tablets without re-pairing.Additional features include an adjustable aluminium scroll ring, dual side-scroll controls for horizontal scrolling and zooming, and support for up to 16 programmable functions using Kensington Konnect software. The TB900 also includes access to Avid Pro Tools Intro+ for audio production workflows.
Key Features and Benefits
- DIAMONDEYE Optical Tracking with Dual Sensors for smooth, highly accurate cursor control for improved productivity and efficiency over traditional mice.
- Up to 1 kHz Polling Rate via wired or 2.4 GHz wireless connection for ultra-responsive performance and fast, accurate cursor control.
- Adjustable Scroll Ring and Dual Customizable Side Scrolls for line-by-line, smooth, horizontal, and zoom navigation.
- Advanced Customization with up to 16 programmable functions using Kensington Konnect software or choose plug-and-play convenience.
- Multi-Device Connectivity supports two Bluetooth connections, one 2.4 GHz wireless connection with government-grade 128-bit AES encryption, and one wired USB-C connection.
- Rechargeable Battery delivers up to four months of productivity per charge. USB-C cable included for in-use charging and wired connection.
- Ambidextrous Ergonomic Design optimized to comfortably accommodate both left- and right-handed users with average to larger-sized hands.
- Windows and macOS Compatibility effortlessly supports Windows 10 or later (32-bit/64-bit), Windows 11 (64-bit only), and macOS 14 or later, for seamless deployment across professional environments.
"Engineers, editors, and creative professionals rely on precise, repeatable control, and traditional mice can lack accuracy and require excessive hand movements which can negatively impact workflow efficiency," said Lisa Schuiteboer-Shuler, Global Marketing Manager at Kensington. "The Expert Mouse Pro TB900 EQ Trackball addresses these challenges with dual-sensor tracking, customizable controls, and multi-device connectivity designed for precision-focused tasks like CAD, video editing, audio production, and graphic design."
The Kensington Expert Mouse Pro TB900 EQ Trackball is backed by a three-year limited warranty and is now available on Amazon and through the Kensington Store. It is offered in two options—a silver ball version (K72469WWMY; SRP $129.99) and a red ball version (K72468WWMY; SRP $129.99)—with the red ball exclusively available on Amazon.

articles.title: Vivo negocia compra da Vero por cerca de R$ 6,3 bilhões • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Vivo negocia compra da Vero por cerca de R$ 6,3 bilhões
Segundo o jornal espanhol Expansión, operação é avaliada em 1 bilhão de euros. Aquisição pode adicionar 1,2 milhão de clientes de banda larga à base da Vivo.
A Telefônica Brasil, dona da Vivo, negocia a compra da provedora de internet Vero em uma operação avaliada em cerca de 1 bilhão de euros (R$ 6,3 bilhões, em conversão direta). Segundo apuração do jornal espanhol Expansión, as conversas com os acionistas da empresa giram em torno desse valor.
As negociações envolveriam principalmente a Vinci Partners e a Warburg Pincus, gestoras que controlam aproximadamente 60% da Vero. A primeira detém cerca de 37,5% das ações, enquanto o fundo americano possui outros 22,5%. As informações sobre a possibilidade de compra começaram a circular no mês passado.
A Vero é a sexta maior provedora de banda larga fixa do Brasil, com aproximadamente 1,2 milhão de clientes. A empresa atende 425 municípios em sete estados: Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paraná, São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso do Sul e Goiás. Sua infraestrutura alcança cerca de 7,2 milhões de domicílios.
A aquisição reforçaria principalmente a atuação da Vivo no Sul e no Sudeste. Segundo dados do ranking das maiores operadoras de banda larga, a Telefônica Brasil tinha aproximadamente 8,5 milhões de acessos de internet fixa em agosto de 2026. Com a incorporação da base da Vero, chegaria a cerca de 9,8 milhões, ainda atrás da Claro, que contabilizava 10,8 milhões.
Além da fibra, a Vero atua como operadora móvel virtual (MVNO), utilizando a infraestrutura da TIM para oferecer planos de celular. A companhia encerrou setembro com aproximadamente 420 mil clientes móveis, crescimento de 56,4% em um ano.
A possível venda ocorre em um momento de resultados mistos para a provedora brasileira. No terceiro trimestre de 2026, a Vero registrou prejuízo líquido de R$ 3,7 milhões, revertendo o lucro de R$ 12,2 milhões obtido no mesmo período do ano anterior, segundo o Teletime.
A receita líquida caiu 3,3% na comparação anual, para R$ 419,8 milhões. A base de banda larga também recuou 5,6%, enquanto o negócio de telefonia móvel apresentou o crescimento expressivo.
Para a Telefônica, a aquisição poderia acelerar a expansão da Vivo em cidades onde a operadora ainda tem menor presença, além de ampliar sua infraestrutura e carteira de clientes. Até o momento, porém, as empresas não anunciaram um acordo definitivo nem divulgaram um cronograma para concluir as negociações. O valor atribuído à operação também não foi confirmado oficialmente pela Telefônica Brasil.

articles.title: Brazilian businessman arrested for attempted murder after planting explosive-filled game console that detonated in electronics store — perp tried to kill business rival, device delivered by unsuspecting motorcyclist working for a delivery service
articles.text:
Brazilian businessman arrested for attempted murder after planting explosive-filled game console that detonated in electronics store — perp tried to kill business rival, device delivered by unsuspecting motorcyclist working for a delivery service
The target suffered minor injuries
A São Paulo businessman has been arrested by police on suspicion of sending a game console stuffed with explosives to the electronics store of a rival in an attempt to kill him. The device then exploded. On Monday, Military Police executed a warrant against Everton Yoshizumi Lima, who is suspected of perpetrating the outrageous attack, G1 reports.
On October 23, 2026, at around 5:30 pm, a delivery person dropped off a video game console at an electronics repair shop, with the cover that it was being left for modifications requested by the customer. Police say the device had an explosive planted inside that was programmed to detonate upon receipt. "Unaware of its contents, the store owner put the video game console in a drawer and continued working," the report states. The device ignited and exploded, causing severe damage and injuring two people: the owner of the store and a friend who was at the scene. The whole thing was captured on video, which you can see by expanding the tweet below:
The device was found to have two explosive charges of the same magnitude inside, but only one of the devices went off, possibly limiting the capacity for damage and injury. The report notes that investigators believe the intent of the device was to kill the victim, given the amount of explosives. The console was delivered to the store by an unsuspecting motorcyclist who was working for a delivery app company and had no idea they were carrying a bomb.
The request appears to have been traced back to Lima, who is the main suspect in the attack. Lima purportedly owns other electronics stores in the area, including two on the same street where this store was recently opened, labeling the motive as "business competition." "The new store had been advertised through a social media campaign and the distribution of flyers," the report states. "Annoyed by the competition, the suspect allegedly decided to eliminate the competitor, according to the line of investigation."
According to the report, Lima was arrested during the course of an investigation into a possible motorcycle theft. It appears that Lima was the owner of the target vehicle, and that police visited in advance, suspecting someone might try to steal it. While checking his data, it was found that Lima had an outstanding arrest warrant for his suspected involvement in the attack.
