articles.title: Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoints now support KV cache aware routing
Today, Amazon SageMaker AI introduces KV cache-aware routing (KV-aware routing), a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints. It uses the cache state that the model container reports. It sends each request to an instance that already holds a long cached match for its prompt and isn’t too busy. It’s for teams that serve large language models (LLMs) with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. You turn it on in two places: add one environment variable to your model so the container reports its cache contents, and set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Your clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.
Here’s the problem it solves: LLM applications such as chat assistants, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), and agents with long system prompts send many requests that start with the same text. A model keeps the work it did on a prompt in GPU memory, the KV cache, and skips that work when the same start reaches the same instance again. In part 1 of this series, we introduced prefix-aware routing for Amazon SageMaker AI, which sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. Prefix-aware routing infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone, so it can’t tell when an instance has evicted that cache.
Prefix-aware routing picks an instance from the request alone. It hashes the start of the request, up to the PrefixLength you configure (bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload, or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API), and sends requests that start the same way to the same instance. It never sees what an instance actually has cached. This works well when every request starts with the same shared text, and less well in two cases:
The cache on an instance changes over time. An instance evicts older KV cache entries when its GPU memory fills up, but the router keeps sending matching requests there as if the cache were still warm.
A conversation starts out short. In a multi-turn chat, each turn adds to the history. While the request is still shorter than PrefixLength, every new turn changes the text the router hashes, so the next turn can land on a different instance than the one that cached the earlier turns. The turns of a conversation stay on one instance only after the request grows past PrefixLength.
In this post, we explain how KV-aware routing works, when to use it, and how to enable, invoke, and verify it on single model endpoints and inference component endpoints.
How KV-aware routing works
KV-aware routing has three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state for the endpoint, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance for each request.
When you turn events on with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG, the container publishes a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts cache entries, and SageMaker AI uses these events to keep the index current. The index holds only pointers: one-way, truncated hashes of cached content, each mapped to the instance or inference component copy that holds it. It never stores prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. When a request arrives, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks up the tokens in the index. The index returns the instances or inference component copies that hold part of the prompt in their cache, and how much of it each one holds. For example, if instance A holds the cached start of a conversation, the next turn of that conversation goes to A. Because the index matches on tokens rather than a fixed number of bytes, a multi-turn history can match in full as it grows. A request that shares only part of its prompt still goes to the instance with the longest match.
The endpoint then picks among these candidates by weighing how much of the prompt each one has cached against how busy it is. A candidate that is too busy is skipped, so if the instance with the longest match is busy, the request goes to the next-best one that is available. If no candidate has a useful match or all of them are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing, as described in Routing overhead and fallbacks. You don’t configure a concurrency threshold for this, as you do with prefix-aware routing. The index also follows the fleet. When you scale in, entries for removed instances are dropped. When you scale out or an update replaces instances, the new instances start with empty caches, so latency can be higher for a short time.
In Figure 1, the endpoint has three instances, A, B, and C. Each instance runs the same model in its own model container (the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container listed in Requirements and limits) and has its own KV cache in GPU memory, so each instance holds different cached content: A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7. When turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives (step 1), the router tokenizes it and looks it up in the managed cache index (step 2). The index shows that A holds the first 6,000 of the request’s 6,200 tokens, so the router sends the request to A (step 3), and A only has to compute the remaining tokens. If A is busy, the router sends the request to the least busy instance instead (step 4). KV-aware routing needs a choice of destinations, so it is active only with at least two instances, or at least two copies of an inference component. With a single instance, every request goes to that instance and the setting has no effect.
Routing strategies on SageMaker AI
With this launch, SageMaker AI offers four routing strategies for real-time endpoints. You set the strategy per production variant in the RoutingConfig of your endpoint configuration.
| Strategy | How it routes | Recommended for | 
| RANDOM (default) | Sends each request to a randomly chosen instance. | General-purpose workloads, non-LLM models, and requests that are interchangeable. | 
| LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS | Sends each request to the instance with the fewest in-flight requests. | Workloads where processing time varies and you want to keep all instances equally busy. | 
| PREFIX_AWARE | Sends requests that share the same prompt prefix, up to PrefixLength, to the same instance. Overflows to another instance at ConcurrencyThreshold. | LLM workloads with shared text at a fixed position at the start of the request, on any serving framework that supports prefix caching. | 
| KV_AWARE (new) | Sends each request to an instance that holds a matching cached prefix, based on cache state reported by the container, weighing match length against load. Falls back to load-aware routing. | LLM workloads on a supported container with multi-turn conversations, frequent cache eviction, or requests that share only part of their start. | 
Prefix-aware or KV-aware
Both strategies send requests to where their prefix is likely to be cached. They differ in how they know where that is, and in what they need from your container.
|  | Prefix-aware routing | KV-aware routing | 
| Source of cache location | Inferred from the request prefix | Cache state reported by the container | 
| Added latency per request | 1.3–1.9 milliseconds in part 1 | A few milliseconds for short prompts, more for long ones, mostly for tokenization | 
| Matching | First PrefixLength bytes (Invoke API) or characters (OpenAI-compatible API) | Tokens, longest cached match | 
| Parameters | PrefixLength, ConcurrencyThreshold | None needed | 
| Container | Any container with prefix caching on | A supported container, with prefix caching and KV cache events on (see Requirements and limits) | 
| Request payload | Any | OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions format | 
Performance
We measured KV-aware routing against random routing in two ways: a large-scale benchmark on production-sized instances, and a smaller, reproducible comparison you can follow in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Benchmark results
In our benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, we ran 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users holding multi-turn chats and document Q&A sessions, with prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing, and with long prompts under load, KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3–48 percent to 80–93 percent. Long prompts gained even at lower load. The gain was smallest with short prompts, where there is less prefill to save. Results depend on your workload. To measure them for your own traffic, use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Routing overhead and fallbacks
Before it routes a request, the endpoint tokenizes the prompt and looks it up in the managed cache index. The lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, but it stays small next to the time a cache hit saves. For text-only requests that use standard options, the tokens it computes are passed to the model, so the prompt isn’t tokenized twice.
If the lookup is slow, finds no useful match, or all matching instances are busy, the endpoint routes the request with load-aware routing, the same behavior as the LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS strategy. The request is still served, without the cache benefit. The same happens when the endpoint can’t tokenize a request, except in the two error cases described in Invoking the endpoint. These fallbacks aren’t reported in the SageMaker AI console or metrics at launch, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working to confirm that routing is effective for your traffic.
With very short prompts there is less prefill to save, so prefix-aware routing can be all you need.
When to use KV-aware routing
Prefix-aware routing needs no changes to your container, but it can’t see what an instance actually holds. KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise. It pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse and that cache is under pressure: long prompts, high load, and instances that run short of GPU memory for the KV cache. When that happens, the container evicts the least recently used parts of the cache, including parts of shared prompts and conversation history.
For example, a support assistant runs on three instances, and each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt. Conversation 1 starts on instance A, which caches the excerpt. Traffic rises, A runs short of memory, and the container evicts most of that excerpt. Instance B recently served another conversation over the same excerpt and still holds its first 4,000 tokens. When the next turn of conversation 1 arrives, prefix-aware routing sends it to A again, and A recomputes the excerpt. With KV-aware routing, A’s container has already reported the eviction, so the index shows that B holds the longest match, and the request goes to B, which recomputes only the remaining tokens. At low load, A wouldn’t have evicted anything, and both strategies would have sent the request to A with the cache intact.
KV-aware routing helps most when requests reuse cached context in ways a fixed-length prefix can’t capture:
Multi-turn conversations: Each turn sends the full conversation history, so the cached prefix grows with every turn. KV-aware routing matches the whole cached history and keeps each conversation on the instance that holds it. This matters most for long conversations. After the managed cache index reflects an eviction, the router doesn’t keep sending the conversation to an instance that has already dropped its cache.
High-throughput inference with shared context: RAG applications prepend retrieved documents, and assistants send long system prompts with every request. KV-aware routing fits when these prompts are long and instances are under memory pressure. With a stable shared prefix and moderate load, prefix-aware routing also fits. Put the shared content first and in the same order: if the same documents appear in a different order, the prompts no longer share a start, so they don’t match.
Workloads where prefix length is hard to tune: With prefix-aware routing, you choose a PrefixLength that covers your shared text without scattering requests that should stay together. KV-aware routing has no prefix length to tune, because it matches on what is actually cached.
Prefix-aware routing is a good fit, with no container changes, if your requests share a stable system prompt or document at the start, your prompts are short, or load is moderate. In these cases, instances have enough GPU memory to keep the shared text cached, so both strategies find it. Prefix-aware routing is also the choice if your container isn’t supported by KV-aware routing, because it works with any container that has prefix caching turned on. If your requests are short and interchangeable, or your model isn’t an LLM, there is little cached context to reuse, so use RANDOM or LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS.
If you aren’t sure which fits, start with prefix-aware routing, run your own traffic against a KV_AWARE endpoint, and compare time to first token, throughput, and hit rate as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Requirements and limits
Before you enable KV-aware routing, check that your container, endpoint, and requests meet these requirements:
Container: At launch, KV-aware routing supports the AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container for SageMaker AI: images with vLLM 0.33.0 or later, or the Amazon Linux build server-sagemaker-cuda-v2.8.0 or later. Prefix caching must be on, which is the default, and KV cache events must be turned on with the SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG environment variable, as shown in How to enable it. SageMaker AI doesn’t set it for you.
Endpoints and instances: Real-time single model endpoints and inference component endpoints, including dynamic Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapters, on GPU instance types. You can also configure KV-aware routing with AWS CloudFormation. Routing is active only with at least two instances for a single model endpoint, or at least two copies of an inference component, which can be on the same instance. With fewer, you can still set KV_AWARE and the endpoint isn’t rejected, but every request goes to the single instance or copy.
Requests: OpenAI-compatible Completions or Chat Completions payloads, sent with InvokeEndpoint, InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream, or the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream isn’t supported. If you set the model field, it must match the value of SM_VLLM_MODEL.
SDK versions: Detailed observability, which you use to track the KV cache hit rate, needs AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) version 2.35.6 or later, or Boto3 version 1.43.31 or later.
SageMaker AI checks these requirements before your endpoint serves traffic. If a check fails, the request or deployment fails with a message that describes what is missing. For the full list of settings, validation behavior, and quotas, see the SageMaker AI documentation.
How to enable it
You turn on KV-aware routing in two places: the model and the endpoint configuration. The example notebook runs every step end to end, for both a single model endpoint and an inference component endpoint.
1. Turn on KV cache events in the model – When you create the model, add SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG to the container environment. Without it, the endpoint has no cache state to route on. The ports in this setting are used only inside the instance, so you don’t open them to your network.
2. Choose KV-aware routing in the endpoint configuration – Set RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the RoutingConfig of the production variant:
If your container image is built for CUDA 13, also set InferenceAmiVersion in the production variant to an AMI that supports it, such as al2023-ami-sagemaker-inference-gpu-4-1. Otherwise the container can fail to start. See Inference GPU drivers.
Check that your account has enough endpoint quota for the instance type and count you choose, and request an increase in Service Quotas if needed.
The same RoutingConfig setting works for inference component endpoints, including dynamic LoRA adapters. For adapters, KV-aware routing chooses among the instances that already have the adapter loaded.
Invoking the endpoint
Nothing changes in how you call the endpoint. Send a Chat Completions payload with InvokeEndpoint, or with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream and "stream": true in the request body:
You can also call the endpoint with the OpenAI Python client through the SageMaker AI OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. The Use the OpenAI-compatible API with SageMaker AI notebook on GitHub shows how, for both single model endpoints and inference components.
KV-aware routing doesn’t apply the multi-tenant prefix isolation from part 1: it ignores the prefix-aware ID header and the prompt_cache_key field. A request that sets a top-level cache_salt field to a non-null value is rejected with a 400 error.
KV-aware routing adds two error cases: a request whose model field names a model that the container doesn’t serve fails with a ModelError, and a request with a non-null cache_salt is rejected with a 400 error. Errors from inference itself are returned as before, and your model container’s own logs in Amazon CloudWatch can help you find the cause. The endpoint doesn’t deliver logs about its KV-aware routing decisions to your account, so use the checks in Verify that KV-aware routing is working, such as cached_tokens per request and the KV cache hit rate, to see how routing behaves.
Verify that KV-aware routing is working
KV-aware routing doesn’t add metrics of its own, so you check its effect on your model. There are three ways to do this.
Check cache hits per request – The container doesn’t report prompt token details by default, so set SM_VLLM_ENABLE_PROMPT_TOKENS_DETAILS to true in the model environment. Each response then includes usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens, the number of prompt tokens that were served from the KV cache. When you send a follow-up turn, or another request that starts the same way as an earlier one, a non-zero value shows that the request reached an instance that held its prefix.
Check model metrics in Amazon CloudWatch – Turn on detailed observability by adding --metrics-config '{"EnableDetailedObservability": true}' when you create the endpoint configuration, using the SDK versions in Requirements and limits. SageMaker AI then publishes the model container’s metrics, including the KV cache hit rate and TTFT. Query them as described in Detailed observability with PromQL.
Compare with the strategy you would otherwise use – For most LLM workloads the real choice is between KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE, so compare those two, and add a RANDOM endpoint as a baseline. Use the same model, instance type, and instance count for each endpoint, and send the same prompts at the same concurrency for the same duration, so that the only difference is the routing strategy. Make sure your test reuses context the way your production traffic does, for example with multi-turn conversations or shared documents. If KV_AWARE and PREFIX_AWARE perform about the same for your traffic, prefix-aware routing is the simpler choice.
As an example of this comparison, we compared RANDOM and KV_AWARE on a small endpoint. We sent the same multi-turn workload to two endpoints that differ only in routing strategy. Each endpoint had two ml.g5.xlarge instances serving Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on a supported container. Each run sent 128 requests: 32 simulated users, each asking 4 questions about a document chosen from 12 documents of about 7,400 tokens. Each question resends the conversation so far, so every question after the first can reuse cached context. We ran two pairs of runs, with RANDOM first in pair 1 and KV_AWARE first in pair 2, and used new documents for each pair so that both endpoints started with empty caches. Table 1 shows the results as pair 1 / pair 2.
| Metric | RANDOM | KV_AWARE | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency average (ms) | 4,124 / 5,100 | 1,235 / 1,314 | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency p50 (ms) | 3,153 / 4,083 | 656 / 700 | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency p90 (ms) | 8,334 / 10,746 | 3,213 / 3,535 | 
| CloudWatch ModelLatency p99 (ms) | 17,779 / 16,249 | 6,876 / 7,238 | 
| Time to first token p50, questions 2–4 (ms) | 1,284 / 1,632 | 237 / 245 | 
| Time to first token p90, questions 2–4 (ms) | 5,039 / 6,101 | 456 / 367 | 
| Time to first token p90, all requests (ms) | 5,003 / 5,683 | 1,465 / 1,759 | 
| Share of prompt tokens served from cache | 0.761 / 0.701 | 0.903 / 0.903 | 
| Run duration (s) | 31.1 / 36.9 | 17.9 / 18.0 | 
| CloudWatch OverheadLatency average (ms) | 13.1 / 8.1 | 27.1 / 27.5 | 
Table 1: RANDOM and KV_AWARE routing under the same workload. Each cell shows pair 1 / pair 2. ModelLatency and OverheadLatency are Amazon CloudWatch metrics for the endpoint. The client measured time to first token and run duration. The cache share is the sum of cached_tokens divided by the sum of prompt_tokens over a run
In both pairs, KV_AWARE had lower CloudWatch ModelLatency (average 1,235 and 1,314 ms against 4,124 and 5,100 ms) and lower time to first token for questions 2–4 (p50 237 and 245 ms against 1,284 and 1,632 ms). Its cache share was higher, at 90 percent in both pairs against 76 and 70 percent. OverheadLatency, the time SageMaker AI spends outside the model container, was 14 to 19 ms higher on average with KV_AWARE. This is one model, one instance type, and one workload with long shared documents, so measure your own traffic as described earlier in this section. Figure 3 shows the model latency charts that the SageMaker AI console displays for the two endpoints.
If neither does better than RANDOM, check that prefix caching and KV cache events are turned on in the container, as described in Requirements and limits.
Example notebook
The example notebook applies the steps in this post to Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on two ml.g5.xlarge instances, the minimum for a single model endpoint, and on an inference component endpoint with two copies. It calls the endpoint with both APIs, shows in the container logs that follow-up requests are served from the KV cache, and doesn’t compare routing strategies. Run its cleanup cells at the end to avoid ongoing charges.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources you created. For an inference component endpoint, delete the inference components first (delete-inference-component), then the endpoint, endpoint configuration, and model (delete-endpoint, delete-endpoint-config, delete-model).
Practical guidance
These three practices help you keep KV-aware routing effective after you turn it on.
Monitor the KV cache hit rate – Keep detailed observability on after launch and watch the KV cache hit rate over time in the SageMaker AI Insights dashboard (Figure 2b), or query it with PromQL, as described in Verify that KV-aware routing is working.
Plan for cold starts – The first request with new context, such as a new document or the first turn of a conversation, has nothing cached on any instance. KV-aware routing speeds up the requests that follow, not the first one.
Plan for cache rebuilds during scaling and updates – As described in How KV-aware routing works, new instances start with empty caches. To soften the latency increase, use a rolling or blue/green update for single model endpoints, or a RollingUpdatePolicy for inference components.
Conclusion
KV-aware routing gives SageMaker AI real-time endpoints a second way to send requests to where their prompts are cached. It uses the cache state that your model container reports, so it follows the cache when instances evict it under memory pressure. Prefix-aware routing from part 1 of this series remains the simpler choice for stable shared prompts, short contexts, and moderate load. SageMaker AI handles routing inside the endpoint for both strategies, so you don’t build or run a routing layer yourself. You turn it on with one environment variable in the model and "RoutingStrategy": "KV_AWARE" in the endpoint configuration.
KV-aware routing is available today in all commercial AWS Regions that support SageMaker AI real-time inference, for endpoints that use a supported container. It is available at no additional charge. SageMaker AI runs and manages the cache index for you, and you pay only for the instances your endpoint uses. KV_AWARE is a new value for the existing RoutingStrategy field, so you don’t need a new configuration object, and older versions of the AWS CLI and Boto3 accept it. To get started, read the documentation, run the example notebook on a small endpoint, and then compare KV_AWARE with PREFIX_AWARE on a copy of your own traffic.

articles.title: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
articles.text:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.
The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.
A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:
Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.
The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII, launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.

articles.title: A qué hora sale GTA 6 en tu país: horarios de lanzamiento para PS5 y Xbox Series X|S
articles.text:
GTA 6 se estrenará el jueves 19 de noviembre de 2026 en PlayStation 5 y Xbox Series X|S, con horarios de lanzamiento que variarán según la región configurada en la tienda digital de cada consola. Rockstar Games eligió un desbloqueo a las 00:00 de la hora local, por lo que el acceso a Vice City no ocurrirá al mismo tiempo en todo el mundo.
El calendario importa porque el esperado lanzamiento de Grand Theft Auto VI será escalonado por husos horarios y porque la descarga exigirá preparación. El juego requerirá hasta 212 GB de espacio libre en la unidad SSD, una cifra que puede extender la espera si la instalación comienza justo cuando se habilite.
GTA 6 se desbloqueará a medianoche en cada región
A diferencia de otros juegos que activan sus servidores a una misma hora global, GTA 6 estará disponible cuando el reloj marque las 12:00 a.m. del jueves 19 de noviembre en cada país o región de la tienda digital.
Para los jugadores de América Latina, incluidos Argentina, Colombia, Chile, México y Perú, el título se habilitará a las 00:00 de la hora local. El mismo criterio se aplicará en España, el resto de Europa, Asia y Oceanía.
Los países con los husos horarios más adelantados serán los primeros en entrar al juego. Nueva Zelanda y Australia tendrán acceso antes que Europa y América, debido a la diferencia de horas.
Estados Unidos podrá jugar desde la noche del 18 de noviembre
Las tiendas digitales de Estados Unidos tomarán como referencia la Hora del Este. Esto permitirá que quienes jueguen desde el centro y el oeste del país accedan durante la noche del miércoles 18 de noviembre.
Estos son los horarios previstos:
- Hora del Este, en ciudades como Miami y Nueva York: jueves 19 de noviembre a las 00:00.
- Hora Central, como Chicago y Houston: miércoles 18 de noviembre a las 23:00.
- Hora de la Montaña, como Denver: miércoles 18 de noviembre a las 22:00.
- Hora del Pacífico, como Los Ángeles: miércoles 18 de noviembre a las 21:00.
En Xbox Series X|S, algunos usuarios suelen modificar la región de la consola para usar el llamado “truco de Nueva Zelanda” y acceder antes. En PlayStation 5, esa alternativa requiere comprar el juego desde una cuenta secundaria creada para esa región.
La predescarga ya está disponible y exige hasta 212 GB
La predescarga de GTA 6 está habilitada desde el 10 de noviembre para quienes hayan reservado la versión digital. En PlayStation 5, se puede iniciar desde la biblioteca de juegos o la PlayStation Store. En Xbox Series X|S, la instalación anticipada se activa desde la Xbox Store después de completar la reserva.
Las copias físicas tampoco incluirán un disco. La caja contendrá un código de descarga, por lo que será necesario conectarse a internet y disponer del espacio suficiente incluso con esa edición.
El lanzamiento nativo estará limitado a PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X y Xbox Series S. No habrá una versión para PC el día del estreno y Rockstar Games no comunicó una fecha para computadoras. Los usuarios de Xbox One no tendrán una edición propia, aunque podrán jugar mediante Xbox Cloud Gaming con la configuración de Xbox Series S.
La campaña podría durar 50 horas y el 100% llegaría a 200
Además de los horarios, la duración de GTA 6 concentra la atención de la comunidad. Según una filtración difundida por el periodista Tom Henderson, la campaña principal demandaría cerca de 50 horas, con alrededor de 100 misiones repartidas en cinco capítulos centrados en Jason y Lucia.
La cifra situaría a GTA 6 por encima de las cerca de 32 horas de historia de GTA V y en una duración similar a Red Dead Redemption 2. El tiempo puede aumentar si el jugador combina las misiones principales con la exploración y las actividades del mundo abierto.
Rob Nelson, responsable de desarrollo y codirector de Rockstar North, relató que una de sus partidas se extendió durante 80 horas. Ese recorrido incluyó objetivos opcionales, interacciones con otros personajes y desplazamientos por el mapa, por lo que no se limitó a la trama principal.
Completar el 100% podría requerir hasta 200 horas, según la misma información. Entre los retos figurarían la identificación y fotografía de más de 170 especies animales en Leonida, además de logros con elementos aleatorios que dificultarían seguir una ruta fija. Rockstar Games no ha confirmado oficialmente estos datos.

articles.title: The Xreal Aura are an impressive first step for Android XR glasses
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Xreal Aura wired Android XR glasses are versatile, powerful, productive, and fun. They're an effective on-your-face computer, and I found them useful for everything from entertainment to gaming. Putting the computer and battery in a puck was smart — and making that puck also a trackpad was a stroke of genius, as if you're ever lost, you can physically take control of navigation with a mouse pointer. The lack of eye tracking makes navigation more finicky than it should be, and the promise of Bluetooth-keyboard-connected productivity was short-circuited by the placement of that cable-connected computer puck, but connecting my laptop through a wired connection (or wireless) was a dream work scenario. Images are sharp, colorful, and immersive, and Gemini on your face is way better than it sounds. They're relatively affordable, and overall this is probably the best Android XR experience available today, and another reminder that the future of mixed reality is probably less Vision Pro and Galaxy XR and more lightweight glasses like these.
- 
Value
- 
Design
- 
Picture Quality
- 
Performance
Reasons to buy
- + Lightweight
- + Sharp visuals
- + Versatile
- + Useful Gemini integration
Reasons to avoid
- - Lack of eye tracking limits precision
- - Productivity with BLE keyboard and compute puck/mousepad is unnecessarily awkward
- - Compute Puck gets warm
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Xreal Aura Android XR glasses: Two-minute review
The list of AR, VR, and XR headsets I've tried is now long, and I'm starting to get a good feel for the pros and cons of these wearables, which range from unwieldy headgear to lightweight glasses, and from headsets and goggles that offer deeply immersive environments to mixed-reality glasses that can, with some caveats, close you off from the outside world almost as well.
As I've traversed the full panoply of wearable styles and capabilities, I've come to realize that I prefer lightweight and less odd-looking over a deeply immersive experience every time.
It's probably appropriate that I got to try the Meta VR Glasses and Snap's Specs just weeks or even days before taking a deeper dive into Xreal's Aura wired Android XR Glasses. All of these specs are less about disconnecting you from the world to immerse you in fully realized AR and VR experiences, and more about finding a middle ground between style and utility, and reality-bending mixed and virtual reality.
The Xreal Aura stand out as the first Android XR glasses, following on the heels of the first XR headset: the Samsung Galaxy XR. Those goggles were designed to compete with Apple's pricey and powerful Vision Pro (a task they mostly accomplished). As with other XR glasses I've tried, here Xreal has moved not only the battery to a wearable brick, but virtually all the compute, too. But Xreal has gone a step further and also added a trackpad surface to the puck for another, sometimes very useful, degree of control.
The Xreal Aura offer the full range of mixed-reality experiences — everything from immersive apps that put you up close and personal with Galapagos tours to games, like Cubism, that highlight the glasses' impressive hand-tracking capabilities.
The Xreal Aura are as good at immersing you in a classic rom-com like How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days, putting you in a virtual, theater-like atmosphere (the electrochromic lenses get quite dark) as they are at extending your desktop workspace into a wraparound screen experience wirelessly, or via a wired accessory cable.
They still look too odd for wearing out and about; but in a home, office, or travel scenario (they come with one of the best, most compact travel cases I've seen so far), they're an appropriate size, and feel good to wear.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The Gemini AI integration is top-notch, and I found myself giving the AI access to my screen so that it could help me identify objects, work out app issues, or just keep me company.
On the downside, while the hand tracking is impressive, the lack of eye tracking meant that I struggled a bit at times to find my target.
$1,099 is not cheap (pricing and availability for the UK and Australia are TBC), but it's worth remembering that this is a complete computer with full support for Google Play apps, and support for everything from console-grade gaming (yes, I connected a Bluetooth game controller) to movies, productivity apps, and powerful AI. Overall, I suspect this is the kind of XR headset most people are looking for, and it's the best example so far of Android XR's promise.
Xreal Aura review: Price and availability
Xreal launched pre-orders for the Xreal Aura in October (with sneak peeks over the last 12 months), and they started shipping in November in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea. The base model, with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, starts at $1,099, and you can upgrade to 16GB RAM and 512GB for $1,299. Xreal has not yet given us a timeline for UK and Australia availability.
Note that if you wear glasses, you might, as I did, need a prescription insert, which cost around $60.
As mixed-reality wearables go, the Xreal Aura are among the cheaper options, costing less than a third of the price of the Apple Vision Pro, and starting at $600 less than Samsung's Galaxy XR headset. It's a full computer with productivity, entertainment, and immersive capabilities thanks to hand- and body-tracking (although, as mentioned, there's no eye tracking). Plus, it has fully baked-in Gemini AI capabilities. For those who want on-their-face computing without looking like they've entered flight school, this might be a very good option.

| Display resolution | 1920 x 1200 pixels per eye | 3552 x 3840 dual (27 million pixels) | 4K per eye (23 million pixels) | 2064 x 2208 pixels per eye | 1920 x 1080 per eye |

Xreal Aura review: Design
The Xreal Aura wired Android XR-powered glasses are lightweight. The 95-gram frames, which I wore for hours at a time, feel somewhat like heavy sunglasses. They're lightweight because they're wired to a roughly half-pound compute puck, which houses the 4,455mAh battery, Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform CPU, 12GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage. The puck is small enough to slip into my pocket, but I did take advantage of the included clip to attach it to my belt.
The glasses look almost identical to Xreal's 1S headset. They ship with optional nose pads, which I did swap out for a better fit, and adjustable stems, which you shift up or down with audible clicks.

View Original
The front is festooned with three lenses: the two wide ones are used for six degrees of freedom hand-tracking, and the center RGB camera (which does include a privacy LED) is what Gemini uses to see your world and what I also used to grab some photos and video.
On the inside are a pair of prisms that direct the Sony Micro-LED imagery to your eyes. There's also a spot to insert prescription lenses that sit right in front of the prisms. Since I wear glasses, I took advantage of this optional feature.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
While these are decent-looking glasses and sunglasses (with the electrochromic lens dimming feature turned on), I'd hesitate to call them stylish. If you were wearing them at home or on a plane, I don't think many people would give you a second look; but equally, don't expect anyone to compliment you on your sense of style.
My Xreal Aura specs arrived with cables for charging the puck and for connecting the puck to the back of the left arm, a cleaning cloth, and a wonderfully compact carrying case that fits perfectly inside my backpack.
Xreal Aura review: Setup and performance
With wearable smart glasses, display quality and performance are inextricably linked. Xreal pairs its X1S spatial chip with the Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite Platform. This silicon drives the Android XR platform with 1,920 x 1200 (per eye) visuals delivered through Sony Micro-OLED screens, and directed to each eye via a pair of prisms. In my experience it's a very good visual system that delivers a relatively immersive 70-degree field of view (considerably better than what I recently experienced with the Snap Spec's waveguide 51-degree FoV).
Before I dig into the quality of the imagery and experiences, let's talk setup.
I have, as I mentioned, tried a lot of these mixed-reality wearables, and I've always been struck by the similarities between the setup process. However, with the Xreal Aura, the process — probably dictated to a large degree by the current state of Android AR — is, if not vastly different, quite distinct.
Hardware-wise, setup is simple., I adjusted the arms to match the view angle I needed for my eyes, put in a different set of nose guards, and then inserted my prescription lenses into a pair of holes just in front of the prisms.
The other crucial piece of hardware is the compute puck. In addition to housing all the processing power, it has a couple of interesting features. First, one flat side is a full-blown trackpad, which does come in handy. There's also a power / sleep / fingerprint reader, which is also useful.
Also on the puck are a volume rocker, vents to help keep the processors cool, and a place to snap in the belt clip. There are also a pair of USB-C ports: one connects to the glasses via a port on the back of the left arm, and the other is there for charging, and to facilitate a wired connection to your computer of choice.
I started by charging the compute puck to 100%, and then ran the included cable from the puck to the rear of the left arm of the glasses; I like that this cable has a right-angle plug so that it doesn't end up jutting out of the back of the stem and, therefore, sticking out behind your ear.
As with other smart headsets, the Xreal Aura guide you through the setup process. Since the system relies on hand-tracking and gesture for control, it quickly guides you through touch calibration. Usually, this involves pinching dots or grasping virtual objects in space. For the Xreal Aura, the system has you put your finger inside a virtual slot that appears at a few virtual distances. It's unlike anything I've seen so far with these types of glasses, but it's fast and effective.
Control and experiences
Broadly speaking, hand-tracking-based mixed-reality systems will never be as good as those that include gaze-tracking. The Apple Vision Pro and Samsung Galaxy XR both combine gaze-tracking with gesture control, but they are also more expensive and bulkier headsets. The Xreal Aura rely on fairly precise hand-tracking, but it wasn't always great for, say, managing windows, or even just for entering my PIN for unlocking the system. For the latter, I came to rely on the integrated puck fingerprint reader (what a godsend).
It's not that the gesture-tracking was bad, but if I wasn't precise in touching what I intended to touch, I could miss my mark. This is one of the reasons why the puck-integrated trackpad sometimes comes in handy. When I was really having trouble, say, selecting a window, I could always turn to the trackpad clipped to my waist.
That said, there were other times when I was very impressed by how well the system tracked my hands and fingers.
Let me give you a quick example: I started playing the app Cubism. This is a fun puzzle game in which you pick up and move 3D puzzle pieces to fit them together in a predefined space. The hand-tracking was so good that, as I picked up and moved, rotated, pulled out, and replaced pieces, I almost forgot it was a virtual experience. It felt quite real and very immersive.
The experiences are as varied as the offerings in the Google Play library, but some apps are better tuned for the XR platform than others.
One of my first experiences was with Galápagos: The Last Eden, which is narrated by the actress Margot Robbie. After one unexpected crash and app reboot, I was soon face to grizzled face with giant island tortoises. I like how the app starts relatively wide-screen and then expands to 360-degree 3D. The footage is sharp and stunning; I also noticed that the Bose-based audio system delivered crystal-clear audio.
I also tried the NBA app, which gave me some cool court-side views of recent games, but I struggled to find a 'tabletop' view that my reviewer's guide promised. What was most interesting, though, is what Gemini told me about the app.
First, though, a digression. Android XR is built around Google's powerful AI platform, and Gemini is always there, if you allow it, to guide you through the device and your worlds. It can see what's on your screen, or right in front of you, and engage in lengthy, contextual conversations. The glasses include a four-microphone array, but you can also summon Gemini by long-pressing the button on top of the right arm.
Back to the NBA app. I was frustrated that my app menu didn't seem to match Xreal's instructions, so I asked Gemini about it, and it told me that the only way I would see the tabletop view was through the Vision Pro version of the app. Whoops! My assumption is that my version of the NBA app is lagging behind, though there was no update available during my testing.
As a naturally 3D system, the Xreal Aura offered me more than a few depth-friendly experiences. Like the Vision Pro, it can take flat images and make them 3D or 'spatial.' I have thousands of photos in Google Photos, and I enjoyed switching them to immersion mode. It's a fun experience, if a little superfluous.
Xreal also supplied me with one of its Xreal Game Controllers ($99), which I used to play Asphalt: Legends. This is one excellent little portable gaming rig, and the 120Hz max refresh rate ensured that all the gaming action was smooth as butter.
The glasses always felt perfectly cool and comfortable, no matter how long I wore them for, or how I used them. The compute puck, on the other hand, gets pretty warm, and you're warned not to block the cooling vents — it's best to wear it on your belt, and not try to use the glasses while the puck is in your pocket.
Let's get productive
The Xreal Aura offer a couple of ways to help you be productive — with the right cable. Xreal sent me a $12.95 USB-C 3 cable to connect my MacBook Pro to the compute puck, after which my laptop launched screen mirroring, and I launched the app on the Xreal Aura. On the Mac, I have the option of Entire Screen, Window or App, or Extend Display.
Through the glasses, I could see what essentially looked like a floating and resizable 50-inch display. I can't really see my physical keyboard through the glasses, but if I were a better touch typist this would be an incredible virtual workstation. I especially appreciate that I didn't have to install any special software on my MacBook Pro.
I'm a bit less convinced about the utility of the Xreal Aura as a standalone work computer. Xreal also sent me an Xreal Keyboard ($79), which unfolds and connects via Bluetooth to the glasses. The idea is that you can set the keyboard on a tabletop and place the puck next to it to use as your trackpad, and then use it like a computer with a giant virtual display.
The virtual display is big, and I opened Google Docs, but the setup felt awkward because the cable for the trackpad goes up to my left ear and therefore runs past where my hands would be on the keyboard, and the cable also obstructed my use of the puck as a trackpad. It doesn't feel like a very natural setup, though I might also get used to it.
Google Maps on the Xreal Aura stands as one of my favorite experiences. I used both hands to glide around and adjust maps, and while it would take a moment or two for each map to fully render, it was always worth the wait. It was just so much fun to use; I even enjoyed it when I let the system drop me somewhere random, and I ended up in Yosemite Valley.
While I didn't have the chance to take the Xreal Aura on a plane, I can already see how they would make an excellent travel companion. Forget watching movies on that tiny seat-back screen; with the Xreal Aura you can have a go-anywhere theater experience,
I started by turning on the electrochromic display: a press of a red button on the bottom of the right arm dims the lenses. Then I opened YouTube and played How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days. The virtual room appeared dark, and all I saw was the large, bright screen. This is how I want to travel.
The AI of it
Wearing the Xreal Aura on your face is like giving Gemini a big, warm hug. If enabled, Gemini can see what you see and watch your screen, ready to hop in and help if you're having trouble. As I was learning how to navigate the Xreal Aura, and kept finding app windows in odd places around my virtual space, it was Gemini that told me I could lock screens to the 'wall', or have them auto-organized.
I showed Gemini my real-world shelf of oddities, and then asked if it could tell me how much my uncut set of Star Trek: The Movie cards might be worth. It was a dim space, and Gemini asked me to get closer. Then it identified them, and we talked about their resale value based on condition.
Throughout my review process I asked Gemini to take screenshots, and every single time it reported back to me that it had done so. When I opened my screenshot collection in Google Photos, however, I noticed that it was missing some of the recent ones. Gemini did not know why they were not there yet, but surmised a system delay. On another later attempt, Gemini admitted that, due to a system issue, the screenshots it reported capturing had not actually been captured. I love how convincingly AI can tell you something that simply isn't true.
I also used Gemini to start video recording, but even though Gemini told me it would, at my request, stop filming, it repeatedly ignored my requests to stop.
Overall, though, I like having Gemini at my beck and call to help me figure things out and understand my world.
Xreal Aura review: Battery
The Xreal Aura's 4,455mAh battery is rated for four to five hours of mixed use, and in my tests I found that I got at least that much.
Yes, the puck gets warm, and that could compromise battery life, but it also includes a fan to help manage the heat, and keep the headset from burning through the battery life too quickly.
How I tested the Xreal Aura wired Android XR glasses
I spent a week with the Xreal Aura, using them to browse the web, use a variety of apps such as Google Maps, watch sports and movies, and play games. I also tested their productivity features, including using the glasses to extend my laptops display.

And of course you can also follow TechRadar on TikTok for news, reviews, unboxings in video form, and get regular updates from us on WhatsApp too.

articles.title: Smart Locks für dein Zuhause: Mit diesen vernetzten Schlössern öffnest du deine Haustür per App
articles.text:
Nie mehr Schlüssel verlieren: Mit diesen Smart Locks öffnest du deine Haustür bequem per App
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Ein Smart Lock ist ein elektronisch gesteuertes Türschloss, das sich ohne klassischen Schlüssel öffnen oder schließen lässt – zum Beispiel per Smartphone, PIN oder Fingerabdruck. Du musst also keinen Schlüssel mehr mitnehmen. Ein Smart Lock ist auch eine praktische Lösung, wenn du Ferienwohnungen vermietest oder regelmäßig Gäste, Lieferant:innen oder Reinigungskräfte ein- und ausgehen lässt. Wir stellen dir drei Modelle aus verschiedenen Preiskategorien vor.
So funktionieren die smarten Türschlösser
Das Grundprinzip ist immer gleich, technische Unterschiede gibt es aber bei der Authentifizierung und bei der Entriegelung. Zunächst müssen Nutzer:innen am Smart Lock ihre Identität nachweisen. Das digitale Türschloss vergleicht daraufhin die übermittelten Zugangsdaten mit den gespeicherten Berechtigungen. Stimmen die Daten überein, gewährt es Zutritt.
Unter den Pioneers Picks stellen wir dir regelmäßig weitere praktische Tools und Gadgets vor.
Ein Elektromotor im Smart Lock betätigt den Schließmechanismus. Je nach Bauart dreht er entweder den gesteckten Schlüssel oder bewegt den Schließzylinder. Dafür benötigt es keinen Stromanschluss, sondern wird meist mit Batterien oder wiederaufladbaren Akkus im Gehäuse betrieben. Die Wahl des Funkstandards richtet sich nach dem Einsatzzweck, der Entfernung zum Schloss und der Einbindung in ein Smart-Home-System. Oft kombinieren Hersteller mehrere Standards in einem Gerät. Diese kommunizieren meist über Bluetooth, WLAN, NFC, Matter, Thread oder Zigbee.
Das Einsteigermodell: Nuki Smart Lock Go
Nuki gehört zu den führenden Anbietern von smarten Türschlössern. Das Smart Lock Go ist ein günstiges Einsteigermodell und lässt sich laut Hersteller innerhalb weniger Minuten installieren. Standardmäßig öffnet das Schloss lokal per Bluetooth: Es erkennt automatisch, wenn du dich in der Nähe befindest, und entriegelt die Tür. Zusätzlich bietet Nuki einen Remote-Access-Service für einmalig 49 Euro an, der über die App von überall aus Zugriff ermöglicht. Du kannst den digitalen Schlüssel mit anderen teilen und festlegen, wie lange die Freigabe gilt. Über den Smart-Home-Standard Matter lässt sich das Schloss außerdem mit Sprachassistenten wie Amazon Alexa oder Google Home verbinden.
Der integrierte Sensor zeigt den Türstatus als „offen”, „geschlossen” oder „verriegelt” an. Er sendet auch Warnungen – beispielsweise wenn die Tür länger als üblich offen bleibt. Das Schloss wird mit vier AA-Batterien betrieben. Alternativ bietet Nuki ein wiederaufladbares Powerpack gegen Aufpreis an. Käufer:innen schätzen die einfache Installation, kritisieren allerdings teilweise die Haltbarkeit, die Konnektivität und den geräuschintensiven Betrieb. Der reguläre Preis liegt bei Amazon bei 149,99 Euro. Im Rahmen einer Black-Friday-Aktion ist das Modell aktuell um 27 Prozent auf 109 Euro reduziert. Laut etablierten Preisvergleichsportalen war das smarte Schloss bisher nicht günstiger zu haben.
Loxeris One: Smartes Türschloss von Abus
Auch Abus bietet smarte Türschlösser an. Das Modell Loxeris One ermöglicht die komfortable Öffnung und Sperrung per App. Du kannst den Zugriff auf das Smart Lock mit anderen teilen und dauerhafte Berechtigungen zum Beispiel an Familie oder Freund:innen vergeben, während Gäste, Dienstleister:innen oder Handwerker:innen einen zeitlich begrenzten Zugang erhalten. Insgesamt kannst du bis zu 28 Personen registrieren. Per App lässt sich auch nachvollziehen, wer das Schloss wann nutzt. Mit der separat erhältlichen Bridge One steuerst du den Antrieb aus der Ferne und bindest ihn in dein Smarthome ein.
Kund:innen sind mit dem batteriebetriebenen Türschloss zufrieden und loben die gute Qualität, die zuverlässige Funktion und die einfache Installation. Für die Nutzung wird ein Schlüssel gekappt und verbleibt im Zylinder. Dieser verfügt zusätzlich über eine Notfunktion, die das Öffnen und Schließen per Schlüssel auch dann ermöglicht, wenn von innen ein Schlüssel steckt. Der reguläre Preis liegt bei 199,95 Euro. Bei Amazon ist das Modell aktuell um 39 Prozent auf 122,95 Euro reduziert. Zusätzlich erhältlich sind ein Fingerscanner, eine Zahlencodetastatur oder eine Fernbedienung.
Maximale Flexibilität mit der Smart Lock Ultra
Die Smart Lock Ultra von Switchbot bietet diverse Optionen, um das smarte Türschloss zu öffnen. Die Auto-Entsperrfunktion nutzt GPS und Bluetooth, um zu erkennen, ob du dich in der Nähe befindest. Auch die Bedienung per App ist möglich. Dort siehst du außerdem den aktuellen Status der Tür. Zum Lieferumfang gehört ein Touch-Keypad mit Zahlenfeld und Fingerabdrucksensor. Insgesamt sollen bis zu 18 unterschiedliche Entsperrungsoptionen möglich sein. Der Hauptakku hält laut Hersteller bis zu neun Monate. Zusätzlich ist das Modell mit einem Notfallakku ausgestattet. Während der Hauptakku lädt, übernimmt der Notfallakku, sodass sich die Smart Lock Ultra weiterhin normal entriegeln lässt.
Herstellerangaben zufolge arbeitet das Modell mit nur 20 Dezibel, was etwa dem Ticken einer Uhr entspricht. Es stehen drei Entriegelungsmodi zur Verfügung, wobei der schnellste die Tür in nur 1,75 Sekunden öffnen soll. Das Vollmetallgehäuse wird mit drei Blenden in verschiedenen Holzmaserungen geliefert, die zu verschiedenen Wohnstilen passen sollen. Kund:innen loben die schnelle Entsperrung und die unkomplizierte Einrichtung. Bei Amazon gilt das Modell als „Bestseller Nr. 1“ im Segment der Türriegelschlösser. Im Rahmen der aktuellen Black-Friday-Aktion ist die Smart Lock Ultra von Switchbot von 249,99 Euro auf 165,99 Euro reduziert. Die Ersparnis beträgt 34 Prozent.

articles.title: Tech orgs push back on Canadian bill that weakens encryption
articles.text:
Lobbyists and executives from Meta, Apple, and Google’s parent company, Alphabet, are mounting a final effort to rewrite Bill C-22 before it officially passes.
The bill, known as the “lawful access” bill, is designed to allow Canada’s investigative agencies and police services to compel tech companies to retain and turn over some previously encrypted data. Although controversial, the Canadian government insists the measures align the country with its Five Eyes and Group of Seven allies.
However, tech companies have pushed back on the lawful access bill for months, arguing that the bill as written would still allow the government to issue secret orders that weaken encryption.
On Monday, leaders from Meta, Signal, and Tailscale argued against the bill at a Senate committee hearing designed to shape its final form. This committee is the bill’s last hurdle before it could potentially pass into law, and it rarely rejects bills—but it often secures amendments.
Now, tech companies argue that the bill goes far beyond what other countries have adopted, and warn that having a backdoor into previously encrypted data could compromise Canadians’ privacy. Yahoo Finance (Bloomberg) added that Meta has argued the law would effectively make its platforms “an arm of the government’s surveillance apparatus.”
Meta even threatened to pull services like WhatsApp from Canada if Bill C-22 passes, according to a CBC News report. Now, Meta is not the only company that is threatening this. Signal stated back in May that if it is asked to comply with Bill C-22, it could pull its services from Canada.
Apple hasn’t gone that far yet, but it previously said it “will never” add a backdoor to its products. Apple also provided the following statement to MobileSyrup:
“At Apple, we believe privacy is a fundamental human right. It’s one of our core values, which is why we minimize the data we collect and design our products from the ground up to protect users’ most sensitive data. While we appreciate attempts to improve C-22, the bill could still undermine Apple’s ability to offer the powerful privacy and security features our users expect from us, including encryption, even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses. You can’t build a backdoor just for the good guys, yet C-22 could force companies to build backdoors into products — something Apple will never do. We are proud of our longstanding cooperation with Canadian law enforcement to protect public safety. Unfortunately, C-22, as drafted, puts the privacy and security of Canadian users at risk.”
The government has been trying to get this bill into law as quickly as possible, with Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree telling the National Post that “my expectation is to get it done before we rise. I want this as law before we rise.”
The federal government has been rushing this bill, including pushing it through the House of Commons right before it rose for summer break in June.
Source: Yahoo Finance (Bloomberg)

articles.title: Por fin: WhatsApp tendrá almacenamiento propio para tus chats y será gratis
articles.text:
WhatsApp está por implementar uno de los cambios más importantes en la gestión de copias de seguridad de su aplicación para Android. La plataforma comenzó a probar un sistema de almacenamiento en la nube propio, el cual permitirá guardar tus chats en los servidores de WhatsApp. Una vez que se despliegue, los usuarios podrán olvidarse de Google Drive como opción para respaldar sus conversaciones.
La beta más reciente de WhatsApp para Android incluye una función conocida como WhatsApp Cloud Storage. De acuerdo con WABetaInfo, esta nueva opción ofrece hasta 2 GB de almacenamiento gratuito para guardar copias de seguridad de chats en la nube. La cantidad sería más que suficiente para el usuario promedio, aunque algunos tendrían que hacer ajustes para dejar fuera algunas fotos o vídeos en su respaldo.
Actualmente, WhatsApp depende de Google Drive para realizar las copias de seguridad en Android. Además de servir como espacio de almacenamiento, la función también nos facilita la vida cuando cambiamos de dispositivo. Solo necesitamos configurar nuestra cuenta de Google en el móvil y WhatsApp se conectará al Drive para restaurar nuestras conversaciones en el nuevo móvil.
El nuevo almacenamiento en la nube de WhatsApp ofrece las mismas funciones que el de Google Drive. La compañía confirmó que las copias almacenadas en sus servidores estarán protegidas por cifrado de extremo a extremo. Esta medida será obligatoria para utilizar el servicio, por lo que los usuarios tendrán que activar el cifrado de copias de seguridad y configurar una passkey o clave como método predeterminado de protección.
WhatsApp regala 2 GB de almacenamiento en la nube gratis
A juzgar por las imágenes, los usuarios podrán elegir entre su proveedor favorito para gestionar las copias de seguridad de sus conversaciones. WhatsApp ofrece la opción de usar el almacenamiento propio o cambiar a Google Drive en cualquier momento.
Si tus respaldos pesan menos de 2 GB, la opción más indicada sería configurar el almacenamiento propio, ya que esto ayudaría a liberar espacio en tu cuenta de Google para usarlo en otros servicios. No obstante, si tienes muchos vídeos o imágenes, lo mejor sería configurar por defecto la opción de Drive para no dejar fuera nada cada que se activa la copia de seguridad.
WhatsApp solo ofrecerá 2 GB a los que tienen una cuenta gratuita, aunque si pagas por WhatsApp Plus, podrás aumentar la cuota hasta 100 GB. La plataforma también ofrece la opción de obtener hasta 4 TB de almacenamiento, aunque deberás suscribirte a un plan de Meta One. En caso de que dejes de pagar la suscripción a Plus o One y tu copia de seguridad exceda los 2 GB, WhatsApp te dará hasta cuatro meses para que la renueves antes de borrar el archivo de su sistema.
Por el momento, el almacenamiento gratuito en la nube solo está disponible en la versión 2.26.46.4 de la beta de WhatsApp para Android. La compañía no ha confirmado si hará lo mismo en iPhone, que actualmente depende de iCloud para subir y guardar nuestras copias de seguridad. Conociendo a la compañía, es probable que esta característica llegue a todos en algún futuro no muy lejano.

articles.title: Black Friday : l’OLED ultralarge de 45 pouces de LG est à moitié prix chez Amazon, 799,99 € au lieu de 1 599,99 €
articles.text:
À dix jours du Black Friday, qui tombe le 27 novembre, Amazon a déjà fait passer un écran gaming OLED ultralarge sous la barre des 800 €. Le LG UltraGear 45GX90SA-B, un 45 pouces incurvé en 3 440 x 1 440 pixels, est affiché à 799,99 € au lieu de 1 599,99 € de prix conseillé : nous ne l’avons pas testé, mais nous détaillons ce qu’il apporte et ce qu’il impose à votre bureau.
Le LG UltraGear 45GX90SA-B est un écran gaming OLED incurvé de 45 pouces au format 21:9, en 3 440 x 1 440 pixels, rafraîchi à 240 Hz avec un temps de réponse annoncé de 0,03 ms. Amazon l’affiche à 799,99 €, soit 50 % sous son prix conseillé de 1 599,99 €, et présente l’offre comme limitée dans le temps.
La remise vise d’abord les joueurs sur PC qui veulent un écran immersif, à condition d’avoir une carte graphique capable de suivre. Elle intéresse aussi celles et ceux qui travaillent avec plusieurs fenêtres ouvertes en parallèle.
Le LG UltraGear 45GX90SA-B est à 799,99 € chez Amazon, contre 1 599,99 € de prix conseillé.
Pourquoi choisir le LG UltraGear 45GX90SA-B ?
- La dalle OLED : Chaque pixel s’éteint individuellement, ce qui donne des noirs profonds dans une pièce sombre. LG annonce la certification DisplayHDR True Black 400 et une couverture de 98,5 % du DCI-P3.
- Le 240 Hz en 3 440 x 1 440 : Cette définition demande moins à la carte graphique qu’une 4K, ce qui aide à approcher les 240 images par seconde que l’écran peut afficher dans les jeux rapides. G-Sync Compatible et FreeSync Premium sont annoncés.
- Le format 21:9 incurvé : Avec sa courbure de 800R, l’image enveloppe le champ de vision en jeu de course, de simulation ou d’aventure. Au bureau, elle laisse la place à deux fenêtres côte à côte.
Du jeu immersif au bureau : ce que change un écran de 45 pouces
En jeu, la courbure de 800R et le format 21:9 jouent la carte de l’immersion : course, simulation, aventure. Les 240 Hz et les 0,03 ms annoncés par LG profitent surtout aux titres rapides, à condition que votre PC tienne la cadence en 3 440 x 1 440 pixels. L’écran embarque aussi webOS, le système de LG : le constructeur évoque des chaînes gratuites et du cloud gaming, utiles pour lancer un contenu sans allumer le PC. Nous n’avons pas testé ce modèle, ces éléments viennent de la fiche du constructeur.
Au bureau, les 992,7 mm de large annoncés par LG offrent la place de plusieurs fenêtres en parallèle, pour le montage, les tableurs ou la programmation. L’écran mesure environ 66 cm de hauteur et 34 cm de profondeur, selon LG. Il convient moins aux petits bureaux, à celles et ceux qui préfèrent une diagonale de 24 à 27 pouces pour le jeu compétitif, ou qui visent la 4K, car la définition reste celle d’un QHD étiré sur 45 pouces.
Face aux écrans gaming OLED plus compacts
Ce 45 pouces ne répond pas au même besoin que les OLED de 27 pouces ou les ultralarges de 34 pouces, nettement plus compacts. Pour comparer les formats et les tarifs, notre comparatif des meilleurs écrans PC gamer reste le point de départ. En face, le 45GX90SA-B apporte une surface d’affichage et une immersion que ces formats n’offrent pas, mais aussi un encombrement que seul un grand bureau absorbe.
✅ Les points forts
- Dalle OLED incurvée (800R) de 45 pouces en 3 440 x 1 440 pixels
- 240 Hz et 0,03 ms (GtG) annoncés par LG
- Compatible NVIDIA G-Sync et AMD FreeSync Premium
- DisplayHDR True Black 400 et 98,5 % du DCI-P3 annoncés
- webOS intégré, avec chaînes gratuites et cloud gaming selon LG
❌ Les limites
- Remise de 50 % calculée sur le prix conseillé de 1 599,99 € affiché par Amazon
- Près d’un mètre de large : un grand bureau est nécessaire
- Définition QHD étirée sur 45 pouces, moins fine qu’une 4K
- Dalle OLED : mieux vaut éviter les éléments fixes affichés longtemps

articles.title: Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra: Gen Z, deep tech and $1 trillion
articles.text:
Fadnavis’ vision for a new Maharashtra: Gen Z, deep tech and $1 trillion
At The Governance Challenge 2026, Maharashtra CM Devendra Fadnavis judged ideas from 13,000+ B-school students and shared his roadmap for a trillion-dollar, drought-free, deep-tech Maharashtra by 2035.
Few sitting Chief Ministers would spend four to five hours judging student presentations. Devendra Fadnavis did exactly that at the summit of The Governance Challenge (TGC) 2026 in Mumbai, where six finalist teams pitched their answers to one question: what can the Government of Maharashtra do to make the state an innovation hub by 2035?
The challenge drew more than 4,400 three-member teams, over 13,000 students from 30 of India’s leading business and policy schools. After several elimination rounds, six teams presented ideas on healthcare, education, farming and access to credit. The Chief Minister, the 18 finalists and Gaurav Goel, founder & CEO of Samagra, which runs the challenge, then joined Shradha Sharma, Founder & CEO at The Bharat Project, YourStory Media for an open conversation.
A government willing to admit it doesn’t have every answer
Fadnavis opened with an unusually candid view of how governments tend to think.
“Normally, in government, we always feel that we know everything, and that we are the ones who will create solutions for every problem. But in my experience of the last 10 years, I feel you need a very fresh perspective to look at every problem.”
The finalists, he said, brought exactly that. They understood technology and how to deploy it, and despite being outsiders to the system, they had clearly thought hard about the problems. Their ideas may not be complete solutions, he added, but they give the government a strong base to build on with its own experience and data.
Why B-schools need a dose of governance
Goel explained that TGC was created to fill a gap in management education. Business school case studies, campus events, internships and placements all lean heavily towards the corporate and startup world, leaving students with little exposure to governance or social impact. TGC tries to change that through immersion, in the hope that the experience stays with students and later draws them towards nation-building.
After the national round, finalists spent two days meeting officials across departments and visiting model schools and primary health centres, while mentors from government and industry helped refine their pitches. The students said the visits upended their assumptions. One admitted that problems look simple from the outside, and that proposing a fix from an air-conditioned room is very different from delivering it on the ground. He was struck by how much infrastructure already exists, including 3D printers in government schools. Others said the competition felt different from the usual hackathons because it pointed towards execution, not just a certificate, and that some teams worked until 3 am refining their ideas.
An 11-year experiment with young talent
For Fadnavis, young people in government is not a new idea. Since 2015, the Chief Minister’s Fellowship, run with IIT Bombay, has placed bright young graduates inside government for a year through a competitive selection process. Some leave jobs at multinationals to join.
One fellowship team built a platform to run and evaluate the state’s farm-pond-on-demand scheme for drought relief and water conservation. The scheme created around 1.5 lakh farm ponds, and the platform won a Prime Minister’s Award. Senior bureaucrats who were sceptical in the early years now compete for fellows, with district collectors asking for two or three at a time.
In 2019, the state also launched a Village Social Transformation initiative with CSR partners across 1,000 villages, asking young people to live in a village for a full year and use CSR funds to fill gaps that rigid government budgets could not. Of 5,000 applicants, roughly 900 to 950 took up the challenge, and not one dropped out.
Goel said Samagra runs on the same belief. Its team of 90 to 100 people has had an average age of 25 to 30 for over a decade. He looks for energy, an impact orientation and raw smarts, and says young recruits are easier to groom because they arrive without baggage.
Experience plus fresh ideas
Fadnavis called Gen Z the first generation born entirely into technology and constantly connected to global best practices. Properly channelled, he said, that exposure produces bright ideas. But he stressed balance: new ideas need mentoring and oversight, and real innovation comes from pairing fresh thinking with experience.
Maharashtra in 2035
Asked what transformation he wants the state to be known for, Fadnavis began with the government machinery itself. Its people, he said, are its most neglected resource, and good work too often depends on an individual minister or officer rather than the institution. Building the state as an institution, with Samagra’s help, is now a priority.
He then set out the economic goal. Maharashtra is a $660 billion economy that he believes can overtake the UAE and Singapore within two years and become India’s first trillion-dollar state economy by 2030. A true welfare state, he argued, must earn before it spends on social programmes. With the state already about 50% urbanised, he wants that urbanisation to drive jobs and sustainable growth.
His vision for 2035 includes a drought-free Maharashtra with water reaching every area, 65% of power from clean sources, and a state that serves as India’s home for startups, frontier technology and deep tech.
Skills over degrees
His advice to students was to stop chasing degrees for their own sake. Future jobs, he said, will depend on the skills people actually acquire. A skilled workforce attracts investment, and investment creates demand for more skilled people. Getting that cycle right would put Maharashtra in a different league.
Innovation for the village
When a student asked what innovation means for a villager with little exposure to technology, Fadnavis gave the line of the day.
“Innovation is a simple solution for a very complex problem. Unless it is a simple solution, it is not an innovation.”
He pointed to the state’s AI advisory tools for farmers and AI models already lifting farm productivity. The problem is that many depend on costly IoT hardware that a farmer with one acre cannot afford. The next round of innovation, he said, must make these tools cheaper and more sustainable.
Purpose first
In closing, Fadnavis told the students that serving the nation does not require a uniform or public office.
Creating jobs, improving livelihoods, lifting people out of poverty and extending healthcare are all forms of service, in any field. Whether they build a startup or chase a unicorn, he urged them to anchor their work in purpose, because purpose matters more than how much they earn.
Shradha called the day a glimpse of what a Viksit Bharat could look like: a Chief Minister who listens, and young people ready to do the work.

articles.title: Surprise! Windows 11 26H2 makes multitasking on 8GB PCs remarkably smooth
articles.text:
The takeaway: With DRAM prices continuing to hit record highs, consumer electronics manufacturers are working on software optimizations to ensure decent performance, even on modest hardware. Microsoft recently claimed that the latest Windows 11 update makes the operating system faster and more responsive on devices with just 8GB of RAM. New reports suggest there may be some truth to that claim.
Earlier this month, Microsoft released Windows 11 26H2 with a series of optimizations that it claimed will improve performance on PCs with just 8GB of memory. According to Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft's EVP of Windows and Devices, the improvements will make Windows up to 20% more responsive and boost multitasking performance by up to 40% on devices with 8GB of RAM.
Early reviews suggest Davuluri's claims may not be just a PR exercise after all. The Verge tested the same 13-inch Surface Laptop with 8GB of RAM before and after installing version 26H2, Build 26300.9974, and found that multitasking performance improved noticeably following the update, with no apparent drawbacks.
According to the report, before the update, running 20 Chrome tabs while streaming a 4K YouTube video and using Slack and Signal simultaneously made the device extremely sluggish. Browser tabs and apps also had to reload whenever the reviewer switched between them. The fan ran at full speed, while Resource Monitor reported between 700 and 29,000 hard faults per second, resulting in a severely degraded experience.
After the update, Windows still slowed down somewhat when performing the same tasks, but the device remained usable. "I could feel things like Task View get a little less responsive, but it was the way you'd expect when taxing a system. Chrome tabs required less frequent refreshes (and) the fan took longer to kick in and ran quieter," the reviewer noted.
Explaining how Microsoft managed to reduce lag on Windows 11 devices with 8GB of memory, Davuluri said the improvements came from better memory compression and more efficient management of which apps remain in memory and which are offloaded to storage. He added that the biggest change involves how the operating system accesses data that has been paged out from RAM to an SSD.
Traditionally, when there isn't enough memory to handle all active data, some of it is moved to the SSD. Since storage drives are considerably slower than RAM, retrieving this data takes much longer than accessing information stored in memory, resulting in slowdowns that can disrupt users' workflows.
According to Davuluri, Microsoft addressed this issue in the latest update by allowing Windows to keep up to an additional 2GB of active data in memory rather than moving it to slower storage. "So an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return," he explained, helping prevent interruptions and slowdowns even on devices with just 8GB of RAM.

articles.title: U.S. Cracks Down on China Renting AI GPUs Through Overseas Data Centers
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
U.S. Cracks Down on China Renting AI GPUs Through Overseas Data Centers
Yesterday, the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released an interim final rule to address remote access to advanced AI chips and servers. This rule significantly addresses a long-standing gap in U.S. export controls, where Chinese companies that are barred from accessing NVIDIA's latest GPUs have been renting overseas computing power instead of purchasing the chips outright. Notably, BIS states that the rule was written by and at the direction of the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council.
Under the new rule, a license is required to ship any advanced accelerators to any data center worldwide that provides more than 12 million "aggregate TPP" of computing power to companies headquartered in Macau or Country Group D:5, which includes China. TPP, or Total Processing Performance, is BIS's metric for chip computing power, calculated as a chip's peak dense throughput multiplied by the bit length of the operation. For example, an H100 rates about 15,800 TPP. "Aggregate TPP" sums up every accelerator in the facility, so the cap equates to roughly 750 H100s or around 330 B200s. The limit also applies to "linked data centers" and indirect access, such as a cloud reseller training models for a Chinese firm. Data centers already serving such customers have 90 days to obtain a license. Only "commercial recommender systems" are exempt, and anything that generates text, images, video, or code does not qualify.The rule also requires a license for advanced AI chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, which the Commerce Department says carry a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. Shipments to U.S.-headquartered companies are exempt if they meet new reporting requirements. Foundries and packaging houses also lose some of the methods to clear advanced-node chips for designers in restricted countries. Finally, the rule formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule, eliminating its country tiers, the Data Center VEU program, and model-weight controls. Reflecting the current trends and the times under the U.S. administration led by Donald Trump, the document uses "Super Intelligence" instead of "AI," citing Executive Order 14434.
Source:
