articles.title: Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Govern and discover records with common metadata in AWS Agent Registry
As organizations build more agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and skills, they need a consistent way to describe, govern, and find them. AWS Agent Registry provides a catalog for registering, approving, and discovering these resources and custom records. Each record carries a name, a description, a protocol descriptor, and an approval status. However, every organization has attributes and facts that it wants to track, and some are unique to that organization, such as its business units, resource owners, risk classifications, and development environments. Organizations want one common definition for each of these attributes, and they want every agent, MCP server, and skill in the registry to carry these facts. Until now, organizations had no way to define these facts in AWS Agent Registry and store them on each record.
Custom metadata schemas are now available in AWS Agent Registry. A custom metadata schema is a set of organization-defined key-value pairs that records in an AWS Agent Registry carry. An administrator defines the schema and applies it to the registry, and all records within the registry must then adhere to the schema. When publishers create or submit records, they supply values for the fields specified in the applicable schema, and AWS Agent Registry validates those values against the schema set by the admin. Approvers can rely on the validated values when reviewing a record, and consumers and agents can use them to discover and filter records. Administrators, publishers, security and governance teams, approvers, consumers, and agents all work from a shared set of facts to govern, discover, and understand the resources in their agentic fleet.
In this post, we follow the AnyCompany organization publishing an MCP server with custom schema definition, enriching that record, and making it available for discovery by humans or agents. We use an MCP server as the example, but the same steps apply to other record types.
How custom metadata works
With custom metadata, an organization can use standardized vocabulary for describing its resources. The registry administrator defines the custom metadata schema: field names, types, allowed values, and whether each field is required or optional. The registry enforces the schema on every record, so a field such as environment has the same name and the same allowed values whichever team publishes the record.
The schema has common attributes that apply to every record type, and you can add dedicated fields that only apply to specific record types. Each field is Text, Enum, URL, or Boolean.
- When a record is created or updated, the registry validates the custom metadata against the schema set up by the admin. 
  - If a record is created without any custom metadata, AWS Agent Registry saves it as NON_COMPLIANT. A team can save work in progress this way, but it can’t submit the record for approval until it has the required fields and values.
  - If a record includes custom metadata with an unknown field, a missing required field, or an invalid value, AWS Agent Registry rejects it with a ValidationException.
- GetRegistryRecord returns the record’s custom metadata values and its compliance status. (COMPLIANT means that the values match the administrator’s schema. It is not an approval. The approvers make that decision.)
- Discovery APIs also allow filtering records based on custom attributes.
What custom metadata makes possible
Because teams can describe the AWS Agent Registry records with the same fields and values, the registry can support and scale governance and compliance.
Ownership and operations
Fields such as environment (prod, staging, or dev), businessUnit, ownerTeam, supportContact, and costCenter record where a resource runs, who is responsible for it, and who pays for it. A configuration management database (CMDB) ID links the record to your existing inventory, and a support-tier field sets expectations for anyone who depends on the resource.
Security and compliance
Data classification, compliance scope such as Payment Card Industry (PCI) or Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), risk tier, scan status, and a scan report URL turn an approval into a check of structured evidence. Your existing scanners, CMDB sync jobs, and classification tools write these values through the API before a record is submitted. You can build your record approval process or automation using these values, as this post shows.
Better discovery
Custom metadata values are indexed for search. A consumer or agent can combine a natural-language query with specific metadata filters, such as environment=prod AND businessUnit=payments AND securityScanStatus=PASSED. Only approved records are returned, so a record that matches the filters but hasn’t been approved stays out of the results. Figure 1 shows how each role, from administrator to consumer, moves a record through schema definition, registration, enrichment, approval, and discovery.
Walkthrough of an MCP record from registration to discovery
AnyCompany operates anycompany-governed-registry, an AWS Agent Registry without auto-approval. Its payments team publishes an MCP record, payments-ledger-mcp, a read-only server for ledger lookups. Existing security and inventory systems enrich this MCP record before an approval function decides whether consumers can discover it.
The five numbered steps in Figure 2 match the walkthrough: define, register, enrich and submit, review, then discover.
Prerequisites
To follow the walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account in a supported AWS Region.
- AWS credentials available to Boto3 and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for AWS Agent Registry.
- Python 3.11 or later and boto3 1.43.113 or later.
- The sample implementation is in the GitHub repo.
The snippets are shortened: cp and dp are the agent-registry-control and agent-registry boto3 clients. The sample repository has the complete code.
Step 1: AWS Agent Registry admin defines the custom metadata schema for the registry
AnyCompany’s admin creates a registry with a custom metadata schema that every record must follow.
- Every record must have its environment, businessUnit, and securityScanStatus fields.
- Records can also carry optional fields that the publisher or automation fills in later: ownerTeam, cmdbId, dataClassification, and securityScanReportUrl.
- MCP servers also record their networkEgress, which is optional.
Figure 3 shows this schema and the values payments-ledger-mcp will carry once enrichment completes in Step 3. The empty autoApprovalRules list means that the registry approves nothing on its own. Every submitted record stays in Pending approval until someone or something approves it. You decide whether that is done by automated checks you build (Step 4 uses an AWS Lambda function), a human approver, or both.
Administrators can also review the schema in the AWS Agent Registry console. Figure 4 shows the common attributes and the MCP-specific field as they appear on the registry’s details page.
Step 2: The publisher registers the server
The payments team’s pipeline registers payments-ledger-mcp with its custom metadata. Its first attempt uses production instead of one of the administrator’s allowed values.
The registry rejects the record. After the pipeline sends prod, the record is created as a compliant draft. This is how the schema keeps every team using the same values.
Step 3: Automation adds additional metadata and submits
Next, AnyCompany’s automation adds what its own systems know: the result from its security scanner, the asset ID from its CMDB, and the approved data classification. It then submits the record for approval.
An update replaces the whole metadata map, so the automation reads the current values, adds its own, and writes them back together. In the sample, the scanner and CMDB calls are stubs that you replace with your own tools. The registry sends a pending-approval event to Amazon EventBridge. In Step 4, a rule that you create passes the event to your approval function.
Step 4: The approval automation decides from the evidence
When the record moves to Pending approval, AWS Agent Registry sends an event to Amazon EventBridge, and an Amazon EventBridge rule is set to invoke a custom AWS Lambda function. Figure 5 shows the console view of payments-ledger-mcp, with the custom metadata values that the approval function reads for its check.
The function reads the record’s custom metadata and compliance status to check that the record is COMPLIANT, the scan PASSED, a cmdbId is present, and the data is public or internal. payments-ledger-mcp passes all four, so the function approves. A record that fails a check is rejected, and the reason names the failed check. In your production systems, you can choose to route records that need a human review, such as those with confidential or restricted data, for manual review instead of being rejected.
Step 5: Consumers find the records from AWS Agent Registry with custom metadata fields as filters
A developer looking for a ledger tool searches the registry and filters on the same fields the administrator defined.
The search returns payments-ledger-mcp because it’s approved and matches all three filters. Agents can run the same search through the registry’s MCP endpoint, https://agentregistry.<region>.api.aws/registry/<registryId>/mcp, which offers search, list, and get as MCP tools. In the GitHub sample, a Strands agent connects to the AWS Registry MCP endpoint and uses a model on Amazon Bedrock. Its system prompt lists the custom metadata fields to filter records on. The agent turns a plain-language request, such as “a production MCP server for payments ledger lookups that passed its security scan”, into a filtered search. It answers with payments-ledger-mcp.
Developers and agents query the same fields the administrator defined, and the approval function checked, so both find only servers that meet your governance rules.
Design the schema for long-term use
Treat the schema as your organization’s shared vocabulary:
- Agree on the vocabulary first. Settle field names and allowed values with the teams that publish and approve records before you create the schema. Schema changes are additive: you can add fields, add allowed values, or make an optional field required, but you can’t rename, remove, or retype a field.
- Expect existing records to lag behind schema changes made after the records were added to the registry. Existing records aren’t rewritten. A record that no longer matches the schema is reported as NON_COMPLIANT and keeps its approval status. The record stays approved, but its next update must meet the new schema. Editing an approved record creates a draft that must be submitted for approval again, and the submit fails until every required field has a value. Until a curator approves the new revision, consumers keep seeing the approved one.
- Put each field at the right level. Use common attributes for questions that apply to every record type, and record-type fields for record-specific facts such as autonomy level for agents.
- Pick the type that fits the field. Use Enums for decision fields that need consistent spelling, Text for external identifiers, and URL for evidence stored behind the source system’s access controls.
- Make a field required only when the publisher can assign a value at registration. For a value that your continuous integration (CI) or automation provides after the record is published, allow an interim value, for example PENDING. In this post, the scan runs after registration, so securityScanStatus has three values: PENDING, PASSED, and FAILED. The publisher writes PENDING, and the enrichment automation replaces it.
- Keep sensitive details out. Leave secrets, internal endpoints, and detailed findings out of broadly readable metadata.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to add custom metadata in AWS Agent Registry to give every record a common set of facts, such as its environment, owning business unit, data classification, and security scan status. Using one MCP server, we showed an administrator defining the schema, a publisher and existing automation filling in the values, an approval function that you build in AWS Lambda deciding approval, and a consumer finding the approved server with metadata filters. Because the administrator owns the schema, every team uses the same fields and values, and that consistency is what makes approvals and searches in AWS Agent Registry dependable.
- Try it yourself: Use the sample at GitHub repo.
- Go deeper: Read the AWS Agent Registry Developer Guide and custom metadata API reference.
- Availability: See supported AWS Regions.

articles.title: Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors.
Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022.
Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.
Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April.
Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results.

articles.title: Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron form unlikely alliance to standardize robot charging as chipmakers push toward unmanned chip fabs — standard specs would allow manufacturer-agnostic charging equipment
articles.text:
Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron form unlikely alliance to standardize robot charging as chipmakers push toward unmanned chip fabs — standard specs would allow manufacturer-agnostic charging equipment
Semiconductor manufacturers are increasing automation to boost the productivity of existing fabs
Samsung Electronics, SK hynix, and Micron are reportedly working together to develop common charging standards for mobile robots used in semiconductor fabrication plants, according to a new report. Representatives from the three companies have reportedly formed an early-stage consultative body to lead standardization efforts, alongside major industry stakeholders such as the Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International (SEMI) industry association.
According to a report by Seoul Economic Daily, the initiative aims to establish common technical specifications that would allow robots from different manufacturers to share charging equipment, reducing the cost and complexity of deploying large robotic fleets across semiconductor manufacturing facilities. The broader goal is to accelerate factory automation, particularly in older fabs, while laying the groundwork for fully autonomous semiconductor manufacturing.
So why are three of the world's biggest memory manufacturers, who are also competitors, coming together to establish standards for the robotics industry? What exactly does the collaboration involve? And what are the implications of something as seemingly minor as robot charging for the broader semiconductor and robotics industries?
Why robot charging is becoming a problem for semiconductor fabs
Soaring demand for semiconductor memory chips used in AI infrastructure has driven manufacturers to automate as many production processes as possible to optimize manufacturing speed and capacity in existing facilities to increase output, while they build additional fabs. Modern semiconductor fabs already have extensive automation systems. However, even these facilities still require human workers for certain operations, such as moving materials between floors and unpacking products, that existing automation systems cannot perform. The issue is even more pronounced in older fabs, which generally have fewer automated material-handling systems and still rely on workers to move wafer containers using manual carts.
One potential solution is to hand these remaining manual operations over to mobile robots, allowing manufacturers to automate tasks without undertaking extensive renovations or installing complex fixed transport systems. These could include autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) that transport materials around the factory, mobile manipulators that combine robotic arms with moving platforms, and humanoid robots capable of performing more complicated handling tasks.
The problem, however, is that these robots come in different builds and configurations, often with their own batteries and accompanying charging infrastructure. A semiconductor fab deploying multiple robot models from different manufacturers could consequently end up requiring separate charging stations for each model. In addition to increasing equipment and maintenance costs, these installations consume valuable factory floor space.
The proposed initiative seeks to address this problem by establishing common charging specifications that different robot manufacturers can adopt. Standardized charging infrastructure would allow multiple types of robots to use compatible charging stations, reducing the need for separate installations and making it easier for semiconductor manufacturers to expand their robotic fleets without adding operational inefficiencies.
What the proposed standard covers and how it would work
The alliance is considering standards covering battery specifications for different mobile robots, charging-station equipment and communication protocols, charging connectors, and battery management systems (BMS). Together, these specifications would establish common requirements for the physical and electronic interfaces involved in charging robots inside semiconductor fabs.
The initial objective is to achieve charging compatibility across different robot models. In addition to letting a fab deploy robots from several manufacturers without having to install a separate charging system for every model, this would also give manufacturers greater flexibility when purchasing new robots, since their choice of supplier would no longer be as heavily influenced by the charging infrastructure already installed in the facility.
A subsequent step would involve integrating robot charging data with the fab's manufacturing execution system (MES), the software that coordinates and monitors manufacturing operations. With access to information such as battery charge levels, robot availability, and production schedules, the system could coordinate when individual robots operate and when they return for charging. For example, robots could be scheduled to recharge during periods of lower demand or while other robots handle critical material transfers, minimizing interruptions to production. This integration would become increasingly important as manufacturers deploy larger fleets of robots across the hundreds of individual processes involved in semiconductor fabrication.
Interestingly, the three chipmakers leading the standardization efforts are primarily customers of industrial robotics manufacturers, not manufacturers of the robots themselves, except for Samsung, which has an established robotics business. The objective is to develop specifications that robotics manufacturers and charging-equipment suppliers can incorporate into their products.
On the other hand, the three companies are not independently creating specifications and dictating them to suppliers. The initiative would likely follow an industry standardization process in which robotics manufacturers, equipment suppliers, and other stakeholders contribute to developing and validating the technical requirements. For now, the project remains in its early stages, with participants still determining which components and interfaces should be standardized and consulting robotics and smart-factory specialists.
Why the chipmaking rivals are joining forces now, and the broader implications
According to DigiTimes, semiconductor industry participants first explored establishing common robotics standards roughly a decade ago, but discussions made little progress until recently. The renewed momentum is largely attributed to the ongoing semiconductor boom, which has coincided with rapid advancements in industrial robotics.
Unprecedented demand for AI-related memory products, along with record financial performance, has given semiconductor manufacturers both the incentive and the financial resources to invest more aggressively in factory automation. While manufacturers are expanding production capacity to meet demand, new fabs take years to construct and bring online. As a result, they are simultaneously looking to squeeze out as much capacity as possible from existing facilities by increasing automation and improving productivity.
As for why Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron are collaborating despite their intense rivalry, the answer likely comes down to shared commercial interests. Incompatible robot charging infrastructure is an industry-wide problem, and all three companies stand to benefit from a common solution. The AI boom has already encouraged numerous partnerships across the semiconductor supply chain, including between companies that are considered fierce rivals, as manufacturers look for ways to overcome common production and infrastructure constraints.
The involvement of these particular companies also gives the initiative considerable weight. Together, Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron control almost the entire global DRAM market. They also operate extensive semiconductor manufacturing networks and represent a substantial potential market for fab-specific robotic equipment. A common set of specifications backed by all three would therefore provide robotics manufacturers with a strong commercial incentive to develop compatible products, potentially shortening development cycles and accelerating adoption.
Although the current collaboration focuses on a relatively small aspect of factory automation, it is a significant step for broader standardization across the semiconductor manufacturing and industrial robotics industries. Common charging infrastructure would make it easier to deploy and manage mixed robotic fleets, while future integration with production management systems could bring fabs closer to operating with minimal human intervention. This longer-term ambition of completely autonomous facilities is already taking shape. Both SK hynix and Samsung have outlined plans to develop an autonomous semiconductor fab by 2030.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Semperis updates Lightning identity security platform to defend against AI agent attacks - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Semperis updates Lightning identity security platform to defend against AI agent attacks
Enterprise identity protection and cyber resilience company Semperis Ltd. today released the latest version of its Semperis Lightning identity security platform, which is designed to help organizations defend against identity attacks by artificial intelligence agents and conventional attackers alike.
Delivered through a single console, the new version of Lightning is said to combine exposure management, attack-path analysis and detection-and-response workflows. Along with Microsoft Corp.’s Active Directory and Entra ID, the new release supports Okta Inc.
Semperis says organizations using Lightning can adopt AI tools for productivity while reducing the risk of agents compromising critical resources. According to Chief Executive Mickey Bresman, identity systems have become “the main control plane” in the agentic age.
Though AI agents move at machine speed through the enterprise, Bresman said, they still depend on the identity fabric for access. With Lightning, organizations are said to be able to create, enforce and monitor what he called “agentic execution boundaries.”
Chief Product Officer Alex Weinert, who joined Semperis in April 2025 after serving as vice president of identity security at Microsoft, said security teams “do not need another flat list of identity findings.” Context on what can actually reach the identity control plane is what they need instead, he said. Agentic identities, he added, are opening new routes to privileged systems.
On the exposure side, Lightning, which now comes with a growing catalog of more than 220 security indicators, continuously scans identity infrastructure for exposures in human and nonhuman identities. The results are then scored, according to Semperis, before being triaged in a single workflow.
The platform’s live identity graph, which Semperis describes as a map of relationships and attack paths, covers routes to domain administrators, privileged accounts and other critical assets. According to the company, remediation guidance from the graph is prioritized by risk so that teams can respond faster.
Nonhuman and agentic identities are discovered automatically, Semperis says, and added to a searchable inventory of every identity in an environment. The company claims Lightning can scale to the largest multitenant, multiforest environments.
Built-in rule templates are designed to detect suspicious activity in Active Directory and Entra ID, such as unusual logons over Kerberos and NT LAN Manager. The company is also offering what it calls generative assistance alongside the templates.
Semperis introduced Lightning in April 2024 with Lightning Identity Runtime Protection, a machine learning-powered identity threat detection service. The company extended its resilience offerings to Okta and Ping Identity Corp. environments in February, when it acquired MightyID Inc.
More than 1,200 organizations, including over 25% of the 100 largest U.S. companies, are said to use Semperis. The company last raised $125 million in growth financing from JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Hercules Capital Inc. in June 2024. Earlier investors include Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. LP, Insight Partners, Ten Eleven Ventures and Paladin Capital Group.

articles.title: Panne Apple : iCloud, l’App Store et Apple Music ne fonctionnent plus, voici ce que l’on sait
articles.text:
Mise à jour 19h10 : Apple reconnaît désormais plusieurs pannes. La liste des services impactés s’est allongée. Apple indique deux problèmes sur « Compte iCloud et connexion » et classe l’App Store, Apple Music et AppleCare sur l’appareil en « panne », le niveau le plus grave de son échelle. L’entreprise n’a toujours donné ni cause ni délai de rétablissement.
Apple a reconnu le problème sans en donner la cause.
En fin d’après-midi, les signalements ont brusquement grimpé sur les sites de suivi de pannes. À 18 h 42, Apple Support, l’App Store et iCloud occupaient les trois premières places des services les plus signalés sur Downdetector.
La connexion au compte en cause
Selon 9to5Mac, des utilisateurs ont été déconnectés d’iCloud sans prévenir, puis ont rencontré des échecs de vérification ou des erreurs inconnues en voulant se reconnecter. Comme ils reposent sur le même compte Apple, d’autres services ont été touchés. L’App Store ne se chargeait plus, et Apple Pay, Apple Music, l’activation des appareils et App Store Connect, l’outil des développeurs, connaissaient eux aussi des problèmes.
Peu avant 18 h 50, la page État du système d’Apple signalait un « problème » pour le service « Compte iCloud et connexion », mais ne donnait ni cause ni délai de rétablissement.

articles.title: Test Samsung Galaxy A18 : pourquoi ce nouveau smartphone va vous séduire… tout en vous frustrant
articles.text:

| Écran |  | 
| Technologie d'affichage | OLED | 
| Diagonale d'écran | 6.7 " | 
| Définition d'écran | 1080 x 2340 | 
| Résolution | 385 ppp |

| Ecran compatible HDR | Non |

| Autonomie |  |

| Puissance de charge (filaire / sans-fil) | 25 | 
| Durabilité |  | 
| Score étiquette énergie | A | 
| Batterie amovible | Non | 
| Certification d'étanchéité | IP64 | 
| Protection d'écran | Gorilla Glass 3 | 
Avec son grand écran Amoled, sa batterie de 5000 mAh et un suivi logiciel solide, le Samsung Galaxy A18 soigne les fondamentaux. Ce smartphone abordable doit pourtant composer avec l'absence de 5G et des performances plutôt modestes.
Avec le Galaxy A18, Samsung renouvelle l'une des portes d'entrée de son catalogue. Le géant sud-coréen préfère cependant peaufiner une formule éprouvée plutôt que de multiplier les nouveautés. Au programme : une dalle Super Amoled 6,7 pouces, un SoC Exynos 1610, 4 Go de mémoire vive et un accumulateur de 5000 mAh.
Lancé en France à 279 € avec 128 Go de stockage, ce modèle améliore son niveau d’étanchéité, change de processeur et promet six ans de mises à jour. La 5G reste pourtant aux abonnés absents, alors qu'elle s'est invitée chez la concurrence à un prix comparable. Les Galaxy A17 5G, Motorola Moto G67 et Redmi Note 17 5G ont en effet quelques arguments à faire valoir.
Difficile de ne pas reconnaître un smartphone Samsung au premier coup d'œil. Le Galaxy A18 reprend les lignes sobres de la famille avec un dos et un cadre en plastique, des tranches plates et des angles adoucis. Le triple module photo prend place dans un îlot noir vertical, une évolution esthétique discrète.
Avec des dimensions de 164,4 x 77,9 x 7,7 mm pour 196 g, il est fin, mais peu maniable d'une seule main. La tranche droite accueille les commandes de volume et d'alimentation sur la petite protubérance caractéristique des Galaxy A, baptisée Key Island. Le lecteur d'empreintes digitales est habilement intégré au bouton d’allumage, en complément de la reconnaissance faciale.
À l'avant, la caméra selfie se niche dans une encoche en goutte d'eau, vestige d'une époque que les poinçons ont pourtant largement enterrée. Les bordures de l'écran demeurent visibles, particulièrement au niveau du menton. Samsung ne cherche donc pas à faire passer son entrée de gamme pour un Galaxy S, ce qui est probablement plus sage.
La façade est occupée à un peu plus de 86 % par un écran protégé par du verre Gorilla Glass 3, un revêtement moins valorisant que le Victus du Galaxy A17. Le constructeur reprend néanmoins un peu de terrain avec une certification IP64, contre IP54 auparavant. Il résiste désormais à la poussière et aux éclaboussures, mais pas à l'immersion… Pour qui a vu le (génial) film Gremlins, ceci est un avertissement à prendre au sérieux.
La connectivité comprend le wifi 5, le Bluetooth 5.3, le NFC pour les paiements sans contact et un port USB-C. Le tiroir situé sur la tranche gauche oblige à choisir entre deux cartes nano-SIM ou une nano-SIM et une carte microSD (jusqu'à 2 To). Ni eSIM ni prise casque à l’horizon, pas plus que de compatibilité 5G. Le haut-parleur est par ailleurs mono, mais il s’avère assez puissant à l'usage.
Pour aller plus loin :
Le Samsung Galaxy A18 dispose d’une dalle Super Amoled de 6,7 pouces au ratio 19,5:9. Elle affiche 2340 x 1080 pixels, soit 385 ppp, et se contente d’un taux de rafraîchissement jusqu’à 90 Hz, quand certains concurrents culminent à 120 Hz. L'Oled apporte malgré tout des noirs profonds et un contraste théoriquement infini, idéal pour profiter de ses films et séries préférés.
Nos sondes ont relevé une luminosité maximale de 763 cd/m², de quoi consulter ses notifications à l'extérieur, même si le plein soleil lui impose quelques concessions. La réflectance d’environ 41 % laisse en effet apparaître des reflets parfois gênants. À l'opposé, le minimum de 1,63 cd/m² permet de lire dans l'obscurité sans transformer le terminal en lampe de chevet.
Côté calibration, le mode par défaut délivre un delta E de 3,91, signe de quelques écarts perceptibles avec les teintes de référence. La température des couleurs approche toutefois les 6500 K attendus (6403 K) avec des blancs légèrement chaleureux.
Le mode Naturel améliore le delta E qui descend à 3,21, mais abaisse la température à 5991 K : l'image prend alors une coloration jaunâtre. On gagne en fidélité chromatique sans forcément obtenir un rendu plus neutre. Dommage que Samsung n'ait pas trouvé un meilleur compromis dès la sortie de boîte.
Le Galaxy A18 est animé par une puce Exynos 1610 associée à un GPU Mali-G68 et 4 Go de RAM. Samsung reste fidèle à une configuration modeste, sans doute plus adaptée à la messagerie qu'aux démonstrations de force. Navigation web, appels, réseaux sociaux, GPS et plateformes de streaming s'exécutent correctement, à condition d'accepter quelques lenteurs. Les changements d'apps manquent en effet parfois de vivacité.
La fonction RAM Plus emprunte une partie du stockage pour épauler les 4 Go disponibles, mais elle ne remplace évidemment pas de véritables puces de mémoire vive. Un point faible qui risque de peser avec les années.
Le bilan se révèle plus encourageant en jeu. Sur notre protocole viSer, l’appareil atteint en moyenne 59 images par seconde (i/s) avec des pointes à 81 i/s. Il peut donc faire tourner des titres légers ou moyennement exigeants, sans prétendre briller pour autant. Les productions les plus gourmandes demanderont fatalement de réduire les réglages graphiques. Bonne nouvelle, nos essais n'ont révélé aucune chauffe excessive.
L'essentiel est donc assuré pour des usages ordinaires, même si l'on aurait apprécié une réserve de puissance un peu plus confortable, surtout pour un smartphone censé traverser plusieurs générations d'Android.
Le Samsung Galaxy A18 reprend le trio photo de son prédécesseur, le Galaxy A17 5G, avec un capteur principal de 50 mégapixels (Mpx) flanqué d'une optique grand-angle ouvrant à f/1,8, un ultra grand-angle de 5 Mpx (f/2,2) et un module macro de 2 Mpx guère utile. Samsung ne propose donc aucune évolution notable, conservant un équipement déjà hérité du Galaxy A16.
Dans de bonnes conditions lumineuses, le capteur principal offre des clichés convaincants avec une exposition correcte, des couleurs naturelles et un bon niveau de contraste. Le piqué se révèle satisfaisant au centre, mais perd en précision sur les petits détails et en périphérie. Quelques artefacts et un bruit numérique à peine gommé par le lissage logiciel ternissent toutefois le bilan.
De nuit, l'appareil montre ses limites. Malgré une exposition maîtrisée et un bruit numérique relativement contenu, les couleurs deviennent fades et délavées, tandis que les zones sombres perdent en lisibilité. Le piqué est acceptable au centre, mais le lissage excessif gomme les détails fins et donne aux illustrations un effet aquarelle, particulièrement marqué sur les bords.
L’ultra grand-angle du Galaxy A18 livre des clichés diurnes décevants. Malgré des contrastes corrects et des inscriptions à peu près lisibles au centre, le capteur de 5 Mpx souffre d’un piqué limité, de textures lissées et d’un bruit numérique visible. Les couleurs sont ternes, l’exposition se montre excessive et une forte distorsion, non corrigée, dégrade davantage les bords de l’image.
Dans la pénombre, rien ne va plus. Malgré une exposition acceptable, la dynamique limitée bouche les zones sombres et les couleurs s'appauvrissent drastiquement. Le piqué s’effondre, le lissage excessif efface les détails et le bruit envahit l’image. Les sources lumineuses aggravent ces défauts, tandis que la forte distorsion en périphérie rend les photos difficilement exploitables.
Le Samsung Galaxy A18 reprend la caméra selfie de 13 Mpx (f/2) des générations précédentes. Les autoportraits s’en sortent convenablement, sans briller, la faute à un lissage prononcé et une exposition parfois approximative. Le mode portrait assure un détourage globalement efficace, quoique trop marqué autour des cheveux. En vidéo, le smartphone se contente d'une captation Full HD à 30 i/s, à l’avant comme à l’arrière, ce qui suffira pour un usage occasionnel ou pour les réseaux sociaux.
Avec sa batterie de 5000 mAh, le Samsung Galaxy A18 n'impressionne pas sur le papier. Pourtant, l'association de cette capacité classique à une configuration peu gourmande produit un excellent résultat. Nous avons en effet mesuré 23 h 26 min d'autonomie en utilisation mixte sur notre protocole viSer.
À titre de comparaison, le Redmi Note 17 5G, pourtant équipé d'un accumulateur d'une capacité de 7700 mAh, avait tenu 20 h 24 min avec le même dispositif. Une journée intensive ne lui fait donc pas peur, et deux jours restent envisageables en usage modéré.
Le passage à la prise réclame en revanche davantage de patience. La charge filaire est plafonnée à 25 W et nos mesures indiquent 1 h 42 min pour atteindre les 100 %. C'est long face à des rivaux nettement plus rapides. Samsung annonce certes 50 % en une demi-heure, mais la seconde partie de l'opération demande de prendre son mal en patience.
La charge sans-fil est absente, sans réelle surprise dans cette gamme. Le bilan reste néanmoins largement favorable : le Galaxy A18 n'est pas pressé de se recharger, mais il met un point d'honneur à espacer les rendez-vous avec sa tétine à électrons.
Notre score de durabilité permet de déterminer l'aspect durable du smartphone, autant pour le consommateur que pour l'environnement. Il s'appuie sur des éléments puisés dans l’étiquette énergie mise en place par l’Union européenne (classe énergétique, scores de résistance aux chutes et de réparabilité, nombre de cycles de batterie avant de tomber sous une capacité de 80 % et résistance de l’écran aux rayures). Nous y ajoutons des critères de durabilité (indice de protection IP, connecteurs standards, durée de garantie et des mises à jour…). Vous trouverez tous les détails de l'analyse dans notre article présentant notre score de durabilité.
Le Samsung Galaxy A18 mise sur un affichage plaisant, une conception plus résistante à la poussière et, surtout, une excellente autonomie au regard de son positionnement tarifaire. Son interface complète et son support logiciel longue durée renforcent son attrait pour les utilisateurs en quête d’un smartphone simple, familier et durable. Il souffre toutefois de plusieurs limites : l’absence de 5G et d’eSIM, seulement 4 Go de RAM et une recharge assez lente. Un modèle endurant et rassurant, donc, mais qui accuse déjà un certain retard technique et s’adresse avant tout aux aficionados peu exigeants, mais attachés à l’écosystème Samsung.
Le Samsung Galaxy A18 se distingue avant tout par son excellente autonomie, supérieure à celle des Redmi Note 17 5G, Moto G67 et Galaxy A17 5G. Son affichage et ses six ans de suivi logiciel jouent en sa faveur, mais difficile d'ignorer l'absence de 5G, les performances timides et la charge lente. Le smartphone de Motorola s'avère en outre mieux équipé, tandis que le Galaxy A17 profite du savoir-faire de Samsung avec une connectivité plus moderne. Un choix difficile à défendre au prix fort.

articles.title: Apple serre la vis aux IA qui fouillent dans les fichiers de votre Mac
articles.text:
Apple tire la sonnette d’alarme sur les agents IA sur votre Mac. Dans un billet à l’intention des développeurs, le géant de Cupertino a levé le voile sur les nouvelles protections incluses dans macOS 27.3, la prochaine mise à jour du système d’exploitation des Mac. Les nouveautés sont déjà disponibles dans la deuxième version bêta de macOS 27.3, actuellement réservée aux testeurs.
Ces protections concernent les applications qui réclament un accès « complet au disque ». Avec cet accès, les applications sont en mesure de lire tout ce qui se trouve sur votre ordinateur, sans la moindre restriction, ce qui ouvre la porte aux abus.
« Avant d’accorder à une application un accès aussi extraordinaire, les utilisateurs doivent comprendre que cela met en danger toutes les données de leur Mac », prévient Apple.
À lire aussi : « Je ressens des vertiges » – le nouveau MacBook Pro pose problème à certains utilisateurs
Apple s’inquiète après deux incidents
Parmi les applications qui réclament un accès au disque dur de votre Mac, on trouve les agents IA, comme Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, OpenClaw, ou Muse. Ils peuvent alors ouvrir vos fichiers, piloter vos applications ou trier vos e-mails à votre demande. Cet accès inquiète évidemment Apple. Un mois avant l’annonce des nouvelles protections, le groupe regrettait que « certains développeurs utilisent l’accès complet au disque d’une manière qui pourrait mettre les utilisateurs en danger, en exposant tout ce qui se trouve sur leur système, y compris les fichiers, les e-mails, les messages et même l’historique de navigation, sans que les utilisateurs en aient pleinement conscience ».
Deux incidents récents ont poussé Apple à réagir. En septembre, un journaliste du magazine Inc. a découvert que Muse, l’IA de Meta, a lu ses messages privés. Il avait pourtant refusé l’accès de ses messages à l’intelligence artificielle. En parallèle, une enquête de Wired a révélé une faille dans l’application Mac de ChatGPT. Cette vulnérabilité aurait pu permettre à des pirates de dérober des données sensibles sur le disque dur. Ces deux incidents surviennent dans un climat d’inquiétude généralisé autour de l’IA. De nombreuses dérives ont été enregistrées ces derniers mois, impliquant notamment ChatGPT, Claude, ou encore Gemini.
« À mesure que les agents IA deviennent de plus en plus performants et autonomes, les risques associés à ce niveau d’accès vont considérablement augmenter », expliquait Apple le mois dernier.
Ce qui change sur votre Mac
Pour protéger les utilisateurs, le géant californien a pris des mesures. Sans surprise, Apple ne bloque pas les agents IA. L’entreprise veut surtout que vous sachiez à quoi vous vous engagez lorsque vous ouvrez les portes de votre disque dur à Claude, ChatGPT, et consorts.
Tout d’abord, l’option « Contrôle de l’appareil et accès aux données » est désormais divisée en deux paramètres distincts. On trouve le contournement des protections du système et des applications, d’un côté, et l’accessibilité, de l’autre. Vous comprendrez mieux ce que vous autorisez. Par ailleurs, Apple va vous encourager à n’ouvrir que les dossiers ou les applications vraiment nécessaires, au lieu de donner accès à tout votre Mac.
De plus, vous pourrez dorénavant demander à une application de réclamer votre feu vert à chaque fois qu’elle veut accéder à vos données. Enfin, Apple met en place de nouvelles règles de transparence. macOS affichera clairement l’étendue des données auxquelles l’application aura accès. Un indicateur apparaîtra aussi dans la barre des menus lorsqu’une application, comme Claude ou ChatGPT, en contrôle une autre. Actuellement, les processus contrôlés par des IA ont tendance à passer inaperçus sur macOS. Rien n’indique clairement et de façon explicite ce qui se passe.
La fenêtre d’autorisation mise au point par Apple se veut plutôt dissuasive. L’avertissement d’Apple prévient que « votre Mac ne pourra pas protéger vos données » face à l’application à laquelle vous ouvrez les portes de votre disque dur. La fenêtre prend aussi le temps de détailler tout ce que l’agent pourra faire, comme lire, modifier, supprimer et exporter toutes vos données, voir vos photos masquées ou supprimées, ou consulter votre historique de navigation. Toutes ces informations doivent vous permettre de prendre une décision éclairée.
À lire aussi : Pénurie de Mac et d’iPad pour Noel ? Apple risque de manquer d’appareils à mettre sous le sapin
Pas de panique pour vos applications actuelles
Les autorisations que vous avez déjà accordées sur votre Mac restent valables. Les nouveaux écrans n’apparaîtront qu’au moment d’approuver une nouvelle demande, ou une nouvelle application IA. Les logiciels de sauvegarde et les outils d’accessibilité, qui ont réellement besoin d’un accès étendu, pourront demander une exception à Apple, précise le billet.
Pour Apple, la question de l’IA sur macOS est très importante. Les Mac mini et les Mac Studio s’arrachent actuellement auprès des passionnés d’IA, qui s’en servent pour faire tourner leurs modèles en local, directement sur la machine. Face aux nouveaux usages, Apple doit impérativement trouver le bon équilibre entre ouverture à l’IA et la protection de la vie privée, l’un de ses principaux chevaux de bataille.

articles.title: Karnataka aims to become global hub for frontier technologies: DK Shivakumar
articles.text:
Karnataka aims to become global hub for frontier technologies: DK Shivakumar
Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar said the strong technology ecosystem in the State gives it the advantage to lead in areas such as AI, biotech, semiconductor and robotics.
Karnataka aims to become a global hub for frontier technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), deeptech, semiconductor, robotics, and biotech, said Chief Minister DK Shivakumar at the inaugural of Bengaluru Tech Summit (BTS) in Bengaluru on Tuesday, citing the state government's enabling policies.
BTS, now in its 29th edition, is themed “AI and Beyond”. Addressing the event, the Chief Minister highlighted that Karnataka has consistently been at the forefront of technology and is well positioned to lead the next phase of global innovation backed by strong IT and startup ecosystem.
The Chief Minister said Karnataka accounted for two out of every five dollars earned by India through software and services exports, which amounted to approximately $173 billion last year.
The state also attracted $9.4 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI) equity inflows in the first half of FY26, accounting for 26.7% of India's total inflows during the period. Bengaluru is home to more than 1,000 Global Capability Centres (GCCs), while over 30 new GCCs brought investments of more than $1 billion into Karnataka in 2025.
Shivakumar said Karnataka was home to more than 24,000 recognised startups, with nearly two out of every five Indian unicorns (startups valued at $1 billion or more) originating from the state.
Bengaluru ranked eighth among the world's startup ecosystems and second in Asia for AI-native startups. Startups in Karnataka have collectively raised approximately $79 billion, while women founders in Bengaluru have secured $13.4 billion in funding.
The state government is also extending financial support to startups working on emerging technologies. Through its ELEVATE initiative, it has supported nearly 1,500 startups with equity-free grants worth $41 million over the past decade.
Under ELEVATE NxT, deeptech startups are eligible for grants of up to Rs 1 crore. Since last year, 33 startups have received equity-free funding totalling Rs 30 crore.
The government has also announced Innoverse, a deeptech accelerator that will support 35 growth-stage ventures over the next five years. The programme aims to help startups move beyond product development and scale up to industrial-level operations.
Another initiative, Government First, aims to make the state government an early customer for startups. A dedicated fund of Rs 25 crore has been earmarked to procure innovative solutions developed by these companies.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is another main focus of Karnataka's technology ambitions. Shivakumar said Bengaluru accounted for nearly 50% of India's AI and machine learning talent.
The state is also building what he described as India's first government-led AI university, alongside an AI Hub that will bring startups, researchers and industry stakeholders together.
An additional Centre of Excellence at IIIT Raichur will focus on expanding AI applications across 13 districts of North Karnataka, particularly in sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, education and small businesses.
Karnataka is also looking to strengthen its position in the semiconductor industry. The state is home to more than 100 fabless chip companies, while Bengaluru accounts for three out of every five engineers working in India's semiconductor capability centres, Shivakumar said.
The state currently accounts for one-fifth of India's electronics exports. Its next priority is to expand beyond chip design and build manufacturing capabilities.

articles.title: Après 50 ans dans l'espace, Voyager 1 s’apprête à franchir une première historique : 1 jour-lumière de la Terre
articles.text:
Ce 18 novembre, Voyager 1 deviendra le premier objet humain à atteindre une journée-lumière de la Terre. Une véritable prouesse pour la sonde lancée en 1977, malgré ses forces déclinantes.
Années 70, cinq ans après le programme Apollo. La NASA envoie dans l’espace deux sondes jumelles, Voyager 1 et Voyager 2, à deux semaines d’intervalle. À leur bord, un disque d’or, gravé de sons et d’images de la Terre, comme un message de l’humanité adressé à d’éventuels visiteurs.
Leur mission officielle est alors limitée : étudier de près les plus grosses planètes du Système solaire, Jupiter et Saturne. Mais l’agence spatiale décide ensuite de prolonger leur voyage. Près de 50 ans plus tard, elles poursuivent inlassablement leur route.
Une distance qui défie l’imagination
Et ce mercredi 18 novembre à 11h16 en France, Voyager 1 se trouvera exactement à une journée-lumière de la Terre, c’est-à-dire la distance que parcourt la lumière en 24 heures. Cela représente environ 26 milliards de kilomètres, une distance qu’aucun objet construit par l’humain n’a atteint. Un message envoyé à la sonde met donc un jour entier à lui parvenir, et sa réponse autant pour revenir.
Car pour rappel, la lumière file à 300 000 kilomètres par seconde : il lui faut 1,3 seconde pour rejoindre la Lune, un peu plus de 8 minutes pour venir du Soleil, et entre 3 et 22 minutes pour relier la Terre à Mars, selon la position des deux planètes. Neptune, la plus lointaine du Système solaire, n’est qu’à 4h10 de lumière, soit près de six fois moins que Voyager 1.
Son trajet est sensationnel : la sonde a survolé Jupiter en 1979, puis Saturne l’année suivante, où elle a observé les anneaux et Titan, la plus grosse lune de la planète. En 1990, depuis les confins du Système solaire, elle prend la célèbre photo « Pale Blue Dot », sur laquelle la Terre n’est plus qu’un minuscule point bleu. Elle pénètre dans l’espace interstellaire en 2012, la région au-delà de l’influence du Soleil. Voyager 2, elle, a emprunté un chemin plus long via Uranus et Neptune. Elle n’atteindra la journée-lumière qu’en novembre 2035.
Un travail monstre pour les maintenir en vie
Mais à bientôt 50 ans, les sondes sont à bout de souffle. Alimentées par une source nucléaire, elles perdent 4 watts de puissance chaque année alors qu’elles en produisaient 470 chacune à leur départ. Le froid extrême du vide spatial n’aide pas, puisqu’elles évoluent à quelques degrés seulement au-dessus du zéro absolu.
Pour faire des économies d’énergie, les ingénieurs du Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) de la NASA n’ont donc pas eu d’autre choix que d’éteindre peu à peu leurs instruments. « Ceux qui consomment le moins d’énergie, mais qui donnent quand même de bonnes données scientifiques, remontent forcément en haut de la liste », explique Jeffrey Hayes, chercheur de l’agence spatiale. De même, l’hydrazine, carburant qui alimente les sondes, risque de geler. Dans ce cas, ce serait « game over », prévient-il. Si les engins poursuivront leur route respective, ils ne pourront plus transmettre aucun signal.
Voyager 1 se dirige désormais vers Gliese 445, une étoile de la Petite Ourse, à la vitesse de 61 000 kilomètres par heure. Elle la frôlera à 1,7 année-lumière dans 40 000 ans.

articles.title: Pusieron a unos agentes de IA a jugar al Minecraft y crearon algo para lo que no estaban diseñadas: la burocracia
articles.text:
La psicología del juego estudia cómo el acto de jugar influye en el desarrollo cognitivo, emocional, social y neurológico del ser humano. Por eso, el juego es uno de los entornos preferidos por los investigadores de IA para estudiar el comportamiento de los agentes de IA y cómo reaccionan al interactuar con otros agentes.
Un experimento, del laboratorio de Y Combinator y Olam Labs orientado a observar las dinámicas de coordinación de grandes enjambres de agentes de IA autónomos impulsados por GPT -6 Sol. Uno de esos experimentos metió a cincuenta agentes de IA en un mundo de Minecraft y Mindustry con una sola orden: "Construir una civilización próspera". No se designó a ningún líder ni se dieron órdenes sobre cómo deberían hacerlo, pero los propios agentes se encargaron de generar roles de liderazgo, racionamiento e incluso burocracia para acceder a los recursos.
Lo primero: designar a un líder. Al principio los agentes se dispersaron a explorar el territorio del juego, cada uno por su lado, pero pronto vieron la necesidad de alguien que coordinara esa tarea de exploración. Así que miraron la lista de nombres de los agentes y escribieron al primero de esa lista: Ada, que recibió 616 mensajes directos del resto de agentes.
Los investigadores no habían insertado ninguna instrucción de liderazgo o jerarquía, pero Ada se convirtió en líder de la colona sin votación ni rivales, solo porque su nombre era el primero. Ada redactó un plan de la colonia, con qué construir y dónde guardar cada cosa. Los demás le pedían aprobación antes de moverse.
La noche oscura alberga horrores. Llegó la primera noche, y con ella el acecho de zombis, esqueletos, arañas y otros enemigos. Esa noche murieron 34 agentes y el grupo cambió de actitud. Comprendieron que estaban en un entorno hostil y se volvieron reacios al riesgo y se encerraron en búnkeres para protegerse. Los autores ven mucho parecido con los agentes de programación de uso diario. Estos se atascan en un paso y se vuelven muy cautos con la seguridad.
Tras la tercera noche, Ada pidió a los agentes que nadie explorara ni hiciera obras grandes por su cuenta. Todos debían esperar en refugios cerrados hasta recibir tareas cortas. Es lo que haría un jefe de equipo prudente tras un mal día. Pero con la prudencia llegó otro problema: la comida comenzó a escasear.
Del reparto de comida al papeleo. Con todos encerrados por precaución y con un poco cantidad de comida, comenzaron a racionarla, y comenzaron a aparecer los oficios y la asignación de tareas: pescadores, cocineros y repartidores. Una agente llamada Inés llevaba la cuenta de quién tenía hambre y qué había en cada cofre de suministros, asumiendo el papel de funcionaria. En tres horas, el grupo cruzó unos 5.900 mensajes organizando el reparto de suministros.
Cada fallo dejaba una norma nueva. Ada lanzó un pollo cocinado a una compañera hambrienta llamada Noor, pero otra agente, Esme, lo recogió y se lo comió. Tras una revisión en el que no se buscaron culpables, el grupo escribió un protocolo de entrega de suministros: las raciones irían en cofres con nombre y no se lanzan. La burocracia y el papeleo nació tras un error en el reparto de recursos, justo como sucede en cualquier oficina u organismo en el que se crean protocolos de actuación.
Qué enseña un juego a los agentes reales. Los juegos se han convertido en un laboratorio barato para ver cómo se organizarán los enjambres de agentes de IA en simulaciones del mundo real. Minecraft ya es un campo de pruebas habitual: agentes de Gemini 4 lo completaron en 27 horas.
De hecho, los juegos han dejado entrever el "carácter" de los distintos modelos gracias a las estrategias que adoptan los distintos grupos de agentes de AI. En otro experimento llevado a cabo por el mismo equipo de investigadores, enfrentaron a dos equipos de diez agentes en Bed Wars, un juego interno de Minecraft en el que los agentes deben destruir las camas de los agentes del equipo rival.
En este escenario, dos equipos de diez agentes Claude Opus 5.5 y diez agentes GPT-6.1 Sol compitieron entre sí. El equipo GPT-6 obtuvo seis victorias frente a tres de Claude. Mientras que los agentes de Claude adoptaron una estrategia más defensiva, comunicándose de forma más formal, los agentes de GPT-6 actuaron de una forma mucho más agresiva utilizando comandos muy abreviados y escribieron scripts de automatización para desmantelar elementos clave.

articles.title: Copia de seguridad de WhatsApp en iPhone sin iCloud: cómo funciona la nube propia de 2 GB
articles.text:
WhatsApp prepara una copia de seguridad en iPhone sin iCloud mediante una nube propia con 2 GB gratuitos, una alternativa que permitiría guardar el historial de chats y archivos multimedia en los servidores de la aplicación. La función se encuentra en despliegue limitado para usuarios de la versión beta en iOS.
El cambio importa porque las copias de WhatsApp compiten por el espacio disponible en iCloud, que Apple limita a 5 GB gratuitos por cuenta. Fotos, documentos, respaldos del iPhone y datos de aplicaciones comparten esa capacidad, por lo que una copia de chats con años de mensajes, imágenes, vídeos y audios puede agotar el almacenamiento.
WhatsApp ofrece una alternativa a iCloud para guardar los chats
La nueva opción aparece en el apartado de copias de seguridad de la aplicación. Desde allí, algunos usuarios pueden escoger el proveedor donde desean almacenar el historial: iCloud o el servicio de almacenamiento en la nube de WhatsApp.
La compañía de Meta prevé asignar 2 GB de espacio gratuito a las cuentas que elijan su servicio. Ese almacenamiento quedaría reservado para las copias de seguridad de la aplicación, sin descontar capacidad del plan de iCloud asociado al iPhone.
Hasta ahora, un usuario que necesitaba más espacio para respaldar conversaciones tenía dos opciones: borrar contenido de iCloud o contratar un plan de pago de Apple. La alternativa de WhatsApp busca separar ambos consumos y dar a los usuarios un mayor margen para administrar los archivos de mensajería.
La medida también modifica la relación entre la aplicación y los servicios de almacenamiento de terceros. En lugar de depender solo de iCloud en iOS, WhatsApp administraría el respaldo desde su propia infraestructura.
El cifrado de extremo a extremo será obligatorio
Las copias almacenadas en la nube de WhatsApp contarán con cifrado de extremo a extremo activado de forma obligatoria. Esto significa que el contenido queda protegido antes de subir a los servidores y que solo el propietario de la cuenta puede acceder a él con el método de seguridad elegido.
Durante la configuración, la aplicación solicitará proteger la copia con una clave de acceso, una contraseña o una clave de cifrado de 64 dígitos. La opción recomendada por defecto sería la clave de acceso, aunque cada persona podrá escoger otro sistema compatible.
La protección tiene una consecuencia práctica: si el usuario pierde la clave o el método de recuperación configurado, podría encontrar dificultades para recuperar el historial. Por eso, antes de trasladar la copia a los servidores de WhatsApp, conviene revisar las opciones de seguridad y mantener actualizado el acceso a la cuenta.
El respaldo cifrado no implica que los mensajes estén disponibles desde cualquier dispositivo o sistema operativo. La copia conserva las limitaciones de compatibilidad de la plataforma.
Más capacidad mediante WhatsApp Plus y Meta One
Los 2 GB gratuitos pueden resultar suficientes para cuentas con conversaciones de texto y pocos archivos. Sin embargo, los historiales que incluyen vídeos, fotografías en alta resolución, notas de voz y documentos suelen ocupar más espacio con el paso del tiempo.
WhatsApp contempla planes de mayor capacidad. La suscripción WhatsApp Plus incluiría 100 GB para copias de seguridad, mientras que Meta One ofrecería planes con hasta 4 TB de almacenamiento, según la modalidad contratada.
Si una suscripción vence, la empresa conservaría la copia más reciente durante cuatro meses. Pasado ese periodo, si el usuario no reactiva el plan, el respaldo se eliminaría de forma permanente.
El respaldo no permite pasar chats de iPhone a Android
De acuerdo con WABetaInfo, la nueva nube no resolverá la migración entre sistemas operativos. Un usuario que guarde sus conversaciones en los servidores de WhatsApp desde un iPhone no podrá restaurarlas directamente en un teléfono Android mediante esa copia.
Para cambiar de plataforma, será necesario utilizar la herramienta de transferencia de chats incluida en la configuración de la aplicación. Esa función permite mover el historial entre dispositivos sin recurrir al respaldo almacenado en la nube.
La disponibilidad sigue siendo gradual. La función fue detectada en la beta 26.45.10.71 para iOS distribuida mediante TestFlight, aunque no todas las cuentas que instalen una versión compatible verán la opción de inmediato. WhatsApp no ha comunicado una fecha para su llegada general a todos los iPhone.

articles.title: U.S. Departments of Commerce and Justice Issue Rare Joint-Statement on the NVIDIA-Megaspeed Investigation
articles.text:
Tuesday, November 17th 2026
U.S. Departments of Commerce and Justice Issue Rare Joint-Statement on the NVIDIA-Megaspeed Investigation
The U.S. Department of Commerce and Department of Justice just issued a rare joint-statement on their ongoing investigation into NVIDIA's dealings with Singapore-based Megaspeed Corporation, a cloud computing firm that had been buying cutting-edge AI GPUs and is alleged to have been involved in the diversion of these GPUs to entities in China, in violation of U.S. export controls for AI compute processors. In their statement, the two Government departments provide a brief timeline of their investigation into Megaspeed, which was initiated by the Department of Commerce as far back as 2024.
In May 2025, investigators from the Commerce department requested records from NVIDIA on their direct and indirect sales of GPUs to Megaspeed. The statement says that NVIDIA put Megaspeed on their "no sell" list in June 2025. In cooperation with Singaporean law enforcement officials, agents from the Commerce department's Bureau of Industry and Security conducted searches at Megaspeed's locations to verify the end-use of AI GPUs purchased from NVIDIA; and interviewed CEO Alice Huang, the woman in the center of the storm that media reports earlier this month alleged to have been an agent of the Chinese state. Following this, the U.S. Department of Justice took the lead role into the criminal investigation of Megaspeed into violations of U.S. export controls.The statement is one of the first Government public-facing mentions of the term "semiconductor smugglers," criminals involved in illegally diverting U.S. high-technology to countries on explicit trade embargoes. In this case, the U.S. has an exhaustive set of export controls for GPUs to China, with a clearly defined process for entities in China to obtain said technology. The statement mentions that as many as 17 defendants across six different investigations have been charged with allegations of smuggling billions of dollars' worth of controlled semiconductors.

articles.title: Nvidia board establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee in wake of Jensen Huang scandal — group to work with independent law, national security, and trade compliance experts
articles.text:
Nvidia board establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee in wake of Jensen Huang scandal — group to work with independent law, national security, and trade compliance experts
It's like closing the corporate barn door after the horse has bolted.
Less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned from the company, Nvidia's board has created its own National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. According to its announcement, the new standing committee will provide high-level oversight of Nvidia’s “national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risk management,” with its National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team reporting directly to the group and to interim CEO Colette Kress.
“Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones said. “As the world’s leading advanced computing company, Nvidia has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges. We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation.”
The rumors of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, have thrown the company into turmoil, especially after his admission and subsequent apology. People have begun digging into details about Ms. Huang, revealing that she was at the center of a tangled web of companies and was reportedly instrumental in importing around $7.5 billion of banned Nvidia chips into China. A deeper investigation also revealed that her husband, Kang Wei, was behind her rise to prominence and seemingly accepted her relationship with the billionaire. It remains unclear if the couple made these shrewd business moves purely for profit or if they were under the control of a hidden third party, but it has certainly exposed the company to additional scrutiny.
The chairpersons of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence have since invited Jensen to a closed-door briefing to discuss Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage,” while President Donald Trump mentioned that the FBI is looking into Jensen Huang’s relationship with Ms. Huang. The U.S. first applied export controls to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, the A100 and H100, in 2022, forcing the company to create the China-market A800 and H800 GPUs that complied with Washington’s performance limitations.
However, the White House lowered the bar once more in 2023, which resulted in the even more watered-down H20, which, nonetheless, remained in high demand. Even though the Trump administration did not implement Biden’s AI diffusion rule, which threatened to outright ban several countries from buying Nvidia AI chips, the president eventually banned the export of H20 chips to China from April to June 2025.
Even before Trump’s total Nvidia AI GPU ban, there have already been multiple reports of smuggling, with one semiconductor analysis firm tracking more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned AI chips exported to China and estimating that up to 1.5 million Nvidia GPUs were smuggled in recent years. Despite that, the former Nvidia chief has always denied the allegations, saying that “There’s no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” Whether the allegations are true or not, it seems that the company is taking the situation seriously and taking steps to plug any leaks. As for Jensen Huang, he may be out of the company, but he still has to face Congress and all ongoing investigations.

articles.title: Exclusive: Cogent Security's DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: Cogent Security’s DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents
Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today launched DefenseOS, an operating system designed for artificial intelligence agents that carry out defensive cybersecurity work inside the enterprise.
Arriving with DefenseOS are two new capabilities, Agent Policies and Agent Automations. The first is designed to give Cogent’s AI agents a deep understanding of the enterprise environment, while the second puts recurring security work on an automated schedule.
Cogent is pitching DefenseOS at security teams that are struggling to keep up as AI speeds up the discovery of vulnerabilities. In October, Microsoft Corp. fixed more than 1,400 security flaws in a single Patch Tuesday release, more than it fixed in all of 2025. The window between disclosure and exploitation has also shrunk, by Cogent’s count, from months in 2024 to only hours this year.
Prioritizing at that pace requires context such as which assets are business-critical, which are exposed to the internet and who owns them. According to the company, that information is spread across documents, teams and tribal knowledge, and most organizations see only a fraction of it.
In its role as the context engine for Cogent, DefenseOS ingests data from scanners, business systems and other security tools. Once the data has been normalized and deduplicated, DefenseOS encodes how the enterprise functions to deliver accurate risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The platform serves as the AI harness that sets the working environment and limits for Cogent’s agents.
The first of the two new capabilities, Agent Policies, is described by Cogent as creating a context layer that builds and grows via agents, turning how an enterprise works into rules. Those rules then shape how the Cogent platform handles asset context, risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The company claims the feature strips out much of the operational overhead that enterprises formerly had to put into running a vulnerability management program.
The second, Agent Automations, acts as the execution layer within DefenseOS. Using it, security teams can build agentic workflows that run automatically to generate alerts and reports, investigate vulnerabilities and deliver remediation guidance on a consistent basis.
Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Geng Sng said recurring reports, known investigations and routine alerts take up a large share of a security team’s week. With Agent Automations, he said, teams can “define that work once” and have Cogent’s agents run it on their schedule.
“Every enterprise runs its security program differently, and moving at machine speed means grasping those differences,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti. “DefenseOS unifies the context of an enterprise environment, surfacing rules into Agent Policies that a customer can codify, and creating the runtime environment for continuous cyber defense led by AI agents.”
The launch follows the release earlier this month of VR-1.1, a new version of Cogent’s frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.
DefenseOS and Agent Automations are available now to all Cogent customers. Agent Policies has launched in beta for new Cogent deployments ahead of general availability at a later date.
Founded in 2025 and staffed by former researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal AI Inc. and Coinbase Global Inc., Cogent says Fortune 500 security teams using its platform have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%. The company has raised $53 million to date, including a $42 million Series A led by Bain Capital Ventures in February.

articles.title: New report finds nearly all UK data centre operators report electrical disruption as 'critical bottleneck' looms
articles.text:
New report finds nearly all UK data centre operators report electrical disruption as 'critical bottleneck' looms
Energy is a major bottleneck for UK data centers
- The UK has a 6GW target for AI capacity by 2030, but its data centers aren't moving quickly enough
- The average connection wait time has grown to 14 months, up from 12 months globally
- One in four say they only discovered an electrical problem after a failure or downtime
Four in five (79%) UK data center operators have blamed electrical or power-system issues for major disruptions, delays or downtime, leaving just 17% confident that they're fully-prepared for future AI workloads, new Fluke research has claimed.
And these challenges are already impacting operations, with around a third (32%) reporting that power problems have already limited their abilities to deploy high-density GPUs and AI workloads.
This is especially alarming given that the UK is targeting 6GW of data center capacity by the end of the decade spanning multiple large-scale AI Growth Zones.
UK data centers are struggling with electricity supplies
With electrical infrastructure now seen as one of the biggest bottlenecks, only 41% say they have real-time visibility across their critical electrical systems. A further quarter (26%) say they only discovered electrical problems after a failure or downtime.
But it's not just the power infrastructure that's problematic – many operators are struggling to hire enough talent, with half (51%) admitting recruiting electrical technicians has become harder. Two in five (38%) say this has directly delayed infrastructure upgrades because they don't have the right people to lead an upgrade team.
As for new projects or expansions, operators are now seeing an average of 14 months to wait for additional grid connections or power capacity – two months longer than the UK average.
"As AI drives unprecedented demand for computing capacity, the electrical infrastructure inside data centres is becoming a critical bottleneck," Fluke Corporation President Parker Burke summarized.

articles.title: Humanity braces for an alien invasion in 3 Body Problem S2 teaser
articles.text:
You might be excused for forgetting about the existence of 3 Body Problem, Netflix’s heady sci-fi series adapted from the award-winning novel The Three-Body Problem by Liu Cixin, the first book in his Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy. After all, it debuted in March 2024. But it was an exceptionally well-done, thematically rich series, and we’re finally getting the second of a planned three seasons in January. Netflix just dropped the first teaser.
(Spoilers for S1 below.)
Created by David Benioff, D.B. Weiss (Game of Thrones), and Alexander Woo (True Blood), the first season followed two primary timelines. In the earlier one, a young Chinese astrophysicist, Ye Wenjie (Rosalind Chao), witnessed her father being beaten to death by Red Guards during the Cultural Revolution. Ye figured out a means of sending an interstellar message to possible extraterrestrial civilizations, receiving a response from a planet called Trisolaris.
The planet had three suns, which wreaked havoc on Trisolaris via unpredictable “chaotic periods”—hence the novel’s title, which refers to a classic problem in celestial mechanics. Despite being warned that the aliens intended to invade and conquer Earth, Ye responded to the message and invited them to do so, bitter and disillusioned by the state of the world. She eventually became an established professor (Zine Tseng played the older version).
In the present day, the consequences of Ye’s fateful decision began to play out, beginning with a series of mysterious suicides by scientists, many of whom had possessed a highly advanced VR gaming headset. Among the dead: a particle physicist named Vera Ye (daughter of Ye Wenjie). Five of her former students (known as the Oxford Five) joined forces to figure out what was going on, eventually finding themselves caught in a global fight to save Earth from the invading Trisolarians (or San-Ti). Another human cult faction was just as intent on enabling the San-Ti invasion, believing they would be spared as a reward, while Ye Wenjie still believed the entire human race deserved to be annihilated.

articles.title: Harvard-Auswertung: 400 Rechenzentren verbrauchen so viel Strom wie ganze Staaten
articles.text:
Harvard-Studie: 400 Rechenzentren verbrauchen so viel Strom wie ganze US-Bundesstaaten
Ein Versuch des US-Bundesstaats Maine, den Bau größerer Rechenzentren für die Dauer von eineinhalb Jahren auszusetzen, scheiterte zwar am Veto von Gouverneurin Janet Mills. Allerdings prüfen mehrere weitere Bundesstaaten entsprechende Schritte.
Wasser auf die Kritiker-Mühlen
In Texas etwa könnte der Erfolg der Demokraten bei den Midterms Baustopps oder Verzögerungen bei KI-Infrastrukturprojekten nach sich ziehen. Eine in Nature Sustainability veröffentlichte Studie von Biostatistiker:innen der Uni Harvard dürfte die Argumentation der Kritiker:innen künftig stützen.
Die Forscher:innen haben in diesem Zusammenhang 403 sogenannte Hyperscale-Rechenzentren in den USA untersucht, die zwischen Mai 2024 und April 2025 in Betrieb waren. In Ermangelung detaillierter offizieller Daten griffen sie dabei auf Satellitenbilder zurück und schätzten den Stromverbrauch sowie den CO2-Ausstoß, wie es bei Wired heißt.
Stromverbrauch wie ganze Staaten
Das Ergebnis: Die rund 400 Rechenzentren verbrauchten in dem untersuchten Zeitraum je nach Auslastung zwischen 68 und 99 Terawattstunden Strom. Das entspricht ungefähr dem jährlichen Stromverbrauch von US-Bundesstaaten wie Indiana, Michigan oder Tennessee und rund zwei Prozent des gesamten US-Stromverbrauchs. Auf europäischer Ebene läge man laut EIA-Daten damit ungefähr zwischen Belgien (79 Terawattstunden Strom) und den Niederlanden (110 Terawattstunden Strom).
Darüber hinaus sollen die untersuchten Rechenzentren zwischen 21 und 31 Millionen Tonnen CO2 ausgestoßen haben – und damit etwa so viel wie Kroatien oder Bosnien-Herzegowina. Dazu kommt, dass mit 54 Prozent mehr als die Hälfte des Stroms aus fossilen Quellen stammt.
Mehr Rechenzentren in Bau und Planung
Die Daten selbst sind allerdings nur eine Momentaufnahme, wie die Forscher:innen selbst einräumen. Schließlich hat der KI-Boom und damit die Nachfrage nach Rechenkapazitäten seit April 2025 noch einmal rasant zugenommen. Mittlerweile sind weitere Anlagen entstanden und bestehende Standorte erweitert worden.
Darüber hinaus dürften aktuell im Bau oder in der Planung befindliche Anlagen noch einmal deutlich mehr Strom verbrauchen. Die rund 400 für die Studie untersuchten Rechenzentren hatten im Schnitt eine Leistung von 40 Megawatt. Geplante Campus-Projekte wie jene von Meta (Hyperion), xAI (Colossus 2) oder AWS (Rainier) sollen zwischen 2.000 und 5.000 Megawatt Leistung haben.
