articles.title: How friends from Coimbatore built GOAT Robotics into an Rs 8 crore business with global reach
articles.text:
How friends from Coimbatore built GOAT Robotics into an Rs 8 crore business with global reach
Starting from a rented 2BHK in Coimbatore, GOAT Robotics grew from Rs 10 lakh in turnover to over Rs 8 crore. Discover how nine engineering graduates pivoted from hotel robots to industrial automation and expanded internationally.
GOAT Robotics, a startup founded by friends who studied B.E. Robotics and Automation Engineering at a private engineering college in Coimbatore, a Tier 2 city, has achieved success by providing robotic services to several countries.
What began with a turnover of just Rs 10 lakh has now grown into a large company that spends Rs 40 lakh every month on salaries alone.
Muthu Vangaliappan, one of the Managing Directors and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of GOAT Robotics, shared the company's success story with us.
The nine founders of GOAT Robotics come from different districts, including Coimbatore, Erode, and Salem. All of them graduated in 2015 with a B.E. in Robotics and Automation Engineering from PSG Engineering College in Coimbatore. After securing jobs through campus placements, they moved to different companies across various states.
“During our college days, the nine of us were a close-knit group. We shared the same dream of studying well and achieving great heights in life. As time passed and we continued working, we began thinking about starting our own business. In 2015, Naveen, Dharmaraj, Mugesh, and I came together to establish a company called Katomaran Technologies Pvt. Ltd.,” said Muthu.
In the initial days, the four friends conducted seminars at colleges and provided robotics-related training to students and aspiring entrepreneurs.
To expand their business, they rented a 2BHK house in Coimbatore in 2018 and formally started operating Katomaran Technologies Pvt. Ltd. This beginning has now grown into a large company generating a turnover of more than Rs 8 crore.
Friends Who Started Their Journey Amid Severe Setbacks
Muthu says they faced several serious challenges and setbacks during the initial stages of their business before recovering.
“While we were providing automation and robotics services to small companies in India, we got an opportunity to work for a few companies in Singapore. We realised that there was always a shortage of around 40% of security personnel there. This led us to start using robotics and automation technology in the security sector.
“We made their work easier and addressed the manpower shortage by introducing various automation technologies, including automated toll gates and cameras, for people traffic, vehicle traffic, utility management, and surveillance. This project gave us good profits and valuable experience.
“We also began introducing robots in hotels. As the years passed, we started thinking about why we couldn't use the same technology in India. With that idea, in 2019, we continuously visited major hotels across India and submitted proposals for using robots,” Muthu shared, recalling the company's early days.
“However, we did not achieve the same level of success that we had experienced in Singapore. This was because the use of robots in India was very limited, and many people were unwilling to adopt them.
“While our business was doing well in Singapore, we faced setbacks when we shifted our focus to India.
Nevertheless, we continued working in hotels, not just with robots but also in areas such as 3D gaming and gaming simulators,” he said.
The Story Behind the Formation of GOAT Robotics
From 2019 to 2022, the team focused extensively on manufacturing specialised robots for hotels. They developed various robots, including room-service robots, hotel room-cleaning robots, bellboy robots, and dispensers, supplying them to five-star and seven-star hotels.
However, during the COVID-19 pandemic, they faced severe difficulties as they stopped receiving orders.
“While our business was progressing this way, five other friends who had studied with us were already running a company called Dotworld Technologies Pvt. Ltd.
“In 2023, their company and ours merged, and we established GOAT Robotics in Coimbatore. GOAT stands for Greatest of All Technologies,” he explained.
“When we started this company, we already had extensive experience in manufacturing, while the new group of friends had significant experience in marketing. Combining the expertise of both teams, we planned to provide automation and robotics-related services to major hotels in India.
“We frequently approached hotels and hospitals, conducted demonstrations, and submitted proposals. That was when we realised an important truth: this business model would work in foreign countries such as Singapore and Malaysia, but it would be difficult in India.
“We realised that we were running fast in the wrong direction. As we reached a point where we risked losing our business, we decided to develop a different category of robotics.”
They first began manufacturing and supplying lifting robots capable of carrying heavy loads. They developed robots for several companies to lift and move heavy objects. Later, they began manufacturing packing robots and providing automation solutions.
“We continued working with small companies through contracts. Within a few months, we received a good response. We then decided to pitch our idea to a major company for the first time.
“We sent our idea to Toyota, and they liked it and signed an agreement with us. Our journey with Toyota began in December 2023,” said Muthu.
From Coimbatore to Serving Countries Across the World
Muthu shared that getting an opportunity to work with a major company like Toyota, despite having started as an ordinary business in Coimbatore, became a major turning point for them.
He continued:
“Although we began our journey with GOAT Robotics in December 2023, we recorded a turnover of just Rs 10 lakh during 2023–2024.
“After that, we recognised our strengths, addressed our weaknesses, and began providing services to companies using various technologies in the robotics and automation sector.”
“During 2024–2025, the GOAT Robotics team began working not only with Toyota but also with several major and multinational companies, including Volvo, Maruti, Suzuki, Pricol, and Timken.
“Our turnover, which was just Rs 10 lakh, increased to Rs 6 crore in 2024–2025.
“Today, we are providing services across several countries, including India, the United States, Australia, Middle Eastern countries, Singapore, and Malaysia,” he said.
“All the members of our team come from middle-class family backgrounds and have faced considerable financial difficulties.
“Therefore, we have started an initiative to make robots accessible not only to large companies but also to small businesses.
“We are manufacturing and supplying robots at affordable prices to entrepreneurs like us,” he added.
From a 2BHK House to a Company Paying Rs 40 Lakh in Monthly Salaries
The company has robots capable of lifting or moving loads weighing 100 kg. It also manufactures robots capable of handling weights ranging from 100 kg to 5,000 kg.
To make robots accessible to ordinary entrepreneurs and micro, small, and medium enterprises, the company manufactures and sells robots priced between Rs 12–13 lakh and Rs 45 lakh, as well as robots valued between Rs 45 lakh and Rs 2 crore.
“Our journey, which began in a simple 2BHK house, has grown to the point where we established our own dedicated 6,000 sq. ft. office in 2024.
“Our company, which started with just nine people in Coimbatore, now employs 77 people.
“We provide opportunities to engineering graduates who are eager to learn and develop their knowledge after completing their education.
“We offer a minimum salary of Rs 30,000. Every month, we spend a total of Rs 40 lakh on salaries alone for the staff and interns working at GOAT Robotics,” Muthu proudly shared, describing the company's growth.
“There are nine of us. This success has been possible because each of us works in teams of two.
“We have divided ourselves into teams based on our experience in manufacturing, communication, service, marketing, and research and development. This division of responsibilities has made it easier for us to achieve success.”
“Every year, the Central Government encourages micro, small, and medium entrepreneurs by presenting awards.
“In 2025, we won the Central Government's Make in India Excellence Award 2025 and received a cash prize of Rs 10 lakh from the government.
“So far in the current financial year alone, we have achieved a turnover of Rs 8 crore.
“Our target is to reach a turnover of Rs 25 crore during this financial year,” he said.
In March 2025, the company raised Rs 2.66 crore (approximately $311K–$320K) in a funding round led by Campus Angels Network, with participation from TiE Coimbatore, NativeLead Angels, Pontaq Ventures, and others.
“Deep Affection Is What Will Make Us Successful”
Muthu also offered some advice to people planning to start a new business and those considering starting a business with partners.
“Those who run businesses with friends or other partners can achieve great success only if they always have deep affection and care for one another.
“When failures occur, they must be willing to make compromises, support one another, face problems positively, and overcome difficult times together. By doing so, they can achieve success more easily.
“Similarly, when starting something worthwhile, we should not wait for the right time. We must understand the risks involved and start the business immediately.
“If we simply watch from the sidelines or hesitate, time will leave us behind, and we may not even be able to begin what we had planned.
“If we lose time, we will neither be able to take risks nor grow,” Muthu Vangaliyappan said, sharing the lessons he had learned from his entrepreneurial journey.

articles.title: Cloud keys leaked in Docker Hub images are stolen within seconds
articles.text:
Credentials and access secrets exposed in public Docker Hub images are being extracted and exploited by attackers within as little as eight seconds of publication.
Two researchers at Stony Brook University, Billy Tsouvalas and Nick Nikiforakis, measured the extraction speed by publishing a total of 300 honeypot images across eight public container registries.
Over a period of four months, the researchers exposed AWS, OpenAI, and Anthropic API keys, along with decoy SSH and database credentials.
They then monitored the use of these keys and placed detection tools to notify them when the images were built, ran, or had a shell opened.
The two researchers presented the experiment and the resulting findings yesterday at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS).
They noted that their images were pulled more than 75,000 times, and the planted AWS keys received over 140,000 API calls from 5,000 unique IP addresses.
The AWS traffic showed a broad pattern, from checking whether the keys worked to listing available resources, and sometimes proceeding to consume them.
The fastest observed use of a planted AWS key came 7.86 seconds after the image was published on Docker Hub. The median time for the first API call was 51.19 seconds, while all 100 AWS keys were used within 15 minutes.
The exposed OpenAI and Anthropic keys were quickly hijacked to exhaust the test-account balances.
Docker Hub accounted for nearly all AWS activity, while Harbor, one of the other registries in the experiment, also saw some AWS key abuse.
The researchers dubbed the automated scanners that interacted with their test images “ContainerBots,” though this is more of a loose umbrella term, as the scans showed no evidence of being coordinated by the same operators.
Monitoring rarely detected anyone actually running the honeypot images, which led the authors to conclude that scanners generally extracted credentials by inspecting image layers directly.
“The scanners interacting with our images overwhelmingly do so through static analysis, e.g., unpacking image layers or querying the registry API to extract filesystem contents, without ever instantiating the container,” explain the researchers.
Exposing secrets this way is common in the real world [1, 2, 3], and revoking the leaked keys requires significant work and coordination.
The researchers recommend that Docker Hub scans images for secrets before pushing them live, and warn publishers if they appear to embed any secrets.
They also suggest restricting or rate-limiting access to Docker Hub’s public feed of recently published or updated images, to thwart mass-scanning tools.
Tsouvalas told BleepingComputer that they reported their findings to Docker in May, along with the full paper, but besides an acknowledgment, they received no follow-up replies.
A small-scale experiment they ran in August to determine whether any defenses had been implemented on the platform showed no changes.

articles.title: Gonzalo (29 años), instalador de placas solares y empresario: "Una instalación básica de 6 paneles cuesta unos 4.000 €"
articles.text:
Aunque instalar placas solares en tu casa parece una inversión difícil de asumir, sobre todo si nunca has pedido un presupuesto y no sabes cuánto tendrás que gastar, lo cierto es que el precio de una instalación básica es más asequible de lo que imaginas. Gonzalo, instalador de 29 años y socio de Efitar Ingeniería, explica que colocar 6 paneles solares en una vivienda cuesta entre 4.000 y 4.500 euros, y lo mejor es que esa cantidad incluye el inversor, el medidor de energía, los trámites de legalización y las licencias.
Como recoge El Español en su información sobre el coste de las placas solares, Gonzalo habló de estas cifras en una intervención en el podcast Sector Oficios en el que habló de cómo ha cambiado el autoconsumo en España. A su juicio, las viviendas unifamiliares y los chalets son las opciones más interesantes porque la electricidad se consume durante las horas de sol, y también señaló que las bonificaciones municipales del IBI y las deducciones del IRPF pueden ayudar a reducir la inversión siempre que se cumplan los requisitos.
Las placas solares producen más electricidad y las baterías también han cambiado
Gonzalo destaca que el rendimiento de los paneles ha cambiado mucho en los últimos años, ya que antes una placa de unos 2 metros cuadrados producía 200 W y ahora existen modelos que alcanzan 600 W con medidas similares. De esta forma, se pueden aprovechar mejor los tejados y abordar proyectos con más posibilidades, y pone como ejemplo cubiertas industriales con hasta 8.500 paneles y parques solares de 300 MW. Además, también recuerda que el coste alcanzó los 400 euros por MWh durante la crisis energética y esto llevó a algunos clientes a amortizar sus instalaciones con baterías en menos de 2 años (aunque, eso sí, matiza que son casos aislados).
A todo esto debemos sumar el interés por los sistemas de respaldo tras el apagón peninsular de abril de 2025. Gonzalo asegura que los equipos más sencillos parten de 150 euros más la mano de obra, mientras que otros sistemas integrados pueden costar entre 800 y 1.100 euros. También destaca la llegada de dispositivos con IA capaces de analizar los hábitos de consumo y gestionar cuándo comprar o vender electricidad a la red utilizando una batería. Eso no significa que cualquier casa con placas pueda seguir teniendo luz durante un apagón, ya que la instalación necesita estar preparada para funcionar sin suministro exterior.
Por último, el empresario también habló de las condiciones laborales de quienes trabajan instalando estos equipos. Y es que el crecimiento de la energía fotovoltaica no solo se nota en los tejados, también en la necesidad de contar con profesionales cualificados. Según explica Gonzalo, un oficial del sector cobra entre 23.000 y 24.000 euros al año, una referencia salarial que ofrece desde su experiencia en un oficio que exige conocimientos técnicos y trabajar habitualmente en altura.

articles.title: À quoi servent ces nouvelles boîtes bleues installées au bord des routes ?
articles.text:
Si vous avez emprunté la RN44 ou la RN4, vous avez peut-être cru apercevoir des radars automatiques de dernière génération au bord de la chaussée. En réalité, ces imposants poteaux métalliques abritent des boîtiers d’écocontribution poids lourds (ECPL). Ce nouveau dispositif a pour but de mettre en place une redevance kilométrique qui cible uniquement les véhicules de plus de 3,5 tonnes transportant des marchandises sur le réseau routier régional.
Des bornes déjà déployées pour taxer dès 2027
Ces nouvelles bornes bleues serviront à appliquer une taxe au kilomètre estimée par la Fédération nationale des transports routiers (FNTR) à environ 15 centimes par kilomètre. La mesure s’étendra sur 525 kilomètres de routes dans le Grand Est, dont 145 kilomètres pour le seul département de la Marne sur la RN4 et la RN44. Thibaut Duchêne, conseiller régional, confirme que ces bornes ne sont pas encore opérationnelles et qu’aucune action préventive ni sanction n’est menée pour l’instant.
Leur déploiement anticipé s’explique par l’attribution d’un marché public qui demande de caler l’installation technique en amont du calendrier. L’objectif des autorités régionales est une mise en service prévue pour le 2 avril 2027. Cette planification évite d’éventuels retards qui repousseraient l’application de l’écocontribution. Le projet suscite la colère des transporteurs qui ont multiplié les mobilisations, comme le 15 octobre devant la Maison de la région à Metz pour exiger la suspension du texte. Des discussions et des négociations restent engagées avec les différents acteurs pour tenter de trouver un accord qui donne satisfaction aux transporteurs.
Un milliard d’euros pour rénover le réseau routier
L’enjeu financier derrière l’installation de ces boîtes bleues n’est pas négligeable dans la mesure où, sur dix ans, l’écocontribution poids lourds doit générer (selon les estimations) un gain d’un milliard d’euros au profit de la Région Grand Est. Une somme importante qui sera intégralement réinvestie dans les travaux de modernisation et de mise à niveau du réseau routier. Elle vient abonder un programme routier régional global d’un montant total de 2,1 milliards d’euros s’étalant jusqu’à l’horizon 2035.
À lire : Deux nouveaux panneaux de signalisation apparaissent sur les routes : voici ce qu’ils signifient
Parmi les chantiers financés, on retrouve en priorité le contournement ouest de Vitry, un projet évalué à 250 millions d’euros. En discussion depuis des années, ce grand projet franchira une nouvelle étape au premier semestre 2027 avec la révision de ses études de faisabilité. Les données récoltées par ces grosses boîtes bleues permettront ainsi de financer les transports régionaux pour les dix ans à venir.

articles.title: Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro
articles.text:
The Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro is a solid mouse built upon an already great foundation. While I will miss the dedicated DPI buttons on the top of the mouse, it’s a great evolution for the DeathAdder line-up. As a fan of the V2 Pro, it’s nearly everything I wanted it to be. The construction is solid, and the upgraded sensors and switches improve performance, and the battery life is tremendous.
Our editors hand-pick related products using a variety of criteria: direct competitors targeting the same market segment, or devices that are similar in size, performance, or feature sets.
The Razer DeathAdder V3 is lightweight, quick, and extremely powerful, and its sensor includes bonus technologies that make it perfect for high performance in competitive games and esports matches.
This is about as good as it gets for fast, wireless, lightweight gaming mice. The DeathAdder V3 Pro is an outstanding mouse. It's comfortable, consistent, has great battery life and feels very nice to use. The side buttons could have been slightly better quality but overall this mouse lives up to its price tag.
The Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro is another interesting effort from Razer that follows on from the logic of the Razer Viper V2 Pro by shedding weight but improving the specs and design in a number of ways.
The Razer Basilisk V3 Pro is a super kitted-out mouse that’s actually a lot of fun to use. While the weight will deter certain hardcore FPS players, it never bothered me. In fact, the sensitivity clutch actually helped me play games better. While Razer’s Synapse software is starting to show its age when it comes to color customization on the Basilisk’s many flashy lights, just about everything else here feels world-class.
A featherweight high-performance esports mouse crossed with the iconic DeathAdder shape and feel. Throw in an impressive sensor and the Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro more than lives up to its Pro naming.
The Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro is one of the most responsive and fun gaming mice I’ve ever used, and also remains one of the most comfortable thanks to minor changes to the mouse’s signature shape. It’s just a shame that for all the above, Razer has upped the price significantly and sacrificed both Bluetooth connectivity and RGB lighting.
The Razer DeathAdder V3 Pro delivers a bevy of improvements to Razer's long running gaming-mouse line that, while not essential, help solidify its spot at the top of the food chain.
The mouse that rules all other gaming mice, the Razer Deathadder V3 Pro is impressive in so many aspects, we’re hard-pressed to find fault in it. It’s expensive, yes, but it’s worth breaking the piggy bank for.

articles.title: AI Framework Autonomously Weaponized Flaws in Real Attacks, Google Says
articles.text:
State-sponsored and cybercrime groups are increasingly adopting generative AI, including multi-agent offensive frameworks, to increase the speed and scale of their operations, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reports.
For the first time, GTIG has identified threat actors using an AI framework to automate both vulnerability discovery and exploitation without human intervention.
The multi-agent framework, called exploit_agent, was discovered on an exposed staging server. It was designed to compare patched and unpatched web application code, identify vulnerabilities, develop exploits, and execute them automatically.
The server also contained data stolen from victims and scripts for post-compromise activities, including reconnaissance and webshell deployment. According to GTIG, evidence pointed to an interest in French media and entertainment websites, as well as the education sector.
Attackers are using frameworks such as Artex, Cairn, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to increase the velocity of their multi-stage intrusions, and rely on LLMs and agentic frameworks to reverse engineer patches at machine speed and rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities.
“Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly,” GTIG notes in its latest AI threat tracker report.
Artex has emerged as the most used AI framework for threat actors, mainly Chinese-speaking groups, but Google and Mandiant also observed attackers using and experimenting with open source frameworks such as Cairn, PentAGI, CyberStrikeAI, and HexStrike AI.
GTIG observed Cairn being used in activity targeting the aerospace sector in the US, and PentAGI being used for systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning across organizations in Asia.
Not only have threat actors experimented with these frameworks and harnesses, but GTIG also observed a Chinese group building its own automated attack framework, likely for use in espionage operations.
“These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation,” GTIG notes.
According to Google, threat actors will continue to adopt these tools and their intrusions will become nearly fully agentic.
“As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity,” GTIG notes.
State-sponsored hackers expand AI use
State-sponsored groups known to have adopted LLMs include multiple Chinese APTs, such as Leaky Castle; Iran-linked APT42, also known as Calanque Ion; and North Korean hackers supporting IT worker activity and running attacks against cryptocurrency organizations, such as Midnight Neptune (UNC1069).
Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) operators too are using LLMs. The Jieyou phishing service, active since March 2026, has a model-agnostic chatbot that allows clients to configure phishing panels and modify templates.
According to Google, threat actors such as state-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are adopting LLMs for content generation and infrastructure design, which improves the quality of long-running influence campaigns.
“This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success,” GTIG notes.
In August 2026, Google discovered an end-to-end IaaS platform that automated the entire IO campaign lifecycle, from persona creation to interactive posting across platforms. A separate commercial contractor was developing an AI-powered platform designed to manage over 100,000 accounts across multiple platforms.
Other threat actors are hunting for credentials that provide access to LLMs to monetize them as part of LLMJacking operations. This type of activity can generate significant usage and billing increases, with cumulative resource abuse reaching $1 million in one case.
The surge in LLMJacking has led to the proliferation of LLM Mixers, illicit marketplaces selling access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure and routing traffic through pools of stolen credentials and compute instances. They offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken ones.
According to GTIG, the wide adoption of LLMs in malicious operations introduces forensic noise that degrades OPSEC and stealth. LLMs can reduce operational reliability, and stealth operators are likely to selectively employ noisy tools for speed and scale while looking to maintain long-term persistence.
“Conversely, we assess with high confidence that actors less concerned with operational stealth, including many cybercrime actors, will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates,” GTIG notes.
“For US critical infrastructure, the danger isn’t just more attacks, but attacks at machine speed. Water utilities, hospitals, and regional electric utilities that struggle to patch on a monthly cycle can’t win that race manually. AI is dramatically lowering the cost and expertise required to conduct sophisticated cyberattacks. Tasks that once required well-resourced teams, from discovering vulnerabilities to exploiting them and moving through networks, can increasingly be handed off to agents. That puts powerful capabilities within reach of smaller, less sophisticated groups,” said Merlin chief strategy officer Matt Hartman.
“This report is an early warning of where things are headed. We should assume these capabilities will spread. Nation-state adversaries and criminal operators are watching closely to see what works. Defenders must do two things at once: nail the cybersecurity fundamentals today and accelerate the shift toward automated defenses that can detect and respond at machine speed,” Hartman added.

articles.title: Un robot armó por primera vez una estructura en órbita sin astronautas, aunque solo terminó una parte
articles.text:
Un robot construyó por primera vez una estructura en el espacio sin ayuda de astronautas, según anunciaron la Agencia de Proyectos de Investigación Avanzada de Defensa de Estados Unidos (DARPA) y el Instituto de Tecnología de California (Caltech). El robot completó una sección de una antena que no pudo terminar.
El equipo de Caltech lo llamó ASTRA. Es un brazo robótico dentro de una caja de cerca de 1 metro cúbico que toma barras y uniones de compuestos de fibra y aluminio desde dispensadores y arma, sección por sección, el borde de una antena reflectora de 1,4 metros de diámetro.
La antena completa debía tener 11 secciones. Dos llegaron ya armadas desde la Tierra y el robot construyó la tercera. Según Caltech, es poco probable que logre más antes de que la misión termine en diciembre de 2026, por falta de tiempo.
Sergio Pellegrino, profesor de ingeniería aeroespacial y civil de Caltech y líder del proyecto, dijo: “Es la primera vez que una estructura se construye de forma autónoma en el espacio”.
Un robot simple, controlado desde la Tierra
ASTRA viajó el 30 de marzo desde la base Vandenberg, en California, como una de 10 cargas del vehículo orbital Vigoride 7, de la empresa Momentus. El cohete fue el SpaceX Transporter-16. DARPA precisó que Momentus alojó el equipo y le dio energía, comunicaciones y cámaras.
Según DARPA, el robot es un sistema sencillo que se mueve en tres ejes lineales. Une los tubos con piezas diseñadas a medida y despliega a la vez una malla reflectante fina, pensada como prueba de concepto para antenas espaciales.
Detor lo describió como un juego de construcción infantil, del tipo Tinkertoys o K’Nex: las barras se unen en nodos, una sección por vez. Agregó que no hay robótica complicada ni algoritmos avanzados, sino “ingeniería sólida” para combinar las operaciones de forma que escalen.
La autonomía tiene límites: Caltech explicó que tres integrantes del equipo enviaban las órdenes y comprobaban el resultado con fotos descargadas desde órbita. Solo hay siete u ocho ventanas diarias de unos 15 minutos para comunicarse con el sistema.
Hubo muchos imprevistos. El equipo repitió operaciones y probó cada solución en una réplica idéntica que tiene en su laboratorio antes de enviarla al aparato en órbita.
Cada sección terminada se empuja hacia el exterior y el robot le fija una película perforada reflectante. Según Caltech, ese material, creado por el equipo junto con la Universidad de Pensilvania, necesita menos tensión previa que las mallas metálicas habituales y permite estructuras más livianas.
Por qué DARPA quiere construir en el espacio
Hasta ahora hay dos formas de poner estructuras grandes en órbita: plegarlas para el lanzamiento y desplegarlas allá, o armarlas a mano con piezas enviadas en varios cohetes. Ambas dependen del tamaño de la cabina del cohete o de astronautas.
Andrew Detor, director del programa NOM4D de DARPA, dijo que el objetivo son estructuras de cientos de metros o kilómetros. “Nada que se acerque a esa escala se puede lograr hoy”, afirmó. Mencionó depósitos espaciales, hábitats, grandes paneles solares y antenas de radio.
DARPA lanzó NOM4D en 2022. Pasó de la idea de una prueba en órbita a un prototipo en el espacio en 15 meses. Solo dos proyectos llegaron a la tercera fase; el otro, de la Universidad de Illinois en Urbana-Champaign, probará en la Estación Espacial Internacional un método para endurecer tubos de carbono.
El prototipo fue completado, sometido a pruebas y entregado a Momentus en menos de 12 meses, según Caltech. Ese plazo incluyó la integración de los componentes antes de su lanzamiento. La experiencia permitirá simplificar y perfeccionar el diseño para futuras misiones, indicaron los investigadores tras la demostración orbital.

articles.title: House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks
articles.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.
Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.
“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman said.
President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.
Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.
Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.
Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman said that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.
“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said in an interview with Inside Climate News.

articles.title: As data centre backlash grows, industry leaders say communities must demand better projects | BetaKit
articles.text:
Communities should ensure innovation is baked into the data centre development process from the get-go, argues Christopher Fazekas, vice-chair of Xnrgy Climate Systems’ board.
“Data centres aren’t going anywhere, but they can be better, so we should make them better, together,” Fazekas said on stage Tuesday morning in Toronto at the MaRS Climate Impact conference. Fazekas spoke during a panel focused on the ongoing public backlash toward data centres, which was reflected in the results of the recent US midterm elections that saw voters broadly reject measures that would have supported development.
“Data centres aren’t going anywhere, but they can be better, so we should make them better, together.”
Christopher Fazekas, Xnrgy Climate Systems
Angus Reid Institute polling shows more than two-thirds of Canadians would oppose having a large AI data centre built near their homes, as many communities have become increasingly concerned about the environmental impact of these facilities, from the water and electricity they consume to the air and noise pollution they create, and where the economic benefits flow. The industry is already feeling the effects: a lack of local support reportedly just drove Telus to pull out of two planned projects in Vancouver.
Arizona-based Xnrgy builds custom air handling solutions designed to help make data centres more sustainable. While Fazekas views the construction of these facilities as inevitable, he acknowledged that the broader data centre industry has thus far “done a terrible job of representing itself” and the value these types of sites could bring to communities. Fazekas and his colleagues believe that the path forward entails more than just building parks and schools.
Fellow panellist Irene Lam, director of client services at Toronto’s Mantle Climate, thinks there is a happy medium between opposing all data centre construction and simply accepting the AI infrastructure buildout on industry’s terms. Her employer is a strategy and risk management consultancy that has engaged the ecosystem on this exact topic.
“We don’t have to unconditionally accept [data centres], but we do need to consider some of the trade-offs that need to be made,” Lam said.
Lam argued that successful projects will require carefully planning these sites around energy system capacity, as well as ensuring communities have input in this process and any decisions that might impact their future.
RELATED: Telus pulls out of two government-backed AI data centres in Vancouver
“We are going to need some of this infrastructure built, regardless,” said Lam. “But the question really is, how do we do this in a Canadian way? How do we build more innovatively, sustainably, and responsibly?”
Lam has already seen a few ways that cities and towns can achieve this, including by ensuring that data centre developers engage with communities early on, establishing clear expectations, and holding these firms accountable through reporting requirements, deadlines, and penalties for non-compliance.
Fazekas echoed this sentiment, arguing that municipalities ought to set a few key ground rules for prospective new builds up front, including eliminating the use of water and evaporative cooling altogether, tackling noise pollution, and requiring sites to generate lasting local employment, such as by setting up corporate campuses nearby, rather than simply exporting processing power.
At the moment, Fazekas said “the only force for innovation … is coming from the industry itself” as it seeks to increase capacity to meet surging AI demand. He thinks greater pressure from communities could accelerate the pace of data centre innovation because more of these facilities are likely to be built, either way.
“The middle ground is an open conversation that demands innovation and demands progress, but also accepts the fact that this is part of industrialization and the new revolution of technology,” Fazekas said.
Feature image courtesy Josh Scott for BetaKit.

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max vorgestellt: Wo der Hersteller bei der globalen Version Abstriche macht
articles.text:
Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max vorgestellt: Wo der Hersteller bei der globalen Version Abstriche macht
Schon seit September 2026 sind das Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max in China erhältlich. Bislang mussten interessierte Käufer:innen in anderen Regionen noch auf eine globale Version warten. Doch diese Wartezeit ist jetzt vorbei. Xiaomi hat offiziell die globale Version der beiden Xiaomi-18-Pro-Modelle enthüllt. Über die Navigation gelangst du schnell zu den Themen rund um die Smartphones, die dich am meisten interessieren.
Xiaomi 18 Pro (Max): Hardware im Detail
Die globalen Versionen des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max stimmen weitestgehend mit der chinesischen Variante überein. Lediglich beim Akku hat Xiaomi Änderungen vorgenommen.
Prozessor
In beiden Xiaomi-Smartphones kommen Snapdragon-8-Elite-Chips zum Einsatz. Das Xiaomi 8 Pro setzt auf den Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, während das Max-Modell den Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 und damit etwas mehr Leistung bekommt. Bei beiden Chips hat Qualcomm die Leistungsaufnahme durch eine Gate-All-Around-Transistorarchitektur verbessert. Die Chips verbrauchen dadurch weniger Energie unter Volllast und werden auch nicht zu warm.
Für die reine Rechenleistung im Alltag verbaut Xiaomi zudem eine Qualcomm-Oryon-CPU mit insgesamt acht Kernen. Im Vergleich zum Vorgänger soll die CPU-Leistung bis zu 13 Prozent besser ausfallen, die GPU-Performance um etwa 44 Prozent besser. Und auch bei der NPU-Leistung, die für die KI-Features zuständig ist, verspricht Xiaomi eine deutliche Verbesserung von 35 Prozent. Wie sich das im Alltag bemerkbar macht, müssen aber noch Tests zeigen.
Kamera
Für die Kameras des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max hat sich der Smartphone-Hersteller mit Leica zusammengetan. Als Hauptkamera dient ein 200-Megapixel-Sensor mit einem lichtstarken Objektiv (f/1,67). Dazu kommt ein Teleobjektiv mit einer äquivalenten Brennweite von 75 Millimetern, das ebenfalls auf einen 200-Megapixel-Sensor setzt. Optisch kann der Zoom sogar auf 150 Millimeter angehoben werden. Ergänzt wird das Setup durch eine Ultraweitwinkelkamera mit 50 Megapixeln sowie einer Selfie-Kamera auf der Front mit derselben Auflösung.
Wer KI beim Fotografieren nutzen möchte, kann auf drei Bildstile zurückgreifen. „B&W Film“ soll Schwarz-Weiß-Aufnahmen mehr Tiefe verleihen, während „Iconic CCD“ dem Bild sattere Farben verleiht. „Modern Vintage“ soll die Details der Aufnahme herausstellen. Bei Porträts und Gegenlicht sorgt die KI dafür, dass Gesichter aufgehellt werden, um die Sichtbarkeit zu erhöhen. Nach der Aufnahme kann die Künstliche Intelligenz zudem das Bild analysieren und Bildzuschnitte für eine bessere Komposition vorschlagen.
Für Videoenthusiasten bieten beide Geräte Aufnahmen mit maximal 8K bei 30 Bildern pro Sekunde. Wer sich mit 4K zufrieden gibt, kann bis zu 120 Frames pro Sekunde aufnehmen. Zudem bieten Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max die sogenannte Log-Videoaufnahme mit bis zu 120 Bildern pro Sekunde. Die logarithmische Aufnahme sorgt für ein kontrastarmes Bild, das sich im Nachgang besser mit Videoschnittprogrammen an die eigenen Farbwünsche anpassen lässt und mehr Dynamik einfängt.
Display
Das Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max bieten jeweils zwei Displays. Auf der Frontseite sitzt der Hauptbildschirm mit einer maximalen Helligkeit von 4.000 Nits und einer maximalen Bildwiederholfrequenz von 120 Hertz. Die beiden Panele sind bei den Modellen technisch identisch und unterscheiden sich nur durch ihre Größe. Das Max-Modell setzt auf ein 6,9 Zoll großes Display, das Standardmodell hingegen auf 6,4 Zoll.
Das Hauptdisplay der Xiaomi-Smartphones bietet einen Privacy-Modus. Wird dieser aktiviert, wechselt das Display auf Privacy-Pixel, die einen engeren Betrachtungswinkel mit sich bringen. Das Ergebnis: Neugierige Blicke von rechts und links schauen lediglich auf ein dunkles Display. Der Privacy-Modus lässt sich dabei auch nur für bestimmte Apps und Benachrichtigungen aktivieren.
Neben dem Hauptbildschirm bieten Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max aber auch noch ein Display auf der Rückseite. Das „Back-Display“ nutzt dasselbe Panel wie der vordere Bildschirm, ist aber deutlich kleiner. Es zeigt Benachrichtigungen, Kartenansichten oder Inhalte, die von User:innen selbst dort angepinnt werden. So können etwa QR-Codes angezeigt werden, die von anderen gescannt werden können. Das Back-Display kann aber auch in Kombination mit der Hauptkamera genutzt werden, um Selfies und Videos im Vlog-Stil aufzunehmen, ohne jemanden mit dem Bildrand abzuschneiden.
Akku
Beim Akku des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max müssen Käufer:innen außerhalb Chinas geringfügige Abstriche machen. Während das chinesische Pro-Modell eine Akkukapazität von 7.000 Milliamperestunden bietet, sind es bei der internationalen Version „nur“ 6.000 Milliamperestunden. Ähnlich gestaltet es sich beim Xiaomi 18 Pro Max. Hier ist der Akku der internationalen Version von 8.500 auf 7.050 Milliamperestunden geschrumpft.
Und auch beim Laden setzen sich die Änderungen fort. Die chinesischen Modelle lassen sich beide mit maximal 100 Watt per Kabel laden. Bei den globalen Versionen erreicht nur das 18 Pro Max diese Geschwindigkeit. Das normale Pro-Modell kann aber immerhin noch mit maximal 90 Watt kabelgebunden geladen werden. Beim kabellosen Laden unterscheiden sich die Versionen nicht. Hier sind jeweils 50 Watt möglich.
Die Software des Xiaomi 18 Pro (Max)
Beide Xiaomi-Modelle werden mit HyperOS 4 ausgeliefert, das auf Android 17 basiert. Features wie Xiaomis Hypercore-Technologie sollen dafür sorgen, dass die Arbeitslast gleichmäßig auf die Prozessorkerne verteilt wird und Daten vorzeitig geladen werden, um das Betriebssystem insgesamt schneller und responsiver zu machen. Wer weitere Xiaomi-Geräte besitzt, kann über den sogenannten Smart Hub Haushalts- und andere smarte Gadgets vom Smartphone aus bedienen.
Wie es bei einem modernen Smartphone fast schon Pflicht ist, ist auch KI mit an Bord des Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max. Hier übernimmt Googles Gemini die Aufgaben als digitaler Assistent. Dadurch können User:innen etwa auf Features wie „Circle to Search“ zurückgreifen, um schnell nach Objekten auf dem Bildschirm im Netz zu suchen. Xiaomi setzt mit HyperAI aber auch noch eine eigene KI ein. Sie kommt etwa bei AI Voice Note zum Einsatz und verwandelt Sprachnotizen in strukturierte Texte.
Xiaomi verspricht bei beiden Modellen eine lange Support-Zeit. Die Geräte erhalten insgesamt fünf neue Android-Generationen per Update. Danach unterstützt Xiaomi die beiden Geräte immerhin noch ein Jahr mehr mit Sicherheitsupdates. Das Xiaomi 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max sollten also mindestens sechs Jahre softwareseitig sicher bleiben.
Xiaomi 18 Pro (Max): Speicher und Preise
Das Xiaomi 18 Pro und das 18 Pro Max erscheinen beide in vier Farbvarianten: Velvet Red, Black, White und Cosmic Blue. Zudem sind die beiden Modelle in je zwei Speicherkonfigurationen erhältlich:
Xiaomi 18 Pro: Speicher und Preis
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 256 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.399 Euro
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 512 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.599 Euro
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: Speicher und Preis
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 256 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.599 Euro
- Zwölf Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher und 512 Gigabyte freier Speicher: 1.799 Euro
Wer direkt zum Marktstart zugreift, bekommt von Xiaomi noch einige Boni geboten. Dazu zählen etwa eine dreimonatige Testversion von Google AI Pro, Youtube Premium und vier Monate Spotify Premium. Interessierte Käufer:innen können sich ihr Smartphone schon jetzt reservieren. Über den Onlineshop von Xiaomi bietet der Hersteller noch Goodies wie Smartwatches und Lautsprecher für alle Vorbesteller:innen.

articles.title: Proton's Lumo, a privacy-focused alternative to ChatGPT and Claude, arrives on desktop | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Proton, the privacy-focused tech company offering alternatives to Google’s and Microsoft’s tools for email, productivity apps, password management, cloud storage, and more, is now bringing its AI app Lumo to personal computers. On Tuesday, the company launched Lumo Desktop for Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to leverage its AI to carry out local tasks on their computer involving connected apps, personal files, and other automations.
The app is designed to offer users more control over their personal data, as consumer AI technology becomes focused more on AI agents that can perform tasks on users’ behalf, rather than just answering questions.
Already, the major model makers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others, offer desktop tools for working with their AI technologies, but doing so invites increased risk to users’ personal data. Only this week, for instance, Apple announced it was addressing those privacy concerns with tightened security settings for apps that request Full Disk Access, as the AI desktop apps do.
Proton’s idea is to offer a set of tools that let its AI access connected apps, files, and folders and automate tasks, but with more personalization over how much access the AI has. The company says users can choose which actions the AI agent takes that will need to request their approval, and it vows that the conversations and information from connected apps and files are never used to serve personalized ads or train AI models.
The new app includes a variety of connectors that support local tools, like file-system access, shell execution, and browser content fetching, as well as Proton’s email app and other third-party services, including Confluence, Dropbox, and Jira.
The connectors also support local and remote MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, which AI agents use to access external data sources.
Proton says that users can decide for each connector which actions Lumo can perform automatically, which require approval, and which are blocked entirely. Users can also turn individual tools off from the Tools menu in their conversation.
In addition, users can set up their own scheduled tasks, where each has its own set of permissions, in terms of what can be handled automatically and what requires approval.
Proton notes that it uses encryption to ensure that only users can read their chat history, not the company. The company also says it keeps no server-side logs, and the limited data it does store is protected under Swiss privacy law. The data is hosted on European infrastructure, outside the scope of the U.S. CLOUD Act, which specifies how law enforcement agencies access data held by cloud service providers.
The company says it’s investing in its infrastructure, with its first Nvidia B300 cluster built on Open Compute Project (OCP) standards now going live in Switzerland.
Similar to other AI apps, Lumo’s desktop app supports Skills, which lets users save instructions, templates, and reference files that Lumo can reuse across their conversations. (An earlier version of this, Custom Lumos, will now be migrated to the Skills format.)

articles.title: 'Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha' (★★★½☆) sorprende con la entrega más trágica de la saga
articles.text:
La esperada precuela de Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha, está a punto de llegar a los cines. La película se convierte en la sexta entrega de la aclamada saga, y también en la segunda de las precuelas de la historia de Katniss. Tras muchos meses con la emoción por las nubes, los fans al fin se reencuentran con el cruel y radical mundo de Panem. Esta vez, además, con una de las tramas más importantes de toda la franquicia.
Y es que Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha nos transporta 24 años antes de los acontecimientos de la primera película, hasta la mañana de la cosecha de los 50.º Juegos del Hambre. Un brutal evento conocido como el Segundo Vasallaje de los Veinticinco. Se trata de una edición especialmente cruel en la que el Capitolio envió el doble de tributos a la arena. Es, también, la edición en la que participó un jovencísimo Haymitch Abernathy, el que posteriormente fuera el mentor de Katniss y Peeta.
El personaje interpretado por Woody Harrelson en las películas originales se ganó el calor del público. Pero ahora, en esta versión rejuvenecida, el testigo recae sobre Joseph Zada. El protagonista de Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha debe demostrar que puede llenar los zapatos de un legado como el de Haymitch. Todo ello acompañado de un reparto de absoluto lujo con nombres como Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin, Glenn Close, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning, McKenna Grace o Maya Hawke.
El trágico pasado de Haymitch
La principal duda que surgía cuando se anunció el desarrollo de Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha era evidente. ¿Es necesaria otra película más de la saga? ¿Tiene este universo algo más que decir? La respuesta ya se vio claramente en el libro del que parte. Y ahora la película da exactamente la misma réplica. Sí. Esta franquicia aún está viva. Todavía quedan historias por contar.
Y de entre todas ellas, esta es una de las más interesantes. El pasado de Haymitch era uno de los grandes interrogantes de la tetralogía original. Alcohólico y deprimido, su presentación no despertaba otra cosa que pena y recelo. Sin embargo, su desarrollo fue formidable. Pronto aprendíamos que se trataba de un personaje roto, sin esperanza, hundido. Poco a poco, el veterano mentor recuperaba la chispa de la vida gracias a Katniss y Peeta. Pero no sabíamos por qué la había perdido en primer lugar.
Ahora, Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha lo explica a la perfección. Porque lo que vemos al principio de la cinta es a un muchacho feliz, enamorado y valiente que vive lo mejor que puede en el Distrito 12. A lo largo de sus dos horas y media, el filme narra cómo Haymitch pudo pasar de un punto a otro tan opuesto. Cómo su mente y su alma se quebraron por completo a raíz de su participación en los Juegos.
Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha es, por tanto, una historia profundamente triste. Es cierto que todas las de la saga lo son. Pero en ellas siempre se vislumbraba un ápice de luz, de esperanza. Trataban sobre el nacimiento (y la necesidad) de una revolución social. Este nuevo filme le da inteligentemente un pequeño giro más oscuro al discurso para no resultar tan repetitivo. Esta vez, el tema central es la supervivencia del individuo, del espíritu de libertad que nace de dentro. Es la lucha contra la opresión del sistema que se recrea en el sufrimiento y el desánimo como mecanismos de poder. Aunque a veces esas batallas, sean tan imposibles que se pierdan.
Más tributos, más espectáculo
Otro de los puntos que destacan en Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha, en este caso no tan para bien, es su duración. La cinta se extiende a más de dos horas y media que, al terminar, se notan. Aunque está dividida en "capítulos" para intentar aligerar el ritmo, a veces se enreda demasiado en sí misma, perdiendo la ligereza de la que sí hace gala durante la mayor parte del metraje.
Hay un pecado en el que la cinta no puede evitar caer. En sus 158 minutos pretende contarnos la vida feliz de Haymitch en el Distrito 12, el desgarrador momento en el que es seleccionado como tributo, su paso por el Capitolio, su entrenamiento, la lucha en la arena y también las consecuencias posteriores en su vida y la de sus seres queridos. Todo ello en profundidad.
Obviamente es una tarea imposible, y ciertas partes se hacen mucho más superficiales y vagas que otras. Tampoco ayuda que se añadan algunas subtramas y personajes que, por esos mismos límites de tiempo, quedan reducidos a elementos prescindibles y olvidables en el esquema general de la cinta. Al final, el equilibrio general está algo desnivelado, lo que le resta puntos pese a que, eso sí, es una película muy entretenida.
Sobre todo porque Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha se hace grande cuando más abraza su escala colosal. Hay secuencias impresionantes en el Capitolio, coloridas y terribles a partes iguales. También en la arena, preciosa, gigante y letal. Y también hay escenas mucho más íntimas y más llenas de vida en ese polvoriento y desdichado Distrito 12. El juego de contrastes que hace la película en cada uno de sus escenarios es muy interesante y ayuda a generar la sensación de espectáculo.
En definitiva, Los Juegos del Hambre: Amanecer en la cosecha consigue sorprender para bien con una de sus historias más trágicas. Es una película triste y cruel con su protagonista que, además, remarca de nuevo el profundo mensaje político de la saga. Eso sí, no es ni mucho menos perfecta. Se hace larga, con algunos segmentos bastante perezosos y olvidables. En cualquier caso, en líneas generales es muy entretenida. Joseph Zada tiene el carisma suficiente para sostener el papel de Haymitch. Y el filme cuenta con las dosis de acción y espectacularidad que se le requieren a una franquicia como esta. A buen seguro los fans de la saga la van a disfrutar enormemente.

articles.title: China engineers behind J-35 fighter jet pioneer 3D-printed load-bearing structures in military aircraft — behemoth 16.4-foot part uses segmented printing and fusion techniques
articles.text:
China engineers behind J-35 fighter jet pioneer 3D-printed load-bearing structures in military aircraft — behemoth 16.4-foot part uses segmented printing and fusion techniques
China has been at this for over two decades, and they're not slowing down.
The Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, the developers of China’s J-35 fighter jet platform, used metal 3D printing to create large primary load-bearing structures for military aircraft applications. Global Times reports the structure is over 16.4 feet (five meters) in length, using segmented printing and fusion techniques.
Shenyang Aircraft Design and Research Institute, a research organization under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), has been working on 3D-printed aircraft components since 2003. The impressively large 3D-printed components are the culmination of decades of research and development of various metal additive manufacturing techniques.
The engineers are no strangers to large 3D-printed components: in 2005, they achieved secondary load-bearing structures; then, in 2012, large primary load-bearing titanium alloy structures, earning additive manufacturing expert Wang Huaming and his team China’s National Technological Invention Award.
Recently, however, the team created a primary load-bearing structure even larger, at over 16.4 feet. The massive component is not printed in one piece, as printing such a large structure faces warping and cracking issues, as stated in Progress and Challenges of Laser Direct Manufacturing of Large Titanium Structural Components, published in the Chinese Journal of Lasers. To avoid these problems, two techniques were employed: Segmented Additive Manufacturing (SAM) and additive fusion joining. It sounds like fancy words to say it was printed separately and welded, and it technically wouldn’t be wrong — but the key distinction is that it is part of the whole workflow; basically, metal 3D printing into the intentionally designed gaps between the components and creating one whole printed piece.
Additive manufacturing eliminates the need for expensive molds and multi-part construction. Titanium alloys are notoriously difficult to machine, cast components are usually weak, and joining parts using bolts and screws is additional labor — metal 3D printing solves all of this by creating a strong printed part in the desired shape in one large piece, minimizing the need for additional fasteners. By eliminating molds, the team can iterate much faster and create more complex structures that would otherwise not be possible with traditional manufacturing techniques.

Jhet Borja is a serial hobbyist who was taking apart toys from childhood and sketching inventions. He now loves doing DIY projects ranging from designing custom 3D-printed parts, building PCs and keyboards, all the way to woodworking. If he's not getting his hands dirty, he's probably brainstorming his next project.
