articles.title: Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Reason over time-series data with OpenTSLM on Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Across industries, decision-making starts with understanding what is changing and why. Industrial organizations collect data that informs decisions across their operations. This data helps prevent production stoppages, diagnose vehicle faults, explain drops in data-center performance, and adjust pricing as supply and demand shift. However, interpreting that data still requires specialist time, and collecting more data does not mean teams can act on it. General-purpose language models like Claude or ChatGPT can help analyze data. However, processing long histories across hundreds of operational metrics as text or images can consume large numbers of tokens, which increases cost.
To help organizations act on this data, Aionic Labs is developing temporal foundation models, including OpenTSLM, an open source family of time-series language models (TSLMs). These models interpret operational measurements, from equipment sensor data to supply and demand, alongside context such as maintenance records, market news, and an engineer’s observations. In doing so, TSLMs help systems recognize emerging problems in recent measurements. Experts can then ask follow-up questions to understand what changed and assess how to respond. TimeNet, the shared data infrastructure for time-series data, provides one format and API to find, build, and load the datasets used to train and evaluate these models. Together, they help organizations understand how their systems change and act before problems become costly.
OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy the model in your own AWS environment. This post explores how Nexthink and Aionic Labs are bringing this capability to proactive IT assistance, then shows how to deploy OpenTSLM and adapt it to your own data using TimeNet.
A customer example: Proactive IT support at Nexthink
Nexthink and Aionic Labs are building toward a digital workplace where employees get help before they need to ask for it. At the center is Spark, Nexthink’s personal IT agent, enhanced with time-series language models that connect device telemetry and context to the problems employees experience. Spark turns that understanding into action: it checks the likely issue, guides the employee through an appropriate fix, and follows up on the result. Proactive assistance becomes part of keeping work moving.
The workflow combines recent device time-series, such as CPU activity, memory use, available disk space, application stability, and connectivity, with timestamped events and device and software context. The TSLM receives the numerical measurements alongside this text context and interprets how the signals change over the observation window.
The TSLM provides Spark with three outputs:
- State summary: Explains the likely issue and the supporting signal patterns, connecting device behavior with the employee’s experience.
- Recommended action: Specifies checks to confirm the issue and a practical action for Spark to offer the employee.
- Expected outcome: Describes the intended improvement and how Spark checks the result.
Device telemetry and context support investigation of a range of issues, including slow performance under high CPU or memory load, recurring application freezes or crashes, and files that fail to synchronize. Resource usage, application events, storage measurements, and connection activity provide different pieces of evidence. Combined with device configuration and software versions, they give the TSLM a broader basis for explaining the employee’s experience and directing Spark’s next checks.
In the illustrative low-disk example in Figure 2, the TSLM connects declining free space, a rising disk queue, and more frequent application hangs with likely employee symptoms, such as a slow computer or difficulty saving files. Spark checks how much space is left and whether temporary files can be removed using an IT-approved cleanup. If the checks confirm that a cleanup is appropriate, Spark shows the employee what it proposes to remove and asks for confirmation. After the employee confirms, Spark runs the cleanup, checks the space now available, and asks whether the problem has improved. If the issue persists, Spark offers to pass the findings to IT support.
TSLMs understand how systems change and help people act on that understanding. For Spark, this means recognizing emerging IT problems and guiding employees toward a solution. The same approach brings time series intelligence to manufacturing, energy, and connected products, turning measurements and context into explanations and intelligent decisions.
Solution overview
The architecture in Figure 3 provides a reusable deployment pattern for time-series applications. SageMaker JumpStart supplies the model discovery and deployment path.
SageMaker JumpStart is a machine learning (ML) model hub that accelerates your ML journey. With SageMaker JumpStart, you can evaluate, compare, and deploy pretrained foundation models (FMs), including the newly available OpenTSLM model. As part of the AWS AI offerings, SageMaker JumpStart provides customizable ML solutions which you can deploy to Amazon SageMaker AI inference endpoints within your AWS infrastructure. It complements Amazon Bedrock, which offers serverless API foundation model inference along with features like customizations, knowledge bases, agents, and guardrails.
Key technical benefits of SageMaker AI and SageMaker JumpStart include:
- Pre-built inference containers – AWS Deep Learning Containers with GPU acceleration, so you can serve the model without building your own image.
- Automatic scaling endpoints – Managed infrastructure scales compute resources based on request volume and latency requirements.
- Inference API – SageMaker real-time inference endpoints with standardized API calls, SDK, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) integration.
- Integrated monitoring – Built-in metrics for throughput, latency, and resource utilization with an Amazon CloudWatch integration.
- Enterprise security – Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) deployment with IAM access control and network isolation options.
The model in SageMaker JumpStart is OpenTSLM-Flamingo. It combines the Gemma 3 4B language model with a time-series encoder and cross-attention layers that let the language model attend to the encoded series. The model has 5.24 billion parameters in total, stored in bfloat16, so its weights take about 10.5 GB of GPU memory.
An application prepares numerical time series and text context, invokes the SageMaker endpoint, and receives the model’s response. The application can present that response to an expert or use it as input to another workflow.
This separation allows the application to control the observation window, select relevant signals, and validate the response before using it. It also makes the model independently adaptable: a new checkpoint can be evaluated against representative cases before the application switches to it.
In addition, we show a tutorial that fine-tunes a pretrained OpenTSLM checkpoint from Hugging Face using ARFBench data loaded through TimeNet. The notebook submits a SageMaker training job that loads ARFBench through TimeNet and fine-tunes the model. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) stores the resulting model artifact, which is then deployed to a separate SageMaker real-time inference endpoint for evaluation.
Prerequisites
For the deployment walkthrough, use an AWS account with an Amazon SageMaker AI domain and a SageMaker AI execution role. The role must be able to create SageMaker models and endpoints in a supported Region, for example a role with the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy. The quick setup for single users creates both. The managed policy grants broad permissions to get started. For production, use a policy that grants only the permissions you need, as described in Amazon SageMaker AI identity-based policy examples. OpenTSLM runs on a single GPU with at least 24 GB of memory and bfloat16 support, and we recommend 32 GB of host memory. The default instance type is ml.g6.2xlarge (one NVIDIA L4 GPU with 24 GB of memory, 32 GB of host memory). In SageMaker JumpStart, OpenTSLM also supports ml.g6.4xlarge, ml.g6.8xlarge, ml.g5.2xlarge, ml.g5.4xlarge, ml.g5.8xlarge, ml.g6e.xlarge, and ml.g6e.2xlarge. In the Service Quotas console, check your quota for “ml.g6.2xlarge for endpoint usage”, or for the instance type you choose. You need a quota of at least 1. If it’s lower, request an increase. See the OpenTSLM JumpStart model card for the model access requirements.
For fine-tuning, use JupyterLab in Amazon SageMaker Studio or a local Jupyter environment with AWS credentials configured to run the accompanying notebook, which submits the training job. The notebook uses the SageMaker default S3 bucket and an execution role. Fine-tuning runs on ml.g7e.2xlarge, so also check your quota for “ml.g7e.2xlarge for training job usage”. Training runs on the job’s managed GPU instance. The notebook itself does not need a GPU. Obtain access to the selected Hugging Face checkpoint where required.
Deploy OpenTSLM with SageMaker JumpStart
To deploy OpenTSLM in SageMaker Studio, complete the following steps:
- In SageMaker Studio, choose Models in the navigation pane, then JumpStart models.
- Search for “OpenTSLM” and choose OpenTSLM-Flamingo Gemma 3 4B. The model page shows the model ID, the license, and the request and response format.
- Choose Deploy.
- On the Deploy model to endpoint form, review the Gemma Terms of Use under License agreement and select the checkbox to accept the end user license agreement (EULA). Keep the default instance type, ml.g6.2xlarge, or choose another supported instance type. Then choose Deploy.
- Wait until the endpoint status is InService. In our tests, this took about 6 minutes. Note the endpoint name, which starts with jumpstart-dft-. You need it to send requests and to clean up.
You can also create the deployment from Python with the SageMaker Python SDK v3. The following example uses ModelBuilder. The model is gated: setting accept_eula=True accepts its license, the Gemma Terms of Use. Review the terms before you deploy. The SDK prints a link to them when it builds the model.
Ask a question about a time series
The endpoint accepts a JSON request with one or more instances. Each instance holds a question, one or more numerical series, and optional context lines. Each series has its values, a name, and a short description of the signal, such as its unit and sampling interval. A series can hold up to 32,768 values. The endpoint scales each series to a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 and passes the original mean and standard deviation to the model as text, so the model receives both the shape and the scale of the signal. Use None for a missing value. The model masks it.
Send the request with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpoint API. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to match your deployment. The calling identity needs the sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint permission. The following synthetic CPU example shows a request.
A request can hold up to four instances, each with 1 to 32 series, and the response contains one answer per instance in generated_text. max_new_tokens accepts values from 1 to 512. The model uses greedy decoding, so the same request typically returns the same answer. A real-time invocation must complete within 60 seconds, and the request body can be up to 6 MB. On ml.g6.2xlarge, the model generates about 20 tokens per second. The endpoint processes the instances of a request in sequence, so response time grows with the number of instances and the length of the answers: an answer of 512 tokens takes about 30 seconds. To stay within 60 seconds, send several instances in one request only with short answers, for example with max_new_tokens of 128. The 6 MB limit also bounds how much series data a request can carry. For long-running requests, you can use asynchronous inference.
You can send the same request with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). Save the request as JSON, for example with json.dump(request, open("request.json", "w")), then run:
Choose an input window that preserves relevant events
OpenTSLM-Flamingo compresses the encoded time series into a fixed-size set of representations before the language model uses it. This bounds the representation passed to the language model, but it does not make the complete system unlimited in memory or guarantee that a brief event remains easy to identify in a very long recording.
Long-context research makes this distinction concrete. TS-Haystack evaluates event retrieval across recordings of different lengths and finds that the evaluated TSLM variants often lose accuracy as the history grows, especially when locating event start and end times. These results motivate testing the chosen checkpoint on the windows and questions used by your application.
Choose a window that contains the event and enough surrounding context to interpret it. For long recordings, compare overlapping windows. Preserve sampling resolution for brief events and align related channels in time. Include units, sampling interval, and the observation period in the text context. Validate both normal and abnormal examples at the intended lengths. The endpoint’s accepted payload size and the model’s useful analysis window are separate constraints.
Fine-tune OpenTSLM on ARFBench with SageMaker
Follow the accompanying fine-tuning notebook for the complete example, from preparing ARFBench data with TimeNet to launching a SageMaker training job and deploying the adapted model.
When should you fine-tune?
Start by testing the pretrained OpenTSLM model on representative examples from your application, and assess how well it answers your questions.
- Use the pretrained model when its answers are correct and its explanations match the signals.
- Improve the input when important information is missing, such as measurement units, sampling rate, system context, or the relevant time window.
- Fine-tune the model when it consistently misses patterns specific to your domain or struggles with your task, even with sufficient context. Use representative signals paired with reviewed answers.
TimeNet provides a consistent way to load the data for training and evaluation. After fine-tuning, compare the adapted model with the original on examples that were not used for training.
Prepare fine-tuning data with TimeNet
ARFBench is a public benchmark of multiple-choice questions about anomalies in Datadog’s software-incident telemetry. We use ARFBench because its multiple-choice answers can be scored automatically, which makes the effect of fine-tuning measurable. The same workflow applies to tasks with open-ended answers, such as the summaries and recommended actions in the Nexthink example. TimeNet serves ARFBench as a versioned dataset: each question is stored with its answer options, its correct answer, and the metric signals. The training job loads ARFBench through TimeNet and the model checkpoint from Hugging Face.
Submit a SageMaker training job and deploy the fine-tuned model
A SageMaker training job runs the OpenTSLM training script on a GPU instance. The job fine-tunes the time-series encoder, the perceiver resampler, the cross-attention layers, and the language model’s token embeddings, and keeps the rest of the Gemma 3 language model frozen. The job saves the fine-tuned model to Amazon S3 in the layout of the Hugging Face model repository and writes the test accuracy before and after training to a metrics.json file. If your SageMaker Studio domain has a default MLflow App, the job also logs the training and validation loss and the test accuracy to it, so you can compare runs in the MLflow UI. In our run on one ml.g7e.2xlarge instance, accuracy on 135 held-out ARFBench questions rose from 5.0% to 45.9%. That is well above the 24.5% that random choice reaches on the full benchmark according to the ARFBench paper. Before fine-tuning, the model left most answers empty. Afterwards, it answered every question with one of the given options. ARFBench serves here as an example application: it shows how to adapt the model to a new task and answer format with a public dataset. The result is not a comparison with other models or an official ARFBench leaderboard result.
The following excerpt from the accompanying notebook starts the training job with ModelTrainer. scripts/train.py loads ARFBench, evaluates and fine-tunes the model, and saves it to FINETUNED_PREFIX.
To deploy the fine-tuned model, create a new real-time endpoint on ml.g6.2xlarge, or another instance type that the JumpStart model supports, with the same container image and environment variables as the JumpStart model, and the inference script that the accompanying notebook provides. Point its model data to the S3 location of the fine-tuned model files. The request format stays the same, so you can send it the requests from the previous section. The accompanying notebook contains the code.
Adapt the workflow to your domain
The same workflow can be adapted to other time-series tasks by pairing signal windows with relevant questions and reviewed answers. Potential examples include interpreting equipment behavior with maintenance context, explaining energy-consumption patterns with operating conditions, and describing activity from wearable measurements. The data, supervision, and evaluation should reflect the domain and the decision the application is intended to support.
Preserve the timing and meaning of the measurements during preparation, and separate training and evaluation data in a way that reflects deployment. For a predictive task, only information available at prediction time belongs in the input. Domain experts should assess whether an answer is grounded in the signals and useful for the intended workflow. For free-text answers, compare them with reviewed reference answers, for example through expert ratings or LLM-as-a-judge, where a language model scores each answer against a rubric.
Clean up
Deployed endpoints continue to incur charges until you delete them. When you finish, delete the endpoint, its endpoint configuration, and its model. If you deployed from SageMaker Studio, run the following commands instead of choosing Delete on the endpoint page, which deletes only the endpoint. The commands look up the configuration and model names from the endpoint name and delete all three. Set ENDPOINT_NAME to the name of your endpoint, for example the default name that starts with jumpstart-dft- for a Studio deployment:
Repeat these commands with the name of the fine-tuned endpoint. Stop the notebook application and remove tutorial-specific S3 data and artifacts that you do not intend to retain. The training job stops when it completes.
Conclusion
Time-series language models connect numerical measurements with the questions, context, and expertise people use to make decisions. Across manufacturing, energy, wearables, and digital infrastructure, they give people and applications a common way to interpret how systems change. The broader opportunity is to connect operational history with language, making past observations more useful in current decisions.
OpenTSLM is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, so you can deploy it to a real-time inference endpoint in your own AWS environment through SageMaker Studio or the SageMaker SDK. TimeNet and SageMaker training jobs provide a path to adapt the model to your domain’s signals and questions.
To get started, explore Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, follow the examples in the AWS Samples repository, and consult the OpenTSLM repository and TimeNet documentation. Start with the public ARFBench example, evaluate it on representative cases, then bring the signals, questions, and expertise from your own domain.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Tratum building offline-capable banking infrastructure for physical economy - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Tratum is developing hardware and embedded financial infrastructure that allows banks and other regulated institutions to extend their services into places where connectivity is unreliable.
Built by YHWH Vision Ventures Technologies Ltd., which was formally incorporated in 2025, Tratum traces its origins to Nigeria’s 2023 cash scarcity crisis, when millions of people had money in their bank accounts but struggled to access or use it.
“If money is increasingly digital, why should access to that money completely depend on a functioning network, a smartphone, a remote server or a particular digital channel at the exact moment someone needs to transact?” said Segun Ademigoke, the startup’s founder and CEO.
At the heart of the ecosystem is the Tratum Node, a secure physical financial endpoint that combines secure hardware, cryptographic device identity, local transaction state and communication capabilities. Under rules set by the institution, a Node can carry out approved transactions locally, record them cryptographically, and then synchronise and reconcile with the bank’s systems once connectivity returns.
“We are not trying to become the bank, replace the central bank or compete with consumer-facing financial institutions. We are building technology that those institutions can use to extend what they already do,” Ademigoke said.
He said the startup is targeting commercial banks, central banks and monetary authorities, with potential applications in digital currency infrastructure and monetary distribution, as well as the merchants and individuals who ultimately use financial services.
Tratum faces competition from several parts of the financial technology stack, including card and POS networks, mobile money platforms, infrastructure providers such as FIS and Fiserv, and companies building offline payment and CBDC technology.
“Our competitive position is not simply “we work offline”. That would be too narrow,” said Ademigoke. “We are building a banking infrastructure layer for the physical economy.”
The startup has so far been funded through founder and family investment, along with government-assisted loan programmes. It has built and field-tested its devices, demonstrated the technology to financial institutions, and is now working towards integrating its first commercial bank into the Tratum network.
“We are not claiming millions of users or large transaction volumes yet. That would be premature,” Ademigoke said. “What we have demonstrated is that institutions are willing to engage with the technology.”
Tratum is pre-launch and pre-revenue. It plans to make money from Node hardware sales, recurring infrastructure and software fees, and transaction and settlement revenue, alongside bank integrations, APIs and licensing. Its internal model targets a selling price of around US$30 per Node and US$150 in annual recurring revenue per active Node.
The startup is currently focused on Nigeria, but its architecture is multi-currency, and it plans to expand into other African markets as regulatory approvals and institutional partnerships fall into place.
Ademigoke said the biggest challenge has been financing the move from validated technology to physical deployment, which requires funding for manufacturing, certification, inventory and integration. Tratum is now raising capital for that phase and is particularly keen to work with African investors.
“We believe Africa should not only be a market for financial technology built elsewhere. Africa can build the infrastructure itself,” he said.

articles.title: How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development Without Overloading Developers' Machines
articles.text:
To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.
In fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".
Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:
With Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.
Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.
Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can
implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the issue, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.
The platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.
Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.
Commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.
Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.
Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

articles.title: DB Info: Die neue Bahn-App soll alles wissen – kennt aber keine Ticketpreise
articles.text:
DB Info: Bahn startet neue App für Informationen – darum kennt sie keine Ticketpreise
Eine neue Bahn-App will Fragen Reisender vor ihrer Fahrt, unterwegs und am Ziel beantworten. Mit DB Info sollen sich zum einen unabhängig vom Anbieter Verbindungen planen lassen.
Zum anderen informiert die Anwendung auch über Verspätungen, Gleiswechsel, Bauarbeiten, bevorstehende Abfahrten, Ankünfte, Gleise sowie Wagenreihungen – und das „konsistent und in Echtzeit zu den Anzeigen im Bahnhof“, wie die Deutsche Bahn mitteilt.
Keine Fahrkarten kaufen – aber den nächsten Kaffee finden
Preisinformationen oder einen Ticketverkauf gibt es in der für iOS und Android verfügbaren und barrierefrei konzipierten App hingegen nicht, weil diese Reisende neutral informieren soll. Zum Informationsumfang gehören aber auch Orientierungshilfen und Angebotsübersichten an Bahnhöfen – etwa zu Bahnsteigen, Schließfächern, Toiletten, Shops und Gastronomie samt Öffnungszeiten.
Aufzüge im Fokus – Lost & Found integriert
Auch Hilfe für mobilitätseingeschränkte Reisende gibt es in der Anwendung, darunter Angaben zu verfügbaren Aufzügen sowie direkten Kontakt zur Mobilitätsservice-Zentrale. In Zügen oder an Bahnhöfen Verlorenes und Vergessenes kann man direkt in der App melden.
Regelmäßig genutzte Bahnhöfe lassen sich ebenso in einer Merkliste speichern wie Aufzüge, auf die man vielleicht angewiesen ist. Dann erhält man bei Ausfällen eine Benachrichtigung.
KI‑Assistent kommt – ebenso wie streckenbezogene Reiseinfos
Die App soll den Angaben zufolge in den nächsten Monaten weiter ausgebaut werden, etwa um einen KI-Assistenten, eine barrierefreie Reisebegleitung von Tür zu Tür sowie streckenbezogene Reiseinformation für Pendelnde und Vielfahrende.

articles.title: Test Sony 75 Bravia 7 II : l'alternative Mini-Led RGB abordable face au très haut de gamme
articles.text:
| Qualité d'image |  | 
| Diagonale d'écran | 55 pouces (140 cm) | 
| Définition | 3840 x 2160 (4K) | 
| Technologie de rétroéclairage | Mini LED | 
| Formats HDR supportés | HDR10, Dolby Vision, HLG | 
| Jeux vidéo |  | 
| Fréquence de la dalle | 120 Hz | 
| Ergonomie |  | 
| Dimensions (L x H x P) | 167.1 x 103.4 x 38.6 cm | 
| Poids | 42.1 kg | 
| Connectique | 4 x HDMI, 2 x USB, Vidéocomposite, Ethernet, S/PDIF optique | 
| Ports HDMI 2.1 | 4 | 
| Système d'exploitation | Google TV | 
| Connexion sans-fil | Bluetooth, Wi-Fi | 
| Protocoles sans-fil | AirPlay 2, Chromecast | 
| Assistant vocal intégré | Google Assistant | 
| Réparabilité |  | 
| Indice de réparabilité | 7.6 /10 | 
Avec son rétroéclairage Mini-Led RGB, un design soigné et Google TV, le Sony 75 Bravia 7 II reprend une partie de la recette du Bravia 9 II, à un tarif néanmoins plus accessible.
Le Sony 75 Bravia 7 II est la déclinaison 75 pouces du modèle 65 Bravia 7 II (65 pouces) que nous avons testé. Les deux modèles sont donc identiques et nous vous conseillons de lire notre test complet pour en savoir plus. Vous trouverez un résumé ci-dessous, dont les mesures proviennent de notre exemplaire de 65 pouces.
Le Bravia 7 II associe une dalle LCD VA à un rétroéclairage Mini-Led RGB, avec des noirs profonds et un contraste convaincant. Sur le 65 pouces que nous avons testé, le Delta E SDR de 2,7 masque toutefois des dérives marquées dans les rouges et les bleus. Le HDR est mieux maîtrisé, avec un Delta E de 1,9, un suivi précis de la courbe EOTF et un pic lumineux de 2164 cd/m² sur une fenêtre de 10 %. De quoi donner de l’éclat aux effets lumineux, avec une compatibilité HDR10, HLG et Dolby Vision, mais sans HDR10+. Le bilan est malheureusement terni par un blooming variable selon les scènes et des dégradés mal gérés, qui laissent apparaître du banding. Les reflets sont aussi beaucoup trop présents, avec une réflectance mesurée à 40,7 %, gênante dans les scènes sombres en pièce éclairée. Enfin, les angles de vision restent étroits : mieux vaut s’installer face à l’écran pour préserver les couleurs et la luminosité.
La dalle 4K 120 Hz du Bravia 7 II permet de profiter d’une fréquence élevée, même si certains concurrents atteignent désormais 165 ou 180 Hz. Les mesures réalisées sur le modèle 65 pouces révèlent néanmoins un comportement contrasté. En 1080p à 60 Hz, l’input lag de 10,4 ms est excellent et assure une réponse rapide aux commandes. À 120 Hz, toujours en 1080p, il grimpe malheureusement à 30,9 ms, un résultat décevant. La rémanence de 30 ms constitue une autre limite : les transitions assez lentes de la dalle peuvent produire des traînées derrière les objets en mouvement, loin de la netteté d’un Oled. Le mode Jeu conserve heureusement une colorimétrie satisfaisante, avec un Delta E moyen de 2,7 en SDR et de 2,0 en HDR. Côté connectique, seuls deux des quatre ports HDMI sont en version 2.1, ce qui pourra devenir contraignant pour brancher plusieurs consoles et une barre de son.
Le pied central du Bravia 7 II soigne le design et facilite l’installation sur un meuble étroit, mais sa hauteur n’est pas réglable. Google TV offre un vaste choix d’applications, tandis que les menus Sony et la barre de réglages rapides sont pratiques. My Cinema permet de préparer des profils associant image et son selon ses habitudes. La télécommande est rétroéclairée et rechargeable en USB-C. Deux ports USB, une prise Ethernet et une sortie optique complètent les quatre HDMI, sans prise casque mini-jack. L’audio est une belle réussite, avec une spatialisation convaincante et des graves présents, mais bien maîtrisés. Une barre de son d’entrée de gamme ne paraît donc pas indispensable. Enfin, le 65 pouces s’est montré sobre : 65,5 W sur notre mire à 150 cd/m², soit 56,2 W/m², et 0,151 kWh pour deux heures de film HDR.
Le Sony Bravia 7 II reprend plusieurs des qualités de son grand frère, le Bravia 9 II, dans un téléviseur Mini-Led RGB plus accessible. Sa luminosité et sa colorimétrie en HDR offrent une belle qualité d’image, dont le rendu se rapproche parfois de celui de notre Oled de référence. Le design est également réussi et le système audio constitue une excellente surprise, avec une restitution ample et bien maîtrisée.
Difficile toutefois de faire abstraction de certains défauts à ce niveau de gamme. Les reflets sont beaucoup trop visibles, les rouges et les bleus manquent de justesse en SDR et le traitement des dégradés laisse à désirer. Le blooming, plus ou moins marqué selon les scènes, vient également rappeler les limites de son rétroéclairage.
Proposé désormais autour de 1200 € en 65 pouces, et 800 € en 55 pouces, le TCL C89L constitue un rival assez costaud sur le terrain du rapport qualité/prix. Il s'avère plus lumineux sur les fenêtres HDR de 2 et 10 %, moins sensible aux reflets et mieux taillé pour le jeu vidéo avec ses quatre ports HDMI 2.1. Aux alentours de 1800 € en 65 pouces et 1300 € en 55 pouces au moment d’écrire ces lignes, les LG C6 et Samsung S92H (Oled) opposent quant à eux un contraste inégalé, l’absence de blooming et une bien meilleure réactivité. Le S92H ajoute même en bonus un excellent filtre antireflet.

articles.title: Obsolescence programmée : Apple renvoyé devant la justice pour entrave à la réparation de ses iPhone
articles.text:
Apple devra s’expliquer devant la justice française au sujet de l’iPhone. L’association Halte à l’obsolescence programmée (HOP) a annoncé ce mardi que le procureur de la République de Paris avait décidé de poursuivre l’entreprise devant le tribunal correctionnel pour « l’emploi de techniques, y compris logicielles, visant à entraver la réparation et le reconditionnement hors de ses circuits agréés ». Une première audience de fixation est prévue le 25 février 2027, et les plaidoiries doivent se dérouler sur quatre jours à partir du 17 juin 2027, selon une source proche du dossier citée par l’AFP et reprise par TF1 Info.
Ce procès fait suite à une plainte déposée par HOP le 7 décembre 2022, et à une enquête confiée à la DGCCRF. Il vise 24 modèles d’iPhone* vendus entre le 17 novembre 2021 et le 23 juillet 2024, parmi lesquels l’iPhone XS, les iPhone SE de 2020 et 2022, les iPhone 12, 13 et 14 ou encore l’iPhone 15 Pro Max. C’est la première fois que le parquet s’appuie sur le délit spécifique d’entrave à la réparation et au reconditionnement, inscrit en 2021 à l’article L441-3 du Code de la consommation. En cas de condamnation, Apple risque notamment une amende pouvant atteindre 5 % de son chiffre d’affaires et pourrait devoir indemniser les consommateurs lésés, rappelle HOP.
La sérialisation, au cœur des reproches
L’association reproche à Apple d’avoir recours à la sérialisation, aussi appelée appariement. Le principe consiste à associer le numéro de série de certains composants, comme l’écran, la batterie ou les caméras, à celui du téléphone. Lorsqu’une pièce est remplacée, le système le détecte, et peut restreindre certaines fonctions si l’intervention n’a pas été validée par Apple. La reconnaissance faciale Face ID a ainsi pu être désactivée après le remplacement de la caméra avant, et l’état de santé de la batterie pouvait ne plus s’afficher après un changement de batterie.
Plus grave encore aux yeux de HOP, ces dysfonctionnements se seraient produits « même quand un appareil est réparé avec une pièce identique et d’origine, dès lors que l’intervention n’est pas adoubée par Apple ». Pour l’association, la pratique limite la réparation chez les réparateurs indépendants, et donc la possibilité de faire réparer son téléphone à un prix raisonnable. HOP rappelle qu’un remplacement d’écran sur les iPhone les plus récents est facturé 489 euros par Apple, contre 161 euros en moyenne en France selon l’éco-organisme Ecosystem.
« La décision du parquet de Paris d’aller jusqu’au procès représente un signal fort pour les consommateurs et un avertissement pour ceux qui mettent en péril le droit à la réparation », se félicite Laetitia Vasseur, déléguée générale et cofondatrice de HOP. « Une condamnation pour obsolescence programmée par entraves à la réparation serait une première historique en France et dans le monde », estime-t-elle.
Apple conteste, et a déjà assoupli ses règles
De son côté, Apple « conteste fermement ces allégations infondées », a fait savoir un porte-parole de la firme de Cupertino. « Nous cherchons toujours de nouvelles façons d’offrir la meilleure expérience possible à nos clients, ce qui implique notamment de concevoir des produits durables, accompagnés de mises à jour logicielles qui permettent aux utilisateurs de conserver leurs appareils plus longtemps. Nous sommes convaincus que la meilleure réparation est celle dont on n’a jamais besoin, et nous continuerons d’innover pour proposer les meilleurs produits au monde », ajoute l’entreprise.
La marque a toutefois fait évoluer sa politique depuis le dépôt de la plainte. Elle a lancé un programme de réparation en libre-service, puis a progressivement autorisé l’utilisation de pièces d’origine d’occasion et la validation de certaines réparations directement depuis l’iPhone. Des avancées que HOP reconnaît, tout en estimant qu’elles « restent à confirmer dans le temps ». Le cadre légal a lui aussi bougé, avec la directive européenne sur le droit à la réparation, qui encadre désormais ces pratiques.
Ce n’est pas la première fois que HOP s’en prend à Apple. Une première plainte, déposée en 2017 après le scandale du ralentissement des iPhone lié à l’usure des batteries, avait abouti en 2020 à une amende de 25 millions d’euros pour pratique commerciale trompeuse par omission, dans le cadre d’une transaction pénale, sans procès. Cette fois, l’affaire sera bien plaidée devant un tribunal. Elle sera la deuxième à porter sur l’obsolescence programmée au sens large, après celle visant le fabricant d’imprimantes Epson, attendu devant le tribunal correctionnel de Nanterre en février 2027. Plus de dix ans après son inscription dans la loi, le délit d’obsolescence programmée n’a encore jamais donné lieu à une condamnation.
*La liste complète n’a pas été communiquée. En toute logique, elle devrait couvrir tous les modèles sortis de l’iPhone XS (2018) à la gamme iPhone 15, soit les iPhone XS, XS Max et XR, les iPhone 11, 11 Pro et 11 Pro Max, l’iPhone SE de 2020, les iPhone 12 mini, 12, 12 Pro et 12 Pro Max, les iPhone 13 mini, 13, 13 Pro et 13 Pro Max, l’iPhone SE de 2022, les iPhone 14, 14 Plus, 14 Pro et 14 Pro Max, ainsi que les iPhone 15, 15 Plus, 15 Pro et 15 Pro Max.

articles.title: Japan takes Fugaku supercomputer offlline after cyberattack
articles.text:
The Fugaku supercomputer operated by Japan's RIKEN Center for Computational Science has been taken offline following a security breach.
The organization says that between November 10 and 13, an unauthorized party exploited the public dashboard displaying Fugaku's operational status to gain access to multiple internal servers.
Although the research center has yet to determine the access method, RIKEN’s investigation confirmed that the intruder accessed some servers to plant malware that targeted user data.
Specifically, the organization says that the following details have been compromised:
- Names, email addresses, and user IDs of 4,222 Fugaku users
- Names and email addresses of 375 Rikyu users
- SSH private keys and access keys stored on users’ computers
- Research data files stored on users’ computers
RIKEN notes that the attacker used some of the access keys in attempts to connect to additional systems, but the investigation did not determine further unauthorized access or theft of research results.
The organization has not attributed the attack, and it’s still working to determine the exact intrusion method.
RIKEN’s Center for Computational Science operates the two supercomputers, making them available to researchers in academia and industry sectors.
Fugaku, which entered shared use in March 2021, is a 537 petaflops supercomputer used in drug discovery, severe-weather forecasting, and simulations of airborne virus transmission. Rikyu is a 64 petaflops supercomputer used in AI scientific research.
In response to the incident, RIKEN shut down Fugaku on November 14, disabled users’ login keys, and asked users to revoke and replace any credentials they had stored on the supercomputer.
RIKEN said Fugaku operations will resume only after it has ensured that it’s safe to do so.
The remediation effort includes addressing the exploited software vulnerability, rebuilding compromised servers, reviewing the network configuration, and implementing advanced AI-driven security measures.
Users are advised to revoke any SSH keys and other credentials stored on Fugaku, and watch out for suspicious emails impersonating RIKEN.
A RIKEN spokesperson told BleepingComputer that they have no more details to share about the incident at the time, but promised to publish updates when the investigation uncovers new findings.

articles.title: Les USA vont nommer des champions de l’IA, et NVIDIA devrait en faire partie malgré la tempête
articles.text:
Washington s’apprête à sacrer les entreprises chargées de porter l’IA américaine à l’international, des « champions ». Et NVIDIA devrait en être malgré le contexte explosif.
Car la semaine dernière, Jensen Huang a démissionné de son poste de P.-D.G après des révélations sur plusieurs liaisons extraconjugales, dont une avec Alice Huang, que le renseignement américain soupçonne d’être une espionne chinoise. Ancienne dirigeante d’une société singapourienne, elle aurait aidé son pays à contourner les restrictions américaines pour mettre la main sur les puces de pointe de NVIDIA.
Les autorités américaines sont aux aguets : dans la foulée, le département du Commerce a durci ses règles à l’export pour éviter ce type de magouilles. Et si l’ex-patron est sous le feu des projecteurs, le gouvernement semble malgré tout vouloir chouchouter sa pépite des semi-conducteurs.
Mieux rivaliser avec les IA chinoises à l’international
Selon le Wall Street Journal, l’administration Trump va en effet désigner un peu plus d’une vingtaine d’entreprises comme » champions nationaux « de l’IA. NVIDIA, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI et Anthropic figureraient parmi elles. Cette annonce va confirmer les ambitions de l’administration Trump formulées il y a un an maintenant, même si jusqu’ici, aucun nom n’avait été dévoilé.
Concrètement, les sociétés sélectionnées pourront obtenir des autorisations d’exportation accélérées pour leurs puces et leurs technologies. Elles bénéficieront aussi du soutien du gouvernement dans leurs activités à l’étranger et d’un accès à des financements fédéraux. Objectif : séduire toujours plus de clients étrangers.
Washington veut leur proposer un « pack » américain, avec puces, modèles et autres produits d’IA vendus ensemble. Et sans surprise, il s’agit surtout d’une autre stratégie pour faire de l’ombre aux solutions chinoises beaucoup moins coûteuses. Une initiative qui rappelle forcément la rivalité sino-américaine lors du déploiement de la 5G, alors que Huawei s’était lancé à l’assaut de l’Europe et de l’Amérique latine.
Un sommet clé se prépare
Le moment est pourtant sensible pour le fabricant de puces. Car Howard Lutnick, secrétaire au Commerce, fait l’objet de nombreuses critiques, son ministère n’ayant pas réussi à combler les failles qui permettent à des entreprises chinoises d’accéder aux puces NVIDIA haut de gamme. Il doit d’ailleurs accompagner Donald Trump en Chine cette semaine, alors que le sommet avec Xi Jinping et Vladimir Poutine se profile.
De son côté, Donald Trump a salué Jensen Huang à maintes reprises, et n’a pas hésité à voler à son secours suite à ces accusations. Pour l’heure, hors de question de sanctionner NVIDIA malgré la négligence présumée de son cofondateur à la veste de cuir.

articles.title: Nvidia creó un comité de su directorio para vigilar las exportaciones de chips y la seguridad nacional
articles.text:
Nvidia anunció el 17 de noviembre que su directorio creó un comité permanente para supervisar la seguridad nacional, el cumplimiento de los controles a las exportaciones y los riesgos del comercio internacional. La decisión llega días después de la renuncia del director ejecutivo, Jensen Huang, y en plena presión de Washington sobre las ventas de chips a China.
La presidenta del nuevo grupo será la directora Suzanne Nora Johnson. Lo integran también los directores Stephen C. Neal y John O. Dabiri. Según el comunicado de la empresa, el comité se reunirá al menos una vez por trimestre, con la gerencia y también en sesiones a puerta cerrada.
Los equipos internos de seguridad nacional y de cumplimiento del comercio global de Nvidia responderán directamente al comité y a la directora ejecutiva interina, Colette Kress, en el trabajo diario. El comité contratará a expertos externos e independientes en derecho, seguridad nacional y comercio internacional.
Harvey Jones, presidente del directorio, afirmó que la tecnología avanzada de chips y la llegada de la inteligencia artificial “y la superinteligencia” plantean desafíos inéditos para la seguridad nacional. Nvidia, agregó, tiene “la responsabilidad y la oportunidad” de liderar a la industria en ese terreno.
La crisis que precede al comité
Huang renunció la semana pasada, según Reuters y Euronews, después de que se conocieran sus relaciones extramatrimoniales, entre ellas una con una mujer sospechada de vínculos con la inteligencia china. Antes de su salida, el directorio había abierto una investigación independiente, a cargo de un comité de directores independientes y asesores legales externos.
En esa declaración, el directorio dijo que no tenía motivos para creer que se hubiera comprometido la seguridad nacional ni secretos de la empresa. El comunicado sobre el nuevo comité no menciona las conclusiones de la investigación ni un plazo para publicarlas.
Reuters señala que la salida de Huang generó dudas sobre los riesgos para la seguridad nacional y sobre la supervisión de las exportaciones de chips de la compañía. Euronews recuerda que Huang había construido una relación cercana con el presidente Donald Trump y que defendió ante el gobierno permitir esas ventas a China.
Washington endurece los controles el mismo día
El lunes, el Departamento de Comercio de Estados Unidos publicó una norma provisional sobre el acceso remoto a chips y servidores avanzados a través de centros de datos en terceros países. La regla busca evitar que se eludan las restricciones vigentes, según Euronews y Stocktwits.
El anuncio de Nvidia llegó un día después de ese paso, mientras Trump viajaba a China para conversar con el presidente Xi Jinping. Según Reuters, el secretario de Comercio, Howard Lutnick, recibió críticas por su manejo de los controles de exportación de chips a China tras el escándalo de Nvidia.
Lutnick acompaña a Trump en la gira por Asia, de acuerdo con un funcionario de la Casa Blanca citado por la agencia.
Nvidia no informó qué cambios concretos habrá en la forma en que controla a quién vende sus chips. El comunicado solo describe la estructura del comité, su composición y su frecuencia de reuniones, y no incluye metas ni plazos de implementación.
Stocktwits informó que Nvidia presenta el 17 de noviembre los resultados de su tercer trimestre del año fiscal 2027 y que, en lo que va de 2026, sus acciones acumulaban una caída superior al 17%.

articles.title: Instagram fine-tunes recommendation systems in India to curb sexually suggestive, violent content
articles.text:
Instagram fine-tunes recommendation systems in India to curb sexually suggestive, violent content
The India-specific measures apply to content recommended from accounts users do not follow and concern what Instagram's algorithms promote, rather than a blanket ban on the content itself
Meta Platforms said on Tuesday that it has fine-tuned Instagram's content recommendation systems in India to curb the visibility of sexually suggestive material and violent content, deploying more advanced artificial intelligence models to identify and filter unwanted posts before they reach users.
The India-specific measures apply to content recommended from accounts users do not follow and concern what Instagram's algorithms promote, rather than a blanket ban on the content itself, the company said.
The announcement comes against the backdrop of increased regulatory scrutiny of social media algorithms in India. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, in an October 10 advisory, asked Meta to review its ranking and recommendation systems to ensure potentially misleading, manipulated or out-of-context material is not disproportionately amplified.
Meta, however, did not say if the changes were linked to the government advisory.
The changes have helped halve the frequency with which users report recommended content compared with a year ago, Meta said in a post on its website.
The platform said it had strengthened default protections over the past year, tailoring its systems to content that users in India have said they do not want to see. The measures apply to recommendations across Reels, Explore and Feed, where Instagram surfaces content from accounts users do not already follow.
As part of the upgrades, Instagram is using more capable AI models to assess content directly against its Recommendations Guidelines, enabling its systems to detect and limit potentially objectionable material proactively rather than waiting for users to report or hide it.
"Today, our systems keep more of this content out of recommendations, including sexually suggestive content and content that depicts violence," Meta said.
The company said the improvements had enabled it to proactively reduce the amount of content in India that does not meet its recommendation standards. It did not disclose the absolute volume of content affected, the proportion of recommendations filtered or the methodology used to calculate the decline in user reports.
Instagram's recommendation standards are distinct from its Community Standards, which govern content prohibited on the platform. Material that violates Community Standards is removed, while content that may be objectionable, sensitive or low-quality but does not breach those rules can remain accessible without being recommended to a wider audience. Content unlawful in a particular country is restricted there, the company said.
Recommendations determine how users discover content beyond accounts they actively follow, giving the platform's algorithms considerable influence over what appears in their feeds and is amplified across the service.
Alongside platform-wide recommendation filters, Instagram offers users controls to customise the content they see and manage interactions on the platform.
Its Sensitive Content Control allows users to opt for less sensitive material across Search, Reels, Explore, suggested accounts and in-Feed recommendations. Instagram said its systems in India already exclude the most mature content from recommendations, with the setting allowing users to further limit exposure to other sensitive material.
Users can also choose to see less political content recommended from accounts they do not follow, flag posts through the "Not Interested" option and filter selected words, phrases and emojis from comments and message requests using the Hidden Words feature. Its blocking function prevents specific accounts from finding profiles, viewing posts or sending messages, including through new accounts they may create.
Teenagers receive additional age-appropriate protections through Instagram's Teen Accounts, introduced in India last year. These accounts automatically place younger users in a 13-plus content setting governed by the platform's age-appropriate content guidelines.
The changes come amid growing scrutiny of social media platforms over online safety, algorithm-driven content distribution and the exposure of younger users to potentially harmful material.
Meta said user feedback, including when people hide posts or select "Not Interested", also informs its recommendation systems and helps identify content audiences do not want surfaced to them.
The company said it would continue to refine its detection systems as user behaviour and technology evolve, with feedback from users in India guiding further changes.

articles.title: Cyber Africa Forum: Benin wants to be Africa’s AI testbed
articles.text:
Benin wants to become a testing ground for Africa’s artificial intelligence (AI) and cybersecurity innovations. Its strategy, according to Mahuna Akplogan, Benin’s Minister of Digital Transformation and Innovation, begins with protecting government systems, developing local expertise and making digital public services more accessible.
“We want to be the test bed of Africa,” the minister said on Monday, November 16, during a media briefing on the sidelines of the sixth edition of the Cyber Africa Forum.
The ambition builds on a digital transformation programme that the minister said had moved more than 550 public services online over the past decade. The next challenge is not simply putting more services on screens, but ensuring that people can use them, institutions can exchange information securely, and local developers can build solutions rather than depending entirely on imported technology.
Security before scale
The minister traced Benin’s cybersecurity priorities to the practical demands of sharing information between government institutions. As those exchanges expanded, protecting the underlying systems became essential.
“So the ranking is just the consequence of our initial goal: data exchange between [government] administration,” Akplogan said. “We need to protect that.”
The response, the minister explained, combined legal and technical frameworks with investment in skilled personnel. Cybersecurity was therefore presented not as an add-on to digital transformation, but as the core infrastructure needed to sustain it.
This fits a broader approach previously reported by TechCabal on Benin’s digital transformation, which highlighted fibre infrastructure, digital identity, and connected government platforms alongside investment in people and partnerships.
For the minister, buying equipment is only part of the task. Public institutions also need staff who can recognise threats, interpret alerts and respond when systems are compromised. Training and incident preparedness remain central to that effort.
Bringing public services closer
With hundreds of public services already digitised, the government’s stated priority is to improve delivery rather than merely increase the number available online.
One proposed tool is AI that can help citizens interact with services in local languages. The minister described work on language integration, although the discussion did not clearly establish which languages are supported or which services already offer those capabilities.
Benin’s ambition reflects a wider push to make AI useful beyond dominant global languages. In March 2026, Nigerian startup Intron expanded its Sahara speech platform to 57 languages, with applications spanning healthcare, courts and government.
Such developments offer regional context, not evidence that Benin has deployed comparable systems. The question for its public services is whether language technology can help citizens complete administrative tasks, rather than simply demonstrating technical capability.
Akplogan also emphasised open-source tools and stronger local expertise as ways to limit technological dependence. That includes developing local talent capable of understanding how systems work, not merely how to use them.
Data sovereignty, experimentation, and proof
Benin’s approach to data sovereignty is more selective than a blanket requirement to keep all government information within its borders.
The minister said each ministry has a technical adviser responsible for AI, who is expected to understand the data the ministry handles. Ministries would identify their critical information to help determine how it should be managed and where it should reside.
Under that approach, more critical data should remain in Benin, while less critical information could be processed abroad.
However, identifying data as less critical does not, by itself, explain how citizens’ personal information will be protected. Asked about safeguards when foreign technology providers process that information, the minister pointed to Benin’s legal framework and proposed classification process.
The response did not specify the practical classification criteria, oversight arrangements or safeguards governing those overseas processing relationships. Those details remain important to assessing how the sovereignty policy will work.
When this journalist asked what a secure, AI-driven Benin would look like in four years, the minister offered an expectation of more locally developed innovations rather than a detailed forecast.
“Even if we try, I mean, hundreds and hundreds of solutions, and we develop that by ourselves, we will find something,” the minister said.
The test-bed ambition rests on that willingness to experiment. Its credibility will ultimately depend on what follows: services people can navigate, institutions equipped to manage threats, and clear protections for the data those systems collect. For citizens, those outcomes will matter more than the volume of technology being tested or the confidence surrounding its launch.

articles.title: Panne à la NSA : voici ce qu’est NSANet, l’intranet top secret des espions américains — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’agence qui écoute une bonne partie des communications de la planète a demandé à ses employés de ne pas arriver tous en même temps au bureau. Le motif n’a rien à voir avec les bouchons autour de Fort Meade, dans le Maryland. Son réseau interne flanche, et des dizaines de milliers de connexions simultanées risqueraient d’aggraver les choses, explique une source citée par Fox News. Pour une maison dont le métier consiste justement à maîtriser les réseaux des autres, la scène ne manque pas de sel.
C’est CNN qui a révélé l’incident mardi 17 novembre, sur la foi de six personnes au fait du dossier. Le réseau touché s’appelle NSANet et sert aux employés de l’agence à faire circuler des informations classifiées.
Du 19 au 30 novembre, le Plaud Note Pro passe à 149 € au lieu de 189 € ! Il enregistre vos réunions, les transcrit et les synthétise pour vous, il suffit d’appuyer sur un bouton. Les Plaud Note, NotePin et NotePin S sont aussi à -20 %. Bref, c’est le moment d’arrêter de perdre du temps au travail !
Selon ces sources, rien n’indique pour l’instant une cyberattaque, et la NSA n’a pas commenté. La source de Fox News parle d’une panne « intermittente » et assure que les communications critiques tiennent grâce à de nombreuses installations de secours. L’incident clôt une semaine pénible pour les infrastructures américaines : panne mondiale de Microsoft (Outlook, Teams) jeudi dernier, arrêt de tous les vols décrété par la FAA, l’aviation civile américaine, à cause de la mise à jour d’un routeur dans l’Arkansas, puis des banques en rade lundi, JPMorgan Chase invoquant un bug logiciel.
NSANet, l’intranet des grandes oreilles
En gros, NSANet est l’intranet maison de l’agence, avec messagerie, smartphone sécurisé, wikis et outils d’analyse.
Il est classé Top Secret/SCI, pour Sensitive Compartmented Information : chaque information y est rangée dans un compartiment réservé à ceux qui ont besoin de la connaître, ce qui limite les dégâts en cas de fuite. Selon le chercheur Peter Koop, qui documente ces réseaux sur son blog Electrospaces, il est chiffré par des boîtiers dédiés, isolé de l’internet public et relie les spécialistes de l’interception des Five Eyes (États-Unis, Royaume-Uni, Canada, Australie, Nouvelle-Zélande).
Il y estimait le nombre d’utilisateurs à environ 30 000 en 2015, tous passés au détecteur de mensonges avant d’obtenir un accès. C’est aussi là que tournent des outils révélés par Edward Snowden, comme MARINA, la base qui stocke les métadonnées internet (qui contacte qui, quand, d’où).
NSANet n’est pas pour autant le seul tuyau du renseignement américain. Il cohabite avec JWICS, le réseau top secret partagé par l’ensemble des agences, et avec SIPRNet, celui des militaires pour les documents classés « secret ». Cette redondance explique pourquoi un responsable actuel et un ancien affirment à CNN que la panne n’empêche pas de transmettre des renseignements urgents à Donald Trump, alors en tournée en Asie. Ces réseaux fermés restent pourtant vulnérables de l’intérieur. Edward Snowden a sorti plus de 1,5 million de documents des réseaux sécurisés de la NSA, d’après la commission du renseignement de la Chambre des représentants, un chiffre que l’intéressé conteste.
L’agence a déjà vécu pire. Fin janvier 2000, le réseau de son siège était resté à terre près de quatre jours, sans trace d’acte malveillant d’après son évaluation interne, déclassifiée depuis. La collecte avait continué, mais le traitement des renseignements était bloqué, et l’audit commandé ensuite pointait des problèmes de gestion connus depuis des années.

articles.title: Costco prevé abrir una nueva macrotienda de 15.000 m² en Madrid: así es el famoso supermercado de Estados Unidos donde sólo puedes comprar con una tarjeta de socio
articles.text:
Costco, la cadena estadounidense en la que sólo se compra con tarjeta de socio, prepara su tercera tienda en la Comunidad de Madrid, concretamente en Torrejón de Ardoz. Con este movimiento, la cadena parece seguir adelante con su expansión en nuestro país.
Suelo e inversión. Costco Wholesale Corporation ha cerrado, a través de su filial en España, la compra de unos 60.000 metros cuadrados de suelo en Torrejón, con una inversión aproximada de 80 millones de euros, cifra cubre toda la apertura y no sólo el terreno.
Cómo será la tienda. Tendrá unos 15.000 metros cuadrados y gasolinera propia, y abriría en septiembre de 2027. Para comprar dentro habrá que ser socio, porque Costco funciona como un club de precios al que se accede pagando una cuota anual. Vamos, que sin tarjeta no se pasa por caja. Y vende la mayoría de sus productos en formatos extragrandes o packs familiares para mover volumen y ajustar precios.
El mapa en España. Con Torrejón, la cadena tendría tres tiendas en la región, junto a las de Getafe y Las Rozas. Fuera de Madrid suma otras tres, en Sevilla, Sestao (Vizcaya) y Zaragoza, además de un almacén logístico en Torija (Guadalajara), datos que recoge la agencia.
La apertura encaja en la estrategia de crecimiento de la multinacional en España, aunque la fecha no es definitiva. Habrá que ver si la licencia municipal llega a tiempo, porque de ella depende ese plazo.

articles.title: Premios Xataka Verisure 2026: sigue hoy nuestra gala y pregala en directo con Ana Brito, muchos sorteos y más sorpresas
articles.text:
Ha llegado el día. Esta noche celebramos los Premios Xataka Verisure 2026, la gran fiesta anual de la tecnología, y lo hacemos donde siempre (en los Cines Capitol, en plena Gran Vía de Madrid), pero con una nueva pareja de presentadores: Ana Brito, humorista, comunicadora y copresentadora del pódcast Poco se habla!, y Jose García, (servidor, Responsable de Productos en Xataka), serán los encargados de conducir la gala y de ir desvelando los ganadores de las 30 categorías.
Los finalistas los habéis elegido vosotros con vuestros votos, que se han sumado a los del jurado para decidir quién se lleva cada estatuilla. Además, tendremos con nosotros a Jimmy Wales, fundador de Wikipedia y ganador del premio Xataka Leyenda 2026, con quien charlaremos sobre el escenario. Si tienes entrada, te esperamos en el Capitol. articles.title: Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix are accused of conspiring to inflate RAM prices, lawsuit moves forward
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Conventional wisdom holds that the rush to build data centers to meet AI demand has more than quintupled DRAM prices since 2025, consequently raising consumer electronics prices. However, a recent lawsuit alleges that the top DRAM manufacturers actually coordinated to fatten their profits, something they've been convicted of before.
A California judge has denied Samsung's motion to dismiss a lawsuit accusing it, Micron, and SK Hynix of colluding to inflate DRAM prices. Spiking DRAM prices and, by extension, RAM prices are the main cause of recent price hikes for PCs, consoles, and other devices.
In Garciaguirre et al. v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. et al., initially filed in June, the plaintiffs accused the trio of neglecting to increase production as AI data center projects siphoned capacity. They argued that in a truly competitive market, at least one player would have increased output to capitalize on rising demand and sell more wafers, prompting the others to react.
Instead, the plaintiffs accuse DRAM manufacturers of deliberately diverting supply from consumer products to HBM server memory and eliminating supply channels to inflate prices. As one piece of evidence, a client reported that all three companies adopted near-identical questionnaires almost simultaneously, asking customers how they planned to use the DRAM they were ordering.
Such behavior suggests collusion, which the lawsuit claims violates Section 1 of the Sherman Act. The section forbids two or more people or business entities from cooperating to restrict trade in a way that harms competition.
This is the third time in roughly the past three decades that Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix have been accused of price-fixing. This week's decision directly references a case in which all three, along with the now-defunct DRAM divisions of Infineon and Elpida, pleaded guilty to cartel-like behavior between 1998 and 2002. However, the three still-operating manufacturers defeated a similar case in 2018.
It remains unclear how long the latest case will drag on or whether it will affect RAM prices anytime soon. Most experts expect demand to outpace supply through much of 2027, if not longer.
Although memory prices are widely blamed for the absurd current state of the GPU market, a recent report also suggests that Nvidia artificially raised demand for data center GPUs (many of which currently sit inert in warehouses) to keep prices high. The GPU maker at the heart of the AI boom has long been accused of financing its own clients, but after cofounder Jensen Huang's ouster as CEO, past statements emerged suggesting that this was a tactic to inflate prices in response to a chip oversupply.

articles.title: Market Research Giant Ipsos Investigating Breach of Internal System
articles.text:
French market research company Ipsos is investigating a breach that hit one of its internal information systems.
The company made the incident public on Monday, November 16, five days after filing a complaint with authorities.
According to Ipsos, the breach has not disrupted its business. “This incident had no impact on our operations or our ability to deliver for our clients,” the company said.
After detecting the incident, Ipsos launched its response process and worked to contain it, bringing in outside security experts to assist with the probe.
“The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident,” Ipsos said.
The company has not said whether any data was accessed or stolen.
“We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously. Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly,” Ipsos said.
The market research giant has not revealed when it detected the breach, which system was affected, or how the intrusion occurred. Ipsos said it could not provide further comment while the probe is underway.
No known cybercrime group appears to have taken credit for an attack on Ipsos.
Established in France in 1975, Ipsos ranks among the biggest market research firms globally. It has nearly 20,000 employees across 90 markets and works with 5,000 clients. Its services rely on data the company collects itself, including from surveys and social media monitoring.
