articles.title: How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How LoanPro built an agentic AI loan servicing assistant with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post is co-written with Mariah Miller from AWS and Colin Terry from LoanPro
Have you ever wondered what the experience is like for the person on the other end of the phone when you call your bank for support? When a borrower calls a lender, the answering agent must pull account data from dozens of fields, transaction histories, and workflow queues to orient themselves before they can help the borrower. All the while, the clock runs. Assembling that context by hand means longer calls, inconsistent service quality, and agent frustration. A loan servicing assistant built on agentic AI changes that.
LoanPro, the operating system for modern lenders, set out to change that. Working with AWS Partner AllCloud and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro built a multi-agent AI assistant that gives servicing agents immediate access to synthesized borrower context and actionable next-step recommendations. Early results show customer call times reduced by up to 15 percent, according to AllCloud’s published case study.
In this post, we walk through the business challenge, the agentic AI architecture built on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the outcomes LoanPro achieved. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with the capabilities you need to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI.
About LoanPro
LoanPro is a modern, API-first lending and credit platform that automates the entire loan lifecycle from origination to payoff. Founded in 2015, LoanPro serves as the system of record for lenders of every type: fintechs, banks and credit unions, and corporates that offer lending as a value-added service. According to LoanPro, the platform serves over 450 lenders, with loans managed on its platform reaching about 31 percent of US households. The platform powers loan management at enterprise scale across the financial services industry.
LoanPro isn’t a lender. It’s the operating system that lenders run on. That distinction matters because LoanPro’s AI strategy is designed to benefit the institutions it serves across the platform, not a single lending operation.
The challenge
One of LoanPro’s core user groups is servicing agents: the people who manage borrower accounts, handle inbound calls, process payments, and resolve issues. During a live customer interaction, an agent might need to review:
- The borrower’s complete payment history, including missed and returned payments.
- Active loan terms, fees, and current balance.
- Prior interactions and open support tickets.
- Available workflow actions such as payment plans, deferrals, or escalations.
Before the AI assistant, agents navigated this information manually, moving through multiple screens and tabs to assemble the full picture. Less experienced agents took longer, and outcomes varied depending on who picked up the phone. LoanPro needed a solution that could:
- Instantly synthesize account data into a coherent summary.
- Recommend the right next action based on account context.
- Deliver more consistent servicing quality across agents of different experience levels.
Solution overview
With the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, LoanPro partnered with AllCloud to design and build a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock. The assistant runs on Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Haiku 5.5, and Claude Opus 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock (see Models at a glance in Amazon Bedrock). Model availability varies by AWS Region. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models in Amazon Bedrock. It’s orchestrated with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Agent logic is built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source framework for building AI agents with tool use. The system coordinates specialized agents through a composer that routes each request to the right specialist, so each agent handles a focused task and can be evaluated and improved independently. The team chose these managed services over building the agent runtime and model access in-house. Amazon Bedrock provides access to leading foundation models through a single API, giving the team flexibility to adopt new models without managing separate endpoints. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a managed agent runtime that removes the operational overhead of running agents in production.
Figure 1 shows this flow in implementation terms. A user request enters through LoanPro API v2 on Amazon API Gateway. An AWS Lambda handler places the request on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. The Agent Interceptor Lambda function then invokes the Loan Summary Agent. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and uses Anthropic’s Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. It reaches its tools through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The gateway finds the right tool in a catalog that the Loan Summary Service registers in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The Loan Summary Tool Lambda function validates the caller’s signature against LoanPro’s single sign-on (SSO) service. It then retrieves account data from LoanPro’s loan management system, which runs on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) behind a Network Load Balancer. The system’s role-based access controls validate the same signature. LoanPro also checks each request against the user’s permissions and compliance controls, then writes the action to its audit trail. The sections that follow describe these pieces: the multi-agent system, the tools it calls, and the gateway.
The architecture has four key components, which combine the pieces in Figure 1 with the composer agent and Invoke API Tool that coordinate and act on them:
Multi-agent architecture with Strands Agents SDK
The solution uses a multi-agent architecture built with the Strands Agents SDK. Rather than a single monolithic model handling every task, specialized agents collaborate to serve different parts of the servicing workflow. One agent focuses on data retrieval and account summarization. Another handles action selection and workflow recommendations. A composer agent routes each request to the right specialist and composes the final response. This separation of concerns makes each agent more straightforward to evaluate, tune, and extend independently.
Tool use: Data Retrieval and Invoke API
The agents retrieve borrower data from LoanPro’s internal systems through tool use, a capability in Amazon Bedrock for calling external functions and APIs. Two primary tools power the assistant:
- Data Retrieval Tool: Fetches account details, payment histories, loan terms, and borrower metadata from LoanPro’s data layer, shown in Figure 1 as the Loan Summary Tool. It spans eight distinct API endpoints, synthesizing around 1,400 fields per account.
- Invoke API Tool: Triggers workflow actions within LoanPro’s platform, such as presenting informational panels to the agent or initiating a predefined automation sequence.
By connecting to LoanPro’s existing APIs, the assistant works with live production data without requiring a separate data pipeline or data warehouse.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway with AWS Lambda
AgentCore Gateway is the secure access layer between the agents and the tools they call. It exposes LoanPro’s APIs to the agents as tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), handles authentication, and manages those connections. AWS Lambda, a serverless compute service that runs code without provisioning or managing servers, provides the integration layer between the gateway and LoanPro’s APIs. The team chose AgentCore Gateway with Lambda over a direct integration for three reasons. It centralizes authentication at a managed entry point, isolates LoanPro’s APIs behind a managed boundary, and lets new tools be added without redeploying the agents. This serverless approach keeps the infrastructure lightweight and scales automatically with request volume. In Figure 1, the Agent Interceptor (an AWS Lambda function) invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime. AgentCore Gateway enforces this access control, screening each request before it reaches the Loan Summary Tool. Because the assistant operates in a regulated lending context, the production deployment pairs these components with additional controls. LoanPro’s role-based access controls and compliance guardrails apply to each request, and AI actions are written to LoanPro’s audit trail and attributed to a named, responsible person.
Integration into LoanPro’s existing web portal
The assistant is embedded directly into LoanPro’s existing web portal, the same interface servicing agents already use. Agents interact with the AI assistant through two components:
- Account summary view: When an agent opens a borrower account, the assistant automatically generates a narrative summary of the account’s health, recent activity, and outstanding issues. Raw data becomes a coherent story about the borrower’s situation.
- Conversational chat interface: Agents can ask follow-up questions in natural language to dig deeper into specific account details. The team describes this as allowing agents to “talk to the loan.” Every agent interaction with the chat interface is logged, maintaining an auditable record of actions taken during a borrower conversation.
Implementation approach
LoanPro built the assistant with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, which pairs AWS applied scientists with customers and partners to accelerate generative AI initiatives, and AllCloud, an AWS Premier Consulting Partner. The three teams designed and built the solution together. What began as a focused engagement now runs in production, serving LoanPro’s servicing agents.
The work was organized into two parallel workstreams:
Workstream 1: Servicing agent assistant
The primary workstream built the AI assistant that is now running in production. Key activities included:
- Selecting and mapping the data sources (application data, loan histories, borrower records) the agent would need to retrieve.
- Developing agent functionality for autonomous data retrieval and intelligent action selection.
- Iterating on prompts to improve retrieval accuracy and output quality.
- Documenting LoanPro’s security model and integration patterns to inform the production roadmap.
Workstream 2: LLM account rule automation advisory
LoanPro had an existing proof of concept (POC) that used a large language model (LLM) to convert natural language into rule automation code for their Clojure rules engine. The core functionality worked, but the solution had known limitations: frequent timeouts, no monitoring, and no deployment strategy. AllCloud conducted architectural reviews and provided recommendations to bring this existing POC to a production-ready state, including a documented production architecture and risk assessment.
Evaluation pipeline
A structured evaluation pipeline validated agent accuracy against benchmarks established by LoanPro’s subject-matter experts (SMEs). The team assembled a benchmark of 150 SME-labeled accounts. Against that benchmark, they measured the agent’s ability to retrieve data, summarize findings, and select appropriate actions, holding it to a 99 percent accuracy target that the agent met. This framework carries forward into production, giving LoanPro a repeatable process for measuring and improving agent performance over time.
Results
Deploying the AI assistant delivered measurable operational impact:
- Up to 15 percent reduction in customer call times (source: AllCloud case study). Across over 800 servicing professionals at LoanPro’s early launch lender partners, agents previously spent 18–20 percent of every call (1–2.5 minutes across 5–7 clicks) orienting to accounts. The AI assistant consolidates that context into a single click, saving 1 to nearly 2 minutes per call. Across those agents, that reclaims up to 9 minutes per operating hour per agent, roughly 120 hours of agent capacity every operating hour.
- Decreased internal ticket volumes by nearly 8 percent (source: LoanPro). Lenders on the platform report fewer support escalations as agents resolve more cases during the initial call.
- Account summaries in under 15 seconds (source: LoanPro internal benchmarks). The narrative summary transforms raw borrower data into a coherent account story within 15 seconds of opening an account, replacing what previously took agents 3–5 minutes of manual navigation.
- Consistent servicing quality. The assistant provides the same level of account context and action recommendations to agents across the platform, reducing variability tied to individual experience levels.
- Compliance-aligned interaction logging. Every action and query the agent makes through the AI assistant is logged, providing an auditable record of interactions during borrower conversations.
- Responsible AI controls. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content filtering and grounding validation to agent responses alongside LoanPro’s compliance guardrails and role-based access controls (RBAC), keeping outputs within policy before they reach a servicing agent and the borrower.
        “The AI assistant has changed how servicing agents work. Instead of spending the first few minutes of every call navigating screens and assembling context, agents now open an account and immediately see the full picture with prescriptive recommendations around the next actions to take. That time savings compounds across thousands of calls.”
— Colin Terry, Chief Product Officer, LoanPro
Looking ahead
Building on the success of the servicing agent assistant, LoanPro and AllCloud are expanding their collaboration. The teams are developing additional AI agents to extend intelligent capabilities across more parts of the lending workflow, moving beyond servicing into areas such as collections and origination support.
The modular, multi-agent architecture makes this expansion practical. New agents can be built and deployed independently using the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore infrastructure, without redesigning the core system. As the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore continue to evolve, LoanPro plans to incorporate new capabilities as they become available.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how LoanPro, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, and AllCloud built a multi-agent AI assistant using Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help servicing agents resolve borrower calls faster and more consistently. The solution retrieves data autonomously, generates account summaries in real time, and recommends next-best actions, reducing customer call times by up to 15 percent.
If you are building agentic AI solutions for customer-facing workflows, here are some resources to explore:
- Amazon Bedrock: Fully managed service for building with foundation models.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: Infrastructure to deploy, manage, and scale AI agents.
- Strands Agents SDK: Open source framework for building AI agents with tool use.
- AWS Generative AI Innovation Center: Accelerate your generative AI journey with AWS experts.
To get started, explore the Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building multi-agent systems, review the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation for deploying agents at scale, or visit the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center to learn how AWS experts can help accelerate your own AI initiative.

articles.title: Fandango Warns Ticket Buyers of Payment Card Data Exposure
articles.text:
US movie ticketing company Fandango is warning customers that payment card information from some purchases made through its checkout page between October 8 and 11 may have been accessed by an unauthorized party.
Fandango says it launched an investigation, assisted by external cybersecurity experts, after learning of a problem affecting the page.
“Our investigation identified evidence that an unauthorized party could access payment card information associated with certain transactions on our checkout page from October 8-11, 2026,” the company says in its notice to customers.
Fandango recently determined which customers’ data was potentially at risk. It has not disclosed how the incident occurred, but says the problem has been fixed and its security processes have since been strengthened.
Potentially exposed data includes the card number, CVV code, expiration date, and billing ZIP code, as well as the customer’s email address. According to Fandango, customer names, Social Security numbers, government-issued identification details, and other account data were not affected.
“Fandango is not currently aware of any fraudulent use of your information as a result of this incident, but nonetheless is informing customers to take appropriate steps to protect their information,” the notice reads.
Affected individuals can sign up for two years of free IDX services, including credit monitoring, dark web scanning, identity theft insurance, and managed identity restoration.
Fandango has not disclosed the total number of impacted customers. Filings with state regulators list 913 affected residents in Oregon and 18 in Vermont.
A notice was also submitted to the California Attorney General’s office, which requires a copy whenever a breach notification is sent to more than 500 California residents.
Fandango, a Versant Media Group brand, handles online ticket sales for more than 31,000 movie screens in the US and also runs the Rotten Tomatoes review site.

articles.title: Just 403 data centers use as much electricity as the whole state of Michigan does in a year
articles.text:
The big picture: Michigan is home to about 10 million people and a big chunk of America's auto industry. Yet a new study estimates that a few hundred data centers scattered across the US used about as much electricity in a single year as that entire state. Strangely, no federal or state agency actually tracks that number, so researchers had to build their own list of these facilities, partly from satellite imagery.
The research, published on Monday in Nature Sustainability, comes from a Harvard-led team. It focuses only on hyperscale data centers – the largest class of facility, mostly run by cloud and AI giants. Operators and utilities aren't required to disclose how much power individual sites draw, so the team combined industry data with satellite checks to compile 403 facilities, then estimated what each consumed between May 2024 and April 2025.
Depending on how hard those sites were assumed to run, their combined usage landed somewhere between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours. The middle estimate of about 82 TWh works out to roughly 1.8% of all US electricity consumption. That upper figure, for comparison, is about what Michigan, Indiana or Tennessee each go through in a year.
Much of that load sits in Virginia. The state's 142 facilities alone use roughly a quarter of the total. Add Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, and those four states account for about half.
Those states run on very different grids, though. Oregon's sites draw on relatively clean power, while those in Virginia, Ohio and Iowa lean much harder on fossil fuels. Across the whole sample, more than half the electricity came from natural gas and coal. And because demand has ballooned so quickly, emissions from these facilities are now more than triple pre-AI-boom estimates.
The real total is probably higher, too, since the study didn't count electricity generated by on-site power plants or anything that came online after April 2025. Lead author Gianluca Guidi also told Wired that some of the campuses being proposed today are "substantially larger than the typical facility" his team looked at.
Those on-site plants have been multiplying fast. Developers stuck in years-long queues for grid connections have increasingly been turning to their own turbines and generators. In August, a Bloomberg analysis counted 99 proposed gas plants meant to power data centers directly. If they were to run at industry-standard rates, they would emit around 318 million metric tons of CO2 a year. That alone would push US power-sector emissions up by about 20%.

articles.title: Nvidia creó un comité para supervisar la seguridad nacional y los controles de exportación
articles.text:
Nvidia creó un comité del directorio para supervisar la seguridad nacional y el cumplimiento de los controles de exportación, una decisión tomada días después de la renuncia de su cofundador y ex director ejecutivo, Jensen Huang, en medio de investigaciones y cuestionamientos sobre la comercialización de chips avanzados.
El fabricante estadounidense informó que el nuevo órgano, denominado Comité de Supervisión de Seguridad Nacional y Control de Exportaciones, revisará las políticas de la empresa en esa materia, los riesgos asociados al comercio internacional y los mecanismos de cumplimiento. La medida llega en un momento de presión política sobre las ventas de procesadores de Nvidia destinados a aplicaciones de inteligencia artificial.
El comité revisará las políticas de seguridad y comercio exterior
El comité estará presidido por la directora Suzanne Nora Johnson y contará con los consejeros Stephen Neal y John Dabiri. Según informó Reuters, sus integrantes se reunirán al menos una vez por trimestre, tanto con ejecutivos de la compañía como en sesiones privadas.
La estructura trabajará con especialistas independientes en asuntos legales, seguridad nacional y controles comerciales. Además, los equipos internos de Seguridad Nacional y Cumplimiento Comercial Global de Nvidia deberán rendir cuentas ante el nuevo comité y ante la directora ejecutiva interina, Colette Kress, en la gestión cotidiana.
La renuncia de Huang elevó el escrutinio sobre las exportaciones de chips a China
La creación del comité se produce después de que Huang dejara la dirección ejecutiva el 12 de noviembre. Su salida siguió a revelaciones sobre una relación con Alice Huang, ex ejecutiva de la firma de computación en la nube Megaspeed, radicada en Singapur, a quien autoridades estadounidenses investigan por posibles vínculos con los servicios de inteligencia chinos.
El Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos no ha llegado a una conclusión pública sobre si Alice Huang actuó como espía. Tampoco existe una determinación pública de que Jensen Huang haya infringido las normas de control de exportaciones. Megaspeed ha rechazado haber desviado ilegalmente semiconductores hacia China y ha señalado que colaboró con inspecciones estadounidenses.
La atención sobre el caso se concentra en los chips de alto rendimiento de Nvidia, utilizados en centros de datos y servicios de computación en la nube. Washington impone restricciones a la exportación de determinados procesadores avanzados al mercado chino por razones de seguridad nacional.
El directorio busca reforzar sus controles mientras define una sucesión
Antes de su dimisión, el directorio de Nvidia había abierto una investigación independiente con asesoramiento jurídico externo para determinar si Huang pudo haber sido objeto de una operación de inteligencia extranjera. La compañía señaló entonces que no tenía motivos para concluir que se hubieran comprometido secretos corporativos o la seguridad nacional.
La empresa, una de las principales proveedoras de infraestructura para la inteligencia artificial, deberá ahora compatibilizar su estrategia global con un mayor escrutinio regulatorio. Kress ocupa el cargo de manera interina mientras el directorio busca un sucesor permanente para Huang.

articles.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
articles.text:
Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.
The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge.
It’s “worse than a bug”
Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”
The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired.

articles.title: Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability
articles.text:
Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.
The announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.
Offline evaluations remain an important part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.
However, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. New user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.
Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.
This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify new scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.
Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.
Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors.Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.
This is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.
Datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.
According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.
They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.
However, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model showed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.
Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.
Datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.
Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.
Datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become new regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.
The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

articles.title: Nvidia's board reportedly 'not considering reinstating Jensen Huang' despite growing support for the ex-CEO and close to 200,000 petition signatures
articles.text:
Nvidia's board reportedly 'not considering reinstating Jensen Huang' despite growing support for the ex-CEO — with Trump saying having him return 'certainly isn't a bad idea'
Petition to bring back Huang is now closing in on 200,000 signatures
- There's been an outpouring of support for ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, including a petition that now has closing in on 200,000 signatures
- Despite that, Nvidia's board reportedly has no intention of bringing back Huang
- President Trump is the latest high-profile figure to lend his support, and Taiwan's tech industry got behind Huang by displaying messages on the Taipei 101 skyscraper
Following the resignation of Jensen Huang, there's been a campaign to reinstate Nvidia's recently departed CEO — but reports suggest that the company's board does not intend to do so.
The Financial Times claims that Nvidia's board is "not considering reinstating Jensen Huang" as CEO, according to anonymous sources with inside knowledge of the situation.
We were told in a previous report from the FT that Huang is mulling a potential return, perhaps buoyed by the open letter signed by his supporters, which now has over 190,000 signatures.
As well as Elon Musk, who is the most prominent name among the high-profile signatories from the tech world, Huang apparently now has the support of US President Donald Trump. The FT quotes Trump as saying: "I think having Jensen go back … that certainly isn't a bad idea."
That's not exactly a wholehearted recommendation, granted, but the gist is clear enough. Trump also noted that the Chinese spy accusations around the woman who Huang had an affair with remain unproven.
In a further show of support for Huang, Central News Agency reports that the Taipei 101 skyscraper (the tallest building in Taiwan) displayed a lit billboard (see the video clip below) with messages aiming to "win back" Huang, including one that simply read "Taiwan ♡ Jensen".
This was funded by some key players in Taiwan's tech industry, including the Taipei Computer Association and Taipei Components Association.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Analysis: thorny succession
With the bring back Huang petition now reaching close to 200,000 signatures (doubtless it'll get there later today), and various displays of support for the ex-CEO (quite literal displays in the case of Taipei), you'd be forgiven for thinking that maybe he does have a chance of making a comeback.
I said that was unlikely yesterday, though, and this new FT report appears to back up that notion in no uncertain terms. This just isn't something the board can consider; at least not based on some generalized shows of support and a petition, anyway.
Nvidia's board has moved on, and is now working on the search for a successor. Approaches have already been made, with the FT informing us that one of the potential candidates Team Green has been in touch with is Rene Haas, the current CEO of Arm.
On the face of it, Haas seems like a strong candidate for the role (and he was previously VP of computing products at Nvidia, albeit some time ago, having left in 2013). Whether he could be persuaded to jump ship from Arm, though, is unclear.
The problem is that taking the reins from Huang is more than a tall order, with the upper structure of Nvidia's top execs very much built around the ex-CEO (Huang seemingly had some 50 or more direct reports, which is a huge number for a chief exec to manage).
This is why there's also talk of perhaps splitting the role into co-CEOs, and that tactic could fly with internal appointments. One theory (as per Business Insider) is that Colette Kress (the CFO and current interim chief exec) and Ian Buck (VP of Hyperscale and HPC Computing) could share the job, taking control over the financial side and product direction respectively. That could be a longer-term semi-permanent co-CEO solution, as it were, while a true successor is worked out.
This uncertainty, and the perceived difficulty of replacing Huang, is why there's suddenly a big cloud of doubt over Nvidia's future. While revenue over the next year (or even longer) is nailed down, what happens beyond that is where the situation gets a lot less clear, and the board is doubtless feeling quite some pressure to be seen as being on top of finding a solution.

articles.title: KI-Angriff ohne Mensch: Google deckt autonomen „exploit_agent“ auf
articles.text:
Angriff ohne Mensch: Google warnt vor vollständig autonomen KI-Attacken
Googles hauseigene IT-Security-Gruppe Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) hat nach eigenen Angaben zum ersten Mal KI-Angriffe dokumentiert, bei denen Kriminelle das Finden und Ausnutzen von Sicherheitslücken mit Sprachmodellen komplett automatisiert haben. Das beschreibt GTIG in einem neuen Bericht.
So funktioniert der „exploit_agent“
Das Framework trägt den Namen „exploit_agent“. Es vergleicht automatisch gepatchte und ungepatchte Versionen verbreiteter Internetsoftware – also Fassungen mit und ohne Sicherheitsupdate, um festzustellen, welche Lücken die Hersteller geschlossen haben. Aus den Unterschieden leitet das Programm dann ab, wo eine Lücke steckt. Findet es eine, schreibt es den passenden Angriffscode selbst und führt ihn aus. Laut GTIG geschieht das „ohne Intervention eines Menschen“. Bei den beobachteten Angriffen zogen die Angreifer Daten von den betroffenen Seiten ab.
GTIG fand außerdem mehrere Skripte, die nach einem erfolgreichen Einbruch automatisch loslaufen sollten. Dazu zählen die interne Erkundung im Netzwerk, Brute-Force-Angriffe mit massenhaftem Durchprobieren von Passwörtern, das Installieren sogenannter Webshells – simpler Hintertüren für dauerhaften Zugriff ohne viel Aufwand – sowie sogar das Löschen der Webshells konkurrierender Angreifer. Die Daten der Opfersysteme deuten laut Bericht darauf hin, dass es dem Verantwortlichen vor allem um französische Websites aus der Medien- und Unterhaltungsbranche sowie aus dem Bildungssektor ging.
Auch andere Gruppen setzen auf KI
GTIG beobachtete auch weitere Cyberkriminelle, die ihre Angriffe mit KI automatisieren wollen. Sie greifen dafür unter anderem auf frei verfügbare Pentesting-Werkzeuge zurück, also auf Software, die eigentlich für legale Sicherheitstests gedacht ist. Auch staatliche Akteure aus Nordkorea nutzen längst generative KI, um ihre Operationen auszuweiten.
Google rechnet damit, dass die Automatisierung weiter zunimmt: „Angesichts der niedrigen Eintrittsbarriere, der einfachen Integration neuer Exploits und des enormen Skalierungspotenzials halten wir es für sehr wahrscheinlich, dass Angreifer diese Frameworks weiterhin in Kampagnen einsetzen werden, die sich gegen Organisationen weltweit richten“, schreiben die Forschenden.

articles.title: Test ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition : la carte graphique du silence absolu, mais à quel prix !
articles.text:
Aucun nouveau GPU à se mettre sous la dent depuis des mois, alors nous en profitons pour tester des modèles qui sortent un peu des sentiers battus. Après la PNY GeForce RTX 5080 Slim, nous faisons aujourd’hui le grand écart en testant la plus imposante des RTX 5080, l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition. Un monstre de près de 40 cm de long pour 2,7 kg !
- Finitions impeccables
- Performances de très haut niveau
- Ventilation très, très discrète
- Chauffe faible des composants
- L'impact de DLSS 4/4.5
- L'écosystème NVIDIA en général
- Tarif public conseillé élevé
- Carte aux dimensions gigantesques
- Carte très proche des 2,7 kg
- Consommation à la hausse
Vous le savez, le test d’une carte graphique prévue pour décliner la génération Blackwell ne revient pas sur les améliorations liées à l’architecture de NVIDIA. Si vous souhaitez en savoir plus sur les nouveautés matérielles et logicielles, nous vous invitons à (re)lire le test de la GeForce RTX 5090 Founders Edition par Colin.
Une carte qui ne rentrera pas dans tous les PC
Voilà bientôt deux ans que la GeForce RTX 5080 a été lancée par NVIDIA avec son modèle Founders Edition, mais aussi – bien sûr – avec de nombreux modèles issus de ses partenaires. ASUS était logiquement l’un d’entre eux et a décliné la RTX 5080 en plusieurs variantes sorties plus ou moins rapidement. Astral, TUF Gaming ou PRIME ont constitué le gros de l’offre du constructeur avant d’être rejointes par le modèle ProArt et des variantes plus spécifiques (White, Hatsune Miku…).
À droite, notez la découpe du carénage à l’image du logo Noctua. © Nerces pour Clubic
Enfin, la dernière GeForce RTX 5080 imaginée par ASUS l’a été en collaboration avec la marque autrichienne Noctua. Celle-ci cherche à se diversifier en multipliant les partenariats comme celui avec Antec sur un boîtier Flux testé dans nos colonnes. La carte graphique issue de cette collaboration est donc l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition et tout son intérêt repose, vous vous en doutez, sur l’intégration d’un système de refroidissement hors normes.
Après tout, Noctua s’est fait connaître grâce à ses ventilateurs et, plus généralement, ses solutions de refroidissement. Cela passe ici par une large chambre à vapeur qui recouvre aussi bien le GPU, que la VRAM et même les VRM. Que tout le monde en profite ! Noctua souligne l’utilisation d’un pad thermique à changement de phase pour assurer le contact entre le dissipateur contenant la chambre à vapeur et les composants.
Le dissipateur dispose aussi de pas moins de 11 caloducs, lesquels font tous 6 mm de diamètre. Quatre d’entre eux sont dirigés vers l’avant de la carte alors que les sept autres sont orientés vers l’arrière. Un dissipateur en aluminium monobloc contient donc le tout et il est surmonté, Noctua oblige, de trois ventilateurs NF-A12x25 G2 PWM. Oui, d’imposants ventilateurs de 12 cm de diamètre pour 25 mm d’épaisseur, dotés de 9 pales chacun.
Notez, à droite, la présence d’un curseur mode « silence » ou mode « performances ». Nous avons utilisé le second mode. © Nerces pour Clubic
Vous l’aurez remarqué, nous insistons énormément sur le système de refroidissement de la carte ASUS car, il faut le reconnaître, c’est à peu près tout ce qui fait sa spécificité. Notez, cela a une incidence plus que notable sur le gabarit du produit. Dès que l’on a le carton en main, on sent qu’ASUS et Noctua ne sont pas là pour rigoler et à l’ouverture, on est impressionné par les dimensions de la bête, c’est encore plus énorme que la GeForce RTX 4090 FE.
Nous nous retrouvons donc en face d’une carte graphique de 385 mm de long, c’est tout simplement la carte la plus longue jamais passée à Clubic. Elle mesure aussi 151 mm de large, ce qui fait qu’elle dépasse largement (environ 4,5 cm) de l’équerre de fixation. Son épaisseur étant de 80 mm, elle occupera quatre emplacements PCI Express. Enfin, son poids est de 2695 grammes ! Il faudra donc la soutenir dans le boîtier pour ne pas risquer une chute, voire la détérioration du port PCIe.
Logiquement, ASUS livre un accessoire de type « support » avec la carte graphique : utilisez-en un autre si vous le souhaitez, mais pas de blague, il en faut un. ASUS livre également un adaptateur 16 broches / 3x 8 broches, car sa carte est – comme toutes les RTX série 50 ou presque – dotée du fameux connecteur 16 broches de NVIDIA. Voilà, il est temps de passer au test à proprement parler.
Protocole de test
On ne change pas une équipe qui gagne et notre protocole de test ne bouge pas le moins du monde depuis le test de la première carte Blackwell, la GeForce RTX 5090 Founders Edition. Nous retrouvons notre configuration à base de processeur Intel 12e génération et de DDR5 G.Skill. Bien sûr, le Resizable BAR est activé dans le BIOS.
L’erreur de configuration/captures s’est reproduite sur CPU-Z. ©Nerces pour Clubic
Configuration de test
- Carte mère : ASUS ROG Strix Z790-E Gaming Wi-Fi II (BIOS 2107)
- Processeur : Intel Core i9-12900K
- Mémoire : G.Skill Ripjaws S5 DDR5-6000 CL28 (2x 16 Go)
- SSD « système » : Kingston KC3000 2 To
- Refroidissement : ASUS ROG Ryujin III 360 ARGB
- Alimentation : be quiet ! Power Zone 2 (1 200 watts)
Autant que possible, nous éliminons les programmes en mémoire vive, et nous nous assurons que les configurations sont proches, matériellement donc, mais aussi d’un point de vue du logiciel.
- Windows 11 Professionnel 64-bit 25H2 v26200.9974
- Pilotes chipset Intel v10.1.20266.8668
- Pilotes graphiques AMD v26.9.2
- Pilotes graphiques NVIDIA v591.74
Aucune difficulté pour brancher l’unique connecteur 16 broches. © Nerces pour Clubic
Qu’en est-il des performances ?
En s’associant à Noctua, ASUS visait un double objectif : un système de refroidissement performant pour limiter la chauffe tout en restant discret et un moyen de pousser un peu les performances du GPU de NVIDIA. Pari tenu ?
3DMark
Même protocole, même ordre des tests et c’est donc avec l’inévitable 3DMark que nous démarrons les mesures de performances. Time Spy Extreme représente la scène de référence, Port Royal est là pour la prise en charge ray tracing alors que SpeedWay constitue la séquence la plus lourde.
Trois scènes aux orientations différentes donc, mais des conclusions qui ne changent pas le moins du monde. Sans grande surprise, l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition est proche des autres RTX 5080, mais notons qu’elle l’emporte systématiquement avec des écarts parfois notables.
Blender benchmark
Nos conclusions sont globalement les mêmes sur Blender benchmark. Il n’est évidemment pas question d’approcher les performances de la RTX 5090, mais le modèle issu de la collaboration entre ASUS et Noctua se paie à chaque fois les autres RTX 5080 passées chez Clubic.
V-Ray benchmark
V-Ray est un outil de mesure spécifiquement conçu pour le ray tracing et à son tour il confirme tout le bien que l’on pense de cette collaboration ASUS/Noctua. Leur RTX 5080 est simplement la meilleure testée à ce jour.
Procyon image generation benchmark
Pour ne pas alourdir le dossier, nous limitons Procyon à son outil de génération d’images. Exprimées en secondes (le score le plus faible est le meilleur), les valeurs ne montrent pas de très grandes différences entre les modèles de RTX 5080, mais c’est une fois encore l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition qui l’emporte.
Performances ludiques
Comme ce fut précédemment le cas sur les modèles de cartes graphiques les plus performants, nous mettons de côté les résultats ludiques en Full HD (1 080p) pour nous focaliser sur les seules mesures en UHD (2 160p) et en QHD (1 440p). Nos tests sont toujours réalisés de la même manière en plein écran, mais synchronisation verticale et G-Sync désactivés. Voici le détail des réglages pour chacun des titres retenus.
- Cyberpunk 2077 : preset RT Overdrive, path tracing ON, ray reconstruction ON, DLSS qualité avec le nouveau modèle Transformer, frame generation MAX (OFF sur la RTX 3090, 2X sur la RTX 4090 et 4X sur la RTX 5090).
- Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora : preset ultra, FSR équilibré, FSR frame generation ON (fixe)
- Black Myth: Wukong : preset cinématique, DLSS équilibré (60 %), frame generation ON
- Forza Motorsport : preset ultra, DLSS équilibré
- Red Dead Redemption 2 : preset ultra, DLSS OFF
- Total War Warhammer III : preset ultra
Nous n’allons pas jouer les surpris, l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition remporte de la tête et des épaules toutes les oppositions ludiques face aux autres modèles de RTX 5080, et ce, qu’il s’agisse des deux versions PNY ou de la Founders Edition. Les écarts restent faibles, mais la persistance de la domination de la carte ASUS/Noctua est bien réelle.
Il ne sera d’ailleurs pas utile d’aller beaucoup plus loin dans les réflexions en passant au QHD (1 440p), les conclusions, comme les écarts entre les cartes, étant sensiblement identiques. L’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition confirme qu’elle est la meilleure joueuse du moment… Exceptions faites des cartes RTX 5090 bien sûr.
De l’efficacité /watt et /euro
Avant de lancer Blackwell, NVIDIA avait promis des optimisations en matière d’efficacité énergétique grâce, notamment, à une gestion plus fine de la consommation. Le test de la RTX 5090 Founders Edition n’avait toutefois pas permis de mettre en évidence de très nets apports. Sans activation de DLSS 4 en tout cas.
Consommation électrique
L’intégration de la solution de refroidissement Noctua ne vient pas modifier les recommandations matérielles : comme sur tous les précédents modèles et comme sur la Founders Edition de NVIDIA, cette RTX 5080 impose l’utilisation d’une alimentation d’au moins 850 W pour être tranquille.
Un petit coup d’optimisation est peut-être passé par là car, au repos, l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition est celle qui consomme le moins de notre sélection. En charge, en revanche, elle se place un cran au-dessus des autres RTX 5080 : avec un système de refroidissement, le GPU peut sans doute davantage prendre ses aises, ce qui expliquerait aussi les performances un peu supérieures.
Efficacité et « rentabilité »
Afin de tenir davantage compte des spécificités de tel ou tel GPU, nous avons décidé d’utiliser deux scénarios pour évaluer l’efficacité énergétique sur un test utilisant le ray tracing, mais aussi sur un jeu compatible DLSS et multi-frame generation.
Nous le disions lors du test de la RTX 5080 Founders Edition, cela reste valable aujourd’hui : « malgré un bond générationnel limité sur les performances brutes, la RTX 5080 propose la meilleure efficacité énergétique de notre sélection ». Un avantage qui ne change cependant pas vraiment d’un modèle de RTX 5080 à l’autre avec, simplement, un tout petit mieux pour l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition, mais alors, tout petit.
Hélas, ASUS et Noctua ont commercialisé leur carte à un prix public conseillé sensiblement supérieur à celui des autres RTX 5080 : 1 599 euros quand NVIDIA lançait sa Founders Edition à 1 179 euros. Forcément, l’indicateur de performances par euro s’en ressent. Cela dit, vous le savez aussi bien que nous, ces prix publics conseillés ne veulent plus rien dire : la carte ASUS/Noctua se négocie plutôt autour des 2 400 euros aujourd’hui. Oui, ça fait très mal pour une « simple » RTX 5080.
N’oublions pas que l’ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition autant que les autres modèles Blackwell mise beaucoup sur la multi-frame generation. Penchons-nous donc sur l’impact que cette technologie peut avoir sur nos deux indicateurs.
En performances/watt, nous sommes un peu surpris de constater un recul de la carte ASUS/Noctua, elle domine encore les modèles PNY, mais s’incline (de très peu) face à la Founders Edition. Plus gênant, l’impact du prix public conseillé est encore plus notable sur cet indicateur : preuve que cette ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition est un modèle singulier qui implique un surcoût notable.
Données (fréquence, températures, rotation des ventilateurs) relevées par GPU-Z : à gauche au repos et, à droite, en charge. © Nerces pour Clubic
Avant de conclure, il nous faut revenir sur le pourquoi de ce surcoût. Nous l’avons largement présenté, le système de refroidissement adopté par ASUS et Noctua est à nulle autre pareil. Il a logiquement un impact sur le prix de la carte, mais aussi – et c’est heureux ! – sur l’échauffement des composants autant que sur les nuisances sonores.
Là, c’est bien simple, elle écrase la concurrence : même au plus fort des sollicitations, nous n’avons jamais atteint les 58°C pour le GPU ou les 65°C pour le hotspot, c’est entre 10°C et 15°C de mieux que les autres cartes. Tout cela, en gardant des ventilateurs en général à moins de 1 000 tr/mn, donc particulièrement discrets (moins de 33 dB). Rien à redire ici, la carte est une merveille.
ASUS GeForce RTX 5080 Noctua Edition : l’avis de Clubic
Sur le principe et les résultats, il n’y a strictement rien à redire à propos de cette carte issue de la collaboration entre ASUS et Noctua. Le système de refroidissement mis en place peut sembler « too much » pour nombre d’utilisateurs, mais il garantit effectivement une dissipation thermique remarquable tout en limitant considérablement les nuisances sonores.
Il s’agit sans aucun doute possible de la plus discrète des GeForce RTX 5080 et elle se trouve être d’ailleurs bien plus discrète que toutes les variantes de RTX série 50 passées entre nos mains. Seuls des modèles équipés de watercooling pourraient faire mieux. Cette efficacité permet au GPU NVIDIA de s’exprimer pleinement et même si les écarts sont faibles, c’est aussi la plus performante des RTX 5080 testées à Clubic.
Hélas, chaque médaille ayant son revers, il faut faire avec une carte graphique absolument monstrueuse qui ne rentra clairement pas dans tous les boîtiers. Attention aussi à bien la fixer car avec pas loin de 3 kg sur la balance, elle va peser sur le port PCI Express. Enfin, et là, nous ne surprendrons personne, son tarif est lui aussi démesuré. Lancée à plus ou moins 1 600 euros, elle est aujourd’hui plutôt autour des 2 400/2 500 euros. On vit vraiment une époque formidable.
- Finitions impeccables
- Performances de très haut niveau
- Ventilation très, très discrète
- Chauffe faible des composants
- L'impact de DLSS 4/4.5
- L'écosystème NVIDIA en général
- Tarif public conseillé élevé
- Carte aux dimensions gigantesques
- Carte très proche des 2,7 kg
- Consommation à la hausse

articles.title: Noté 9/10, le nouveau Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max et sa station complète perdent 200 € pour le Black Friday — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le Robot Vacuum 6 Max prend la suite du Robot Vacuum 5 Pro, qui nous avait déjà marqués par son rapport performances/prix. La recette évolue peu, avec une station complète, une navigation par LiDAR et l’ajout d’un rouleau serpillière pour nettoyer en profondeur sur son passage. Noté 9/10 dans notre test, ce modèle combine une aspiration efficace et un déplacement précis dans la maison. Pour le Black Friday, il profite d’une réduction de 200 euros sur la boutique officielle.
Les forces du Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max
- Un rouleau serpillière efficace pour le nettoyage humide des sols
- Une navigation précise grâce à son LiDAR rétractable
- Une puissance d’aspiration annoncée à 35 000 Pa par Xiaomi
Affiché d’ordinaire à 999,99 euros, le Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max descend à 799,99 euros sur le site de la marque jusqu’au 30 novembre. L’offre est également valable sur le site d’Amazon.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le YUKA mini 2 500 passe à 599 € au lieu de 799 € ! Plug & Play, sans fil périmétrique à enterrer, zéro installation prise de tête. Bref, déballez, lancez, et dites adieu à la tonte !
Une station discrète et un robot bardé de capteurs
Xiaomi a trouvé une formule qui fonctionne, et le design reste proche de la génération précédente. Le Robot Vacuum 6 Max dispose d’une station grise dont le sommet cache une trappe donnant accès aux deux réservoirs d’eau. Le sac à poussière se loge derrière une trappe amovible en façade. Xiaomi annonce 75 jours sans avoir à le vider, d’après ses tests dans un logement de 120 m² nettoyé une fois par jour.
Le robot reprend le même gris, avec des pare-chocs plus foncés. Sur le dessus, une tourelle réunit les boutons On et Home ainsi que le LiDAR. Si ce bloc casse un peu l’harmonie de l’ensemble, il a l’avantage d’être rétractable : en s’abaissant, il permet au robot de se faufiler sous les meubles bas, dès 9,3 centimètres de hauteur libre. Ce capteur laser pilote la cartographie rapide du domicile et fonctionne en duo avec le capteur 3D et les deux caméras infrarouges situés à l’avant pour éviter les obstacles et les objets qui traînent au sol.
Une aspiration solide et un lavage par rouleau
Côté aspiration, Xiaomi annonce 35 000 Pa pour ce Robot Vacuum 6 Max. Un chiffre à prendre avec des pincettes : la marque le mesure directement au moteur, alimenté par une source externe, pas au ras du sol. Grâce à ses deux brosses latérales avant qui rabattent les saletés vers sa brosse principale anti-enchevêtrement (capable de sectionner cheveux et poils d’animaux), il nettoie efficacement sols durs comme tapis.
Le gros changement concerne toutefois le lavage : le robot associe un patin rotatif déporté à un rouleau-serpillière, et la station lave ensuite le rouleau à 85 °C avant de le sécher à l’air chaud à 50 °C. Lorsqu’il croise un tapis, il relève automatiquement ses serpillières pour ne pas le mouiller.
Enfin, côté autonomie, le Robot Vacuum 6 Max embarque une batterie de 6 400 mAh (en hausse par rapport aux 5 200 mAh du 5 Pro) qui lui assure une belle endurance. Lors de nos essais sur une surface d’environ 50 m² au sol, un cycle standard combinant aspiration et lavage pendant deux heures n’a consommé que 28 % de batterie. Même en poussant tous les réglages au maximum avec un double passage, il tient 3 h 30 avant de descendre à 10 % et de retourner automatiquement à sa base pour faire le plein.
Pour le détail de nos essais, rendez-vous sur notre test du Xiaomi Robot Vacuum 6 Max, qui revient sur chaque étape du nettoyage.

articles.title: Estados Unidos oficializa la investigación contra Megaspeed por el presunto desvío de chips de Nvidia hacia China
articles.text:
El Departamento de Comercio y el Departamento de Justicia de Estados Unidos confirmaron el 16 de noviembre que investigan a la empresa singapurense Megaspeed por presuntas infracciones a los controles de exportación de semiconductores sensibles, incluidos chips fabricados por Nvidia. En una declaración conjunta, los dos organismos precisaron que la pesquisa se inició en 2024 tras detectar actividad sospechosa vinculada a un posible desvío de esos componentes y advirtieron que aplicarán la ley ante cualquier conducta delictiva que se compruebe.
Según el comunicado oficial difundido ese día, el origen de la investigación fue el monitoreo proactivo que el Departamento de Comercio realizaba sobre el movimiento de semiconductores con restricciones de exportación. Al identificar indicios de un posible desvío en las operaciones de Megaspeed, las autoridades abrieron una investigación formal por posibles infracciones a los controles vigentes.
Joint Statement from Department of Commerce and Department of Justice on Megaspeed Investigation. https://t.co/aAdtN9aDfF
— U.S. Department of Commerce (@CommerceGov) November 17, 2026
Ambos organismos aclararon que, si bien no suelen pronunciarse sobre pesquisas en curso, en este caso consideraron que divulgar los hechos era de interés público.
El Departamento de Comercio solicitó registros a Nvidia y la empresa sumó a Megaspeed a su lista de “no vender”
En mayo de 2025, investigadores del Departamento de Comercio requirieron a Nvidia documentación sobre ventas directas o indirectas a Megaspeed. El pedido buscaba establecer si la firma singapurense había accedido a chips de alto rendimiento a través del fabricante estadounidense.
Un mes después, en junio de 2025, Nvidia incorporó a Megaspeed a su lista de “no vender”, medida que implica el cese de cualquier transacción comercial con esa compañía.
Nvidia no respondió de inmediato a las consultas de medios fuera del horario habitual, según informó Reuters.
Agentes de Estados Unidos y Singapur inspeccionaron las instalaciones e interrogaron a la directora ejecutiva de Megaspeed
También en junio de 2025, agentes de la Oficina de Industria y Seguridad (BIS) del Departamento de Comercio, con la colaboración de autoridades de Singapur, llevaron a cabo una verificación presencial en las instalaciones de Megaspeed para constatar el uso final de los productos. En esa instancia, entrevistaron a Alice Huang, entonces directora ejecutiva de la compañía.
Tras esa acción, el Departamento de Justicia asumió el liderazgo de la investigación penal. Megaspeed informó el 16 de noviembre de 2026 que Huang dejó formalmente la empresa el 30 de agosto de 2025 y que la compañía inició una investigación interna sobre sus operaciones.
El caso surgió en el marco del escándalo protagonizado por Jensen Huang, exCEO de Nvidia
La investigación tomó estado público en las últimas semanas, luego de que trascendiera una relación extramarital entre Jensen Huang, fundador y entonces presidente ejecutivo de Nvidia, y Alice Huang, exejecutiva de Megaspeed. Autoridades de Estados Unidos sospechan que Alice Huang mantuvo vínculos con esfuerzos de espionaje chinos, acusación que Beijing rechaza.
Según Reuters, la agencia no pudo verificar de forma independiente esas acusaciones, que también difundieron otros medios, entre ellos The New York Times. Dos fuentes citadas por la agencia indicaron que las agencias de inteligencia de Estados Unidos aún analizan el vínculo de Huang con el Ministerio de Seguridad del Estado chino, y que las pruebas reunidas hasta ahora apuntarían a que era un activo de inteligencia —alguien que compartía información— antes que una espía entrenada.
Jensen Huang renunció a la presidencia ejecutiva de Nvidia el 12 de noviembre de 2026 tras hacerse públicas las revelaciones.
Megaspeed, el mayor comprador de chips Nvidia en el sudeste asiático, bajo la lupa de Singapur
Megaspeed es el mayor comprador de chips de Nvidia en el sudeste asiático y es señalada como posible canal de desvío de semiconductores avanzados hacia China, pese a las restricciones de exportación vigentes. El gobierno de Singapur acordó continuar las conversaciones con Washington sobre el caso.
Las autoridades de la ciudad-estado tienen prohibido el reingreso de Alice Huang a su territorio, mientras continúa la investigación sobre Megaspeed y otras seis personas. La policía singapurense no halló pruebas suficientes para imputarla por declaraciones falsas sobre compras de servidores, pero la advirtió por haber minimizado su rol en la empresa.
Las sanciones por control de exportaciones aumentaron 18 veces respecto de la administración Biden
En el plano institucional, el caso también generó tensiones entre el Departamento del Tesoro y el Departamento de Comercio. El secretario del Tesoro, Scott Bessent, responsabilizó públicamente al titular de Comercio, Howard Lutnick, por no haber supervisado de forma adecuada las exportaciones de chips. Lutnick fue citado a testificar ante el Comité Bancario del Senado el mes próximo.
Por su parte, Jensen Huang acordó comparecer ante el Comité Especial de la Cámara de Representantes sobre China para explicar si su relación comprometió la seguridad nacional. La Casa Blanca anunció el 16 de noviembre nuevas restricciones al acceso de China a chips de inteligencia artificial de empresas como Nvidia.
En el comunicado conjunto, el Departamento de Comercio y el Departamento de Justicia destacaron su historial en casos similares: bajo la administración Trump, 17 acusados en seis investigaciones independientes fueron imputados por presunto contrabando de semiconductores valuados en miles de millones de dólares.
Según el mismo comunicado, las sanciones monetarias en casos de controles de exportación registraron un aumento de 18 veces frente a la administración Biden. Ambos organismos reiteraron que los semiconductores sensibles son “uno de los activos más valiosos y estratégicos de la economía estadounidense” y que mantendrán la vigilancia contra quienes intenten comprometer la ventaja tecnológica del país.

articles.title: 720 796 propriétaires de BMW sont priés de garer leur voiture dehors et loin des maisons aux États-Unis à cause d'un « risque d'incendie »
articles.text:
Voilà un problème dont tout propriétaire de berline ou de SUV BMW se serait bien passé. La National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), l’agence américaine chargée de la sécurité routière, vient de rappeler 720 796 voitures BMW en Amérique du Nord. En cause, un risque d’incendie avéré, y compris lorsque les véhicules sont stationnés et que le moteur est éteint. Pour éviter tout incendie dans un garage fermé ou un parking souterrain, il faut impérativement laisser sa voiture stationnée à l’extérieur, loin des bâtiments et des autres véhicules, jusqu’à ce que les réparations soient effectuées.
Un connecteur électrique mal étanchéifié
Le dysfonctionnement provient directement de la pompe à eau du véhicule. La NHTSA précise dans un communiqué qu’un connecteur électrique mal étanchéifié sur la pompe à eau peut se retrouver exposé à l’eau et provoquer un court-circuit, ce qui augmente le risque d’incendie. Cette alerte concerne une bonne partie de la gamme du constructeur allemand : les BMW Série 3, Série 5, X1, X3, Série 2 Coupé, Série 3 Break et Série 2 Cabriolet.
À lire : Jusqu’à 828 km d’autonomie : le nouveau BMW iX4 prend l’avantage sur ses concurrents
Pour les conducteurs concernés, la NHTSA indique qu’une solution est en cours d’élaboration et sera disponible gratuitement chez les concessionnaires BMW dès sa mise en service. À ce stade, le constructeur a déjà recensé une dizaine d’incidents susceptibles d’être liés à cette défaillance, même si aucune victime n’est heureusement à déplorer.
Une seconde intervention obligatoire et une série noire pour BMW
Cette campagne d’intervention prend une tournure particulièrement délicate pour l’entreprise bavaroise. L’agence américaine souligne en effet que les véhicules concernés avaient déjà été rappelés en 2024 pour ce même problème de pompe à eau et doivent aujourd’hui être réparés une nouvelle fois. De plus, la dizaine d’incidents recensés par BMW s’est produite exclusivement sur des véhicules qui avaient pourtant déjà été réparés lors de cette première vague.
À lire : Moins de 3 heures de recharge pour traverser toute l’Europe : l’exploit fou de la nouvelle BMW i3
C’est une vraie série noire pour le constructeur. En effet, en février dernier, BMW avait déjà dû rappeler 600 000 véhicules à travers le monde en raison d’un risque d’incendie causé par une pose défectueuse du faisceau de câbles du tableau de bord. Seulement deux semaines plus tôt, le groupe avait également confirmé le rappel de centaines de milliers d’exemplaires dotés d’un relais de démarreur présentant un risque de court-circuit et d’incendie.

articles.title: Researchers hijack Hugging Face account for popular Kokoro AI model
articles.text:
A Lack of ownership verification on the Hugging Face platform allowed researchers to take control of Kokoro, a text-to-speech model used in projects from Google, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Amazon Web Services.
An attacker hijacking the account could use it as a distribution channel in supply-chain attacks, potentially leading to data theft or code execution.
However, the researchers demonstrated a stealthier attack: they modified the model's weights so it produced audio that differed from the input text, without changing the underlying application code.
Because only the weights change, there is no malicious code or signature for malware scanners to detect, the researchers say.
"We changed what this model says by fine-tuning its neural weights. Same input text. Same voice file. Same configuration. Same inference code — not a single line touched in the application that runs it," said security researcher Alon Hertz.
Kokoro is an open-weight model that converts text into speech. It supports multiple languages and has more than 50 voice presets.
Although its developer, Hexgrad, has not pushed an update since April 2025, the project continues to be popular, with nearly 13 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face. The GitHub repository and the Python package on PyPI also went silent around the same time.
Kokoro is supported by developer tools from Google, NVIDIA, and Intel, including software for voice agents and on-device speech synthesis. AMD and Amazon Web Services have also published guides demonstrating its use in AI-agent workflows.
Hertz and his team took control of the Kokoro account on Hugging Face by simply registering the domain used by the original owner and resetting the login password.
Over the past weekend, the researchers registered the “hexgrad.com” domain listed on Kokoro’s public DONATE.md file and used it to perform a password reset on the publisher’s account.
They then ran a controlled test in which they modified Kokoro’s model weights in 87 seconds using a gaming GPU, causing the model to produce poisoned output.
Hertz says the team tested the modified Kokoro model locally using its normal inference pipeline, but never uploaded the modified weights to Hugging Face, as that would likely put at risk many production systems depending on the model.
The researcher underlines that an update would still carry all the hallmarks of a legitimate release, as tests from another account showed that Hugging Face would not flag anything as suspicious.
Despite the takeover, the publisher appeared the same, just like the file delivery route, the format, and the architecture. File sizes would be similar, and the release would contain no malware.
A broader trust problem
The researcher notes that the supply-chain risk from compromised publisher accounts distributing altered weights via routine updates to systems that automatically fetch new revisions is significant.
Kokoro was just a high-profile example the team used to highlight the issue.
Hertz says even non-hijacked accounts could pose a risk, as anyone can curate an ostensibly legitimate image for a period of time, then push a malicious update at some point.
“Hugging Face does not vet publishers. It doesn’t verify whether an account is still held by its original, legitimate owner — or by whoever quietly took it over last week. It doesn’t vet the models or datasets those accounts upload,” Hertz says.
“The same unvetted weights and datasets flow through mirrors and converted versions, GitHub releases, package registries, deployment guides, and direct downloads across the entire open-model ecosystem,” added the researcher.
Hertz reported the issue to Hugging Face, hoping for quick action, but received no response.
BleepingComputer has also contacted Hugging Face for comments, but we have not received a response yet.

articles.title: Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
articles.text:
Elastic
View Brand Publisher
Elastic{ON} Mumbai: Why context, not the model, is the real AI advantage
At Elastic{ON} Mumbai, CEO Ash Kulkarni argued that every business already owns what AI models lack. The rest of the day showed what it takes to put that context to work.
As AI models become available to everyone, the advantage for enterprises is shifting to something no model providers can supply: the context that makes AI useful to a specific business. Elastic{ON} Mumbai took on that challenge, bringing together the people building and running AI in India’s enterprises to work out how to make their data count.
The Elastic{ON} Tour 2026/2027 stopped in Mumbai on September 30, bringing developers, SREs, IT and security leaders and practitioners to JW Marriott Mumbai Sahar under the theme ‘Forge the Future’. Across keynotes, live demos, customer and partner sessions, and a hackathon awards ceremony, one idea kept returning: context is what turns a widely available model into a lasting business advantage.
Context is your moat
Ash Kulkarni, CEO of Elastic, who grew up a short distance away in Vile Parle, opened by tying the company’s name to the city. “Mumbai has stretched, it has evolved, it has transformed. It has never broken,” he said.
That adaptability matters, he argued, because AI is moving faster than any earlier technology shift, and the models driving it share a blind spot. “None of these models have any understanding of your business. They don’t understand your data,” Kulkarni said. “The bottleneck is the context.”
Every industry now faces startups trading human capital for token capital. What they cannot copy, Kulkarni said, is a company’s accumulated learnings, experience, and data on how best to serve its customers and partners. “That context is your moat.”
The challenge is that context is scattered. Customer information alone sits across CRM, entitlement, and ticketing systems. Kulkarni’s answer is a bridge that connects it all, securely and with privacy built in, to any model. The result, he said, is “actual intelligence”: the reasoning power of the model combined with the context of the business. Delivering that has meant evolving Elastic’s core engine.
Making context affordable
Ajay Nair, GM, Elasticsearch and Platform, Elastic, picked up the thread. “The model’s only half the equation,” he said. An agent that does not know a customer has raised ten support tickets might still send them a renewal pitch, and that will not go well.
Nair said most teams make their models rebuild context from scratch every time a question is asked, an approach he called “top-down” context that burns tokens on every query. The more efficient pattern is “bottom-up”: deriving relationships, metadata, and risk factors once, keeping them fresh, and handing models a ready-made picture.
That is the idea behind the Elastic Context Engine, which Nair announced on stage and which is now in private preview.
Context at work in operations and security
The same foundation runs through Elastic’s observability and security solutions. Vinay Chandrasekhar, Director of Product Management, Observability, Elastic, demonstrated Elastic nightshift AI SRE, an AI agent that surfaces problems no alert was set up to catch, tests several root-cause hypotheses in parallel, and shows every step of its reasoning. Kulkarni noted that it gets better at investigating “within the context of your environment”, adding: “It’s not generic.” Elastic has since announced nightshift in private preview on Elastic Observability Serverless.
James Spiteri, Senior Director of Product Management, Elastic, argued that “the SIEM has never mattered more”. He previewed what has since launched as AlertZero, the agentic layer built into Elastic Security. Specialised groups of agents, called Watches, triage alerts, hunt for threats, and investigate incidents, learning from how a team already works, while analysts decide which actions need their approval. AlertZero is now available in technical preview across Elastic Cloud, self-managed, and air-gapped environments.
A day built with the community
Beyond the keynotes, customers carried much of the program. On the morning panel, moderated by Ravindra Ramnani, Head of Field Engineering at Elastic India, leaders from Axis Bank, Standard Chartered Bank, and Easebuzz debated whether enterprises can observe, audit, and explain what their AI agents do. Nykaa joined AWS to describe how its SREs now investigate incidents by querying logs conversationally with Elastic AI Assistant. Afternoon breakouts featured Network18 on AI governance, Qualys on closing the SOC loop with agentic AI, and Standard Chartered Bank on standardising observability across 40 countries, alongside community sessions from Iron Mountain, Jolera, and Sprinklr.
Partners showed how they ground AI in enterprise context. Google Cloud explained how its agent tooling and Gemini models work with Elastic retrieval to turn sensitive enterprise data into trusted context without moving it. Microsoft and Elastic walked through OverflowAI, Stack Overflow’s retrieval-first architecture, in which Elasticsearch hybrid retrieval grounds Azure OpenAI in the community’s validated answers.
The community also had its moment on the main stage, as the Forge the Future Hackathon awards recognised the top teams from the Grand Finale held in Bengaluru on September 18 and 19. Frustrated Engineers took first place, followed by Sandboxed in second and Defcon in third. Powered by Elastic and AWS, the hackathon challenged teams to build explainable, production-ready AI agents across search, observability, and security.
Models will change. Context stays.
Kulkarni closed with commitments that put a customer’s context, not any single model, at the centre. Elastic will stay model agnostic, he said, because “there is no winner yet, and there will likely never be a single winner.” It will also run wherever customers do, in the cloud or self-managed.
Models will keep getting better. The context that makes them useful belongs to the business, and Elastic{ON} Mumbai made the case that connecting the two is where the lasting advantage lies.
