articles.title: How Ubini is teaching machines to understand Edo language
articles.text:
When Stephanie Ohumu’s grandmother died in 2023, she took with her recipes the family could no longer recreate, words Ohumu relied on her to explain, and cultural knowledge that had never been written down.
“It used to be that if I encountered Edo words in the wild, I’d text my grandma or call her and she would translate for me,” Ohumu said. “Not just that, there are meals we cannot make the way we grew up eating them because they were never written down and we don’t know how to make them. All of that went away.”
Her grandmother’s death made Ohumu, a journalist and artificial intelligence expert, realise how much Edo culture existed only in the memories of older people, with little preserved for future generations. “Language is a repository of knowledge. It took my grandmother dying for me to really understand that,” she said.
The loss also raised questions about how languages like Edo, a language spoken by an estimated 2 million people across seven local government areas in Edo State, southwestern Nigeria, would survive in an increasingly digital world. Ohumu worried that the lack of reliable digital material would leave such languages poorly represented in artificial intelligence (AI) systems, increasing the risk of convincing but inaccurate translations and responses.
These concerns led her to found Ubini in 2024. The bootstrapped company is building a digital corpus of Edo oral histories, recipes and other cultural heritage. It aims to preserve knowledge that might otherwise disappear while creating machine-readable data for language technology and source material for films, books and other creative works.
Ubini has interviewed about 20 people and transcribed more than 20 hours of recordings. It has also produced Mia Mia, a 27-minute documentary featuring Maria Evbagharu Osazee, an 85-year-old woman reflecting on her life and the cultural loss she has witnessed.
The gap in African-language data
Africa has more than 2,000 languages, but few have the digital resources needed for natural language processing. Many are underrepresented in AI training datasets, leaving developers with little material to build tools that understand or communicate in languages such as Edo.
A 2026 study by Kedir Hussen and six other researchers, published in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, examined large and small language models’ support for African languages. It identified 41 African languages supported by the models and 23 publicly available datasets, finding that more than 98% of African languages were unsupported.
Ohumu said tests of existing AI models showed that their Edo responses could sound convincing while containing inaccurate translations.
“Claude can write a convincing enough cosplay of Edo, but it fills it with a lot of nonsense,” she said. “It’s really dangerous because if you don’t know the language, you wouldn’t know that.”
In one example, a model translated “download” as “D-A-N-L-O-D”, reproducing an English pronunciation instead of providing an Edo equivalent. Ohumu described it as a parody of how an Edo speaker might pronounce the word.
She attributes such errors partly to the limited Edo material available online.
“I’ve done extensive research on this, and there’s probably stuff I haven’t seen yet,” she said. “The largest one is, oddly enough, Jehovah’s Witness. They have translations of the Bible and other devotional books in the language.”
Some existing materials, she found, were also heavily influenced by English. “It’s like seeing Pidgin English being passed off as English. So there’s a lot of Anglicising happening,” she said.
For Ohumu, language loss also erodes vital knowledge. She recalled reading a study about indigenous communities where understanding of a plant’s medicinal value existed in only one language.
“So when that language goes extinct, our understanding of what that plant can do as well dies,” she said.
The shortage of reliable data also affects AI development. Edo is tonal, so differences in tone markings can change a word’s meaning. Models trained on incomplete or inaccurate material risk reproducing errors in translations and generated speech.
Ohumu believes a reliable Edo dataset could support practical applications, including voice-based services for people more comfortable communicating in the language. She cited financial services that would let market women carry out banking transactions through audio commands in Edo.
Such applications depend on verified language data—the precise gap Ubini is setting out to address.
Building an archive
The decision to focus on Edo is both personal and practical. Ohumu said she grew up in Benin City and has community connections across Edo State, giving Ubini access to people with specialised knowledge and making it easier to organise recordings without the cost of entering an unfamiliar market.
The company focuses on people over 70 years old who speak Edo as their first or main language, capturing everyday conversations, ceremonial speech and knowledge no longer widely shared. Its current collection covers people’s life experiences and food, including recipes, ingredients and the stories behind particular meals.
“We want everyday speech, but we also really want ceremonial speech as well,” Ohumu said. “And we also really want knowledge that is already outside of the mainstream.”
Ubini deliberately seeks diverse contributors to avoid disproportionately representing particular backgrounds, dialect groups or communities. For its current food collection, it is concentrating on women, who Ohumu said have historically been responsible for much of the cooking. Future collections will cover bead-making, traditional guilds and wood carving.
Ohumu estimates that Ubini needs at least 250 individuals, with an average of two hours of recordings each, to capture a broader range of speakers and knowledge.
The company works in quarterly research sprints, selecting a subject for each collection before identifying potential contributors. Researchers approach people in communities where the team has existing connections, explain the project and seek their participation.
Consent is central to the process. “It makes no sense to be documenting your culture if you’re going to be disrespectful to the custodians of it,” Ohumu said. “Sometimes people say no, and you have to leave it at that.”
Researchers also record contributors’ ages, occupations and backgrounds to establish whose knowledge the archive represents.
After the interviews, researchers manually transcribe conversations in Edo and translate them into English.
“Edo is a tonal language, so depending on where you put the markings, the meanings can differ greatly,” Ohumu said. Each initial transcription undergoes quality assurance by two University of Benin professors, who review and correct the text.
Finding people proficient in written Edo has proved difficult. Fluency in speaking the language does not necessarily translate into accurate writing, while automated tools such as Whisper and Granola have fallen short.
“The transcription is a lot harder than I thought it would be,” Ohumu said. “I knew it was going to be difficult because our languages are oral. It means that even people who have a very high proficiency in it cannot write it.”
Ubini currently has three transcribers working with its lead researcher, Elliot. The team also searches for out-of-print books and visits university libraries to study Edo grammar, word origins and spelling conventions.
Ohumu had expected a larger pool of people proficient in written Edo. Although she had read about a state government initiative to train young people to write the language, she discovered it had been discontinued.
“So that pipeline of people who are proficient in writing it wasn’t significantly built,” she said. “I do think that to scale, I will have to build this.”
She plans to train more transcribers as the project grows, particularly because poor initial drafts require repeated corrections before entering the archive.
Ubini aims to collect 50 hours of audio by December 2026. It hopes to have 150 hours transcribed and translated by the end of 2027, supported by 30 transcribers, and to build a 250-hour corpus by 2029.
The finished material is organised into XML files containing speaker turns, Edo transcriptions, English translations and information about contributors and recording contexts. Ohumu eventually wants to include phonetic transcriptions, but for now, her priority is documenting the language while its most fluent speakers are still alive.
“The first bit is just finding the people who speak it before they die and getting it out in a machine-readable version,” she said.
From language data to stories
For Ohumu, preserving Edo is only the beginning of Ubini’s ambition. She believes the language holds cultural knowledge and stories that can be developed into films, books and other media products
“The entire point of the company is this thesis: I think that within my language and all of the knowledge that it holds, there’s a repository of media IP,” she said. “It’s insanely valuable. And I think it’s untapped.”
She compares the opportunity to South Korea before K-dramas and K-pop gained international popularity, believing Edo culture holds stories that could reach wider audiences if developed and told well.
Ubini has begun exploring that possibility with Mia Mia, a 26-minute documentary about Maria Evbagharu Osazee, an elderly Edo speaker who reflects on the cultural changes she has witnessed throughout her lifetime. The film’s title is an Edo expression meaning “to forget”.
Ohumu said the documentary emerged from a research visit to a village to document Osazee’s knowledge.
“We were in the community to talk to the woman and her story was amazing, and I was like, okay, let’s make a film out of this,” she said.
Mia Mia premiered at the Uncolonial Film Festival in Germany in August 2026 before being selected for the Human Screen Festival in Tunisia in November, where it had its African premiere. It is also scheduled for its Nigerian premiere at the Kano Indigenous Languages of Africa Film Market and Festival later in November.
The film also enriches Ubini’s archive, with raw footage—including conversations excluded from the final cut—added to the dataset. The material serves two purposes: preserving the language and providing source material for creative work.
“The creative economy bits can’t be a thing that happens when we have a large enough corpus that makes sense,” she said. “It has to happen as we are doing it. And I think that one of the entry points that has the least barrier to entry is food.”
For Ohumu, the opportunity lies in developing stories from a culture she believes mainstream media has underrepresented. “I’m not building an app, I’m building stories, stories that don’t currently exist because we’re not speaking the language the way we should and the way they are stored,” she said.
Finding a sustainable model
Ohumu sees licensing Edo-language data as Ubini’s quickest route to revenue, but believes media products will provide more sustainable income in the long run.
“I do think that licensing is the lower-hanging fruit. Absolutely,” she said. “But I do think that the bulk of the sustainable funding will come from media products, whether that be selling a strong enough story to Netflix or Prime or EbonyLife, or developing it ourselves.”
Ubini has been self-funded since it began in 2024. Keeping costs down has depended on building within her existing networks and areas of experience.
“If you build at home and if you build around your circle of competence and if you build in industries where you’ve stayed for a bit, it really cuts down the cost,” she said.
Yet the project is reaching a point where that approach is becoming harder to sustain. The biggest expense so far has been transcribing and verifying the recordings.
“All that we’ve done so far, I can comfortably fund, but we’re starting to reach the point where it’s not as comfortable anymore,” Ohumu said. “The really expensive layer has been transcription and that QA process, to be very honest with you.”
She is now seeking funding to expand Ubini’s work. Whatever form it takes, she wants capital that gives the project room to grow without pressure for immediate returns.
“I’ll have non-equity diluting 200k. That’s important to me. Or even if it is an investment instead of a donation, it’ll be patient money. There’s no other way this works,” she said.
Over the next year, Ohumu plans to expand the team, improve transcription quality, and collect and transcribe an additional 100 hours of audio as Ubini works towards its 2027 and 2029 corpus targets.
For Ohumu, however, the work is bigger than the prospect of building a profitable company. She said she would continue preserving Edo even if Ubini never made money.
“Even if this company doesn’t make one naira, I’m still going to do this anyway,” she said. “That’s how strongly I believe in it.”

articles.title: Los robots humanoides de Xiaomi trabajan un turno completo de ocho horas en su fábrica de coches eléctricos
articles.text:
Xiaomi ha publicado un vídeo en X en el que dos de sus robots humanoides cubren un turno de ocho horas en su fábrica de coches eléctricos, clasificando los embellecedores laterales de la consola central. Según la compañía lo han hecho por su cuenta, detectando y corrigiendo sus propios fallos sobre la marcha, y de ser real su autonomía estaríamos ante una notable demostración.
Ocho horas en la línea. Xiaomi publicó el vídeo el 3 de noviembre de 2026, el mismo día en que la compañía recogía dos premios en Wuzhen, en la Conferencia Mundial de Internet. En las imágenes se ve a los robots sacando las piezas de unos contenedores y colocándolas en los huecos de unos estantes, con un contador del tiempo de trabajo acumulado y rótulos que marcan el vídeo como autónomo y acelerado hasta 100 veces.
Según Xiaomi, los robots cubrieron toda la producción diaria que necesitaba ese puesto, coordinándose además con el sistema de control de la línea, y la empresa lo presenta como un paso más hacia su uso en la industria. Vamos, que el escenario es un puesto de trabajo real de la fábrica.
El tercer paso del programa. Es el tercer hito de un programa que Xiaomi lleva todo el año enseñando en público. En marzo puso a sus humanoides de “becarios” en su fábrica de Pekín, colocando tuercas autorroscantes, y anunció una tasa de éxito del 90,2% durante tres horas seguidas, con un ritmo suficiente para cumplir el ciclo de 76 segundos de ese puesto. En julio aseguró haber subido esa tasa al 98% y añadió dos puestos más complicados, entre ellos el de clasificar estas mismas piezas.
A finales de 2025 el consejero delegado de Xiaomi, Lei Jun, ya avanzó que la compañía desplegaría robots humanoides a gran escala en sus fábricas en un plazo de cinco años. Además, Xiaomi ha anunciado que su modelo de IA de código abierto Xiaomi-Robotics-1, entrenado con más de 100.000 horas de datos de manipulación del mundo real, ha empezado a En una de esas pruebas trabajó más de 30 minutos seguidos, recorrió tres habitaciones y encadenó más de 50 tareas.
¿Cuánto hay de autónomo? Xiaomi no ha dicho cuántas piezas clasificaron los robots, qué tasa de acierto tuvieron durante las ocho horas ni cuántas veces tuvo que intervenir una persona, unas lagunas que también señala Interesting Engineering. Tampoco explicó en su publicación cómo se mantuvieron con batería durante todo el turno. Eso sí, el propio vídeo da una pista, porque según la agencia china CLS, los robots pararon dos veces a cargar, a las tres horas y dos minutos y a las seis horas y tres minutos de trabajo acumulado, y uno de los rótulos de Xiaomi marca el equipo como “en carga”.
Y todo esto importa porque “autónomo” en un vídeo de robots puede significar casi cualquier cosa. Los Optimus de Tesla que se vieron en el evento We, Robot de 2024 estaban en parte controlados a distancia por persona, y Tesla no lo reconoció hasta después del evento. A principios de diciembre de 2025, otro Optimus se cayó en una demostración en Miami llevándose las manos a la cabeza, como haría un teleoperador al quitarse unas gafas de realidad virtual.
Para ser justos con Xiaomi, la empresa publicó tasas de éxito y tiempos de ciclo de sus pruebas anteriores, algo que va más allá de lo que Tesla ha contado nunca sobre el rendimiento de Optimus en tareas reales. De hecho, Tesla no prevé entregar Optimus a clientes externos hasta finales de 2027, aproximadamente.
Atentos a las ruedas. Uno de los momentos más interesantes del vídeo llega hacia el minuto 1:37. En un fragmento que Xiaomi titula como “material caído, colaboración entre varios robots”, un torso humanoide montado sobre una base con ruedas se acerca a echar una mano a los dos robots con piernas, y según el relato de CLS lo hace para recoger una pieza que se le había caído a uno de ellos.
Y no es lo único que va sobre ruedas en esa escena, porque los contenedores de piezas los mueven robots móviles autónomos, el mismo tipo de plataformas que llevan años transportando material en las fábricas de coches.
En cualquier caso, si la demostración fue realmente autónoma durante ocho horas con los robots resolviendo sus propios errores, es una de las más impresionantes que se han visto con humanoides, aunque siempre hay que tener prudencia.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
- November 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
- A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Petri Jalanko, Marja H. Leppänen, Bert Bond, Jari A. Laukkanen, Timo A. Lakka, Eero A. Haapala. Associations of Physical Activity and Sedentary Time From Childhood to Adolescence With Cognition in Adolescence: The PANIC Study. Pediatric Exercise Science, 2026; 38 (3): 268 DOI: 10.1123/pes.2025-0083

articles.title: Pretxt Emerges Stealth With $5M Seed and an AI Supervision Tool
articles.text:
Pretxt, with offices in Aspen, CO, and Dublin, Ireland, has emerged from stealth with $5 million seed funding raised from Deciens Capital, Howdy Partners and Service Provider Capital. Pretxt enters the emerging category of firms providing technology to prevent AI agents escaping their guardrails and causing unintended harm.
AI is more like a person than like traditional computer code: it doesn’t simply run; it receives, interprets, misinterprets and responds to ambiguous instructions. It is the combination of misinterpretation and wide agency of response that results in AI agents going rogue and potentially causing harm.
Since it is impossible to categorically exclude ambiguity in language (which is how we instruct the agents), our only alternative method of controlling them is to limit their agency. But too stringent a limitation of agency could become an unacceptable restriction on a potentially huge business benefit.
So, without a new category of supervision control, it is likely that we cannot have beneficial AI agents without also having potentially dangerous rogue agents. This requirement for a new control is leading to the emergence of a type of cybersecurity product that attempts to recognize a potentially harmful agentic action at runtime and control it before it can cause harm.
Pretxt is announcing just such a product which it describes as AI Supervision, “a purpose-built runtime technology to supervise AI agents as they work, guiding them back on course before mistakes become business consequences.”
Rather than neutering the capability of an agent, explains Aaron Costello, Pretxt co-founder and CTO, “We say, ‘Okay, you give an AI agent the same level of access as an authorized employee, and we will continuously monitor the manner in which it interacts with systems and other people. We will validate and ensure that all such interaction conforms with your business standards and operates in the same way that you expect your employees to operate.”
If the agent exceeds its expected authority or deviates from its authorized purpose, Pretxt doesn’t simply shut it down – it ‘steers’ the offender back on track. It’s a bit like having an experienced supervisor permanently on the shoulder of a trainee, who just steps in when necessary, with, “Don’t do it like that, do it like this instead.”
‘Steering’ is governed by context, continues Costello. “We ask new customers to onboard and connect their AI agent to our product, so we can immediately see the agent’s instructions and understand its purpose. As we watch it in operation, we learn how it speaks. We see what tools it can access, and we learn what abilities it has been given – such as ‘send’ an email, ‘post’ to LinkedIn, or ‘update’ a database.”
The customer then explains to Pretxt, I never want my AI agent to do x, or I only want my agent to do y, or see this kind of data. “It could be anything,” adds Costello. “The information is imported into Pretxt’s own AI. It becomes the context for acceptable behavior and is hooked into anywhere within the agent that could potentially violate the agent’s intended purpose and constraints.”
He gives the example of a customer service agent used by a medical practice to help patients book an appointment. Pretxt may have been told by the medical practice, ‘I never want this agent to give medical advice.’ “What we do,” he continues, “is hook into every single occasion the AI agent interacts with the user. Our own agent will look at this interaction and check whether it contains medical advice. This is done in real time. If it does contain medical advice (which we know should not be offered), we prevent it. But not by shutting down the agent, because that would leave patients unable to book appointments. We use a different approach that we call ‘steering’. If we detect medical advice, we invisibly talk back to the agent and effectively tell it, ‘You tried to give medical advice. Please continue to help the user with their booking request, but do not attempt to give medical advice again’.”
This is the purpose of Pretxt’s AI supervision app – not to shut down wanton AI agents, but to keep them safe, and prevent them straying from their predefined constraints.
Related: US Agencies Detail Incident Response Practices for Rogue AI Agents

articles.title: Seattle police bomb squad buys $360,000 Spot robot dog, already planning to get a second
articles.text:
What just happened? Boston Dynamics' quadrupedal robot, Spot, continues to find work in law enforcement. Rather than a Black Mirror-style machine of mass destruction, the robotic dog is now being used by Seattle police's arson/bomb squad. It cost the department $360,000, and it plans on buying another one.
The Seattle Police Department (SPD) writes that Spot was purchased with Federal Emergency Management Agency grant funding approved by the Seattle City Council in April 2026. The approval was granted after the robot was assessed for potential privacy and security risks.
The SPD notes that Spot is a lot lighter, nimbler, and easier to maneuver than the bomb squad's five other robots, which traverse on treads. Spot's ability to climb stairs is going to be a big advantage over the older robots.
Using Spot's robotic arm, an operator can locate a door handle, open the door, and send the robot into a room containing a suspected explosive without anyone having to enter. The operator can then manually control the arm to lift the device and place it in a safe container. The entire process can be carried out from nearly a mile away, keeping both the operator and the public at a safer distance.
The introduction of Spot, which also packs a 360-degree camera and a microphone, has raised familiar concerns about weaponized robots and AI making life-or-death decisions. But Seattle police said Spot can't be equipped with weapons, doesn't use AI to make independent decisions, and doesn't use facial recognition tech.
Police spokesperson Detective Shane Weatherford said the plans to buy a second Spot robot were already in the works. The SPD never said how many times the current Spot has been deployed, why it needs a second unit, or how it will pay for the next robot.
Police officials said the device would address unspecified "critical gaps" in equipment needed for detecting dangerous objects and preventing terrorism, according to a city record.
The Seattle Times highlights the $360,000 this Spot model costs and the apparent lack of specifics from the SPD about why the price was justified or how often it's being used. Buying another of these robots, which will push the total bill to almost three-quarters of a million dollars, will likely raise plenty of eyebrows.
This isn't Spot's first deployment in a law enforcement setting. In 2019, the Massachusetts State Police bomb squad leased one of the robots for use as a "mobile remote observation device."
The NYPD deployed a heavily modified Spot known as Digidog in 2020. It led to plenty of backlash, so the NYPD terminated its $94,000 lease in 2021, only to bring Digidog back two years later.
More recently, it was reported that ICE wants to spend up to $2 million on Spot robots.

articles.title: Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Responsible AI for agentic AI: A phased roadmap for platform and application teams
Companies build agentic AI platforms to govern the applications, tools, skills, models, and storage that agents use. The nondeterministic nature of generative AI models introduces a complexity that previous software development practices didn’t anticipate. Consider a real estate app that generates property listings from retrieved data: does it accurately reflect the property, or hallucinate features that don’t exist? Or a customer service agent grounded on internal knowledge bases: can you verify that it doesn’t surface confidential information?
Until recently, responsible AI (RAI) was model-centric, scoped to the machine learning development lifecycle: training, testing, and inference. Models didn’t reason, use tools, or take actions. When the conversation extended to model-powered systems, it covered statistically bounded situations you could test against known inputs. Generative AI powered applications and agents changed this. The systems now reason, act, compose tools dynamically, and interact over multiple steps, expanding both the scope and the depth of what responsible AI must cover.
Organizations are turning Responsible AI, which includes the pillars of security and privacy, veracity and robustness, fairness, safety, controllability, explainability, transparency, and governance into a growth strategy by addressing its expanding scope early. When enterprises adopt agentic AI at scale, the positive and negative impacts come hand in hand. As Wade and Wirtz observe in the Harvard Business Review, trust is becoming a competitive differentiator. The same capabilities that personalize at scale can also surveil and discriminate, and organizations that govern them earn stakeholder confidence. Robinhood, for example, built a generative AI financial crimes agent on Amazon Bedrock with strict data governance. They achieved a 20% efficiency gain while maintaining regulatory compliance. Structuring these practices across platform maturity is the next step. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Application teams. Application teams, sometimes called Workstream teams, build and own agents on the platform.
This post provides a condensed, actionable roadmap for the Platform team and Application teams building on agentic AI. It’s designed to be read together: the Platform team sets up the guardrails. Application teams build within them. Both need a shared language for where they are and what good looks like. We provide a Responsible AI Assessment Skill, that maps the AWS Responsible AI Lens pillars to a three-phase maturity model: governance foundations, pilot deployment, and evaluation and hardening. For each phase, it shows which responsible AI pillars are critical and when to revisit them. An accompanying scorecard lets both application teams and the platform team assess where they are today and iterate as their applications mature.
Note: This post covers the key questions to ask at each phase. It leaves out step-by-step implementation details. This post also doesn’t provide legal or compliance advice. Always consult your legal team.
The challenge
In conversations with customers building agentic AI platforms, four challenges surface consistently.
- Unpredictable runtime behavior: nondeterministic outputs, goal drift, and cascading failures where one agent error propagates across services. A financial services company in Germany found that multi-agent orchestration amplified a single misclassification into policy violations across three downstream services.
- Data exposure and authority boundaries: Scope every agent to its intended tenants, data, systems, and actions. Isolate session context so each session starts with data residency at the access layer, and grant privileged access through least-privilege, task-bound permissions that agents can’t modify themselves. Agents then act only in the systems and with the authority they were explicitly given.
- Regulatory velocity: EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, and upcoming legislation are creating compliance requirements faster than governance can adapt. Proving compliance for nondeterministic systems requires continuous evaluation, which should be monitored and revisited with a predefined cadence (for example, daily, weekly, or monthly).
- Team collaboration: organizations lack a shared framework defining who owns what across the agent lifecycle. A media company in the UK flagged that segregation of duty between developer and deployment teams is undefined for agent workloads. The Platform team builds guardrails that application teams work around, and application teams defer responsibility they assume the platform handles.
Solution: A three-phase responsible AI maturity framework
In this post, we define an agentic AI platform as described in AgentOps: Operationalize agentic AI at scale with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a system for building, deploying, and operating AI agents securely at scale, covering governance, build and operations, evaluation, and observability. Your responsible AI posture should mature progressively alongside this platform. We break the journey into three phases and present prioritized responsible AI pillars across a customizable 12-week implementation timeline, allowing the platform team to establish a solid responsible AI foundation while their first use cases take shape.
Phase 1: Governance foundation
Focus pillars: Governance, security and privacy
In this phase, assess project fit, risks, and ethics, secure legal and compliance approvals, and define the trust model for AI agents. The application teams classify risks for each planned use case using a risk rubric. The Platform team focuses on establishing the core landing zone infrastructure, for example, setting up the overarching monitoring and access control, and governing newly onboarded agents and use cases from the start.
Critical tasks to consider in this phase include:
Security and privacy
- Evaluate access to data and systems needed by each agent and assess potential impact. This lays the foundation for the knowledge grounding strategy.
- Implement foundational data security and data exfiltration protection with data classification, data access control, logging, data integrity, and data access monitoring.
- Build a map of the data that is shared between agents like organizational knowledge bases and the subjective data like context graphs which individual agents might need. Then establish access boundaries and assign read/write permissions accordingly.
Governance
- Define a risk classification rubric aligned to your regulatory obligations (EU AI Act risk tiers, financial services industry requirements, and so on). Assign Low / Medium / High / Unacceptable risk levels to each planned use case and document the control requirements each risk level triggers. Gather relevant documentation and traceability requirements.
- Before onboarding agents, the underlying models need to go through a vetting procedure. The procedure covers a series of evaluations with safety and reliability criteria. Catalog approved models based on capability, latency, and cost.
- Implement a process to centrally register and govern products like agents, shared tools and skills deployed in your organization for centralized visibility and consumption. Every product gets registered with owner, risk tier, and regulatory scope. If a resource (agent, tool, skill) isn’t in the registry, it can’t be discovered and managed by the organization.
Phase 2: Pilot deployment
Focus pillars: Safety, veracity and robustness, controllability, security and privacy
Deploy your first agent that serves measurable business value. With the template and developer guidance provided from the Platform team, application teams implement orchestration patterns, memory, guardrail baselines, knowledge grounding, and tool use patterns. Risks identified in the foundation phase must now be addressed through a set of concrete controls in a pilot implementation.
In this phase, application teams consider the following concerns:
Safety
- Guardrails. Platform team establishes foundational personally identifiable information (PII) redaction filters for model I/O and tool calls. Provide a set of guardrails rules ready to be applied. Application teams then set content moderation thresholds explicitly based on the use case the agent serves. Configure human escalation for low-confidence responses.
- Policies. Define which agent can access what tool and how. Augment with fallback scenarios in case of policy violations.
Veracity and robustness
- Knowledge grounding with checks: Even with the right context, models can still hallucinate or misrepresent the provided sources. Therefore, configure contextual grounding checks to verify every response is correctly grounded in relevant data. For regulated use cases, activate automated reasoning for verifiable outputs. Implement a process to curate and update your knowledge sources. Define how out-of-domain requests are classified and handled.
Controllability
- Implement a process for Human-in-the-loop approval for high-risk or on-behalf-of actions as circuit breakers. Define criteria for when an agent must defer to a human approver/reviewer (for example, confidence below threshold, safety guardrail triggered, or a high-stakes decision). Log escalation events for later audit and analysis.
- Provide permission audits to the end-user to grant/revoke access provided by human users or agents that granted permissions to sub-agents to gain transparent control.
- Activate end-to-end observability with session-level, trace-level, and span-level telemetry. Emit structured traces for agent decisions, guardrail invocations, and tool calls. Implement distributed tracing across multi-agent and multi-tool workflows to support full reconstruction of agent reasoning paths. Add dashboards for 360-degree observability and cost-control.
Security and privacy
- Establish least-privilege access controls. Define policy-based authorization rules for tool-level access using declarative policy languages. Apply granular access policies for agent actions and per knowledge source.
Phase 3: Evaluation and hardening
Focus pillars: Fairness, explainability, transparency, security and privacy
You have seen your first agent deliver business value. But how can you demonstrate it to a regulator, an auditor, or a board? How do you detect and help prevent unauthorized events on the system? In the third phase, evaluation stress-tests the fairness thresholds, and bias benchmarking. Hardening turns those findings into fixes.
This phase includes the following workstreams:
Fairness
- Model-level fairness testing: Check model cards for fairness metrics and restrict model access to a list of pre-approved models tested for common biases. In case there is no metric provided, test bias and alignment yourself using established benchmark sets such as Compositional Evaluation Benchmark (CEB) or Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM). Monitor whether outputs and routing treat demographic groups equitably.
- Agent-level fairness testing: Evaluate whether end-to-end agent routing, including tool selection, and resource allocation treats user groups equitably.
- Fairness regression monitoring: Set up automated pipelines to detect fairness drift over time as models are updated or new data sources are added.
Transparency
- Enforceable transparency for machine generated content: Attach machine-readable provenance labels to every reusable output, so downstream consumers can verify origin. Enforce mandatory AI-presence disclosure in user-facing interactions.
- Decision audit trails: Each agent action is logged with enough detail to reconstruct the reasoning path for a given outcome. For instance, what did the agent access, when and with which identity.
Explainability
- Compile an audit report for a fictional audit or appeal: Make sure you can quickly assemble the relevant data and understand how a decision was made.
- User-facing explanations: Provide end-users with on-demand, plain-language summaries of why an agent took a specific action or made a recommendation.
Security and privacy
- Continuous evaluation: Set up evaluation pipelines and evaluate before and after deployment. Document the results. Implement alerting mechanisms to be notified when metrics fall below a predefined quality threshold.
- Conduct penetration testing and red-team evaluations targeting agent-specific threat models: prompt injection, tenant isolation under concurrent access, token exchange with misconfigured profiles, and long-running async agent tasks. Define a Security Incident Response runbook specific to AI agent safety events. Configure automated alerting for safety-critical events.
- Fine-tune release criteria (evaluation scores, security scan results, fairness metrics) iteratively based on production feedback. Build deployment gates into your continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline. Nothing reaches production without meeting the release criteria for its risk tier.
When to revisit
Responsible AI isn’t a one-time implementation. As the platform evolves, each dimension must be periodically reassessed. The following table gives some examples to define both standing review cadences and event-driven triggers for re-evaluation.
| Standing Cadence | 
|  | 
| Triggers | 
|  | 
Example use case and implementation
Consider the following case: A bank builds a multi-agent loan processing platform. The platform features an intake agent, risk scoring agent, compliance agent, and customer communication agent.
Phase 1 (Governance foundation): The platform team gathers legal requirements for their use case, for example those stemming from the EU AI Act and financial regulation, and registers agents at High-risk tier (financial decisions affecting individuals) using the AWS Agent Registry. They use a secure landing zone built with AWS Control Tower with foundational logging and access control active and configure tenant isolation to help prevent cross-customer leakage. The team documents residual risk and scope for each agent: for example, if the intake agent produces unexpected data, the risk scoring agent processes its output without independent verification.
Phase 2 (Pilot deployment: Validation and rollout): Risk scoring uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases grounded in regulatory lending documentation. Automated Reasoning checks verify denial decisions conform to documented criteria (conformance, not causal explanation). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails redact PII data before customer communication. To address the multi-agent trust gap: the scoring agent confirms key applicant data from source systems rather than solely relying on the intake agent’s extraction. Each agent is bounded to required tools through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions, and the team uses Policies in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to further restrict the risk scoring agent to read-only access on the customer segment the agent is approved for. A case where the Automated Reasoning check returns a result other than VALID (for example, SATISFIABLE or TRANSLATION_AMBIGUOUS), or where the applicant’s risk score falls within the marginal band (for example, ±5 points of the threshold), is automatically escalated to a human credit specialist (human-in-the-loop review) before the decision is communicated. Escalation events are logged with the triggering condition for audit.
Phase 3 (Evaluation and hardening: Continuous monitoring): Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, run on every pipeline push. CI/CD blocks deployment if an evaluation result is below releasing criterion or per-subgroup fairness metrics drifts beyond threshold. Red-team exercises (independent security team) test realistic security threats on the intake agent to verify that it can’t influence scoring. Human review of denial decisions, moving to after-the-fact review through an appeals process after 2,000 aligned decisions over 60 days. AI usage in the decision process is disclosed transparently to customers. Every automated decision is traced end-to-end using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It captures OpenTelemetry spans that can be automatically aggregated into a single distributed trace ready for auditing and appeals.
How to measure maturity
Frameworks serve as aspirations, while measurements provide accountability. Questions like “Can you list the risk tier for a use case?” will necessarily arise when the platform is operational from stakeholders like CISOs or auditors. To leave you prepared, we provide a repository with a set of questions that you can use to gauge your current posture and identify improvement areas before your system goes live.
We also package the questionnaire as a portable skill for AI Agents like Amazon Quick, and AI coding assistants like Kiro, Claude Code, and Codex. The AI walks you through each phase and assesses your responsible AI posture along the dimensions on a scale from 1–5. Scores below 4 indicate substantial risks that should be remediated. Scores of 4 or higher indicate residual risk that might be acceptable when acknowledged on a case-by-case basis. The AI also provides actionable recommendations for improving your Responsible AI posture.
Conclusion
Responsible AI (RAI) is a continuous, evolving effort. We recommend organizations implement RAI pillars through the AgentOps journey. These best practices cover governance policies, evaluation gates, and production telemetry into agentic AI platforms. This creates the feedback loop that keeps fairness, safety, and transparency continuously measured and improved.
This framework is a starting point, not an exhaustive compliance checklist. RAI practices vary by industry, use case, and requirements. Organizations should consult their own legal, compliance, and ethics teams to tailor these recommendations to their specific regulatory obligations and risk profiles.
For a comprehensive treatment of responsible AI across workload types, refer to the AWS Well-Architected Responsible AI Lens, which provides detailed best practices, design principles, and evaluation criteria for each of the eight pillars discussed in this post. For industry-specific guidance, consult the Financial Services Industry Lens and the Healthcare Industry Lens, which address sector-specific regulatory and ethical requirements. Get started today by installing the RAI assessment skill from this repository and evaluating your organization’s RAI posture with your preferred AI agent.

articles.title: Moto G77 (256 GB) registra desconto agressivo de 40% na Black November • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Moto G77 (256 GB) registra desconto agressivo de 40% na Black November
Moto G77 conta com tela AMOLED de 5.000 nits, câmera principal de 108 MP e bateria prometida para até 37 horas de uso. Oferta com pagamento no Pix pelo Mercado Livre
O Moto G77 (256 GB) está em promoção com 40% de desconto no Mercado Livre. O smartphone sai por apenas R$ 1.509 no Pix em oferta na Black November 2026. Anunciado em março pela Motorola por R$ 2.499, se destaca pela ficha técnica equilibrada, com destaques para a tela brilhante e câmera principal de alta resolução.
O celular utiliza um painel Extreme AMOLED de 6,8″ que reproduz cores intensas, além de entregar resolução Super HD (superior ao Full HD) às imagens. O brilho máximo de 5.000 nits que o Moto G77 promete atingir em circunstâncias de baixa ou nenhuma luminosidade, sendo um dos mais fortes do segmento intermediário. Enquanto a taxa de 120 Hz assegura experiência fluida de modo geral.
O dispositivo traz uma câmera avançada de 108 MP. O sensor principal conta com estabilização óptica (OIS), zoom de 3x para manter a nitidez mesmo a distância, e recursos de IA via Moto AI. Na parte traseira, ainda há uma ultrawide de 8 MP. Enquanto a lente frontal de 32 MP, possui a função Detector de Sorrisos para aprimorar os resultados das selfies.
Equipado com o processador Dimensity 6400 e 8 GB de RAM física, o celular da Motorola com 256 GB de armazenamento entrega desempenho somente para tarefas básicas. Portanto, é mais voltado para usuários com pouco interesse para rodar jogos e executar multitarefas.
Em relação a construção, o celular utiliza uma carcaça de plástico combinado a certificação IP64, com resistência completa a poeira só que limitada a respingos d’água. Por outro lado, a certificação militar MIL-STD-810H garante a aprovação em condições extremas de pressão, temperatura e outras circunstâncias.
A bateria de 5.200 mAh sugere autonomia para mais de um dia de uso intenso, com promessa pela Motorola de até 37 horas de uso, incluindo reprodução de músicas e vídeos. O componente suporta apenas carregamento com fio de até 30 W.
O Moto G77 (256 GB) com promessa de atualizações até o sistema Android 19 está com 40% de desconto no Mercado Livre, por apenas R$ 1.509 no Pix.
A Black November segue até o dia 27 quando ocorre a Black Friday 2026, seguida pela Cyber Monday (30) que fecha o mês com as últimas ofertas. Confira na página do Achados as melhores ofertas de eletrônicos com a nossa curadoria e sem rabo preso!
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life
articles.text:
Fine art sculptor Natalie Rosen is seen at work for the California Science Center, shaping space shuttle Endeavour's external tank and other foam-covered components that are now debuting on display in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center/collectSPACE.com
Fine art sculptor Natalie Rosen is seen at work for the California Science Center, shaping space shuttle Endeavour's external tank and other foam-covered components that are now debuting on display in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center/collectSPACE.com
Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
She is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.
Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
The only fully authentic display of a space shuttle in its launch configuration opens to the public at the California Science Center in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
Credit:
California Science Center / ZGF Architects/Mike Kelley
The only fully authentic display of a space shuttle in its launch configuration opens to the public at the California Science Center in Los Angeles on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
Credit:
California Science Center / ZGF Architects/Mike Kelley
“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”
Rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.
ET-94
For those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.
The 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.
To protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too quickly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.)
The only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.
After the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.
Natalie Rosen shapes a foam ice frost ramp that was later installed in a series of ramps along the outside length of external tank ET-94 for the display of space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
Natalie Rosen shapes a foam ice frost ramp that was later installed in a series of ramps along the outside length of external tank ET-94 for the display of space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” said Rosen.
“Orange” peel
There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.
“It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.
By the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.
“And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen said.
Sculptor Natalie Rosen, poised atop a high platform in 2024, works on touch-ups to the foam on the forward intertank stringers for the external tank on vertical display with the space shuttle Endeavour in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
Sculptor Natalie Rosen, poised atop a high platform in 2024, works on touch-ups to the foam on the forward intertank stringers for the external tank on vertical display with the space shuttle Endeavour in the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
It was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”
“If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she said.
Replicating that pattern was not easy.
“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”
Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.
“She had to come up with a lot of new processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he said.
In the vertical
Some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.
“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen said. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”
Even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.
External tank restoration specialist Natalie Rosen applies close-out foam on external tank ET-94’s aft longeron area, preparing it for display with the space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
External tank restoration specialist Natalie Rosen applies close-out foam on external tank ET-94’s aft longeron area, preparing it for display with the space shuttle Endeavour at the California Science Center’s new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center in Los Angeles.
Credit:
California Science Center
Now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a new frontier.
“In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” said Rosen.
“So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she said.
The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

articles.title: Microsoft Releases .NET 11: C# 15 Union Types, Native AOT CLI Host, and CoreCLR by Default in MAUI
articles.text:
Last week, Microsoft has released .NET 11, the latest version of its development platform, together with C# 15, F# 11, ASP.NET Core 11, .NET MAUI, and Entity Framework Core 11. The release is a Standard Term Support (STS) version and will be supported for two years.
As stated in the announcement, .NET 10 remains the Long-Term Support option, while .NET 8 and .NET 9 reached end of support on the same day, November 10, 2026. The release coincided with this year's .NET Conf, held from November 10 to 13.
C# 15 is the default language version for projects that target .NET 11. It adds union types, declared with the union keyword, and the compiler checks switch expressions over them for exhaustiveness. Closed hierarchies limit derivation to the declaring assembly.
The language also gains collection expression arguments, extension indexers, and labeled break and continue statements, while the memory safety work stays in preview. F# 11, according to the release, lowers compiler memory use and reduces collection allocations in FSharp.Core.
In the SDK, the CLI now starts through a Native AOT host by default and keeps the MSBuild server warm between invocations. The dotnet test command gains run-level timeouts and failure limits, and container publishing can produce reproducible digests. In the runtime, Runtime Async remains a preview and is turned on with a feature flag.
The JIT removes more bounds checks and improves devirtualization. As described in the documentation, the release also raises the minimum hardware requirements, and the x86/x64 baseline moves to x86-64-v2.
The libraries add Zstandard compression to System.IO.Compression, new Process APIs for running a process and capturing its output, and four in-memory stream adapters. System.Text.Json supports C# unions and JSON Lines output, and LINQ gains a FullJoin operator.
ASP.NET Core 11 adds asynchronous validation and generates OpenAPI 3.2 documents by default, which the release notes list as a breaking change. SignalR can refresh authentication without reconnecting.
Blazor receives a CacheView component for static server-side rendering, client-side validation for static SSR forms, and an opt-in automatic circuit pause for inactive tabs. An experimental package with AI components for Blazor is also available.
.NET MAUI now uses CoreCLR as the default runtime, with Mono still available and Native AOT as an opt-in option. As reported, XAML Incremental Hot Reload is on by default for Debug builds, XAML namespace declarations are implicit, and the Microsoft.Maui.Controls.Compatibility package no longer ships.
Entity Framework Core 11 requires .NET 11. It generates fewer unnecessary joins, translates FullJoin, supports complex types and JSON columns with TPT and TPC inheritance, and adds experimental vector search for SQL Server.
Other changes in this release are the dotnet new mcpserver template, the dotnetup toolchain manager in public preview, .NET Skills for coding agents, opt-in modern visual styles in Windows Forms, and reliability fixes in WPF.
On Reddit, the reaction was mixed. Several developers welcomed union types as a replacement for hand-written result classes, and others said that .NET 11 and .NET 10 share the same end-of-support date.
The most upvoted comments argued that AI coding tools have made new releases feel less exciting. Other users criticized the code fix for non-exhaustive switch expressions and asked for the decimal conversion change to be more visible.
For interested readers, the full release notes and the list of breaking changes are available in the official .NET 11 documentation.

articles.title: Physical AI company Promise Robotics announces $40-million Series B round | BetaKit
articles.text:
A Toronto startup using AI and robotics to accelerate homebuilding has attracted $40 million CAD in Series B funding.
The news: Promise Robotics, which uses a combination of AI software and robotics to build modular, prefabricated homes, announced the closure of its Series B round on Tuesday. The round was led by White Star Capital, with additional participation from Horizons Ventures, Radical Ventures, and Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments).
From the source: “Homebuilding can’t scale on trade labour alone,” said Promise Robotics CEO and co-founder Ramtin Attar in a press release. “We’re building the production infrastructure the industry can scale on; a network of intelligent factories … this round lets us extend that network.”
The context: Promise Robotics uses AI to take building designs, break them into modular pieces, and then fabricate them via AI-controlled robotics. Those prefabricated pieces are then delivered to a construction site and assembled by crews of human workers. The company has factories in Calgary and near Edmonton in Nisku, Alta. It’s also planning an expansion south of the border in Phoenix and has signed deals with Texas’ D.R. Horton, a major residential developer in the US.
Promise Robotics plans to use the funding to expand its production infrastructure and research and development capacity. It also has plans to expand its workforce from 85 to more than 100 employees, according to reporting from The Globe and Mail.
Final thought: Access to affordable housing has been a persistent issue in Canada for decades, with the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) estimating that an undersupply of housing has driven up prices. Canada has reacted to that forecasting by pledging to build 500,000 new homes per year, though reporting from the Canadian Housing Research Network pegs the current rate of construction at closer to 200,000. Promise Robotics has pitched its model as a way to improve productivity, increase capacity, and accelerate construction timelines.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy of Promise Robotics.

articles.title: Jensen Huang says he would be 'honored' if allowed to return as Nvidia CEO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In the first public statement since his resignation, Nvidia founder Jensen Huang signaled his willingness to return as CEO if the board decides it is in the company’s best interest.
Huang’s statement, posted in full on X, reads as follows:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA. 
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO. 
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.
Jensen
Huang resigned after reports of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and another with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is suspected of working with Chinese intelligence services. Nvidia’s chip exports have faced intense scrutiny since the revelations, and Huang is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1.
In Huang’s absence, Nvidia has formed a new executive committee to oversee export control compliance.
Still, many investors and employees associated with Nvidia have called for Huang to return as CEO, at least until an investigation can provide clearer evidence of guilt. An open letter circulated earlier this week attracted the signatures of more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees, as well as prominent tech figures like Elon Musk, Amjad Masad, and Travis Kalanick.
“We are concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process,” the letter reads. “If the Board believes his continued absence is necessary, provide a specific, evidence-based explanation of why it serves NVIDIA’s best interests.”
Still, many see such a return as unlikely. On Monday, an unnamed source on Nvidia’s board told The Washington Post there were no plans to reinstate Huang. There’s also significant resistance to the idea in Congress, where Huang still faces significant questions about his role in chip exports to China-linked firms.
Reached by Politico, one senator called Huang’s reinstatement “one of the worst ideas I’ve heard today.”
