articles.title: Avec la Watch S5 41 mm, Xiaomi ouvre ses montres sous Hyper OS au paiement sans contact et sans restriction
articles.text:
Avec la Watch S5 41 mm, Xiaomi ouvre ses montres sous Hyper OS au paiement sans contact et sans restriction
Moins de six mois après sa Watch S5 au grand format 46 mm, Xiaomi pense aux petits poignets et décline sa montre en une version bien plus compacte. La Watch S5 41 mm adopte un positionnement un peu plus design et gagne surtout une fonction qui change la donne : la compatibilité avec Google Pay.
Il était temps. Si nous avons testé, au printemps 2026, la Watch S5 de Xiaomi, d’ailleurs réussie dans l’ensemble, nous avons relevé un point d’achoppement : sa puce NFC autorisait les paiements sans contact, mais seulement dans le cadre de rares partenariats, notamment avec Revolut. Changement de cap avec la déclinaison 41 mm de la tocante - vu son design, largement pensé pour un public féminin au petit poignet - qui prend en charge une fonction qui change la donne : Google Pay est au menu. Il devient donc possible de payer avec une carte Visa ou Mastercard, par exemple, depuis la Watch S5 41 mm.
Xiaomi Watch S5
Tournant sous HyperOS, ce qui lui permet d’ailleurs d’être connectée à un smartphone Android comme à un iPhone, la montre embarque un écran Oled niché dans un boîtier épais de 9,9 mm et pesant 36 g, dans la moyenne des appareils de son format. On apprécie le choix de matériaux respirant la qualité - un cadre en inox assorti d’une lunette en céramique - et, même si Xiaomi privilégie un système d’attache propriétaire, la déclinaison de ses bracelets en moutures plus ou moins sportives, allant du cuir au silicone.
Une montre polyvalente pensée pour le design
Cette montre polyvalente se veut assez sportive, sans aller jusqu’au raffinement des modèles les plus outdoor. Xiaomi promet le suivi de plus de 150 types d’activités et inclut à son appareil des capteurs standard dédiés à la mesure de la fréquence cardiaque et à celle du taux d’oxygène dans le sang. S’y ajoute bien sûr un GPS. Côté santé, pas d’ECG au menu, mais un suivi du stress et une surveillance du sommeil que le fabricant annonce plus précis que sur ses précédentes générations de montres.
L’atout de ce type de produit tient à son autonomie : si le nombre d’applications disponibles sur HyperOS reste limité, il se distingue par une endurance annoncée jusqu’à 14 jours. Mais aussi à son prix, contenu en soi : comptez 229 à 249 € selon la finition choisie… Néanmoins, la compacité, le design et le paiement sans contact imposent un surcoût à l’appareil, puisque sa version 46 mm est facturée à ce jour environ 195 €.

articles.title: La Chine fait voler un avion électrique à 10 moteurs : l'Europe est définitivement à la traîne
articles.text:
Airbus et Boeing viennent peut-être de se faire ridiculiser par un concurrent chinois baptisé Comac. Ce 14 novembre 2026, le constructeur aéronautique chinois a fait voler pour la première fois le Comac CE-25A, un petit avion uniquement équipé de moteurs électriques.
Un premier vol habité pour le CE-25A, un petit avion électrique chinois
Ce samedi, le CE-25A a décollé de Binzhou, dans la province de Shandong, avec deux pilotes et un ingénieur d’essais à bord. L’avion est resté en l’air 16 minutes et 38 secondes exactement, parcourant 60 kilomètres environ. Comac indique que l’appareil a fonctionné normalement et que ces indicateurs de performance ont répondu à ses attentes.
En vérité, ce n’est pas la première fois que l’avion quitte le sol : en février dernier déjà, l’avion avait volé en total autonomie, sans personne à son bord. Puis ont ensuite été réalisés 19 vols de validation sans pilote avant d’y placer de vrais humains. Ce vol du CE-25A était donc la première démonstration de Comac d’un avion commercial électrique chinois avec un pilote.
Dévoilé pour la première fois à Shanghai en 2023, il aura fallu trois ans seulement à Comac pour développer cet avion. Il est conçu pour transporter 19 passagers sur des liaisons régionales courtes ; son autonomie ne lui permet pas d’aller plus loin. Selon les données communiquées par le constructeur, il affiche une masse maximale au décollage de 10 tonnes, une vitesse de croisière de 300 km/h, une altitude de croisière de 2 400 m et une autonomie annoncée de 400 km. Cet avion dispose de dix ventilateurs électriques carénés installés au-dessus des ailes. Fini les gros moteurs ou les turboréacteurs : Comac fait le pari de multiplier les petits moteurs électriques.
Une prouesse technique dont l’Europe et les États-Unis ne sont pas capable
Faire voler un avion électrique de 10 tonnes avec équipage est une prouesse car à cause de cette masse, il faut des batteries énormes et denses et trouver le bon équilibre entre poids et puissance. Les petits avions électriques existent depuis longtemps, mais concevoir un avion commercial avec plusieurs places à bord est une autre histoire. Pour le moment, le CE-25A n’est pas certifié, mais ça ne saurait tarder. Avec cet avion, la Chine poursuit sa stratégie de décarbonation entamée dans tous les secteurs.
Pour le moment, en Europe ou aux États-Unis, chez Airbus ou Boeing, aucun avion 100% électrique de cette envergure n’a profité d’une démonstration. Il y a bien le français Aura Aero qui développe l’ERA, un avion régional hybride électrique de 19 places dont le premier vol est prévu en 2027. Outre-Atlantique aussi on s’intéresse à l’électrique avec le X1 de Heart Aerospace, mais il est surtout là pour développer des appareils hybrides également. Pour rester dans la course, les constructeurs européens et étatsuniens vont devoir pousser la manette des gaz. D’autant plus que Comac vient concurrencer Airbus aussi sur les avions longs courriers.

articles.title: Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset; Menopause in India’s public health agenda
articles.text:
Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset; Menopause in India’s public health agenda
The company is betting on a cheaper S1Z scooter and in-house battery manufacturing to win back customers, though the long-term success of its reset depends on retail registrations, supply chain stability, and margin recovery.
Dear Reader,
India’s deeptech ecosystem just got a major capital boost. Multi-strategy asset manager Oister Global has launched the Oister Deep Tech Fund, targeting up to Rs 600 crore to back revenue-generating Indian startups. The fund will build a concentrated portfolio of eight to ten mature companies in the frontier tech ecosystem.
Meanwhile, upGrad has launched upGrad Next, a workforce advisory business that will help organisations redesign how they structure, hire, reward and develop employees amid workplace changes due to AI. The move expands upGrad’s corporate offering as it moves beyond skilling into higher education, professional courses, study-abroad services and enterprise learning.
In other news, India’s deeptech companies raised $914 million in 257 rounds in 2025, 34 times the 2016 level. The harder test is turning research and prototypes into commercial products, according to Speciale Invest’s report, India’s Deep Tech Revolution - From the Lab to Growth and Exits.
Edtech companies aren’t the only ones betting big on AI learning. Government programmes are also rapidly expanding India's talent pipeline. According to the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, the Skill India Digital Hub’s SOAR programme now offers 50 AI and AI-application qualifications, drawing over 517,000 enrolments and certifying more than 100,000 learners as of August 2026.
Elsewhere, a new kind of revolution is brewing. About 3.76 crore rural women belonging to self-help groups have achieved Lakhpati Didi status. The Centre’s rural livelihood initiative aims to create 6 crore Lakhpati Didis by March 2029. Additionally, 5.70 crore women have been identified as Potential Lakhpati Didis.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset
- Menopause in India’s public health agenda
Here’s your trivia for today: Which global payments giant began in 1966 when a group of California banks formed the ‘Interbank Card Association’? (Scroll down for the answer)
Analysis
Ola Electric’s dealer-led model reset
EV company Ola Electric is abandoning its direct-to-consumer model and shutting most company-owned showrooms by December 2026 to transition into a dealer-led business. While the broader electric two-wheeler market grew significantly, Ola’s revenue dropped sharply amid severe service backlogs, consumer complaints, and regulatory store closures over missing trade certificates. To recover, Ola rapidly established over 319 dealer outlets, shifting inventory costs to partners and boosting wholesale orders.
Key takeaways:
- The company is betting on a cheaper S1Z scooter and in-house battery manufacturing to win back customers, though the long-term success of its reset depends on retail registrations, supply chain stability, and margin recovery.
- The company's Q2 FY27 revenue dropped by 39% to Rs 421 crore even as the wider electric two-wheeler market grew.
- Between September 2023 and August 2024, the maker of electric two-wheelers received 10,644 complaints through the National Consumer Helpline. Of these, 3,389 concerned service delays and 1,899 were about delayed deliveries, according to media reports.

Health and wellbeing
Menopause in India’s public health agenda
Millions of women in India navigate menopause with little to no support from family or even their healthcare providers. That’s why the Karnataka government’s recent order for a three-month pilot of Ruthu Taare, its Mid-Life Women’s Health and Menopause Programme, in Dakshina district is a welcome step in the right direction.
Key takeaways:
- The programme will feature dedicated clinics, comprehensive health screenings, mental health assessments, nutrition counselling, and referrals for women aged 35 and above.
- The pilot will organise dedicated clinic sessions every Wednesday at primary health centres, taluka and district hospitals. Designated medical colleges may organise special clinics on Saturdays.
- The Ruthu Taare initiative is important because it attempts to bring menopausal care into mainstream conversation and integrate it into public healthcare.
News & updates
- Lawsuit: Intel is facing a shareholder lawsuit alleging the US chipmaker concealed the severity of a slump in its PC business. The class-action complaint follows a grim financial forecast that sent Intel's stock plunging nearly 29% in a single day, wiping out roughly $140 billion in market value.
- Charity: Warren Buffett has announced that he is donating roughly $5.47 billion in Berkshire Hathaway shares to four charities led by his adult children. Accompanying his annual Thanksgiving gift, the legendary investor stated that his confidence in the conglomerate he built over six decades remains “as strong as ever.”

articles.title: El nuevo Xiaomi 18 Pro es oficial y llega a España: lo ponemos frente a frente con el anterior para ver sus diferencias
articles.text:
Xiaomi ha elegido este 17 de noviembre para hacer oficiales sus nuevos Xiaomi 18 y Xiaomi 18 Pro Max. Sus antecesores, los Xiaomi 17 Pro, se hicieron el año pasado muy virales por llevar una pantalla trasera, aunque estos no desembarcaron en España. La película ha cambiado con esto nuevos teléfonos y, aunque no tenemos la opción de comprar los dos en nuestro país, vamos a echar un vistazo por las principales diferencias entre ambos modelos Pro para ver cómo ha sido la evolución de la gama alta del fabricante chino.
Xiaomi 18 Pro
Principales diferencias entre los Xiaomi 17 Pro y 18 Pro
Xiaomi estrena su propia pantalla de privacidad
A nivel de diseño, ambos teléfonos mantienen un aspecto muy similar y unas dimensiones que no cambian demasiado, más allá de un poco más de grosor y peso para el nuevo Xiaomi 18 Pro. Sin embargo, hay un cambio importante en ambas pantallas, especialmente en la principal.
Esta, que crece 0,1 pulgadas, estrena una nueva tecnología llamada Xiaomi HyperRGB 2.0. Esta se basa en una nueva estructura de píxeles que, según promete la compañía, mejora tanto la nitidez como la eficiencia energética. El otro cambio importante es que tanto este móvil como su versión Pro Max estrenan su propia pantalla de privacidad, muy en la línea de lo que ya vimos con el Galaxy S26 Ultra. Es decir: un sistema por hardware que reduce la visibilidad de la pantalla desde los laterales para evitar miradas indiscretas. Y será configurable, tanto en la pantalla completa como para apps o notificaciones. También sube de 3.500 a 4.000 nits de brillo máximo.
Turno ahora de la pantalla trasera. Xiaomi no ha especificado su tamaño, aunque sí que también llega a 4.000 nits de brillo máximo y que tiene una tasa de refresco de hasta 120 Hz como la del Xiaomi 17 Pro. Donde hay mayor cambio es a nivel de funciones, estrenando una muy útil de traducción con IA: colocando el móvil entre ambos, las dos pantallas mostrarán el idioma del interlocutor que tiene delante.
El Xiaomi 18 Pro llega con el primer procesador de 2 nm de Qualcomm
Ambos dispositivos utilizan un procesador de Qualcomm, aunque el Xiaomi 18 Pro utiliza el Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, fabricado en 2 nm. Esto implica que se trata de un procesador más eficiente, algo que tiene impacto directo en la autonomía del dispositivo (hablaremos de la batería a continuación). En este sentido, podemos hablar también de un salto de rendimiento.
¿Y a nivel de memoria? Dependiendo de la configuración, el Xiaomi 17 Pro estaba disponible con 12 o 16 GB de memoria RAM LPDDR5X. Sin embargo, el nuevo modelo llega únicamente con 12 GB de RAM LPDDR5X, aunque sí que podremos elegir entre dos capacidades diferentes: 256 o 512 GB.
Repite el silicio-carbono, pero con menos capacidad
El silicio-carbono está haciendo que veamos cifras enormes de mAh en muchos móviles, especialmente de fabricantes chinos. Aquí se produce algo curioso, y es que el Xiaomi 17 Pro tiene más capacidad de batería que el Xiaomi 18 Pro: 6.300 mAh frente a 6.000 mAh. Hay que tener en cuenta que esto es una cifra aislada y que la autonomía depende de otros muchos factores, pero es un dato a tener en cuenta.
También existe una pequeña diferencia en lo que a la carga rápida se refiere. Mientras que la inalámbrica se mantiene idéntica (50 W), también carga un poco más rápido por cable el Xiaomi 17 Pro (100 W) que el 18 Pro (90 W).
Mejora en resolución para dos de sus cámaras
Llegamos a otro de los puntos donde hay mayor cambio entre ambos dispositivos: las cámaras. Tanto el sensor frontal como el ultra gran angular se mantienen iguales, pero sí que hay diferencias importantes en las otras dos cámaras. La cámara principal del 18 Pro sube hasta los 200 megapíxeles (frente a los 50 megapíxeles del anterior teléfono), lo que es ideal para hacer recortes posteriores a la hora de editar.
Algo similar ocurre con la cámara que falta, el teleobjetivo. En esta ocasión también pasamos de 50 a 200 megapíxeles, que en esta ocasión es de 1/1,56 pulgadas. Esta cámara, según explica Xiaomi, ayuda a que el sistema fotográfico del móvil sea muy versátil, puesto que cuenta con un zoom óptico de hasta 150 mm y la posibilidad de telemacro a 12 cm para imágenes muy cercanas.
No hay sorpresa: tiene precio de gama alta
El Xiaomi 18 Pro es un teléfono de gama alta con todas las letras, algo que se va a ver reflejado en el precio. Aquí no podemos hacer una comparación directa entre ambos dispositivos, puesto que el Xiaomi 17 Pro no llegó a España. Sí que podemos hablar de cifras concretas: este último partía el año pasado de los 4.999 yuanes, unos 682 euros al cambio. Eso sí, es una cifra engañosa porque los precios finales fuera de China suelen ser más altos por impuestos o distribución, entre otras cosas.
El Xiaomi 18 Pro, como ya hemos explicado más arriba, llega en dos configuraciones diferentes. La más económica de las dos, que es la que tiene 256 GB de almacenamiento, cuesta 1.399,99 euros. Eso sí: tiene un descuento de lanzamiento de 250 euros, más 50 euros si se compra desde la app.
Si prefieres el doble de almacenamiento (es decir, 512 GB), el precio sube hasta los 1.599,99 euros. Esto es exactamente lo que cuesta la versión más económica del Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.
¿Merece la pena el Xiaomi 18 Pro?
En este tipo de comparativas solemos dar los principales motivos por los cuales merece la pena el nuevo dispositivo o, al contrario, es mejor apostar por el de la generación anterior. No tiene sentido en esta ocasión, puesto que no podemos acceder al Xiaomi 17 Pro en España. Lo que sí tiene es ver cuáles son los puntos fuertes y débiles del nuevo modelo Pro para que así puedas ver si te merece la pena (o no) lanzarte a por él.

articles.title: Karra Elejalde, actor, 65 años: “No hay animal, mineral, ni vegetal más nocivo para el planeta que el ser humano”
articles.text:
Karra Elejalde hablaba de cine (de él, de su trabajo, de su vida) y Ana Trasobares le preguntó sobre sus creencias. Entonces contestó: “Sí, soy creyente, creo en el planeta. Y porque soy creyente, creo que no hay animal, mineral ni vegetal más nocivo para el planeta que el ser humano”.
El actor (Vitoria, 1960), que cumplió 66 años en octubre de 2026, hizo una llamada de atención sobre el planeta y sus recursos. Su declaración continuaba con otras referencias personales: “Y también creo en Gaia, y en la serendipia y en que estoy indignado porque nadie me ha contado qué he venido a hacer aquí”.
Hijo de un músico y un ama de casa, Elejalde es un actor que ha mezclado el humor y el drama. En este momento llevaba más de tres décadas en el cine y ya había dado vida al personaje de Ocho apellidos vascos, que le había hecho conocido por un público más amplio.
Fama por trabajo
En la misma conversación decía que nunca había aspirado a ser un actor famoso. “Nunca he querido ser un actor famoso, ni popular. He querido ser un actor prestigioso, un actor que lo hace bien”. Y la fama es una consecuencia lógica de que las cosas funcionen en esta profesión.
Su paso por el cine comenzó en 1987. Antes de Ocho apellidos vascos (2014), trabajó con Juanma Bajo Ulloa, Julio Medem, Álex de la Iglesia, Pedro Almodóvar, Icíar Bollaín e Imanol Uribe. También con Manuel Gutiérrez Aragón. Como guionista y director ha hecho “Año Mariano” y “Torapia”.
Con “Ocho apellidos vascos” consiguió uno de sus mayores éxitos populares. En ella interpretaba a Koldo, un padre que iba poco a poco mostrando su faceta más tierna con el andaluz (Dani Rovira), que se hacía pasar por vasco y pretendía ser su yerno.
Aspiraba a hacer bien su trabajo y también en esto tenía su opinión. Lo resumía en una frase: “La mejor forma de vender una película es hacer un buen trabajo”, sentenciaba.

articles.title: Flipper Devices launches $399 ‘Flipper One’ Linux-based multi-tool
articles.text:
Flipper Devices, the company behind the popular Flipper Zero pentesting device, has launched a crowdfunding campaign for Flipper One, a portable Linux computer and networking multi-tool.
Despite global RAM shortages and unpredictable price fluctuations, the company said Flipper One will launch at $399, a price that reportedly covers production costs and leaves no profit margin.
Flipper Devices said the device’s RAM and UFS storage account for half of the total hardware cost, but after years of development, they decided not to hold back now.
“Instead of waiting for perfect market conditions or raising the price, we’re moving forward with the Kickstarter campaign,” reads the press release Flipper Devices shared with BleepingComputer.
“We aim to make Flipper One as accessible as possible without building a profit margin into the hardware's price.”
Flipper One is a portable computer that runs a Debian-based system called Flipper OS, and features built-in Wi-Fi 6E, Gigabit Ethernet, and an eSIM.
It can manage up to five network uplinks, act as a hotspot, run VPNs and firewalls, and connect to an external display over USB-C.
It is a separate product from Flipper Zero, focused on IP networking and on-device computing.
In May, Flipper Devices asked the community to help build it, highlighting the project's complexity and listing several ambitious goals.
Development appears to have progressed at a good pace since then, and the company is now preparing to build the first actual units of the Flipper One.
The company says that Flipper One already runs on the mainline Linux kernel, while USB-C DisplayPort patches are under review for inclusion in the mainline Linux.
Work continues on memory power efficiency and removing the remaining closed-source boot components.
The campaign also offers LoRa (support for MeshCore, Meshtastic, Reticulum, and walkie-talkie mode), a 5G modem, and software-defined radio expansion modules (full specifications to be disclosed).
The Kickstarter campaign for Flipper One will run between November 17 and December 17, with the goal of funding the first production run.
Device shipment for the first buyers is estimated for July 2027, and the package will include the device and a USB-C cable.
Flipper Devices also relied on Kickstarter to launch its iconic Flipper Zero in 2020, since then selling over 1 million devices.
Flipper Zero reached its funding goal within eight minutes and raised $4.8 million from crowdfunding in 30 days.

articles.title: Why BitLipa thinks fragmentation hurts stablecoins
articles.text:
Stablecoins—blockchain-based digital tokens pegged to fiat currencies—have made it possible to move dollar-denominated value across borders in seconds, offering businesses an alternative to international bank transfers that can take days. Yet, moving a digital dollar between wallets is not the same as delivering money to someone who needs it in their local currency.
That distinction is becoming increasingly critical as payment companies turn to stablecoins to settle international transactions.
A business moving money from Kenya to South Africa can convert Kenyan shillings into USDT—the dollar-backed stablecoin—transfer the tokens across a blockchain, and convert them into South African rand. The blockchain transfer may take seconds, but the transaction still depends on finding counterparties willing to buy the shillings, supply the stablecoins, and provide enough rand to complete the payout.
Your money crossed the blockchain. Why hasn’t it arrived?
Follow a payment from Kenya to South Africa. Watch where the money moves—and what happens when the destination runs out of local-currency liquidity.
No actual funds are transferred.
Tap to remove or restore liquidity.
Your payment begins in Kenya
You fund the transaction in Kenyan shillings. The payment provider must collect the funds before arranging the cross-border transfer.
A liquidity provider converts the money
A provider supplies the stablecoins needed for the cross-border leg. A blockchain cannot create a missing buyer or seller of local currency.
USDT crosses the blockchain
The digital-dollar transfer may settle in seconds. But a successful blockchain transfer is not the same as a successful local-currency payout.
The payment needs South African rand
A local provider must have enough rand available to fund the payout. With destination liquidity available, the payment can continue.
Payment blocked: no rand liquidity
The USDT transfer succeeded, but the recipient cannot be paid through this route because the destination provider has no usable rand. Restore liquidity to continue.
The recipient gets paid
When destination liquidity is available, the recipient can be credited. Institutions may still need to settle and reconcile their balances afterwards.
Illustrative simulation, not a live payment or exchange-rate quote. Actual routes depend on payment providers, counterparties, currency availability, compliance and settlement arrangements.
In markets where those counterparties are scarce, the transaction can remain expensive or difficult to complete, regardless of how quickly the stablecoins move.
This exposes the core limitation of stablecoins as cross-border payment infrastructure. While they can reduce the time and cost of transferring value between financial institutions, they do not automatically resolve liquidity shortages, disconnected payment networks, or regulatory barriers that make cross-border transfers complex.
The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) reached a similar conclusion in its 2026 Annual Economic Report, finding that stablecoin payments perform unevenly once currency conversion spreads and the costs of entering and exiting digital assets are included.
Where the payment breaks
Apollo Eric, the chief executive officer and founder of BitLipa, a Kenyan payment infrastructure company, has encountered this problem while building a business that connects local payment providers through stablecoin settlement.
Founded in 2019, BitLipa initially operated a peer-to-peer (P2P) crypto remittance platform before pivoting to infrastructure for businesses. It now connects payment companies, banks, mobile money operators (MMOs), and liquidity providers to facilitate collections, payouts, and cross-border settlement.
According to Eric, the company processes roughly $100 million a month. Around 70% of its transaction volume involves mobile money collections, with payouts accounting for the remaining 30%.
The more revealing aspect of its operation is what happens between collection and settlement.
When a business needs to move money from Kenya to South Africa, BitLipa’s system identifies available liquidity providers, compares their rates, and selects a route to convert and deliver the funds. The recipient can be paid before the underlying balances between the institutions are fully settled, Eric told TechCabal in an interview.
He noted that actual settlement and reconciliation can take a further one to two days. That creates two distinct measures of payment speed: the time required to credit a recipient, and the time required to settle obligations between the institutions involved.
Stablecoins can accelerate the latter process where both parties hold sufficient digital assets. However, when a transaction begins and ends in local currencies, access to domestic liquidity remains essential.
This friction is particularly pronounced in less liquid African markets.
Eric said Burundi, Malawi, Mozambique, Ethiopia, and several Central and North African markets remain difficult corridors for sourcing liquidity, despite stablecoins’ promise of rapid transfers. In Burundi, for example, the core challenge is finding buyers for Burundian francs.
A payment company holding francs cannot necessarily convert them into dollars or stablecoins at a competitive rate. While there may be strong demand to send money into Burundi, there is often insufficient demand for flows in the opposite direction.
This imbalance makes liquidity expensive to provide. Companies may need to hold local currency balances for longer, commit additional capital, or source counterparties outside their existing networks. The blockchain cannot create the missing buyer.
The fragmentation problem is bigger than blockchains
Stablecoin fragmentation operates at two levels.
The first is technical. Stablecoins circulate across multiple blockchains, including Ethereum, TRON, and Solana. Tokens issued on one network are not automatically transferable to another, even when they represent the same underlying currency. As a result, stablecoins are not technically interchangeable across chains.
Moving value between networks often requires exchanges, bridges, or issuer-supported transfer mechanisms, adding costs and operational risk.
In its 2026 report, the BIS said this is a problem, warning that the expansion of competing blockchain networks can divide liquidity and weaken interoperability.
The second, and potentially more consequential, problem is financial.
A liquidity provider holding USDT in Nigeria cannot necessarily meet demand for local currency in Mozambique. A company with enough stablecoins to settle a transaction may still lack access to the banks, mobile money networks, or local counterparties required to complete the payout.
Consequently, liquidity can be abundant globally yet remain inaccessible within a specific payment corridor.
This helps explain why adding more stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks, and payment companies does not automatically make cross-border payments cheaper. Each additional network may expand access, but it can also create another isolated pool of liquidity that cannot easily be deployed elsewhere.
For businesses, the relevant question is not how much stablecoin liquidity exists globally, but how much can be converted into the required currency, in the required location, when a payment is due.
The correspondent banking dilemma returns
Traditional international payments face a similar constraint. Banks rely on correspondent relationships to access foreign currencies and payment rails in markets where they lack a direct presence. These arrangements often require pre-funded accounts, multiple intermediaries, and additional compliance checks.
That structure can be costly, yet it also provides access to established liquidity networks, credit lines, and clearing systems that allow institutions to manage obligations.
Stablecoin-based payment companies are now building their own versions of these networks.
Rather than relying exclusively on correspondent banks, they connect exchanges, market makers, local payment providers, and businesses holding different currencies. Some providers pre-fund destination accounts to execute payouts immediately and settle the underlying obligations later.
The intermediaries have changed, but the underlying economic requirement has not: an institution or counterparty at the other end must supply the destination currency and bear the cost of holding it.
The traditional banking system has another advantage that is less visible to customers. Banks can reduce the amount of money they need to move by offsetting payments travelling in opposite directions.
Consider two businesses: one needs to send $1 million from Kenya to South Africa, while another needs to send the equivalent of $800,000 in the opposite direction.
If their payment obligations can be matched, only the equivalent of $200,000 needs to be funded externally, ignoring fees and currency movements.
Without that matching, the providers may need liquidity for both transactions.
Stablecoins make it easier to transfer the settlement asset, but they do not automatically create the relationships, liquidity-sharing arrangements, or netting mechanisms needed to reduce the amount of capital committed.
This is why payment orchestration and liquidity management may become more valuable than the stablecoin transfer itself.
The next competition is over liquidity
The challenge for stablecoin payment companies is now shifting from moving tokens to organising fragmented financial markets.
BitLipa’s approach is to connect multiple liquidity providers and payment institutions, allowing its system to compare available rates and identify counterparties capable of completing a transaction.
The company wants to make liquidity sourcing more competitive rather than depend on one provider in each market.
But this model also has limitations. Connecting more providers improves access only when those providers have usable liquidity. It cannot eliminate foreign exchange (FX) restrictions, create demand for an unwanted currency, or remove the capital required to fund one-sided payment corridors.
Traditional finance is also evolving. The BIS’s Project Agorá has tested a shared platform using tokenised commercial bank deposits and central bank reserves, demonstrating that blockchain-related technology can improve cross-border settlement without relying on privately issued stablecoins.
The competition is consequently not simply between stablecoins and banks. It is between different ways of connecting currencies, institutions, and liquidity.
Stablecoins may ultimately become a standard settlement instrument for cross-border payments. But that would not make every payment corridor equally accessible or inexpensive.
The companies best positioned to benefit may be those that can source local currencies, match opposing payment flows, and reliably deliver funds through domestic payment systems.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse in Australia - a personal AI agent built for everyone - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Muse is now available in Australia. It is the world’s first personal AI agent built for everyone to help users stay on top of tasks and do everything from shopping and monitoring emails to planning workouts and creating designs.
Meta says it built Muse from the ground up and can do more than just answer questions.
It can help keep you get organised, find information, compare products and prices and even explore property listings.
From day one Muse will have connector partnerships with Canva, Domain, Kogan, Mecca, Officeworks, RealEstate.com.au, Sweat, ShopBack and Ticketek.
More connector features will roll out in the coming weeks.
The Canva connector, for example, will allow Muse users to design visuals and content Muse also makes it’s possible to explore property listings on Domain and RealEstate.com.au.
On the shopping front, Muse can also be used to look for value electronics and appliances through Kogan.com, beauty products through Mecca, office supplies, furniture and other devices from Officeworks and tickets through Ticketek.
And with ShopBack, Muse makes it possible to compare prices and earn cash back and rewards for flights, hotels, and shopping.
Muse also works with popular services including Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, and Shopify.
Muse will be available on iOS and Android and at muse.ai and the app can work on your smartphone and on a browser on Mac and Windows computers.
Tech Guide has been using Muse for a few days in an early preview and we gave it access to our email so it could give us an overview of our inboxes so it can highlight and summarise the emails that needed our attention and action.
Users can interact with Muse with their voice in real-time conversations on mobile, web, or Mac so you’re able to talk through an idea or a query and let Muse get to work.
It’s also possible to customise your Muse character and give it a name.
Spaces is another custom experience you can create within Muse simply by describing your idea.
Spaces is home to your ideas, plans, and projects whether it’s planning a wedding or planning a trip.
“With the festive season coming up, the timing couldn’t be better. From finding and buying the perfect gift to planning and booking a holiday, Muse is designed to take work off Australians’ plates,” says Will Easton, Managing Director, Meta Australia and New Zealand.
“As local experiences roll out, familiar services will make Muse even more useful in everyday life.
“And people stay in control, including choosing what Muse can access and approving purchases before they happen.”
Muse is run on MuseSecure VM, which is a dedicated cloud computer that securely stores data and credentials for the services you connect while keeping passwords and payment methods out of the agent’s reach.
Users can decide what Muse can access and will always check with you before any actions including sending an email or making a purchase.
Muse is available now for Australian users on iOS, Android, and Muse.ai and will be coming soon to Meta AI glasses.
Muse is free for most of what people need but subscription plans will be announced soon for those who want to do even more.

articles.title: Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
articles.text:
Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution
- Date:
- November 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Innsbruck
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed a new way to determine whether quantum simulations can be trusted, solving a growing problem as quantum computers become too powerful for conventional machines to check. Demonstrated on a 51-qubit system, the technique measures uncertainty and provides verifiable error margins that could help unlock the full potential of quantum computing.
- Share:
As quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.
The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.
Quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.
A New Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy
The breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.
Quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can quickly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.
But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," says Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties."
Rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the new approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify important interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.
"From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy."
Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator
To evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.
After this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, showed that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.
This represents an important step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.
Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems
The next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.
"This is particularly important because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important."
The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.
Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.
"After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," says Peter Zoller.
This shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how quickly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.
The findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

articles.title: Modder finds a way to play Nintendo 64, SNES, and Genesis cartridges on a Sega Dreamcast
articles.text:
TL;DR: Playing retro games on consoles from newer generations usually requires either official backwards compatibility or running ROMs through an emulator. However, modder Throaty Mumbo has unveiled a way to play physical cartridges on a Sega Dreamcast, sidestepping the legal concerns that often accompany emulation. Instead of relying solely on emulation, the project combines multiple methods to run code from other consoles on a Dreamcast.
Dreamcart is a series of cartridge readers that can play Super NES, Sega Genesis, and NintendFo 64 games on a Sega Dreamcast. The readers aren't for sale, but the project's GitHub repository contains instructions for building and programming them.
Since the Nintendo 64's cartridge slot is detachable, Throaty Mumbo could use it as the basis for a custom cartridge reader to load an N64 game's assets onto other devices, such as the much more powerful Dreamcast. The device also incorporates the Raspberry Pi debug probe, the Pico SDK, and KallistiOS-based software.
A disc burned with dcload-ip loads the retro software onto the Dreamcast via a controller port. The Dreamcast memory card stores progress for N64 games that normally require a controller pack.
Playing Super NES and Sega Genesis games proved relatively simple as emulation for these consoles is quite advanced, and the Dreamcast is more than up to the task. Here, the cartridge readers simply load modified versions of Super Famicast and Genesis Plus DC, emulators designed for the Dreamcast. The process resembles Bleemcast, which drew multiple lawsuits for emulating PlayStation games on the Dreamcast when both consoles were still actively sold.
However, running Nintendo 64 titles proved much trickier and required combining multiple methods. Since N64 emulation is less mature, especially on the Dreamcast, performance was too poor for games to be playable, so Throaty Mumbo resorted to recompilation, which has become popular for making unofficial PC ports.
A handful of Nintendo 64 titles, such as Super Mario 64, Mario Kart 64, and Doom 64 have already received unofficial Dreamcast ports, and Dreamcart runs them perfectly from their original cartridges. This circumvents the need to dump or pirate games to load ROMs onto the Dreamcast.
Unfortunately, this method only supports the few titles with dedicated ports. Throaty Mumbo managed to play other games, such as Kirby 64 and Cruis'n World, via static recompilation, which converts Nintendo 64 code in seconds. While performance isn't perfect, it's quite playable and easily preferable to N64 emulation on the Dreamcast.
Recent updates to the GitHub page suggest improvements are on the horizon.

articles.title: Nvidia presentó un modelo de IA que enseña a robots a hacer tareas viendo videos de personas
articles.text:
Nvidia presentó en la Conferencia sobre Aprendizaje de Robots (CoRL) de Austin, Texas, GR00T 2, un modelo de inteligencia artificial (IA) que aprende tareas a partir de videos de personas y las traslada a robots. La empresa publicó los resultados de sus pruebas y dijo que liberará el modelo en diciembre de 2026.
Hasta ahora, enseñar una tarea a un robot exigía que un operador lo manejara a distancia durante horas, un proceso lento que había que repetir para cada modelo de máquina. GR00T 2 busca reducir ese trabajo: ve cómo una persona realiza una acción y la reproduce con el cuerpo del robot.
El sistema funciona distinto a sus antecesores. Predice a la vez el video de lo que ocurrirá en los segundos siguientes y los movimientos que lo producirán, y luego ejecuta esos movimientos. Nvidia lo llama modelo de acción y mundo, y lo construyó sobre Cosmos, su plataforma de simulación.
Para entrenarlo, la empresa usó 402.730 horas de video grabado por personas con cámaras en la cabeza mientras trabajaban, 10.184 horas con pinzas manuales y 23.500 horas de robots manejados a distancia. Nvidia también publicó 100.000 horas de ese video, con licencia que permite uso comercial y no comercial.
Los resultados: de 40% a 95% con cinco demostraciones
En una prueba con 50 tareas que el robot no había practicado, el modelo completó 40 al menos una vez sin ninguna demostración propia, con un éxito promedio de 40%. Con una demostración por tarea el promedio subió a 71%, y con cinco, a 95%.
Esas cinco demostraciones sumaron menos de tres minutos de datos del robot, y el ajuste posterior tomó unos 30 minutos en una sola tarjeta gráfica RTX 5090, de las que se usan en computadoras de escritorio para juegos. Los robots de las pruebas encendieron fósforos, armaron camiones de juguete y prepararon yogur con banana, según la página de Nvidia.
La propia documentación de la empresa matiza la cifra. TechRepublic señala que las 50 tareas se eligieron entre aquellas que ya habían superado 80% de éxito tras cinco demostraciones, por lo que el resultado no demuestra igual desempeño ante cualquier tarea nueva.
Nvidia presentó además GR00T 2 Turbo, una versión más pequeña que funciona dentro de un robot humanoide. Cada predicción tarda 124 milisegundos en la computadora integrada Jetson Thor. Con ella, un humanoide sirvió palomitas de maíz en las 48 pruebas y despejó una mesa en 93% de los intentos.
Límites que reconocen los investigadores
The Decoder recoge las dificultades que el grupo admite. El modelo todavía no procesa datos directos de tacto y a veces pasa por alto errores sutiles, como un tornillo que quedó a medio girar. En una tarea de limpiar un líquido con una toalla bajo el pie, el humanoide acertó en menos de la mitad de los intentos.
Para armados largos, Nvidia combina el modelo con otro programa de lenguaje que divide el trabajo en pasos. Con esa ayuda, los robots armaron juguetes en al menos 97 de cada 100 intentos. Ese programa vuelve lento el proceso: en la clasificación de basura, el robot esperó en promedio más de siete segundos entre decisiones.
Nvidia afirma que Foxconn aplica GR00T 2 en la automatización de la fabricación de servidores, que Siemens lo evalúa para usos industriales y que la empresa Nexuni prueba con él el manejo de ropa en lavanderías.
Jim Fan, director de robótica de Nvidia, presentó el modelo en la conferencia. Dijo que los pesos del modelo, es decir, los parámetros que lo componen, y su versión Turbo se publicarán en diciembre de 2026 como código abierto, junto con el método de entrenamiento para pasar habilidades de un robot a otro.

articles.title: MSP ScreenConnect Servers Targeted in Month-Long Campaign
articles.text:
Dozens of MSP ScreenConnect servers have been targeted in a month-long campaign exploiting a vulnerability patched in September, cybersecurity firm Huntress reports.
The attacks, ongoing since at least October 20, aim to exploit CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score of 9.9), a critical missing authorization and improper privilege management bug that allows for files to be transmitted and executed during a connection without authorization or confirmation.
ConnectWise patched the security defect on September 8, and CISA added it to the KEV catalog on September 11. Huntress warned at the time that exploitation started on August 20.
Now, the cybersecurity firm says a new wave of attacks is targeting ScreenConnect instances, with a focus on managed service provider (MSP) servers.
The hackers exploit CVE-2026-84869 via requests to run a guest-pushed batch file that connects to a Telegram bot and installs a rogue ScreenConnect client.
“Attackers appear to be spraying servers blindly: Since October 20, we’ve seen at least 688,000 guest ‘run file’ requests for update*.bat hit 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses, waiting for any technician to join,” Huntress says.
According to the cybersecurity firm, the activity is different from the recently observed campaigns targeting ScreenConnect instances with the SCKit malware toolkit and with unauthorized sessions from machines posing as crypto exchanges.
The exploitation of CVE-2026-84869, it explains, allows attackers to push malicious files to technicians’ machines and get their own clients to execute them when the technician joins the session. The technician sees no prompt when the files are executed.
“An MSP technician’s workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target. When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files,” Huntress notes.
In one attack, a rogue ScreenConnect client disguised as Windows Update was installed and spawned within nine seconds of the host client running the guest-pushed bat file.
As part of another, the guest machine pushed a text file two seconds after the technician joined the session, and the technician’s client ran the file three seconds later.
In October, a targeted attack hit an MSP server: the attacker joined as a guest in three real sessions the technician had created and asked the client to execute a file designed to drop a script into the technician’s computer’s Startup folder.
Organizations should update technicians’ ScreenConnect host clients to version 26.6.5 or later, along with all the Access agents ConnectWise lists.
