articles.title: Ten Years On, Google Updates the SRE Book for the AI Era
articles.text:
Google has announced a completely rewritten second edition of their seminal book Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems, ten years after the original book was first published. The book updates thinking on site reliability engineering (SRE) to encompass modern cloud architectures, platform engineering and AI workloads, whilst keeping the original emphasis on applying good software engineering techniques to operations work.
Announced by Google's SRE programme manager Betsy Beyer and software engineer David Huska, the new edition is positioned as a response to a production environment that has changed substantially since 2016, when the first edition appeared. The authors argue that the central problem is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining reliability as systems become more distributed, interdependent and continuously changing.
"Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before."
Betsy Beyer and David Huska, Google Cloud Blog
The original SRE book became influential because it gave a public account of how Google operated large-scale services. It described practices such as service level objectives (SLOs), error budgets, toil reduction, incident management and postmortems. InfoQ's 2016 review noted that the book presented SRE as the application of software engineering to an operations function, with engineers expected to automate repetitive operational work rather than simply respond to it.
The second edition does not present SRE as a fixed set of practices. Instead, it describes how those practices have changed as organisations have moved from early cloud migration and monolithic applications towards microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless systems and internal developer platforms.
One of the clearest changes over the years concerns SLOs and error budgets. Google says that teams once relied on basic availability metrics and manually applied error-budget policies. The revised guidance describes user-centred, multi-tiered SLOs, dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Reliability practice itself has evolved away from infrastructure uptime alone and towards measures that describe the effect of failures on users.
Observability has also evolved, and the book's new edition talks this through. The first edition's world of static dashboards, basic logs and manual alert triage has given way, in Google's account, to OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing and automated anomaly correlation. The aim is not merely to collect more telemetry, but to reduce the time between an alert and a credible explanation of what has failed.
Automation is the third major area of revision. Google describes a movement from custom scripts addressing isolated tasks towards declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms and self-healing systems. This aligns with the platform-engineering model now common in larger organisations: reliability capabilities are built once into a platform and consumed by product teams, rather than being reimplemented by every team.
Reliability testing has also changed. Google contrasts scheduled game days and synthetic load tests with continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing and live production canary verification. The practical implication is that resilience becomes part of the delivery pipeline rather than an occasional exercise performed before a major release.
"Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification."
Betsy Beyer and David Huska, Google Cloud Blog
Capacity management is another area where the book has been updated. Google says that manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment and optimisation for GPU and TPU clusters. This matters because AI training and inference workloads can concentrate demand on scarce accelerated computing resources, making capacity planning, networking and cost control more operationally significant.
Generative AI inevitably appears in the second edition, in two facets. First, SRE is presented as a discipline needed to operate AI infrastructure. The book covers the reliability of large GPU and TPU clusters, network topologies, non-deterministic model outputs, latency behaviour and the pipelines used for training, fine-tuning and data processing. These are different operational problems from those posed by a conventional stateless web service.
Second, AI is presented as a tool for reliability engineers. The post welcomes generative AI support for incident triage and postmortem writing, natural-language queries over telemetry, and predictive models that identify resource bottlenecks before they cause an outage. The examples in the announcement mostly place AI in a supporting role, gathering and organising evidence for engineers, rather than claiming that AI can replace operational judgement. Recent industry activity appears to support this, with InfoQ reporting in October 2026 that Datadog had released Scout, a specialist model intended to investigate production problems inside its Bits AI SRE product. Other vendors are exploring similar territory, including Honeycomb's Canvas Agent, Splunk AI SRE and New Relic's SRE Agent. InfoQ also reported in February 2026 on Google Cloud SREs using the Gemini CLI during real outages; using AI to help engineers work through incidents, rather than as an autonomous replacement for on-call staff.
The announcement also revises the organisational side of SRE. Google describes a move beyond dedicated SRE teams attached to particular applications, towards hybrid models, platform-engineering integration and reliability champions embedded in product teams. This has come about because many organisations cannot staff a central SRE team for every service, so reliability expertise has to be distributed more widely.
Despite the technological updates, Google argues that the underlying culture has not changed. The authors restate the importance of reliability-focused culture and expand the book's coverage of the human aspects of systems engineering. David Blank-Edelman made a related point in a presentation, You Are Asking the Wrong Questions (about Reliability and SRE), delivered at InfoQ Dev Summit Boston in 2025. He argued that reliability work should start from the customer's perspective rather than the component's perspective, and described SRE as fundamentally collaborative. He also challenged the conventional focus on a single root cause, favouring an examination of the contributing factors behind a failure.
The second edition is available in physical format through Google Books and in digital format from O'Reilly. For teams already practising SRE, its value is likely to lie less in introducing familiar concepts than in showing how those concepts have been adapted for platforms, distributed systems and AI-heavy infrastructure. For organisations earlier in their reliability journey, it remains a substantial reference on how to make operations a software-engineering problem rather than a collection of manual tasks.

articles.title: Schlüssel vergessen? Google Wallet öffnet künftig deine Haustür
articles.text:
Schlüssel vergessen? Google Wallet öffnet künftig deine Haustür
Erst vor einigen Wochen hat Google zahlreiche Neuerungen für die Wallet-App angekündigt. Darüber können User:innen etwa seither Quittungen einscannen und abspeichern. Jetzt folgt schon die nächste Neuerung, wie das Unternehmen in einer Ankündigung schreibt. Preview-User:innen können aktuell ein Feature ausprobieren, mit dem sie ihre Haustüren über Google Wallet entsperren können.
Google Wallet: So können Haustüren entsperrt werden
Das ist möglich, indem die Wallet-App mit kompatiblen Smartlocks kommuniziert. Im Grunde können User:innen also einen digitalen Zugang in ihrem Smartphone speichern und den physischen Schlüssel zu Hause lassen. Wenn sie die Tür wieder entsperren wollen, müssen sie lediglich das Smartphone außen an das Smartlock oder ein Keypad halten und schon schließt sich das Schloss selbstständig auf.
Diese beschriebene Variante nutzt NFC am Android-Smartphone, um mit dem Smartlock kommunizieren zu können. Hat das Smartphone auch noch einen Ultrabreitbandsender, kann auch die zweite Entsperrmethode genutzt werden. Dadurch sendet das Smartphone schon aus größerer Entfernung den Befehl, die Tür aufzuschließen. Kommst du also mit Einkäufen in den Händen zurück, wird die Tür automatisch geöffnet und du kannst einfach hineingehen.
So praktisch das Feature auch ist: Um es nutzen zu können, müssen einige Voraussetzungen erfüllt sein. Für die NFC-Entsperrmethode gibt Google ein Smartphone mit Android 9 oder höher vor. Für das Entsperren aus der Ferne muss der UWB-Sender den Aliro-Standard unterstützen. Google nennt hier als kompatible Smartphones die eigenen Pixel-10-Pro-Geräte und aktuellere Modelle sowie ausgewählte Samsung-Galaxy-Smartphones.
Zu guter Letzt musst du aber auch noch ein kompatibles Smartlock besitzen. Zum Launch des Features unterstützt die Google Wallet vorerst nur das Aqara 400, das Schlage Sense Pro und das Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Das Aqara-Modell kann direkt mit NFC und UWB entsperrt werden. Beim Schlage-Gerät wird UWB nachgereicht, während das Nuki-Smartlock auf NFC beschränkt bleibt. Google betont, dass die Funktion aktuell noch von Preview-User:innen ausgetestet werden soll. In den kommenden Wochen soll das Entsperren dann aber für alle Wallet-Nutzer:innen ausgerollt werden.

articles.title: Ataque hacker atinge quase 200 sites e coloca usuários de iPhone na mira
articles.text:
Um ataque cibernético comprometeu ferramentas utilizadas por quase 200 sites de grandes empresas e organizações ao redor do mundo. A ofensiva atingiu páginas da BBC, IKEA, Zoom, CNN, Salesforce e Air France-KLM, entre outras, e tentou roubar informações financeiras, desviar criptomoedas e explorar vulnerabilidades em dispositivos da Apple.
O incidente aconteceu na segunda-feira (16) e foi identificado pelo pesquisador de segurança Scott Helme, fundador da plataforma de monitoramento Report URI. Segundo a investigação, 178 organizações foram afetadas pela distribuição de códigos maliciosos por meio da Optimizely, empresa que oferece ferramentas para personalizar páginas e testar diferentes versões de sites.
A estimativa considera 188 arquivos de JavaScript infectados, encontrados em análise de 1.611 arquivos da plataforma. O número real de organizações atingidas pode ser maior, segundo Helme. Entre os nomes identificados, estão BBC, Zoom, CNN, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Ledger, Peacock e Air France-KLM.
A própria Optimizely confirmou o incidente e informou que um invasor explorou uma vulnerabilidade em sua ferramenta Experimentation para inserir códigos maliciosos em projetos de clientes.
Como os hackers conseguiram atingir tantos sites?
- O ataque explorou uma característica da plataforma: cada cliente utiliza um pequeno arquivo de JavaScript fornecido pela infraestrutura da Optimizely. Esse código permite executar experimentos e modificações nas páginas, incluindo a inserção de scripts personalizados;
- Os criminosos conseguiram introduzir código malicioso nesses projetos de clientes. Como os arquivos continuavam sendo distribuídos pelos servidores da Optimizely, os navegadores dos visitantes os carregavam como se fossem componentes legítimos;
- Na prática, os invasores transformaram uma ferramenta confiável em canal de distribuição de malware;
- A investigação de Helme identificou três versões do código utilizado na campanha. Algumas direcionavam os navegadores para um domínio externo controlado pelos criminosos; outras escondiam o endereço por meio de codificação ou carregavam cópia do malware diretamente na página;
- A origem exata do acesso não autorizado a tantos projetos diferentes ainda não foi esclarecida pelos pesquisadores.
Malware tentava roubar cartões e criptomoedas
O código malicioso tinha diferentes funções, que podiam ser executadas de acordo com o dispositivo e as ações de cada visitante.
Uma delas era substituir endereços de carteiras de criptomoedas pelos endereços controlados pelos invasores. Dessa forma, uma pessoa que copiasse uma chave de recebimento para realizar uma transferência poderia acabar enviando o dinheiro diretamente aos criminosos.
O mecanismo conseguia alterar endereços em textos, formulários, links e até na área de transferência do dispositivo.
Outra função era capturar informações de cartões de pagamento, incluindo número, data de validade e código de segurança (CVV). O malware monitorava formulários próprios dos sites e tentava enviar os dados coletados aos servidores dos invasores.
Segundo a investigação, campos de pagamento incorporados por serviços externos, como Stripe e Adyen, não estavam ao alcance desse mecanismo específico.
O código também tentava coletar cookies não protegidos contra acesso por JavaScript e capturas de tela das páginas visitadas.
A análise identificou movimentações de criptomoedas em carteiras associadas aos invasores. Entretanto, não foi possível determinar quantas transferências vieram efetivamente de vítimas do ataque.
iPhones e iPads também estavam na mira
Um dos aspectos mais preocupantes da campanha foi a tentativa de explorar dispositivos móveis da Apple.
O código malicioso identificava a versão do sistema operacional utilizada pelo visitante e, em seguida, tentava carregar ferramentas de exploração conhecidas como Coruna e DarkSword.
Segundo a análise da Report URI, o mecanismo direcionava diferentes versões dessas ferramentas conforme a versão do iOS:
- iOS 13 a 17: o código tentava carregar o conjunto de exploração Coruna;
- iOS 18: a campanha utilizava ferramentas associadas ao DarkSword;
- iOS 26: foi identificada uma cadeia separada que, naquele momento, apenas coletava informações sobre o dispositivo.
Em aparelhos com iOS 18.6 ou versões anteriores, as páginas afetadas podiam ser recarregadas a cada 60 segundos na tentativa de repetir a exploração.
A presença dessas ferramentas não significa que todos os dispositivos que acessaram os sites tenham sido infectados. A investigação identificou tentativas de exploração, mas não confirmou quantos aparelhos foram efetivamente comprometidos.
Leia mais:
- De geladeiras a criptomoedas: o Brasil está pronto para enfrentar hackers turbinados por IA?
- Falha no iOS permitia gravação de áudio sem permissão do usuário
- Rede confidencial de comunicações da NSA sai do ar nos EUA
- IA acelera ataques cibernéticos e amplia incidentes nas empresas
Optimizely confirma invasão e corrige vulnerabilidade
Em comunicado publicado em sua página oficial de status, a Optimizely confirmou que um agente não autorizado explorou vulnerabilidade em sua ferramenta Experimentation para inserir JavaScript malicioso em projetos de clientes.
A empresa afirmou que corrigiu a falha, removeu os códigos injetados dos projetos afetados e tomou medidas para proteger as contas dos usuários envolvidos.
Também foram implementadas proteções adicionais para impedir que códigos não autorizados voltassem a ser distribuídos pela plataforma.
A página oficial classificou o episódio como incidente em monitoramento, e não como completamente resolvido.
Em entrevista à ABC News, a companhia informou ainda que, na região dos Estados Unidos, as recomendações continuavam sendo entregues e atualizadas. A expectativa era de que a qualidade do serviço voltasse ao normal ao longo daquele dia.
Zoom e IKEA investigam possíveis impactos
Algumas das empresas afetadas também começaram a tomar providências.
A Zoom informou à ABC News que desativou preventivamente a Optimizely em seus ambientes de produção. A companhia afirmou que, até aquele momento, não havia identificado impactos nos dados dos clientes e que continuava monitorando a situação.
A IKEA também confirmou estar ciente do problema envolvendo o fornecedor terceirizado. A varejista afirmou que investigava possíveis consequências para seus serviços digitais e clientes, destacando que a proteção das informações dos consumidores era prioridade.
Outras companhias também adotaram medidas preventivas. A Salesforce desativou scripts da Optimizely enquanto investigava alterações não autorizadas. A Equifax interrompeu o uso da plataforma e afirmou não ter encontrado evidências de comprometimento de seus próprios sistemas.
O HSBC, por sua vez, declarou que scripts não autorizados não estavam ativos em seus sites.
Por que o ataque acende alerta para a segurança da internet?
Em outro artigo publicado nesta terça-feira (17), Scott Helme chamou a atenção para um problema recorrente na segurança digital: a dependência de códigos fornecidos por empresas terceirizadas.
O pesquisador explica que organizações costumam adotar processos rigorosos para revisar os programas instalados diretamente em seus servidores. No entanto, muitas vezes permitem que scripts externos sejam carregados e executados automaticamente nos navegadores dos visitantes.
Isso cria um risco: mesmo que a infraestrutura de uma empresa esteja protegida, uma vulnerabilidade em um fornecedor de software pode abrir caminho para ataques contra seus clientes.
Uma análise de 256 sites das organizações afetadas também revelou falhas nas proteções adotadas pelas empresas. Apenas 24 (15%) tinham uma Política de Segurança de Conteúdo (CSP, na sigla em inglês) suficientemente restritiva para bloquear o código malicioso.
Outros 68 não utilizavam essa proteção, enquanto 50 tinham configurações que permitiam a execução do malware e o envio de informações aos servidores dos criminosos.
A CSP é um mecanismo de segurança que permite aos administradores determinar quais fontes podem fornecer códigos e para quais destinos uma página pode enviar informações.
Helme também recomenda o uso de mecanismos como o Subresource Integrity (SRI), que permite ao navegador verificar se um arquivo externo corresponde à versão esperada, além de ferramentas para monitorar alterações nos scripts carregados pelos sites.
Para o pesquisador, o episódio demonstra que confiar em um fornecedor não deve significar executar automaticamente qualquer código que ele disponibilize.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Meta launches Direct, a stand-alone messaging app for Instagram | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta is testing Direct, a new stand-alone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account.
With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain users who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform.
Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the company says it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.
The new app also gives the company a way to keep these users within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem, even if they don’t use Instagram itself.
Besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes, and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs.
Meta says users can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes.
Users in Turkey and Thailand can sign up for Direct using their email address or phone number. Those with an existing Instagram account can log in using the same username and password, and their existing conversations will be synced across both apps.
Meta says only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time.
The company also says it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young users. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits.
Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts.
Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries.

articles.title: Why Glowtify made an unlikely bet on industrial manufacturing | BetaKit
articles.text:
When Marc Allard and his team started knocking on the doors of industrial manufacturers, they brought donuts.
The CEO and Co-Founder of Montréal-based Glowtify wanted to understand how these businesses found customers, and what was preventing them from reaching more. The team travelled through Québec and the United States, visiting factories and speaking with operators from Saguenay to Michigan and Idaho.
“Many of these people aren’t reachable from ‘traditional’ marketing channels that other SaaS brands might be used to,” Allard said. “So, we found another way.”
“Sometimes the sexiest market isn’t the right one.”
A little sugar helped his team get through the door, where they found businesses with decades of technical expertise and established reputations but little online visibility beyond their existing customer networks.
Allard came from a different world. His background was in website development and e-commerce, and Glowtify had originally built its AI-powered marketing platform for online retailers. The software helps businesses develop marketing strategies, plan campaigns, create content for any digital channel, and manage their online presence, with support from human strategists.
Some of Glowtify’s strongest customer relationships, however, were emerging among industrial manufacturers. While online retailers typically have established marketing systems, many manufacturers have little infrastructure or staff dedicated to marketing. Glowtify could help manage much of that work for them.
“I’ll admit I was hesitant to leave the e-commerce and marketing world behind,” Allard said. “I had a website development agency and this was our bread and butter.”
The factory visits, along with the company’s early success with industrial customers, made it clear that Glowtify had found an underserved market. By February 2026, Allard had enough evidence to narrow the company’s focus to industrial manufacturers and the service companies and suppliers in their ecosystems. Its industrial business has since grown more than fivefold.
The limits of an offline reputation
Allard heard from manufacturers that were seeing fewer new customers, as well as declining revenue from existing ones. Some wanted to enter new markets but had very little information online about what they actually did, the equipment they used, and the products they made.
Marketing was often somebody’s second job at these companies, if it was anybody’s job at all. In July, 72 percent of Glowtify’s customer accounts had no employees dedicated entirely to marketing. Allard met presidents who wrote their company’s web copy and salespeople handling marketing work between customer quotations.
“Whatʼs framed as a desire to be seen and be noticed is actually an urgent need to generate new business by opening digital marketing channels,” Allard said.
Glowtify began helping manufacturers turn their existing expertise into technical articles, case studies, and other content about their capabilities. American Precision Electronics, a US manufacturer serving specialized industries, had spent 35 years growing largely through referrals. After working with Glowtify to make its technical capabilities easier to discover, website quote requests increased eightfold over eight weeks.
New pressures mean new priorities
The need to reach new buyers has become more pressing for some Canadian manufacturers, and the focus has shifted to diversifying partners globally. Allard said many businesses were already exploring new markets before tariffs added urgency to those plans.
Québec-based Groupe Mundial, for example, used the Glowtify app to explore opportunities to work with European manufacturers that needed production capacity in North America. Its existing facilities could help those companies establish operations in the region.
Reaching those kinds of customers means manufacturers need to make information about their capabilities, equipment, and experience available to buyers who may never have heard of them.
Geographic expansion is just one priority for manufacturers. In September, Glowtify conducted dozens of interviews with customers and prospective customers about their marketing goals. Some needed to recruit skilled workers, while others wanted to pursue larger contracts.
“The findings helped tap into the nuance around manufacturers’ challenges. We learned the desire to be visible is all about getting more of the right type of quote requests. And we learned that expanding current contracts is possible, but there’s no system to get that done fast, especially when no one is dedicated to marketing. And hiring is always top of mind: getting talent to apply for jobs is a consistent hurdle to jump, which requires investment in showing why you’re a better place to work than the shop down the road,” Allard said.
Many Québec businesses are also preparing for ownership changes after decades under the same family or founder. Making their expertise and reputation easier to find online could help them reach new customers as those businesses change hands.
The opportunity close to home
By August, industrial customers accounted for over 60 percent of Glowtify’s customer base, up 12x from the beginning of the year. The company has also reported improvements in sales conversion and customer retention since the pivot. Glowtify developed its approach and product vision working with manufacturers in Québec and Canada, and is now quickly penetrating the US market.
The decision to focus on manufacturing also has personal significance for Allard. His family has a history of entrepreneurship in the mining industry in Thetford Mines, Québec, and he has a lot of admiration for people who have spent decades building industrial businesses. During a recent trip to Dallas, Texas, the team met a fourth-generation foundry owner whose company dates back to 1886.
“We have a saying: the businesses that build the world deserve to be known,” Allard said. “We’re championing that fully.”
Marc Allard,
Graphite Ventures
“These companies are now in the middle of a major innovation curve: they need to update how they reach buyers who are getting younger and changing how the business operates. And that requires an investment in marketing,” Allard said.
Graphite Ventures, an investor in Glowtify, supported the company’s decision to pursue manufacturers. According to Allard, general partner Kevin Madill encouraged Allard to consider the opportunity in an industry that had received little attention from marketing software companies.
“Sometimes the sexiest market isn’t the right one,” Madill said. “There is often a larger, more profitable, less obvious one. I encouraged Marc to think hard about where Glowtify could solve the most important and urgent problem for customers, and which markets were underserved by competitors or alternative solutions.”
Allard still sees considerable opportunity among manufacturers that have invested heavily in production technology, including robotics and automation, but continue to rely on comparatively basic marketing systems.
“It might be contacts on a spreadsheet, or even a pen and paper,” Allard said. “Tradeshow and marketing calendars are on the wall in an office, not in a project management software.”
The lack of established marketing infrastructure could make it easier for some manufacturers to adopt newer technology and become AI-native marketing organizations without having to replace complicated legacy systems. It’s an advantage Allard believes manufacturers can build on.
“We have a saying: the businesses that build the world deserve to be known,” Allard said. “We’re championing that fully.”
PRESENTED BY
Check out Scale Canadian for more stories of those building in Canada and scaling globally.
All images courtesy Graphite Ventures.

articles.title: Xiaomi renueva su gama alta con el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max y el Xiaomi 18 Pro: pantalla trasera... y mucha IA
articles.text:
Xiaomi renueva su gama alta con el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max y el Xiaomi 18 Pro, dos nuevos terminales con unas especificaciones sobresalientes y una propuesta centrada especialmente en la IA y con la seña de identidad de su pantalla trasera que promete seguir ampliando funcionalidades.
Los dos terminales, pertenecientes a la Pro Series de la compañía, hacen gala de la gama Elite de Qualcomm, montando un Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 para el caso del Pro Max y Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 para el modelo Pro, pero no es lo único que ofrecen en lo alto de la lista de especificaciones.
De nuevo, repite con dos tamaños: por un lado, el Xiaomi 18 Pro, que cuenta con una compacta pantalla de 6,4 pulgadas y una anchura de 72 mm que facilita un uso cómodo con una sola mano, y el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, que crece hasta las 6,9 pulgadas.
En este sentido, su sistema de cámaras Leica Dual de 200 MP promete ofrecer alguna de las mejores experiencias de foto y vídeo en la gama alta, y además se incorporan algunas funciones muy interesantes, marca de la casa, como su pantalla Privacy Display con HyperRGB 2.0.
Xiaomi vuelve a apostar por la pantalla trasera... y mucha IA en los 18 Pro
No obstante, la clave de estos nuevos Xiaomi 18 Pro Max y el Xiaomi 18 Pro es, como decimos, su pantalla trasera, a la que Xiaomi llama Back Display. La compañía no ha escatimado nada en esta pantalla trasera, puesto que está construida con el mismo panel M11 de la pantalla principal, por lo que sus especificaciones son altísimas: hasta 4.000 nits de brillo máximo, tasa de refresco LTPO de 1 a 120 Hz, un diseño unificado bajo cristal (Unified Underglass) que integra tanto la pantalla como las cámaras bajo una única lámina de vidrio, y resistencia a golpes y caídas firmada por Gorilla Glass Victus 2.
La pantalla trasera no es solo atrezo. Además de las funciones de cámara para selfies de grupo o modo espejos para sacar toda la calidad de la cámara trasera para selfies, también tiene otras funciones interesantes. Xiaomi destaca AI Interpreter, una funcionalidad que convierte las dos pantallas en una herramienta de traducción en tiempo real o, gracias a la integración de la IA y la app de GenAI Apps, que trae el vibe coding a los smartphones y permite crear miniaplicaciones y usarlas en la pantalla trasera. Xiaomi dice que hay más de 50 aplicaciones predefinidas con funciones personalizables para la back display.
Como siempre, uno de los puntos fuertes de la Pro Series de Xiaomi es su sistema de cámaras. La compañía vuelve a firmar con Leica, y en el caso del Xiaomi 18 Pro ha optado por una cámara principal con Leica UltraPure y una lente óptica Leica Summilux f/1.67, además de un teleobjetivo de tipo periscópico llamado Power Prism que combina redirección de la luz y enfoque en un único componente óptico combinado con un sensor de 1/1,56 pulgadas. Además, en el caso del Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, se incluye un sensor Light Fusion 960L, que proporciona un elevado rango dinámico de 16,2 EV para escenas a contraluz.
En cuanto a vídeo, Xiaomi 18 Pro Series admite grabación hasta en 4K a 120 fps en Dolby Vision, además de perfil Log de 10 bits y resolución 8K a 30 fps y todas las funciones de IA que te puedas imaginar, tanto en foto como en vídeo, impulsados por el modelo de imagen con IA integrado en el dispositivo.
Xiaomi tampoco se ha olvidado de la batería. El Xiaomi 18 Pro Max alberga una impresionante batería de 7.050 mAh con carga HyperCharge por cable de 100 W e inalámbrica de 50 W, mientras que el Xiaomi 18 Pro cuenta con una batería de 6.000 mAh con HyperCharge de 90 W por cable y 50 W inalámbrica.
Xiaomi 18 Pro: precios y disponibilidad
Respecto a su precio y disponibilidad, el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max estará disponible en cuatro colores: Negro, Blanco, Azul Cósmico y Velvet Red, y en 2 variantes de almacenamiento con los siguientes precios:
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max 12GB + 256GB: 1.599,99€
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max 12GB + 512GB: 1.799,99€
Por su parte, el Xiaomi 18 Pro estará disponible también en cuatro colores: Negro, Blanco, Azul Cósmico y Velvet Red, y viene con 2 variantes de almacenamiento con los siguientes precios:
- Xiaomi 18 Pro 12GB + 256GB: 1.399,99€
- Xiaomi 18 Pro 12GB + 512GB: 1.599,99€
Con motivo del lanzamiento, Xiaomi tiene algunas promociones en mi.com: para el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (en cualquiera de sus dos variantes) con descuento directo de 300 € y para el Pro normal un descuento directo de entre 250 € y 350 €, dependiendo del almacenamiento.

articles.title: Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
articles.text:
Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives.
Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
Meta’s chief AI officer posted an AI video of a top competitor. It’s allowed under Meta’s AI policy.
Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse.
Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened. Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents.
Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness.
Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram.
Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Integrating QPUs into Supercomputing Centers Using Slurm HRES Plugins | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Quantum processors are being integrated into supercomputing centers worldwide. National programs in North America, Europe, and Asia are driving the installation of quantum processing units (QPUs) alongside high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Every supercomputer will eventually be a hybrid quantum-classical device, drawing on quantum processors to expand what’s possible in scientific research.
The scientists that will become the first power users of quantum-GPU supercomputing already run their simulations and workflows on HPC systems. Chemistry, weather modeling, engineering simulation, and other traditionally HPC-centric fields stand to benefit from quantum acceleration for certain workloads. For these scientists, the QPU is simply another accelerator, alongside the CPUs and GPUs that supercomputing centers already provide.
Making quantum computers readily available, easily programmable, and familiar to access, reserve, and execute at scale is imperative for scientific researchers to be able to adopt quantum processors into workflows. Until now, a key missing piece has been a workload manager. Slurm 26.11 changes that with Hierarchical Resources (HRES) plugins, which allow a site to schedule a QPU as a native, cluster-level resource through a short, portable Lua plugin.
This post covers why QPUs have not fit the previous scheduling models Slurm used for CPUs and GPUs. It then explains the solution: how HRES models a QPU, and what HRES plugins add in Slurm 26.11, including the API callbacks and capabilities that middleware teams build on. It also addresses how community-driven interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI have already built open source plugins on these APIs, as well as initial adoption by the quantum ecosystem and supercomputing centers.
Building quantum-GPU supercomputing
Integrating a QPU at a supercomputing center requires more than just its physical installation. The QPU must be networked with the existing computing infrastructure, and users must be able to request it at job submission the same way CPUs and GPUs are requested. Its usage must be tracked, monitored, and accounted for, and it must abide by site-specific policies. In other words, the scheduler, or workload manager, must manage the QPU like it would any other computing resource.
Until now, schedulers have had no native way to model a QPU, so most integrations are repeatedly custom-built for each new supercomputing site or QPU builder. The cost of that fragmentation falls on everyone involved:
- Users face a different interface at every site.
- Administrators must maintain custom code that complicates upgrades.
- QPU vendors rebuild their integration for each customer, with no portability.
- Global systems integrators (GSIs) cannot deliver a repeatable deployment.
On the QPU side, open source efforts such as QRMI and QDMI are unifying how such devices are described to, and controlled by, HPC software. What has been missing is a unified interface in the scheduler used by supercomputing centers for integrating QPUs into HPC deployments.
Why existing Slurm resource models don’t accommodate QPUs
A QPU is typically a cluster-wide accelerator, not part of a node. Slurm generic resources (GRES), the mechanism used for GPUs, belong to individual compute nodes. Modeling a QPU as a GRES binds it to one node, so only jobs on that node can use it. If that node fails, for example, the QPU stays unreachable until an administrator reconfigures the cluster.
Many integrations instead combine licenses, which represent cluster-wide resources, for scheduling, and use SPANK plugins for the user interface and node setup. This approach works, but it has several problems:
- Idle nodes: Without a license, SPANK only acts after Slurm has allocated nodes, so a job can hold compute nodes idle while it waits for the QPU.
- Two-flag requests: Nothing stops a job from passing device options without holding the license.
- Multiple QPUs: Hosting several QPUs on one cluster is difficult, because their SPANK plugins compete for the same command-line options.
- Upgrade risk: In practice, many SPANK plugins tie third-party code to Slurm internal APIs, so every Slurm upgrade risks breaking the integration.
- No device awareness: Slurm cannot tell on its own when a QPU is recalibrating or offline, so it keeps starting jobs that cannot use the device until it is back online.
How HRES plugins in Slurm 26.11 enable integration
Slurm 26.11 introduces an HRES plugin interface to address these gaps, so that the HPC and quantum communities can integrate with Slurm without changing Slurm itself. Its first implementation, hres/lua, runs a short Lua script. The plugin reports device health to the scheduler, accepts device options as part of the resource request, and runs setup and teardown code at each stage of the job.
A site describes the QPU as a cluster-level HRES in resources.yaml and points it at the plugin. The two files divide the work. resources.yaml holds site-specific details and policies, such as endpoints and which nodes can reach the device, under the system administrator’s control. The plugin holds the device logic, so the community or a QPU vendor can write it once and ship it to every site that deploys Slurm 26.11.
Modeling a QPU as a hierarchical resource
HRES was added to Slurm 25.05 as a beta feature and is the evolution of licenses. Like a license, an HRES is a count of a resource that does not belong to any single node. Unlike a license, that count is associated with a specific set of nodes: the ones allowed to use it (Figure 1). Slurm 26.11 also starts to allow more dynamic modeling of the relationship between nodes and HRES.
An HRES is defined in resources.yaml, in the same directory as slurm.conf. Each resource has one or more layers, and each layer has a name, a list of nodes, and a count. For a QPU, the simplest definition is a single layer covering the nodes that can reach the device, with a count of one. The plugin block attaches the Lua script and its site-specific settings:
- resource: qpu
  mode: MODE_1
  plugin:
	type: hres/lua
	config:
  	- name: path
    value: /etc/slurm/hres_qpu.lua
  	- name: endpoint               	# site settings, never secrets
    value: https://qpu-gateway.example.org
	maintenance_cycle: 30            	# seconds between health checks
  layers:
	- layer_name: qpu1
  	nodes: ["node[0001-0123]"]
  	count: 1
With this definition, a request is satisfied when a layer that overlaps the job’s allocated nodes has enough of the resource available. A job that requests the QPU runs only on nodes in that layer. Jobs request the resource with --resources=qpu:1.
The middleware is the boundary between HPC and QPU
In the model shown in Figure 2, neither Slurm nor the Lua plugin talks to the QPU directly. A third-party access middleware sits between the HPC system and the QPU and provides a unified interface to different quantum hardware APIs. The middleware is therefore the boundary between the HPC system and the QPU.
Slurm treats the QPU as a single schedulable unit. It decides whether the unit is available, which job holds it, for how long, and from which nodes. Importantly, Slurm does not orchestrate anything inside the unit: calibration, error correction, and device control stay within the QPU and its own software runtime. The approach therefore applies both to today’s noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices and to future error-corrected systems.
The plugin translates between the two sides. It asks the middleware for status and reservations, and reports the results to Slurm in Slurm’s terms: whether a layer is disabled, whether a job can start, and a payload for the job’s nodes.
HRES plugin APIs
The current implementation of HRES plugins runs a Lua script written by the community or a device vendor.
Lua
A Lua plugin is a plain text file that vendors can ship and update independently of Slurm’s release cycle. It does not link against libslurm, whose API changes each release, so it does not need rebuilding for every Slurm upgrade. Lua is also fast, embeds cleanly in C, and is already used by Slurm’s job submit and CLI filter plugins. The script must sit at the same path on the controller and on every node, and since most of its functions run as root or as SlurmUser, only root should be able to write to it.
Key capabilities include:
- Stackability: slurmctld creates a separate plugin context for each resource that defines a plugin. One cluster can host several QPUs, and several QPU types, without the option collisions that SPANK plugins run into.
- Site configuration: Endpoints and other settings live in the plugin’s config list, which Slurm hands to the plugin without interpreting it. The configuration, the job’s arguments, and any payload travel with the job to its nodes, where the job’s user can read them. This means that none of them may hold secrets.
- User inputs: Users append name=value arguments to the request, for example --resources='qpu:1[shot=1000]'. Slurm passes them to the plugin without interpreting them, which removes the need for a second command-line flag.
- Health checks: Every maintenance_cycle seconds, a maintenance callback asks the middleware whether the QPU is ready, and sets or clears disable_layer on each layer to stop or resume allocation from it.
- Job start and end: Once a job is scheduled, and before its nodes are allocated, a controller prerun can admit or hold it, so the job never holds idle nodes while it waits for the QPU. Because the prerun holds the controller’s job lock, slow work, such as reserving the QPU, belongs in an optional asynchronous prerun, whose payload Slurm sends to the job’s nodes. If the job does not start, a revoke callback undoes the reservation, and a controller epilog releases it when the job ends.
- Failure handling: A callback can return ESLURM_HRES_REMOTE_FAIL to report that the external service is unavailable rather than broken. A failed prerun then leaves the job pending, and a failed node prolog or epilog does not drain the node.
A plugin implements the callbacks in Table 1, in the order they run for a job.
| Callback | Runs | Example QPU use | 
|---|---|---|
| hres_create_context  | slurmctld, for each resource with a plugin, when the configuration is read. Every layer shows nothing used at this point | Check the service is reachable and set up connections or state | 
| hres_maintenance  | slurmctld, every maintenance_cycle seconds | Query the middleware for status; set or clear disable_layer on each layer | 
| hres_controller_job_prerun  | slurmctld, once the job is scheduled and before its nodes are allocated, under the job lock | Admit or hold the job, for example against a cached device status | 
| hres_controller_job_async_prerun (optional)  | slurmctld, in a separate thread while the job is configuring | Reserve the QPU on the service; return a payload for the job’s nodes | 
| hres_controller_job_revoke  | slurmctld, when the job does not start after its prerun succeeded | Undo the reservation | 
| hres_node_job_prolog  | Each node of the job, once, before the Prolog script | Start an access service or write per-job files | 
| hres_node_task_prolog  | slurmstepd, in each task as root, before it starts | Privileged per-task setup | 
| hres_node_user_task_prolog  | slurmstepd, in each task as the user, just before it starts | Per-task setup as the user | 
| hres_node_task_epilog  | slurmstepd, after each task exits | Per-task cleanup | 
| hres_node_job_epilog  | Each node of the job, once, after the Epilog script | Stop the service; remove per-job files | 
| hres_controller_job_epilog  | slurmctld, after all the job’s node epilogs, before its resources are returned | Release the reservation | 
| hres_destroy_context  | slurmctld, before the configuration is read again | Close connections and free anything the script holds | 
hres_create_context and hres_destroy_context also run on slurmctld whenever it reads its configuration
Most integrations need only a few callbacks. The following skeleton shows the shape of a plugin: a health check, an admission decision before any nodes are allocated, and a release when the job ends. The middleware_* calls stand in for the middleware’s own client library.
-- Callback names, arguments, fields, and return codes are Slurm's hres/lua API.
-- middleware_* calls are placeholders for your middleware's client library.
  -- Health: slurmctld, every maintenance_cycle seconds
function hres_maintenance(ctx, layers)
  local ready = middleware_status(ctx.config.endpoint)
  for _, layer in ipairs(layers) do layer.disable_layer = not ready end
  return slurm.SUCCESS
end
-- Admission: once the job is scheduled, before its nodes are allocated
function hres_controller_job_prerun(ctx, job, prep)
  if not middleware_can_admit(ctx, prep.plugin_args) then   -- cached, no network
	return slurm.ESLURM_HRES_REMOTE_FAIL                	-- the job stays pending
  end
  return slurm.SUCCESS
end
-- Release: after the job's node epilogs
function hres_controller_job_epilog(ctx, job, prep)
  middleware_release(ctx.config.endpoint, prep.payload)
  return slurm.SUCCESS
end
-- The remaining required callbacks return slurm.SUCCESS.
Community integration examples of HRES plugins
The teams that build QPU access middleware usually write the HRES plugins. Two of those communities, QRMI and QDMI, have released open source plugins built on the Slurm 26.11 APIs. Both admit jobs only while the QPU is available, and in both, the layer’s count sets how many jobs can use a QPU at the same time. The QRMI plugin acquires access to the QPU for each job before it runs. The QDMI plugin only admits jobs, and each job then queues its work with the provider. With either plugin, sites running Slurm 26.11 can connect their clusters to quantum computers from multiple providers.
QRMI: Acquiring the QPU for each job
Each HRES resource is named after a resource in the QRMI configuration file. Before a job runs, the plugin books access to the QPU with the user’s own credentials, in a separate thread outside the scheduler’s critical path, and releases it after the job ends. Depending on the backend, the booking is a reservation or a session. Existing applications run unchanged, because jobs see the same environment variables as with the QRMI SPANK plugin. For the complete configuration, plugin and a containerized test cluster, visit the QRMI HRES plugin repository.
QDMI: Leaving the queue to the provider
Each HRES resource is one device, named after its QDMI device ID. The plugin’s maintenance callback checks the device’s status and admits jobs only while it reports itself as idle or busy. The plugin reserves nothing: each job submits its work through QDMI, and the provider’s queue schedules it on the device. For the complete configuration and plugin, visit the MQSC Orchestrator.
Learn how more organizations in the quantum ecosystem are integrating HRES plugins:
User job submission
From the user’s side, the two integrations look and feel the same. A job script requests the QPU by its HRES resource name just as it requests nodes or GPUs, and runs in the partition that contains the HRES assigned nodes. Slurm holds the job until the plugin reports that the QPU is available and, where the middleware supports it, reserved. The template below works for either integration; only the resource name changes.
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my-hybrid-job
#SBATCH --nodes=4
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --resources=<qpu_resource>
srun ./my_hybrid_app
Get started with Slurm HRES plugins
Slurm 26.11 gives QPUs a native place in the scheduler. An HRES models the QPU as a cluster-level resource tied to the nodes that can reach it, and a Lua plugin connects that resource to the middleware that manages the device. Because the Lua plugin is designed to hold little to nothing site-specific, a vendor or community project can write it once and every Slurm site can reuse it, while administrators keep control of their own policies.
By design, this approach is valid for today’s generation of quantum computers and for future fault-tolerant systems, making it a lasting choice for supercomputing centers deploying quantum devices.
Ready to get started? Deploy the QRMI HRES plugin or the QDMI HRES example, or use them as starting points for your own integration. To learn more, check out the Slurm 26.11 release notes, and read the HRES documentation and the resources.yaml reference.
Acknowledgments
We thank the QRMI and QDMI communities for building on HRES plugins and for their contributions to this post.

articles.title: Alerte sur GTA 6 : un faux téléchargement du jeu cache un logiciel qui vole vos données
articles.text:
À deux jours de la sortie de GTA 6, Avast met en garde contre un faux téléchargement du jeu. Derrière une prétendue version complète circule actuellement un infostealer, un logiciel conçu pour voler les données des joueurs.
Un faux téléchargement du jeu le plus attendu de l'année, GTA 6, circule sur le Web, et il peut faire des dégâts. Les experts d'Avast nous indique ce mardi 17 novembre avoir identifié ce piège, qui mène d'un PDF d'apparence sérieuse jusqu'à une fausse page Google Drive, et en détaillent chaque étape. Il promet la version complète du jeu de Rockstar, mais livre en réalité un programme malveillant. L'arnaque est taillée sur mesure pour piéger les joueurs les plus impatients, à seulement deux jours d'une sortie attendue depuis treize ans.
Un GTA 6 gratuit trop beau pour être vrai
Le premier maillon de ce piège cyber autour de GTA 6 est un document PDF se fait passer pour un guide de téléchargement du jeu. Sur les captures transmises par Avast, rien ne cloche au premier regard. On a un large bouton « Download Now » (Télécharger maintenant), un résumé fidèle du jeu, qui cite Jason, Lucia et l’État de Leonida, et même un lien vers le site officiel de Rockstar. Le document pousse le culot jusqu’à recommander de vérifier la page avant de télécharger. Tout ce vernis de sérieux sert à endormir la méfiance des joueurs.
Le bouton renvoie vers un site baptisé getallsoft[.]co, alors que le PDF est signé… « Getarsoft ». La page, intitulée « Grand Theft Auto VI Download – Latest Version », est datée du 24 octobre. Avec ses rubriques Windows, Antivirus ou PC Games, le site se présente comme une vaste bibliothèque de logiciels gratuits, ce qui ressemble fort aux plateformes qui diffusent des copies piratées, souvent piégées. La page se trahit toute seule d'ailleurs, car elle reconnaît que GTA 6 ne sortira que le 19 novembre, et uniquement sur PS5 et Xbox Series, et elle propose quand même de le télécharger gratuitement dès aujourd’hui. Un jeu qui n'est pas encore sorti, et encore moins sur PC, ne peut évidemment pas se télécharger.
Un nouveau clic mène à une page qui imite Google Drive, rebaptisée « GDrive », où attend une archive ZIP présentée comme mise en ligne le 10 novembre. La page affiche un fichier scanné et un transfert soi-disant sécurisé, mais son adresse n'a rien à voir avec Google. Et l'archive pèse plus de 700 Mo, une goutte d'eau face aux 212 Go que réclame le vrai jeu, selon la console. À l'intérieur, vous l'aurez compris, il n'y a pas de Vice City, mais un infostealer, c'est-à-dire un voleur d'informations, dans le détail un programme qui fouille l'appareil pour en extraire des informations personnelles, comme des identifiants ou des mots de passe.
Aucun GTA 6 sur PC, et c'est le meilleur indice
On insiste, GTA 6 ne sort que sur PS5 et Xbox Series X|S, le jeudi 19 novembre à minuit, heure locale, et Rockstar n'a annoncé aucune version PC. Tout fichier qui prétend contenir le jeu complet avant cette date, a fortiori pour ordinateur, doit donc être considéré comme suspect. Les experts d'Avast expliquent que les escrocs profitent aussi des rumeurs de fuites pour rendre leurs pièges plus crédibles.
Ce n'est pas la première alerte en tout cas sur le jeu. Il y a quelques semaines, Avast avait déjà repéré plus de 200 noms de domaine liés à GTA 6 en seulement 24 heures, dont près de 10 % présentaient un risque élevé ou moyen. Dans le lot, on retrouvait de fausses précommandes, des sites imitant les boutiques de Rockstar ou de PlayStation, des téléchargements frauduleux et des faux jeux-concours. Les arnaqueurs du Web exploitent toutes les facettes d'un jeu dont les précommandes numériques frôlent désormais les 15 millions d'exemplaires.
Pour jouer sans risque, il n'existe qu'une voie, celle des boutiques officielles de Sony et Microsoft, ou les revendeurs habituels, dont les boîtes ne contiennent d'ailleurs qu'un code de téléchargement. Ceux qui veulent vraiment prendre de l'avance ont une option à disposition. Sur Xbox Series, l'astuce de la Nouvelle-Zélande permet, en principe, de lancer le jeu dès mercredi midi. Et si vous avez déjà ouvert un fichier douteux, ne traînez pas et lancez une analyse antivirus, changez vos mots de passe depuis un autre appareil, en commençant par votre messagerie et vos comptes de jeu.

articles.title: The fake photos are gone. INEC’s bigger problem remains
articles.text:
Nigeria’s electoral umpire, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), says it has removed artificial intelligence-generated photographs from its voter register. But a more consequential part of the disclosure concerns the people who helped put them there: some of the commission’s own personnel.
With the 2027 elections approaching, the controversy raises questions that cannot be settled by deleting suspicious images. INEC needs to explain how questionable photographs entered the register, why its registration checks did not prevent their inclusion, and whether its newly announced image-capture restrictions will close the gap. The commission says it is replacing external webcam-based uploads with photographs captured directly through an approved application.
On November 11, 2026, the commission said it had identified 54 registration personnel across 10 states for possible disciplinary action over registration irregularities. This does not establish that all 54 uploaded synthetic photographs or committed criminal offences. It does, however, show that the inquiry extends beyond applicants submitting questionable information to officials responsible for protecting the registration process.
“But the ones involving our own staff, where it is our own staff that did so, that one is within our control,” Mohammed Kudu Haruna, INEC’s national commissioner for information and voter education, said during a PUNCH Media Foundation webinar on November 11. “They have been flagged,” he added. “Obviously, they are going to face disciplinary action.”
The allegations potentially extend beyond workplace misconduct. Section 23 of the Electoral Act 2026 criminalises knowingly transmitting materially false registration declarations and procuring the registration of fictitious or ineligible persons. Whether particular personnel committed those offences requires investigation; being flagged is not a finding of guilt. Haruna’s assurance of disciplinary action leaves a further question: will cases supported by evidence of criminal conduct also be pursued in court?
Beyond the photograph
The involvement of registration personnel changes the nature of the problem. Electoral bodies must anticipate inaccurate information from applicants. But when authorised staff allegedly circumvent registration protocols, the issue becomes whether the institution can enforce its own safeguards.
AI may add a technological dimension, but the investigation must address fundamental questions of institutional control. Who could upload or replace a photograph? What checks were required? Could one official make changes without independent review? And are there records showing who altered each entry?
Deleting suspicious images addresses the visible problem. Establishing how they entered the system is necessary to prevent a recurrence.
So far, the disclosures do not establish that an external cyberattack compromised the register or that manipulated photographs resulted in fraudulent votes. These possibilities should not be presented as confirmed findings.
What the numbers mean
The figures surrounding the cleanup also require careful interpretation. INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan said 1,608,660 invalid registrations had been removed. Separately, reports say the commission reviewed 268,000 contested cases, rejecting 217,722 and retaining 50,278.
Published accounts have not clearly explained how these figures relate to one another, so they should not be added together automatically. Neither should the 1.6 million figure be described as the number of AI-generated voter records.
The cleanup covered several irregularities, including duplicate entries and deficient registration records. Synthetic or manipulated photographs were one concern within that broader exercise.
The distinction matters because imprecise figures can turn an administrative problem into allegations that the available evidence does not support. At the same time, a large deletion figure does not explain what the commission detected, how it verified each category, or whether the underlying weaknesses have been addressed.
The 50,278 records retained after adjudication are equally important. Suspicion alone does not establish ineligibility. A credible cleanup must prevent invalid registrations while protecting eligible voters from wrongful exclusion.
Discipline is only the beginning
INEC says the register was published in preliminary form to allow public scrutiny and objections before final certification. That process can help identify errors before an election, but it should not replace safeguards that ought to operate during registration.
Both things can be true: public inspection may have helped expose irregularities, while their discovery points to weaknesses that the commission must address. INEC’s credibility will depend on its ability to explain what went wrong and how its internal controls are changing.
The proposed disciplinary action is a starting point, not a completed accountability process. The identified personnel must be allowed to respond to the allegations, and the commission must distinguish between mistakes, negligence and deliberate falsification. Disciplinary action should also not be confused with criminal prosecution, dismissal or conviction.
Beyond individual sanctions, Nigerians need to know what investigators found, which procedures failed and what corrective measures have been introduced. While personal information may require protection, INEC can still disclose its institutional findings.
The policy test ahead
INEC said in October it is finalising an AI policy, but the controversy raises questions about whether that framework will address only AI-generated campaign content or also the commission’s own systems, personnel and use of automated tools.
“We have that policy. Very soon, we will concretise it, and we will be able to share it with the media,” Haruna said at the November 11 webinar.
The timing is significant. With presidential and National Assembly elections scheduled for January 16, 2027, the policy was still awaiting publication roughly two months before polling. More importantly, the registration exercise had already exposed irregularities that the framework could have helped prevent.
A useful policy must go beyond broad warnings about artificial intelligence. It should clarify who can access and alter voter records, what verification is required before photographs are accepted, how suspicious submissions are escalated, and who independently reviews sensitive changes. It should also establish clear responsibilities for staff and supervisors, with decisions documented and open to audit.
The absence of a published standalone AI policy does not prove that INEC had no existing safeguards, nor does it mean earlier publication would necessarily have prevented the irregularities. The commission must explain whether controls were missing, inadequate or deliberately bypassed. Its own admission of staff involvement makes that distinction central.
Ultimately, Nigerians need more than assurances that suspicious photographs have been removed or that personnel will face discipline. They need evidence that the registration process is secure, that eligible voters will not be wrongly excluded and that those entrusted with the register are accountable.
The photographs can disappear quickly. The reason they were accepted must not disappear with them; otherwise, the next AI-generated image may be harder to detect, while the institutional weakness remains unchanged.

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, primeras impresiones: mucho más que una pantalla trasera para llamar la atención de los más fanáticos
articles.text:
Grabar un vídeo con la cámara trasera de un móvil tiene un inconveniente bastante evidente: no puedes verte mientras lo haces. Parece una tontería, pero para quienes nos dedicamos a crear contenido puede ser un problema, especialmente cuando queremos aprovechar la mejor calidad posible sin depender de otra persona que nos ayude a encuadrar. Xiaomi lleva tiempo experimentando con las pantallas secundarias, pero con su nuevo Xiaomi 18 Pro Max parece haber encontrado una aplicación que, al menos en mi caso, tiene muchísimo sentido.
He tenido la oportunidad de probar el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max en París, coincidiendo con su presentación oficial y, aunque todavía es pronto para sacar conclusiones definitivas, hay varias cosas que me han llamado especialmente la atención. Su pantalla trasera es la novedad más evidente, pero después de utilizar sus cámaras, especialmente de noche, tengo claro que este teléfono es mucho más que una simple pantalla para llamar la atención.
La pantalla trasera es mucho más útil de lo que parece, aunque tiene un problema
Evidentemente, lo primero que llama la atención del Xiaomi 18 Pro Max es el enorme módulo fotográfico que encontramos en su parte trasera. En él, además de las cámaras desarrolladas junto a Leica, Xiaomi ha integrado una pantalla AMOLED completamente táctil que permite consultar información, interactuar con determinadas funciones e incluso utilizarla como visor cuando hacemos fotografías o grabamos vídeos. Y precisamente esto último es lo que más me ha gustado.
La posibilidad de grabarme con las cámaras principales mientras veo exactamente cómo estoy encuadrando me parece una auténtica maravilla. La pantalla tiene un tamaño más que suficiente para comprobar que todo está correctamente colocado, responde perfectamente a las pulsaciones y permite tanto iniciar grabaciones como hacer fotografías. Incluso incorpora controles por gestos para disparar sin tocar el teléfono, algo especialmente práctico cuando queremos colocarlo sobre una superficie y grabarnos a cierta distancia.
Para quienes creamos contenido, esto puede suponer una diferencia importante. Hasta ahora, lo habitual era recurrir a la cámara frontal para comprobar el encuadre, sacrificando parte de la calidad que ofrecen los sensores traseros. Con esta solución podemos aprovechar el sensor principal de 200 megapíxeles sin renunciar a vernos durante la grabación. Además, la pantalla tiene muchísimo brillo y no he tenido ningún problema para utilizarla en exteriores, incluso en las condiciones de luz que hemos tenido estos días en París.
Pero Xiaomi quiere que esta pantalla sirva para algo más. Podemos personalizar su apariencia, consultar el calendario, utilizar cuentas regresivas o crear tarjetas mediante inteligencia artificial para determinadas tareas. Por ejemplo, es posible configurar recordatorios para beber agua o temporizadores Pomodoro, entre otras muchas cosas.
Son funciones interesantes y todavía tengo que dedicarles más tiempo, aunque aquí aparece mi principal duda: ¿hasta qué punto vamos a acostumbrarnos a utilizar una segunda pantalla cuando ya tenemos una principal que funciona perfectamente? Creo que ese será uno de los mayores retos para Xiaomi.
Más allá de estas funciones, la pantalla trasera también permite controlar la reproducción de música en aplicaciones como Spotify, además de consultar las notificaciones que recibimos. Eso sí, por ahora sus posibilidades son bastante limitadas, ya que podemos ver que hemos recibido un mensaje, pero no responderlo directamente desde esta pantalla.
Tampoco es posible visualizar las fotografías que nos envían, únicamente aparece el aviso de que hemos recibido una imagen. Xiaomi también tiene previsto incorporar la navegación con mapas, aunque esta función todavía no está disponible. Por tanto, creo que aún tiene bastante margen de mejora para convertirse en algo realmente útil en el día a día.
También hay un pequeño detalle que conviene tener en cuenta. Las cámaras están integradas prácticamente al mismo nivel que la superficie trasera, por lo que al interactuar con la pantalla resulta relativamente fácil tocar alguna de las lentes sin querer. No es ningún drama, pero habrá que acostumbrarse a mantenerlas limpias para evitar que una simple huella termine afectando a nuestras fotografías.
Por lo demás, el diseño me ha convencido bastante. Estoy utilizando la versión en color negro, con un acabado mate que apenas retiene las huellas y que también se extiende al marco de aluminio. El resultado es un teléfono elegante, limpio y agradable al tacto, aunque debo reconocer que el acabado rojo, que también he podido ver en persona, me parece todavía más bonito. Eso sí, con sus 235 gramos, estamos ante un dispositivo grande y pesado, algo que conviene tener presente.
Hay otros detalles curiosos, como la integración de una de las salidas de sonido en el propio módulo de cámaras o la reubicación del emisor de infrarrojos en la parte trasera, dos decisiones que ayudan a mantener un diseño más limpio. También encontramos un botón dedicado a funciones de inteligencia artificial en el lateral izquierdo que, si bien puede resultar útil para acceder rápidamente a herramientas como las notas de voz, al menos por ahora, me parece más una curiosidad que una característica realmente determinante.
Sus cámaras Leica me han sorprendido especialmente de noche
Si hay algo que me ha dejado especialmente buenas sensaciones durante estos primeros días, ha sido el apartado fotográfico. Xiaomi ha apostado por una cámara principal Leica de 200 megapíxeles con sensor Light Fusion 960L y tecnología HDR LOFIC, acompañada de un teleobjetivo, también de 200 megapíxeles, con una distancia focal equivalente a 75 mm. Sobre el papel ya estamos hablando de un sistema al nivel de los mejores dispositivos del mercado, pero lo interesante es comprobar cómo responde fuera de las condiciones ideales.
Y precisamente las condiciones no han sido las mejores. Durante mi estancia en París hemos tenido cielos bastante nublados, lluvia y muy pocas oportunidades de fotografiar con buena iluminación. Sin embargo, esto me ha permitido comprobar algo que me ha sorprendido muchísimo: el comportamiento de la cámara principal por la noche. El nivel de detalle es fantástico, el ruido está extraordinariamente controlado y las fotografías mantienen un contraste que, personalmente, me ha encantado.
De hecho, hay una cosa bastante curiosa que he observado durante las pruebas. La imagen que aparece en el visor antes de disparar no tiene demasiado que ver con el resultado final que encontramos después en la galería. El procesado marca una diferencia considerable, especialmente cuando hay poca luz, y consigue fotografías con un aspecto muy cuidado. Evidentemente, no estamos hablando de sustituir una cámara profesional de objetivos intercambiables, pero los resultados que he conseguido hasta ahora me parecen excelentes.
También me gusta mucho el tratamiento del color que Xiaomi sigue desarrollando junto a Leica. Podemos elegir entre diferentes estilos, como Leica Vibrant, Leica Authentic o el perfil Original, pero personalmente me quedo con el segundo. Ese contraste más marcado y el ligero oscurecimiento de los bordes le dan a las fotografías una personalidad que me resulta especialmente atractiva. Incluso en días grises como los que hemos tenido en París, creo que el resultado tiene muchísimo encanto.
El teleobjetivo tampoco se queda atrás. Sus 200 megapíxeles permiten conseguir fotografías con un nivel de detalle muy alto y, lo que más me ha sorprendido, es que mantiene una calidad estupenda incluso cuando cae la noche. Además, permite enfocar a distancias bastante cortas, de hasta 12 centímetros según Xiaomi, por lo que también podemos utilizarlo para fotografía telemacro. Es una de esas funciones que pueden pasar desapercibidas, pero que ofrecen bastante juego cuando queremos fotografiar objetos pequeños o capturar detalles sin acercarnos demasiado.
No todo es perfecto, eso sí. El ultra gran angular es claramente la cámara que menos me ha convencido. Aunque sus 50 megapíxeles cumplen razonablemente bien durante el día, hay una diferencia apreciable respecto al sensor principal y al teleobjetivo. Por la noche esa distancia se hace todavía más evidente y tengo la sensación de que Xiaomi necesita apoyarse bastante en el procesado para conseguir fotografías aceptables. No diría que es una mala cámara, pero está un escalón por debajo de las otras dos, especialmente cuando hablamos de grabación de vídeo.
Y hablando de vídeo, todavía no he podido exprimir todas sus posibilidades, aunque las primeras pruebas también han sido positivas. El Xiaomi 18 Pro Max permite grabar hasta en 8K a 30 fps, además de ofrecer 4K a 60 fps, que personalmente considero la opción más equilibrada para el día a día. También tenemos 4K a 120 fps para grabaciones a cámara lenta y compatibilidad con Dolby Vision. La calidad de imagen me ha gustado y la estabilización funciona muy bien, pero necesitaré hacer más pruebas antes de valorar este apartado en profundidad.
Un móvil de gama alta con muy pocas pegas, al menos por ahora
Más allá de las cámaras y la pantalla trasera, el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max transmite las sensaciones que esperamos de un teléfono de su categoría. Su panel principal de 6,9 pulgadas tiene una calidad de imagen fantástica, una respuesta táctil excelente y un brillo que no me ha dado ningún problema. Además, incorpora una tecnología de privacidad que limita la visibilidad desde determinados ángulos, aunque es una de las funciones que todavía tengo pendiente probar con más detenimiento porque de primeras no he notado que sea algo diferencial ya que apenas se nota.
En cuanto al rendimiento, pocas sorpresas. El Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, fabricado en 2 nanómetros, ofrece una potencia más que suficiente para cualquier tarea que he realizado hasta ahora. HyperOS 4 también me ha dejado buenas sensaciones: todo funciona con una fluidez excelente, las aplicaciones responden rápidamente y no he encontrado ningún problema durante estos primeros días. El lector ultrasónico de huellas sigue siendo rapidísimo y el desbloqueo facial, aunque utiliza reconocimiento 2D, también funciona correctamente.
La batería es otro de los apartados que prometen bastante. Este modelo incorpora 7.050 mAh de capacidad gracias a la tecnología de silicio-carbono, junto con carga rápida de 100 W por cable y 50 W de forma inalámbrica. Durante las jornadas de fotografías que he realizado en París ha respondido bien, pero todavía no tengo datos suficientes para hablar de autonomía real. Prefiero reservarme esa valoración para cuando pueda comprobar cómo se comporta después de varios días de uso intensivo.
Después de estas primeras pruebas, tengo la sensación de que Xiaomi ha conseguido un teléfono muy completo, especialmente para quienes damos mucha importancia a la fotografía y al vídeo. El sensor principal y el teleobjetivo me han parecido excelentes, el rendimiento está a la altura de lo esperado y el diseño tiene detalles interesantes. También ayuda que su posicionamiento de precio resulte algo más contenido frente a determinados rivales, especialmente si tenemos en cuenta las promociones de lanzamiento.
Pero si hay algo que realmente puede diferenciar a este Xiaomi 18 Pro Max es su pantalla trasera. Para grabar contenido ya le he encontrado una utilidad clarísima, y solo por eso me parece una incorporación muy acertada. La gran pregunta es si conseguiré integrarla en otras actividades cotidianas o si terminará siendo una función que únicamente utilice cuando necesite grabarme. De momento, las sensaciones son muy buenas, aunque todavía quedan bastantes cosas por comprobar antes del análisis definitivo.
Precio y disponibilidad del Xiaomi 18 Pro Max en España
En cuanto a precios, el Xiaomi 18 Pro Max llega oficialmente a España en cuatro colores: negro, blanco, azul cósmico y Velvet Red. La marca ha confirmado dos configuraciones de almacenamiento, ambas con 12 GB de RAM, cuyos precios oficiales son los siguientes:
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max de 12 GB + 256 GB: 1.599,99 euros.
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max de 12 GB + 512 GB: 1.799,99 euros.
Sin embargo, Xiaomi ha preparado una promoción de lanzamiento que permite ahorrar 300 euros en cualquiera de las dos versiones al registrarse y realizar la compra a través de mi.com. De esta forma, los precios quedan así:
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max de 12 GB + 256 GB: 1.299,99 euros.
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max de 12 GB + 512 GB: 1.499,99 euros.
Estas ofertas estarán disponibles desde el 17 de noviembre de 2026 hasta el 6 de enero de 2027, tanto en la tienda online oficial de Xiaomi como en sus establecimientos propios. Además, la compañía ofrece financiación de hasta 24 meses sin intereses para ambas configuraciones, así que tenemos muchísimas opciones disponibles para poder hacernos con él a muy buen precio.
