articles.title: Apple to add Face Unlock to iPhone Duo in future software update - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple is adding facial unlock for the new iPhone Duo in the next iOS 27.3 update which will use the front-facing camera when the device is in the closed position.
Many iPhone Duo customers were surprised to find out the device did not have Face ID but instead used Touch ID for security.
We know many customers, most coming from a previous iPhone, found it jarring not to have the instant unlock that Face ID provides.
READ TECH GUIDE’S iPHONE DUO REVIEW HERE
Apple has responded to these reactions and decided to remedy the situation with this new facial unlock feature which is only available on the lock screen.
Facial unlock will still require Touch ID to authenticate.
Touch ID will be required again after 45 minutes of inactivity.
The new feature needs to be enabled in the settings under Touch ID and Passcode.
Touch ID will still be required to authorise Apple Pay and access your passwords folder.
Apple has also added Close To Lock feature, which, as its name suggests locks the iPhone Duo when you close it.
Closing the iPhone Duo without this setting just transfer what you’re viewing to the front screen.
This feature can be activated in the Display & Brightness settings.
These features have just been released to developers in the beta for the iOS 27.3 software update.
Customers can expect the update to be available in early December.

articles.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
articles.text:
AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
Using AI to make bionic vision smarter and more precise, scientists are bringing the possibility of restoring sight to people with blindness one step closer to reality.
- Date:
- November 12, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Barbara
- Summary:
- Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.
The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.
Published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.
"Building a model in the abstract is one thing," said Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab."
How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes
For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.
Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.
The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.
Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back."
The new findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.
Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man
An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.
At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.
When researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.
Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.
To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.
Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.
AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise
When the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The new approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.
Another important discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.
This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.
"Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler said. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation."
The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.
Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person
A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.
This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.
The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.
Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.
The AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.
By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.
"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler said. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around."
A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight
The research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration."
The project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.
Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.
Rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of California - Santa Barbara. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler, Eduardo Fernández. Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex. Neuron, 2026; DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

articles.title: Las leónidas pueden ser la mejor lluvia de estrellas del año o la más decepcionante. Esta noche toca lo segundo
articles.text:
Si pensamos en una lluvia de estrellas abundante, en el hemisferio norte seguro que nos vienen a la mente las perseidas. En el sur son más de gemínidas, porque tienen lugar cuando allí es verano, como pasa con las perseidas en el norte. Ambas suelen regalarnos espectáculos de más de 100 meteoros por hora, muy agradables de ver. También hay otras igual de potentes, como las cuadrántidas.
Más allá de eso, la mayoría de lluvias de estrellas suelen pasar desapercibidas. Sin embargo, hay algunas que normalmente pasan sin pena ni gloria, pero que en algunos momentos de la historia superaron con creces a perseidas y gemínidas. Es el caso de las leónidas, que en 1966 dieron lugar a una tormenta de más de 144.000 meteoros por hora. Esta noche será el pico de esta lluvia de estrellas. ¿Qué podemos esperar de ellas?
Más estrellas de las que se pueden contar. En 1966, el científico jefe del planetario Hayden de Nueva York, Kenneth L. Franklin, calculó que la noche del 17 de noviembre tendría lugar la lluvia de estrellas más abundante que ningún humano vivo hubiese visto jamás. Según sus predicciones, las leónidas bombardearían el cielo, superando los 100.000 meteoros por hora. Tal fue su emoción que animó a todo el mundo a acudir a Central Park para tumbarse en el césped y disfrutar del espectáculo. Lamentablemente, las nubes impidieron el espectáculo, por lo que los allí presentes no pudieron calcular si el astrónomo estuvo en lo cierto. Sin embargo, en otros puntos de Estados Unidos y del resto del mundo sí pudieron hacerlo.
Trece astrónomos reunidos en el pico Kitt, al sur de Arizona, llegaron a contar 40 meteoros por segundo, lo cual equivale a 144.000 por hora. Es cierto que es una extrapolación y puede que no se mantuviese esta tasa de forma estable hora tras hora, pero aun así fueron muchísimos meteoros. De hecho, la mayoría de personas que disfrutaron del espectáculo contaron que se veían tantas estrellas fugaces que era imposible contarlas. Incluso hubo quien señaló que la imagen era tan brutal que sentían la necesidad instintiva de protegerse de la caída abrumadora de estrellas sobre ellos.
Este año. ¿Podremos ver este año lo mismo? Pues no, la verdad es que no. Ni de lejos. Las leónidas se forman a partir de los escombros que deja atrás el cometa Tempel-Tuttle, que pasa por el sistema solar cada 33 años y un tercio. La mayor parte del polvo que deja a su paso se queda muy cerca del cuerpo principal del cometa, por lo que es importante que se encuentre bien cerca de la Tierra para que nos topemos con sus escombros en nuestro particular recorrido alrededor del Sol. La última vez que el cometa se acercó al máximo al sistema solar fue en 1998. Por eso hubo lluvias muy potentes en 1999, 2001 y 2002.
Actualmente está a 1.790 millones de kilómetros del Sol, por lo que, como mucho, puede que nos crucemos con unos pocos escombros que el cometa dejó atrás hace mil o dos mil años. Eso significa que tendremos de 10 a 15 meteoros por hora, o incluso algún periodo suelto sin una sola estrella fugaz visible. No pierdes nada por intentarlo, así que ojo al cielo a partir de las 23:45 UTC (00:45 de la madrugada el 17 al 18 de noviembre, hora peninsular española).
Diferencia con las perseidas y las gemínidas. Las perseidas suelen dejar unos 100 meteoros por hora y las gemínidas alrededor de 140 meteoros por hora, aunque parece que las primeras van disminuyendo y las segundas aumentando muy lentamente. A pesar de ese cambio paulatino, en general nos dejan un espectáculo bastante fijo en el cielo. Esto se debe a que el rastro de su objeto de origen, el cometa 109P/Swift-Tuttle para las perseidas y el asteroide (3200) Phaethon para las gemínidas, es mucho más ancho y distribuido. No es necesario que pasen muy cerca de nosotros para que nos crucemos con sus escombros.
Otro gran año. Desde que existen registros, hubo otro año con una gran tormenta. Y es que, según los científicos de la época, en 1833 se llegaron a ver más de 100.000 meteoros por hora con las léonidas. De hecho, los cálculos de 1966 de Franklin se basaron justamente en que la posición del cometa iba a ser muy similar a la de aquel año, por lo que cabía esperar otra tormenta colosal. En acercamientos posteriores, como el de 1998, la Tierra pasó por el borde de los escombros, por lo que hubo muchos, pero no muchísimos.
¿Veremos otra tormenta así? Si en 1998 hubo un acercamiento y este se produce cada 33 años, estamos cerquísima de volver a disfrutar de una gran tormenta de meteoros con las leónidas, ¿no? Esta sería la opción lógica sin tener en cuenta más factores. Desgraciadamente, según los cálculos realizados por astrónomos, está previsto que en 2029 Júpiter desvíe al cometa de su trayectoria actual, por lo que nos dejará sin espectáculo colosal. Aun así, puede que haya un buen estallido en 2034. No habrá 100.000 meteoros por hora, pero quizás sí 2.000. Al final, las lluvias de estrellas más impredecibles suelen ser las más emocionantes.
Imagen | Clay Banks (Unsplash)
En Xataka | Lo que los astrónomos creían iba a ser una aburridísima supernova ha desvelado un enigma del polvo galáctico

articles.title: Corma Receives $125 Million to Train Foundation Models for Defensive Cybersecurity
articles.text:
Cybersecurity startup Corma has raised $125 million in a Series A funding round, bringing the total raised to $185 million and its valuation to $1 billion.
Led by NEA, the investment round saw additional support from previous backers Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.
Founded in 2025 and headquartered in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, Corma emerged from stealth mode in August with a frontier foundation model specifically designed for defensive cybersecurity.
Corma says AI’s offensive capabilities have grown exponentially over the past several months, while its defensive capabilities have not, and it aims to fill that gap.
The startup trains frontier foundation models and deploys them as AI agents alongside existing security tools to audit security data and correlate signals across environments to improve defenses and help security teams respond to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.
“Cybersecurity is now a battle of intelligence against intelligence, and Black October made that impossible to ignore,” said Corma co-founder and CEO Alon Pluda.
“Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand,” Pluda added.
Related: Daylight Lands $80 Million for AI-Powered Security Operations
Related: Finite State Raises $27 Million to Secure Software and Firmware in Connected Devices

articles.title: FBI warns of an open-source AI hacking tool that can breach networks in under three hours
articles.text:
What we know so far: The FBI says that hackers are using an AI-driven penetration testing tool called Artex to automate attacks that used to require skilled human operators. The software connects to large language models and handles the scanning, exploitation and lateral movement on its own, and in some cases it has gone from first targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours."
Artex belongs to a growing category of open-source AI penetration testing platforms. Victims linked to the tool so far include IT management firm ConnectWise and thousands of its customers, security vendor Barracuda, and a group of South Korean financial institutions.
Security teams use this kind of software to probe their own defenses before attackers do the same. The FBI says attackers have taken the same capability and turned it outward against financial services firms, government agencies, technology and defense companies, telecom and internet providers, and law firms.
The tool's design explains much of its appeal. Operators can connect Artex to hosted frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI, open-source models, or models built outside the US. Once connected, Artex usually begins by scanning a target network quickly for weak spots. It then goes after simple flaws, such as poor protections and exposed or stolen passwords, to get an initial foothold. From there it moves toward databases, mailboxes and other stores of sensitive information.
The FBI describes Artex intrusions as "noisy," meaning they produce large volumes of traffic and data that can set off a victim's defensive alerts. Speed makes up for the noise, though. The tool works faster than most human responders can investigate, so an alert may arrive while the attacker is already spreading through the network.
Artex was first released publicly in July, and the advisory ties it to several campaigns since then. In South Korea, attackers used it against a number of financial institutions, and the breaches were blamed largely on weak security, including missing multi-factor authentication. Personal data belonging to at least 68,000 people was stolen.
The biggest known operation involved ConnectWise. The FBI confirmed Microsoft's earlier finding that hackers used Artex to breach the company and reach the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
Microsoft has said the attackers are likely Chinese, and they used the tool to steal data from the affected customers. ConnectWise did not respond to a TechCrunch request for comment on the FBI's findings.
Barracuda's breach shows how small the opening can be. The company said financially motivated criminals using Artex found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda never revoked after it stopped working with that vendor.
With that credential, the attackers reached stores of credentials Barracuda uses to collect data from its customers' systems. The company said its logs were not detailed enough to rule out access, so it decided to "assume the worst" and rotated all of its customer credentials.
Arve Kjoelen, Barracuda's chief information security officer, described what this means for traditional security operations. "Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished," he wrote.
A Barracuda spokesperson told TechCrunch that the company "directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials." The spokesperson did not say how many customers were affected.
After the attacks, Artex's developer made the software closed source to stop further misuse. The FBI says the change came too late to prevent further misuse. The earlier open-source version is still circulating and remains "widely accessible," so anyone with a copy and access to a capable model can still run it.
The tool's own infrastructure has also proved poorly secured. Last week, researchers found hundreds of Artex systems exposed on the public internet with no password, most likely because of mistakes or misconfiguration. One of them was the system used in the South Korean attacks. Exposed instances like these could let outsiders take over ready-made hacking setups without building their own.
None of the intrusions described so far relied on new exploits. Artex succeeded by finding the same problems attackers have always used, such as missing multi-factor authentication, leaked passwords and credentials left active after a vendor relationship ended. What has changed is that an AI agent can now find and use those weaknesses faster than many defenders can react.

articles.title: How Canada gets to space on its own terms | BetaKit
articles.text:
Today on The BetaKit Podcast, we’re talking about space.
Why? First and foremost: space is cool as hell. I think most people, at some point in their life, at least consider being an astronaut like our two guests today, the CEOs of Nordspace (Rahul Goel) and Canada Rocket Company (Hugh Kolias).
“It takes us—to launch our small rocket—six months just to get an approval. We can do that in 24 hours in the United States. We can drive our rocket down to the States like a lot of companies have—and they never come back.”
Rahul Goel
There’s another reason: this year’s BetaKit Most Ambitious issue was focused on sovereign technology, nation building, and all the invisible infrastructure Canadians rely on that we don’t currently own or control. It turns out that a lot of that infrastructure lives in space, which we desperately need access to, let alone control of.
SpaceX is scaling back its rocket ride-share program. It could cut off Canada’s access to space. Or, according to our guests, it could be the catalyst for Canada’s sovereign space goals, leading to significant strategic and financial windfalls. In Budget 2026, the federal government earmarked previously committed capital toward sovereign space capacity.
But what does sovereign space capacity look like? And how will it get built?
Our two guests this week, who joined shortly after they were on stage together at tech festival Nrth in September, have significantly different (perhaps competitive) visions of how this will happen. But you’ll find that their debate on how to get to space, while sometimes tense, is always respectful.
Why? Getting to space is hard. Very hard.
And ultimately, they both share the same goal: ad astra Canada.
So prepare for launch, and let’s dig in.
PRESENTED BY
The BetaKit Podcast is presented by Float.
Float follows the friction, so your team doesn’t have to live with it. See what that looks like for Canadian businesses.

articles.title: Instagram's new tool for creators targets unauthorized reposts and AI-modified videos | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Instagram is introducing a new tool to help creators protect their original videos, the Meta-owned company announced Tuesday. The feature, called “content protection,” is already available on Facebook and is designed to detect when creators’ original videos are being used without their permission. The company is also expanding the tool to address AI content, not just conventional reposting.
The announcement comes in response to creators’ concerns over how easily original content can be copied and redistributed across social media platforms, especially considering how generative AI has made it easier to manipulate existing videos.
Instagram says the content protection tool continuously scans Instagram for unauthorized uses of creators’ protected videos. When Instagram detects a match for one of a creator’s Reels uploaded by another user, it sends the creator an alert. Creators can then choose to block the video from being viewed on both Instagram and Facebook to hide the matched content. They can also choose to add an “original by” label on the content that links viewers of the matching video back to their original video.
Additionally, creators can choose to keep the match visible while monitoring its performance or release their claim on the reel, allowing it to remain visible on Meta’s platforms.
The tool will also begin detecting AI-generated videos that reuse audio from creators’ original content, even when the visuals have been altered. This update will initially be tested with a small group of creators in the coming weeks. The company plans to expand access to this feature to creators who enroll in content protection on both Instagram and Facebook.
Instagram says it’s exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repost others’ work.
Creators who are eligible for content protection will see a notification in their activity feed. Once they enroll, every original video they post to Instagram going forward is automatically protected. They can also choose to retroactively protect eligible videos they’ve already posted by manually selecting them.
If creators have permitted certain profiles to use their work, such as their second profile or a brand, they can add them to their allow list so their videos won’t be flagged as matches.
Tuesday’s announcement marks another step in Instagram’s ongoing efforts to give creators greater control over their content and protect the originality of their work.

articles.title: Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave
articles.text:
On a harried Saturday afternoon at Denver International Airport, I had the good fortune of sitting just a few feet from Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey. It shouldn’t have come as a surprise. He, I, and 3,500 or so others had just left “What’s Next,” a conference organized by Majority Democrats, a group dedicated to charting a path for the suddenly — and shockingly? — victorious party.
Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave
At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.
Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave
At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.
Frey, who rose to national prominence amid ICE’s brutal Operation Metro Surge, had come to the conference in Denver to listen, not to speak. “I’ve never been to one of these things before,” he said. He had flown in for a day and, like everyone else in attendance, is curious to see where the party goes from here. He said he hopes Democrats do two things with their newfound power. “One, act with urgency. And second, don’t fuck it up.”
Another conference-goer sitting nearby chimed in: “Abso-fucking-lutely.”
Democrats, unaccustomed to winning, have seemingly learned from the folly of Republicans’ 2024 sweep. Where Donald Trump’s return to power was falsely attributed to a vibe shift of seismic proportions, born of voters’ preoccupation over DEI and desire to say slurs, Majority Democrats has a simpler explanation for the blue tsunami: It’s the economy, stupid. Everything is falling apart, and even just getting by feels more expensive than ever. The midterms were a rejection, not an endorsement: Voters rejected data centers, they rejected war, and they cast their lot with the side that promised to give them what they want.
The Democrats understand this is not a cultural victory. Even the hollow center of the Democratic Party has, at long last, realized voters don’t necessarily want what they’re selling — they just want to afford to live. It’s gas and groceries all the way down. This analysis would almost verge on Marxist if it wasn’t put forth by an organization comprising the party’s new, young moderates. Majority Democrats describes itself as an alternative to three unpopular, ineffective factions: the “gerontocratic establishment,” the “activist left,” and the “MAGA right.”
The Democrats want you to know they’ve changed. This is no longer the party of “Kamala is brat” or “Pokémon Go to the polls.” They are, in fact, “A Different Kind of Democrat.” They’ve abandoned hollow identity politics and sworn off toxic factional infighting. They really, really care about affordability — for real. They even have the merch to prove it.
Attendees at What’s Next wore their convictions on their sleeves, and also their chests, and also their heads. There were hats that read “pay your taxes” and hats identifying the wearer as a “new deal democrat,” both in all lowercase because the Democrats would also like to remind you that they are once again the youth party. At a separate merch stand, there was a T-shirt declaring “America!” and another T-shirt posing an existential question, also in all lowercase: “how did fucking computers become the thing and machines became the thing that does art? and humans are like the ones in amazon warehouses like shouldn’t robots be working so we can paint?” This second shirt, a friend pointed out, is an uncredited reference to a joke alt-comedian Stavros Halkias made on Theo Von’s podcast. And there was the Our Get Along Shirt, a sartorial exercise in magical thinking that summed up the ethos of the What’s Next conference. The Democrats were in control. Having realized the folly of fighting each other, they would instead channel their energy into fighting for the American people.
The illusion of harmony was shattered early into the programming when a small group of dissenters heckled Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the soon-to-be speaker of the House. “We’re asking you to listen to us now,” one of the protesters shouted after the moderator, Fox News’s resident Democratic host Jessica Tarlov, attempted to placate them by saying she’d be asking Jeffries about the youth vote. “When is the time for a Green New Deal? When is the time for an arms embargo?” The protesters’ cries were drowned out by the crowd’s chants of “HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM, HA-KEEM.”
Jeffries, ever the politician, was unfazed by the altercation. “I’m from Brooklyn,” he told his visibly uncomfortable interlocutor. “This is light work.” The protesters were whisked away, and the interview continued as if the interruption had never happened. Democrats would be gracious in victory.
This new way of doing things was best summed up by Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who told reporters that she and her new colleague, Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, had plenty of debates in the car en route to campaign events — though she declined to say what the debates were about. (Slotkin has identified as a Zionist but has also voted against providing certain military aid to Israel. El-Sayed has called Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide.) “Abdul and I do not agree on everything, but we agree on the really big, important thing, and that is making sure we have a middle class in this country,” she said. “When I see elected officials spending their time fighting the progressive-versus-moderate battle, I know that person didn’t actually learn a damn thing from the election.”
Throughout the weekend, speaker after speaker urged Democrats not to squander their newfound control of Congress by bickering among themselves. At the airport, notorious Democratic operative Lis Smith, an adviser to Majority Democrats, told me the midterms sweep was a rejection of Trumpism, not a sign that voters prefer one style of Democratic politics over the other. “A big takeaway of the election was that there’s no one way to be a Democrat, and that’s in part how we were able to have such a big victory,” she said. The calls for unity were reminiscent of the slogan of one doomed 2016 presidential campaign: Stronger Together. This time, however, they may be onto something — at least for now.
“It’s easy to have Pete Buttigieg and Ro Khanna onstage when we’re all riding the same high,” one staffer told me on the final night of the conference. But what happens when it’s actually time to govern?
For all the talk of unity, there was plenty of tension at What’s Next — sometimes overt, more often simmering beneath the surface of what organizers described as a congenial event.
There was tension toward the establishment, as characterized by Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s announcement that he was challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) for Senate majority leader. There was tension between speakers’ repeated exhortations to get “big money” out of politics and the fact that Majority Democrats is largely bankrolled by hedge fund billionaire Stephen Mandel, a major investor in companies powering the AI boom. (Several attendees I spoke to described What’s Next as hands down the most luxe Democratic event they’ve been to, on par with the party’s national conventions. The snack station was stocked with full-size candy bars.) There was tension between all the populist posturing and the nightly afterparties at the Ritz, where 2028 contenders, staffers, and hangers-on of all types drank well after last call. And notwithstanding the recent blue tsunami, there was tension between Democrats’ persistent unlikability and the conference’s poptimism-tinged branding.
Everything was a little too cute. Majority Democrats staffers wore custom Dickies-style jackets with their names embroidered on the front. Highlight reels played between each main stage speech. The opening-night happy hour, sponsored by the Searchlight Institute — a think tank founded in 2025 with the stated goal of weakening the influence of liberal groups like the ACLU and the Center for American Progress — was Western-themed, though hardly any attendees strayed from the blazer-and-lanyard dress code that is de rigueur in liberal policy circles. The conference lineup was announced via a music festival-style flyer. The halls were decorated with stylized posters of the politicians in attendance, many of whom seemed to be soft-launching their 2028 presidential campaigns.
“The organizers here want a big tent — one big enough even to invite anti-establishment voices like me,” Khanna, one apparent presidential aspirant, said from the stage. “I’m all for a big tent. I’m not for a shallow one. A big tent cannot mean that we water down principle for political expediency.” He called on the new Democratic-controlled Congress to pass Medicare for All, codify a path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, abolish ICE, and cut off funding to Israel, which he said was committing an ongoing genocide against Palestinians. All of this got huge cheers from the audience — some of whom, one presumes, also applauded Jeffries just one day earlier.
Depending on whom you ask, What’s Next was either a concerted effort to rally Democrats around an affordability agenda or moderates’ cynical attempt at co-opting voters’ populist rage. Across the street from the Mission Ballroom, a small group of protesters with Indivisible unfurled a giant banner that read “NO SCHUMER CORONATION.” Members of another group, posted up by one of the side stages hosting the “Do Issues Matter?” panel, told me they hoped the Democrats didn’t abandon their commitment to immigration reform and abortion rights. At the “AI safety breakfast,” one advocate of tech regulation told me there was little daylight between the organizations putting on the conference and its affiliated events — Majority Democrats, the Searchlight Institute, and the pro-AI regulation PAC Tomorrow Together — and the flailing Abundance movement. “They’re rebranding because no one likes abundance,” she said. “This is counter-programming to the populist left. They took a bunch of AI safety money to put on things like this.”
There were notable absences. Vermont senator and erstwhile presidential candidate Bernie Sanders was not in attendance, and neither was New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, whom the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America recently urged to run for president. Slotkin may have name-checked El-Sayed, but he wasn’t there, either. Not even Colorado Rep.-elect Melat Kiros – a member of the Democratic Socialists of America who won her race in a landslide and now represents the very district where the conference was held – was present. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, a member of Majority Democrats who helped organize the event, told The Washington Post that he had personally invited Ocasio-Cortez.
Still, there were other representatives of the party’s left wing milling about, including Khanna, Van Hollen, and Angie Nixon, a DSA-backed Democrat who came within 3 percentage points of winning a Florida Senate seat. And regardless of their political leanings — and counter to the Democratic Party’s 2024 message that the economy was just fine, actually — nearly every single speaker decried the steadily increasing economic divide separating America’s billionaires from the shrinking middle class and the growing ranks of the working poor.
“We just won in a historic fashion, and I think everyone feels good about that,” said Morris Katz, a 26-year-old digital strategist whose roster of previous clients includes New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. (Katz was also the driving force behind Senate contender Graham Platner, who dropped out of the race after being accused of sexual assault.) “I think everyone is united under an anti-billionaire focus on affordability and corruption, and there’s a lot to feel good about.”
And what about the billionaire funding this very conference?
“If there are people who want to support where we’re headed, and the things we’re doing, great, everyone’s welcome,” Katz told me. The difference, he said, is whether Democrats let themselves be co-opted or corrupted by their donors. He pointed to outgoing Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott — who supercharged tech development in the state and whose campaign was largely funded by Elon Musk and data center developers — as an example of what could go wrong. “There’s a quid pro quo there that needs to be avoided at all costs. We need to be the anti-Big Tech party.”
Democrats are already heading in that direction. Khanna pointed out that one-third of the nation’s wealth is concentrated in the Silicon Valley district he represents. Jerusalem Demsas, founder of the liberal publication The Argument, urged legislators to rein in AI development. (“I know everyone here is in a good mood, and it’s about to not be a good mood,” she said before reminding the assembled legislators and political operatives that “what comes after winning is governing.”) At a press conference after her speech, Slotkin called for the establishment of a bipartisan, bicameral committee on AI akin to midcentury bodies created to regulate nuclear power. “While we’re bickering with each other — Democrats and Republicans — there’s an opportunity cost, and we have not done what we need to do on AI,” she said. “If we were healthy politically, we would have been working on this for five years straight.”
There was an obvious undercurrent of technopessimism throughout the weekend. News of the nationwide FAA ground stop broke minutes before a panel titled “How Weird Will AI Make 2028?” Though a faulty router was ultimately identified as the culprit, attendees — myself included — couldn’t help but speculate whether an AI cyberattack, or even just shoddy implementation of the FAA’s new AI tool, was actually to blame.
“It was clear that there is just a huge interest in AI here, and grappling with it, that sits across the party,” Rob Flaherty, the cofounder of the AI safety PAC Tomorrow Together told me. Flaherty’s organization hosted an off-the-record breakfast on AI safety. “We built it for 100 people, and 600 people showed up,” he said. The coffee ran out almost immediately, though there were somehow enough burritos to go around. Tomorrow Together’s polling, which was shared at the breakfast, indicates that voters don’t just hate data centers but have broadly soured on AI. They tie AI developments to broader economic concerns like rising utility bills and a worsening job market. Most importantly, voters don’t think the companies can be trusted to regulate themselves.
“Now it’s on Democrats to not just channel the anger and be the vessel for that anger but to actually enact the things that are going to alleviate the pain that people are feeling,” Flaherty told me.
But for Flaherty, who previously worked for Biden’s and Harris’ presidential campaigns, the conference “was less about a policy agenda and more about a theory of power” — one articulated by Bernie Sanders a decade ago. “If you look at the way people — James Talarico on down, Hakeem Jeffries on down — were speaking, it doesn’t sound dissimilar from the kinds of things Bernie was raising in 2016,” said Flaherty. “He rightly — and I was working on the other side — identified some of the economic discontent that a lot of people are feeling.”
Still, there’s a difference between Sanders’ vision of Medicare for All and, say, a public option — or what 2020 presidential hopeful Pete Buttigieg described as “Medicare for all who want it.” Both fall under the broad umbrella of universal healthcare, but the distinctions matter. Absent nitty-gritty policy discussions, however, it’s easy to get the sense that all voters — and all Democrats — want the same thing. Perhaps this is why, even among the professional Democrats in attendance, I met people who told me they wanted Democrats to prosecute ICE agents, enact a $25 an hour minimum wage, and pack the Supreme Court. At a certain point, I became desperate to find someone whose politics were a little more tepid.
My pleas were answered by Uriel Espinoza, a local Democrat whose friends introduced him as a centrist. Espinoza’s friends insisted that I join them for happy hour at a nearby brewery. (Espinoza said he rejects the centrist label, but broadly disagrees with the Democratic Socialists of America’s manifesto.) Their car wasn’t big enough to fit us all, but it didn’t matter. As four of us piled into the back seat of a Tesla whose driver — another member of the friend group — was blasting Drake, Espinoza told me he had once identified as a conservative. At the bar, he and another friend said the conference had been fun, if a little “East Coast consultant-y.”
Here was the mythical moderate voter in all his glory. He was even wearing a cowboy hat. And what did he want? Immigration reform, universal healthcare, and an economy that isn’t stacked against working people. There was a time, Espinoza told me, when he felt betrayed. “On certain things — like Israel, Gaza, Palestine, immigration — we are looking to our elected officials at the highest level, and we feel that they aren’t really delivering, or differentiating himself from Republicans,” he said.
I told him he sounded almost like a leftist.
“I’m also surprised, myself, because I’ve never thought of myself — and I don’t think of myself — as a socialist,” he told me. “I’m an entrepreneur. I’m pro-business, I’m pro-economy, but I’m also, at this point, pro-results.”
Update, November 17th: This piece has been updated to include Uriel Espinoza’s description of his political leanings.

articles.title: GoDaddy's new AI builder app lets SMBs turn an idea into a website faster than ever
articles.text:
GoDaddy's new AI builder app lets SMBs turn an idea into a website faster than ever
GoDaddy's comprehensive AI site builder is now available
- GoDaddy's AI website builder already supports 90+ third-party integrations
- You can build and operate an ecommerce site with payment platform support
- Early usage data shows it being a hit among service-based businesses
GoDaddy has launched Airo AI Builder, its own agentic operating system designed to create advanced websites.
Positioned as much more than a setup tool, Airo will instead let users both create and continue to refine their sites via a simple conversational interface, with website spanning both simple portfolios as well as web apps, online stores, online booking systems and more.
From launch, the agentic system already supports integrations with over 90 third-party tools including Slack, Notion and HubSpot, focusing on tasks like accessing databases and managing customer relationships.
GoDaddy launches Airo AI Builder
The company recently released research which found service-based businesses accounted for more than one-third of the sites created, including health and body (13%), home and property (12%) and business services (11%) sectors. Food and travel (13%) also accounted for a large number of sites created, all of which are not typically associated with having extensive tech teams or expertise – making effective website building a challenge for many.
During Airo AI Builder's beta phase in the summer, around one-tenth of the use cases even included rebuild and reimagine projects – businesses looking to update or modernise their sites, who may not previously have had the right skills or resources.
On the ecommerce front, GoDaddy offers its own Payments platform but it also has a partnership with Stripe to let users collect payments, but more are set to come.
"For anyone who has found building a website a burden, it opens up the opportunity to take that first step, then keep improving as their customers’ needs and their business evolve," marketing-led growth VP Selina Bieber said, positioning Airo as a more comprehensive platform designed to see users through more than just the initial build.

articles.title: Así era 'Avengers: The Kang Dynasty', según Kevin Feige: un gran plotwist y su conexión con el Doctor Doom
articles.text:
A falta de un mes para el estreno de Avengers: Doomsday, el jefe máximo de Marvel, Kevin Feige, ha desvelado cuáles eran los planes originales para la quinta entrega de los Vengadores. Hace unos años, el filme iba a titularse Avengers: The Kang Dynasty. Pero todo cambió con el despido de Jonathan Majors, actor de Kang el Conquistador, tras ser declarado culpable de malos tratos a su pareja.
Durante todo este tiempo, los fans siempre han asumido que aquel hecho llevó a Marvel a tener que cambiar de planes y buscar un nuevo villano. Por eso, finalmente se decantaron por el Doctor Doom, para el que trajeron de regreso a Robert Downey Jr. Sin embargo, Kevin Feige ha confesado que no fue exactamente así como sucedió todo. Y es que, al parecer, en Marvel ya estaban maquinando cambios para Avengers: The Kang Dynasty.
"Era una situación muy delicada. No queríamos precipitarnos y tomar decisiones imprudentes en materia de empleo. La gente cree que hubo una relación de causa y efecto con los problemas de Jonathan, y es cierto que eso aceleró algunas cosas. Pero el desastre ya estaba muy avanzado antes de eso", explica el CEO de Marvel en una entrevista a Empire.
"Quantumania no tuvo la acogida que nos hubiera gustado. Hay muchos aspectos de la película de los que estamos orgullosos, y el desempeño de Kang es uno de ellos. Pero ya en aquel momento estábamos haciendo cambios [en The Kang Dynasty]", asegura entonces. "Probablemente se habría seguido llamando Avengers: The Kang Dynasty, pero habría servido como introducción para el Doctor Doom a mitad de esa película", revela.
El Doctor Doom era el villano secreto de Avengers: The Kang Dynasty
Es decir, los últimos planes de Marvel para Avengers: The Kang Dynasty pasaban por presentar un gran plotwist con su villano. En lugar de convertir a Kang en el principal enemigo, a mitad de película se revelaría que, en realidad, el Doctor Doom estaba detrás de todo. El Conquistador solo sería un personaje presentado para despistar y sorprender con el gran secreto. O, al menos, eso es lo que promete Feige, pues sus declaraciones parecen cuanto menos oportunistas.
Sea como sea, lo cierto es que Kang ya no está en el Universo Marvel. Ahora, el Doctor Doom ya ha tomado las riendas como el villano principal de la Saga del Multiverso. Y aunque de una manera rápida y apresurada, lo cierto es que en la compañía no lo están haciendo mal para convertirle en una amenaza a la que temer. Muy pronto podremos ver todo su poder en Avengers: Doomsday, que se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: 1998 KY26: Warum ein Asteroid plötzlich die Wissenschaft verblüfft
articles.text:
Physik-Rätsel im All: Warum Asteroid 1998 KY26 plötzlich beschleunigt
Der erdnahe Asteroid mit der Bezeichnung 1998 KY26 bewegt sich nicht allein nach den Gesetzen der Schwerkraft durch das All, sondern erfährt senkrecht zu seiner Umlaufbahn um die Sonne eine zusätzliche, sogenannte nichtgravitative Beschleunigung. Bislang vermuteten mehrere Wissenschaftler:innen hinter dieser Bahnabweichung unsichtbar verdampfendes Wassereis im Inneren des Himmelskörpers, doch wie in einer im Fachmagazin Icarus veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist, erweist sich der Gesteinsbrocken für dauerhafte Eisvorräte als deutlich zu warm.
Für die Untersuchung haben die beiden Raumfahrtingenieure Korbin Hansen und Masatoshi Hirabayashi vom Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta im US-Bundesstaat Georgia ein dreidimensionales Computermodell eingesetzt, das die Wärmeleitung von der Oberfläche bis in den Kern des rund elf Meter großen Körpers berechnet. Ihren Simulationen zufolge liegt die Temperatur selbst an den kältesten Stellen im Durchschnitt eines Sonnenumlaufs bei mindestens 212 Kelvin, was minus 61 Grad Celsius entspricht, während Wassereis im Vakuum selbst unter einer schützenden Gesteinsschicht nur unterhalb von 145 Kelvin beziehungsweise minus 128 Grad Celsius über längere Zeiträume stabil bleibt.
Warum 1998 KY26 am Georgia Institute of Technology durch den Eis-Test fällt
In der Astronomie galt der Himmelskörper seit einigen Jahren als Kandidat für einen sogenannten „dunklen Kometen“, also einen Körper, der zwar äußerlich wie ein gewöhnlicher Gesteinsasteroid ohne leuchtende Staubwolke aussieht, aber durch ausströmendes Gas wie durch kleine Steuerdüsen aus der Spur gedrückt wird. „Den Ergebnissen unseres Temperaturmodells zufolge würde auf 1998 KY26 zu viel Wasser entweichen, als dass sich Eis im Untergrund halten könnte – das grenzt genauer ein, woraus der Asteroid besteht“, schreiben Hansen und Hirabayashi in ihrer Arbeit, über die auch Sciencealert berichtet.
Wenn verdampfendes Eis – in der Fachsprache durch den direkten Übergang vom festen in den gasförmigen Zustand als Sublimation bezeichnet – tatsächlich die Ursache für die gemessene Bahnabweichung wäre, müsste der Asteroid pro Sekunde rund 0,03 Gramm Wasser verlieren und hätte seine Vorräte bereits nach 62 Jahren restlos aufgebraucht. Selbst ohne diese Schubwirkung würde ein Wasseranteil von einem Prozent der Gesamtmasse bei den berechneten Temperaturen innerhalb von gut 2.000 Jahren verschwinden, zumal der schnell rotierende Brocken vermutlich ein zusammenhängender Felsblock, ein sogenannter Monolith, ist und die Sonnenwärme dadurch viel besser ins Innere leitet als ein lockerer Trümmerhaufen-Asteroid aus Geröll und Staub.
Sonnenlicht statt Wasserdampf: Wie Strahlungsdruck den Asteroiden 1998 KY26 antreibt
Dass Forscher:innen überhaupt auf die Idee eines verborgenen Eis-Antriebs kamen, lag an veralteten Annahmen über die Größe des Objekts, das seit Ende der neunziger Jahre auf etwa 30 Meter Durchmesser geschätzt wurde. Erst im September 2025 zeigten Beobachtungen unter der Leitung des Astronomen Toni Santana-Ros von der spanischen Universität Alicante an den Teleskopen der Europäischen Südsternwarte (ESO), die im Fachjournal Nature Communications erschienen sind, dass 1998 KY26 lediglich elf Meter misst und sich alle 5,35 Minuten einmal um die eigene Achse dreht.
Durch das rund zwanzigmal geringere Gewicht und eine helle, stark eisenarme Gesteinsoberfläche, die 55 Prozent des einfallenden Sonnenlichts zurückwirft, genügen bereits konventionelle physikalische Kräfte, um den leichten Brocken merklich von seinem Kurs abzulenken. Wie ein Team um den Wissenschaftler Davide Farnocchia vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory der US-Raumfahrtbehörde Nasa im Fachblatt The Astrophysical Journal Letters vorgerechnet hat, lässt sich die rätselhafte Beschleunigung durch den mechanischen Strahlungsdruck des Sonnenlichts sowie den sogenannten Jarkowski-Effekt erklären, bei dem die verzögerte Wärmeabstrahlung der aufgeheizten Oberfläche einen schwachen Rückstoß erzeugt.
Raumsonde Hayabusa 2 der Jaxa steht 2031 vor einem schwierigen Manöver
Trotz der deutlichen Ergebnisse aus Atlanta bleibt eine Einschränkung bestehen, da auch das neue Wärmemodell auf Annahmen beruht und unklar ist, wie lange sich 1998 KY26 schon auf seiner heutigen, sonnennahen Umlaufbahn befindet, die ihn bis auf knapp unter den Abstand zwischen Erde und Sonne an unser Zentralgestirn heranführt. Endgültige Gewissheit über die Beschaffenheit soll im Juli 2031 die Raumsonde Hayabusa 2 der japanischen Raumfahrtagentur Jaxa liefern, die sich bereits auf dem Weg zu dem Kleinkörper befindet.
Für die Ingenieur:innen der Jaxa bringen die jüngsten Erkenntnisse handfeste Probleme mit sich, weil sie die Mission ursprünglich für einen rund dreimal größeren und halb so schnell rotierenden Zielkörper geplant hatten. Da auf dem elf Meter kleinen, trockenen Felsblock abseits der Pole die Fliehkraft stärker wirkt als die eigene Anziehungskraft, wird jedes Annäherungs- oder gar Aufsetzmanöver der Sonde zu einem riskanten Unterfangen, bei dem aufgewirbeltes Material oder ein unkontrollierter Abpraller die Instrumente gefährden können.

Researchers at Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), A*STAR, and National University of Singapore (NUS) published “Self-Supervised Attention-Based Virtual Metrology for CMP MRR Prediction.”
Excerpt
“In this paper, we propose Global Regression Pretraining (GREP), a self-supervised, attention-based framework for CMP* MRR prediction. GREP learns temporal representations from unlabeled sensor signals through global proxy-target regression, followed by supervised fine-tuning for MRR estimation. The framework is evaluated against a feature-engineered supervised baseline under three conditions: limited labeled data, sensor noise, and temporal process drift. “
