articles.title: En 1895 descubrimos una estatua romana de bronce en Pamplona. Ahora los arqueólogos intentan aclarar su mayor misterio: su sexo
articles.text:
En 1895 un grupo de operarios estaba excavando en la calle Navarrería de Pamplona para construir un edificio de viviendas cuando, para pasmo de los responsables de la obra, encontraron una gran estatua de bronce que mostraba una figura cubierta con una toga romana. A la pieza le faltaba la cabeza y estaba muy deteriorada, pero no tardó en llamar la atención de los arqueólogos. Ahora, más de 130 años después, siguen haciéndose una pregunta: ¿Qué representa exactamente? ¿Se trata de un joven o de una adolescente?
La cuestión es más importante de lo que parece.
¿Qué diablos es eso? Una pregunta parecida debieron de hacerse hace 131 años los obreros que removían la tierra del casco antiguo de Pamplona (se cree que a la altura del número 16 de la calle Navarrería) para construir un edificio.
Para sorpresa de los operarios y del constructor José Aramburu y Elizaga, los trabajos dejaron al descubierto una estatua de bronce de 127 cm que mostraba un cuerpo humano cubierto con una elegante toga. El primer arqueólogo en describirla fue Juan Iturralde y Suit y en 1911 ya la vemos referenciada (con foto) en una obra de Julio Altadill.
¿Y cómo apareció la figura? Muy deteriorada. A la pieza le faltaba la cabeza, estaba estropeada por el paso de los siglos y había sufrido daños, probablemente tras caerle encima una losa de piedra. Aramburu y Elizaga, el dueño de la estatua según la legislación de la época, la cedió a la Comisión Provincial de Monumentos de Navarra para que la examinaran, lo que permitió a los arqueólogos hacerse una primera idea de lo que tenían entre manos: la escultura, romana, se dató hacia el siglo II d.C. Nada sorprendente si se tiene en cuenta que apareció en la antigua Pompelo.
Sin embargo, la pieza estuvo poco tiempo bajo la custodia de la Comisión Provincia de Monumentos. Solo unos años después, hacia 1904 o 1906, Aramburu la reclamó y los historiadores le perdieron la pista durante décadas.
De hecho, como recuerda el Museo de Navarra, estuvo en paradero desconocido hasta 2015, cuando se localizó en una colección particular norteamericana. En 2022 el Gobierno llegó a un acuerdo temporal con su propietario para que la pieza pudiese regresar a España y en 2023 dio un paso más allá, al pactar su compra por 620.000 dólares, cerca de 575.000 euros.
¿Qué muestra la estatua? Esa es la pregunta del millón. Y el epicentro de una intensa disputa entre expertos que ya ha dado pie a varios artículos académicos, como recordaba estos días Vicente G. Olaya en El País. ¿Qué muestra exactamente la figura? ¿Se trata del cuerpo de una adolescente? ¿Es un torso masculino? ¿Estamos ante un genius loci, un espíritu protector?
Durante un tiempo se dio por sentado que el bautizado como ‘Togado de Pompelo’ mostraba una figura masculina de la primera mitad del II d.C., un joven ataviado con una túnica talaris que le alcanzaba hasta los tobillos. Pero esa explicación no convence a todos los expertos.
¿Es una adolescente? Esa es la idea que desliza un comunicado publicado hace justo un año por la Dirección General de Cultura-Institución Príncipe de Viana. En él las autoridades navarras se hacen eco de un estudio de Carmen Marcks-Jacobs y Hans Rupprecht Goette que sostiene que la escultura muestra en realidad “la figura de una romana de entre 10 y 12 años”.
En su opinión, la escultura representa a una niña ataviada con una toga praetexta, una vestimenta usada durante la infancia y que nos confirma su condición de ciudadana. El mismo análisis plantea que lo que la escultura sostiene en su mano derecha es un haz de espigas, un símbolo de fertilidad.
¿Asunto zanjado? Para nada. Sigue habiendo historiadores convencidos de que la primera interpretación era la correcta y el Togado de Pompelo nos muestra a un varón. Esa es de hecho la postura que sostiene Javier Andreu-Pintado en un artículo recién publicado en ‘Cuadernos de Arqueología de la Universidad de Navarra’.
Su análisis sostiene que “las evidencias iconográficas, históricas y contextuales respaldan la identificación masculina tradicional y cuestiona la nueva hipótesis por su escaso apoyo en paralelos arqueológicos y fuentes antiguas”. El paper incluye además un tirón de orejas a las administraciones por dar por buena una teoría “antes de alcanzar consenso científico”.
¿Es el único que opina así? En su crónica para El País, Vicente G. Olaya recoge comentarios de otros expertos que confirman que el debate efectivamente está lejos de estar resuelto. ¿Muestra la estatua un togado masculino? ¿Representa a un genius? ¿Y si la pieza es una reelaboración y combina dos representaciones, masculina y femenina?
¿Qué nos dice la vestimenta, una cuestión relevante dado que la toga praetexta era una prenda usada básicamente por hombres que ya habían superado cierta edad? Son preguntas interesantes porque, como se recuerda con frecuencia, el Togado de Pompelo no es una obra cualquiera: en toda la península solo se han hallado dos estatuas togadas en bronce de la época romana. La otra es el Togado de Periate, parte de la colección del Museo Arqueológico de Granada.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
- November 7, 2026
- Source:
- University of Regensburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

articles.title: Google Maps change radicalement : Gemini peut organiser vos vacances et prendre vos rendez-vous
articles.text:
Google Maps vient d’être enrichi d’une nouvelle fonctionnalité baptisée « Demander à Maps ». Il serait question de « la plus grande mise à jour de Google Maps depuis plus de dix ans », selon Google. Le principe est simple : Gemini est intégré à Google Maps pour vous aider à planifier vos vacances, réserver vos plats ou encore prendre des rendez-vous à votre place. Voici tout ce qu’il faut savoir.
Gemini se transforme en guide de voyage
La fonctionnalité « Demander à Maps » se présente sous la forme d’une fenêtre conversationnelle disponible aussi bien sur le web que sur l’application Google Maps. Google précise que cette fonctionnalité est basée sur les données de plus de 300 millions de lieux et sur les avis de plus de 500 millions de contributeurs.
À travers la fonctionnalité « Demander à Maps », l’utilisateur peut par exemple demander à Gemini d’établir un itinéraire de vacances sur plusieurs jours. Il pourra par ailleurs bénéficier de la section « À savoir avant de partir » qui donne des conseils pratiques, des informations en temps réel sur la météo, des informations sur le stationnement à chaque étape ou encore des indications sur les péages. Il peut par ailleurs poser toutes sortes de questions, comme « Où est-ce que je peux recharger mon téléphone au plus vite ? », « Trouve-moi un court de tennis public éclairé pour jouer ce soir » ou encore « Conseille-moi des événements à proximité ». Gemini peut par ailleurs comparer des hôtels.
Bien entendu, il n’est pas nécessaire d’être en voyage pour utiliser « Demander à Maps ». L’utilisateur peut poser n’importe quelle question concernant son environnement direct.
Gemini peut prendre des rendez-vous et réserver des plats à votre place
Gemini intégré à Google Maps ne se limite pas à répondre à des questions et à donner des indications : l’assistant IA est aussi capable d’effectuer des actions. Google explique qu’un utilisateur peut par exemple demander à l’application de rechercher des restaurants correspondant à ses envies et de préparer une commande à emporter en ajoutant automatiquement les plats au panier. L’utilisateur n’aurait qu’à fournir certaines indications et à valider le panier final. De son côté, l’IA tiendrait compte lors de ses recherches des adresses enregistrées par l’utilisateur et de ses besoins alimentaires spécifiques. Cette fonctionnalité sera prochainement disponible via Uber Eats.
Gemini serait même capable de prendre des rendez-vous à votre place. Ainsi, si vous demandez à Gemini « Trouvez-moi un rendez-vous pour une manucure à 16 h près de chez moi », l’IA se chargera de trouver une place pour 16 h dans un centre situé près de chez vous.
Gemini intégré dans Google Maps sera aussi capable de répondre à des questions par rapport à vos listes. Ainsi, si vous lui demandez « Parmi mes adresses enregistrées, lesquelles ont une table pour 5 dans 30 minutes ? », l’assistant IA devrait vous fournir les adresses correspondant à votre requête. À noter toutefois que Google ne précise pas comment Gemini entre en contact avec les professionnels, les restaurants et les magasins. Enfin, précisons qu’il sera possible de connecter la fonctionnalité « Demander à Maps » à Gmail, afin que Gemini tienne compte de vos rendez-vous et réservations en ligne.
La fonctionnalité « Demander à Maps » est disponible dès maintenant en France. Par contre, la section « À savoir avant de partir » et les réservations de plats et de rendez-vous seront déployées prochainement.

articles.title: Liquidation judiciaire pour la start-up française de vélos électriques Anod
articles.text:
Fondée en 2022 en Vendée par Arnaud Malrin et son père Christophe, la jeune entreprise Anod n’est plus. Le tribunal de commerce de La Roche-sur-Yon a prononcé la liquidation judiciaire de la société le 21 octobre 2026. Cette décision a été publiée au Bodacc, le bulletin officiel des annonces légales des entreprises, le 6 novembre, et relayée par nos confrères de Transition Vélo. Anod cesse ainsi son activité et ses biens seront vendus pour rembourser ceux à qui elle doit de l’argent, dans la mesure du possible.
Le jugement fixe la date de cessation des paiements au 21 avril 2025. D’après le tribunal, Anod ne pouvait donc déjà plus régler ses dettes avec l’argent disponible dix-huit mois avant sa liquidation. Le liquidateur désigné est Maître Thomas Humeau, de la Selarl Humeau. Il est chargé de recenser les dettes et de vendre ce qui peut l’être.
Du 10 au 30 novembre, le LUBA mini 2 AWD 1000 passe à 1 199 € au lieu de 1 499 €, support de lavage offert ! Vision IA tri-caméra, sans fil périmétrique, tonte des bordures, adaptation à toutes les conditions de luminosité… Bref, il a tout pour tondre à votre place !
De l’argent public, des investisseurs et deux vélos en deux ans
Au cours de son existence, Anod a levé des fonds et obtenu plusieurs aides publiques pour développer son vélo électrique, qui associe un moteur à récupération d’énergie et des supercondensateurs pour réduire, puis supprimer, la batterie lithium-ion.
Une campagne de financement participatif sur la plateforme Sowefund lui a rapporté environ 630 000 euros, et la Région Pays de la Loire lui a apporté 310 000 euros. Surtout, en décembre 2024, l’entreprise a décroché 1,7 million d’euros au concours i-Nov du plan France 2030 pour son projet Mona, un programme de recherche et développement de 3,7 millions d’euros.
Du côté des produits, en revanche, le parcours a été plus chaotique. Le premier vélo, l’Hybrid, était proposé en précommande à 3 499 euros dès mars 2024, avec une petite batterie lithium de 76 Wh en complément des supercondensateurs. Anod l’a abandonné en septembre 2025, après un problème chez son fournisseur de batteries et des risques d’incendie détectés lors de nouveaux tests. D’après Arnaud Malrin, aucun acheteur n’avait été livré. Il a été remplacé par l’Anod Hybrid 2, affiché à 2 990 euros, qui se passe complètement de lithium et dont les premières livraisons étaient prévues en décembre 2025.
Notre avis sur l’Anod Hybrid 2
Nous avions pu tester l’Anod Hybrid 2. Nous lui avions attribué la très bonne note de 8/10 à l’époque. Le moteur MHR1, l’électronique, le système S.A.F.E., les brevets et la marque Anod font partie de ce que le liquidateur peut vendre. Aucune reprise n’a été annoncée pour l’instant.

articles.title: California Sues OpenAI, Seeking Court-Ordered Changes After the Hugging Face Hack
articles.text:
California’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against OpenAI on Monday in an effort to force the ChatGPT-maker to change its business practices over a July cybersecurity incident in which its artificial intelligence system hacked into another company on its own.
In the lawsuit filed in San Francisco Superior Court, Attorney General Rob Bonta alleges that OpenAI misled and endangered the public and users of its services by knowingly developing advanced AI models without necessary safeguards. He says the company’s actions could put critical infrastructure, institutions and the public at risk, which makes it a “public nuisance” under state law. Bonta says OpenAI is a public nuisance, and he wants a judge to order the company to change its ways and give up any profits generated by what he claims are the company’s risky business practices.
OpenAI announced an “unprecedented cyber incident ” on July 21, when its AI agent hacked into another AI company, Hugging Face, after escaping from what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment known as a sandbox. OpenAI said its AI used stolen credentials and discovered a previously unknown vulnerability to access Hugging Face’s servers.
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that has been identified by every major AI lab.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” Pusateri wrote in an email to The Associated Press. Those steps include publishing detailed technical and independent reports, strengthening safeguards, and creating a framework to identify when AI agents act in a way that doesn’t match the company’s instructions or goals, Pusateri said.
“We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry,” Pusateri wrote.
In the lawsuit, Bonta says OpenAI’s promises about safety and security are deceptive.
“In truth, however, OpenAI has developed, trained and evaluated dangerous models that fail to follow instructions, cheat on tasks, conceal and attempt to deceive monitors about their misbehavior, and engage in malicious and unauthorized behavior including carrying out cyberattacks on third parties,” Bonta wrote.
He also noted that early last month, OpenAI reported that it had discovered that internally deployed agents were able to suppress monitoring alerts and disable monitoring. A month later, the company published a research report finding that as AI models become more capable, they become more difficult to supervise, he wrote.
“Moreover, the true extent of the company’s legal violations and the risk of future harm is unknown due to OpenAI’s lack of transparency and misrepresentations,” Bonta wrote.
OpenAI was already being sued by at least eight states that say the company’s popular chatbot model is hurting children and deceiving adults by giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging paranoia and coaching people to kill themselves or hurt or kill others. The lawsuits contend the ChatGPT chatbots are pretending to be agreeable and compassionate while preying on the vulnerable and teenagers.
In a statement released last month in response to those lawsuits, OpenAI said it had built safety protections into ChatGPT for children and that it would continue to improve the model.

articles.title: COP 31: Auch die Weltklimakonferenz geht die Umweltfolgen des KI-Booms nicht an
articles.text:
COP 31: Auch die Weltklimakonferenz geht die Umweltfolgen des KI-Booms nicht an
Sowohl Schätzungen der Internationalen Energieagentur als auch der Vereinten Nationen kommen zu dem Schluss, dass sich der Energieverbrauch durch Rechenzentren in der Zeit von 2025 bis 2030 verdoppeln wird – vor allem wegen der steigenden KI‑Nutzung. Im Angesicht dieses massiv steigenden Energieverbrauchs sollte man sich eigentlich freuen, dass das Thema auch bei der noch bis zum 20. November 2026 laufenden Weltklimakonferenz COP 31 in Antalya zur Sprache kommt.
Eigentlich – denn was die türkisch-australische COP-31-Präsidentschaft zu dem Thema vorgelegt hat, eignet sich nicht im Geringsten, um den Auswirkungen des KI-Booms auf die Umwelt gerecht zu werden. Dabei klingt es ja eigentlich nicht schlecht. Immerhin erklären die Unterzeichner des Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge „ihr gemeinsames Ziel, KI zu einem Teil der Klimalösung zu machen“. Und zwar indem sie „nachhaltig betrieben, effizient konzipiert, transparent gemessen und für alle zugänglich“ wird.
Konkrete Ziele? Fehlanzeige
Die KI-Selbstverpflichtung sieht für die Unterzeichner:innen insgesamt vier Aufgaben vor: Aufbau und Betrieb von KI‑Infrastruktur sollen nachhaltig erfolgen; KI soll über ihre Lebensdauer hinweg verantwortungsvoll entworfen, verwaltet und beschafft werden; Bewertung und Auswertung der Umweltfolgen von KI sollen unterstützt werden; der Einsatz von KI für den Klimaschutz soll finanziell unterstützt werden.
Wie genau das passieren soll? Wer weiß. Das Papier nennt lediglich ein paar Beispiele, wie man das theoretisch machen könnte. Konkrete Anforderungen ergeben sich aus den Exempeln derweil nicht. So könnte man, wie das Dokument als Beispiel vorschlägt, mehr Rechenzentren mit Strom aus emissionsarmen Quellen versorgen – oder eben auch nicht.
Dafür kann aber jeder mitmachen. Unternehmen, Investoren, Forschungseinrichtungen, internationale Organisationen, staatliche und nichtstaatliche Stellen – sie alle werden in dem Dokument angesprochen. Auch explizit die Zivilgesellschaft – ohne aber zu erklären, welche Rolle sie überhaupt einnehmen soll.
Letztlich ist das Dokument ohnehin nicht rechtlich bindend. Umso unsinniger ist es, keine echten Minimalforderungen zu stellen. Selbst die US-amerikanischen KI-Firmen, die bisweilen Gasturbinen für den Betrieb ihrer KI-Rechenzentren nutzen, könnten das Papier guten Gewissens unterzeichnen. Was nützt ein breiter Konsens, wenn der nur darauf hinausläuft, dass niemand wirklich etwas ändern muss?
Es geht um mehr als nur Strom
Die wachsende Zahl an KI-Rechenzentren benötigt nicht nur Energie. Auch der Wasserbrauch ist enorm. Einer UN-Prognose zufolge soll er sich in der Zeit von 2025 bis 2030 mehr als verdoppeln und dann mehr als neun Billionen Liter betragen. Das entspricht dem Wasserverbrauch von 1,3 Milliarden Menschen.
Zusätzlich steigt die Menge an Elektroschrott. Einer Nature-Studie zufolge könnte der KI-Ausbau bis 2030 zwischen 1,2 und fünf Millionen metrische Tonnen Elektroschrott zur Folge haben. Das gemeinnützige Basel Action Network rechnet sogar mit einem deutlich höheren Müllaufkommen.
Beide Probleme werden zwar zu Beginn des Dokuments genannt, später gibt es aber – im Gegensatz zur Energie – keine Erwähnung mehr davon. Damit fällt es auch nicht unter die vier Ziele, zu denen sich die Unterzeichner:innen bekennen sollen.
Deus ex Machina: Die KI als Klimaretter?
So vage das Dokument dabei bleibt, wie man den klimaschädlichen Auswirkungen von KI habhaft werden könnte, so optimistisch werden die potenziellen Vorteile skizziert. KI unterstütze schon „Maßnahmen zur Eindämmung, Anpassung und Stärkung der Widerstandsfähigkeit“ und könne „die Umsetzung der Klimapolitik beschleunigen sowie die Verbreitung von Lösungen vorantreiben“.
„Citation needed“, würde es auf Wikipedia heißen. Denn die tatsächliche Nettowirkung ist umstritten. Vor allem Tech-Unternehmen, aber auch Wissenschaftler:innen, haben immer wieder Modellrechnungen aufgestellt, nach denen KI am Ende zu einer Senkung des CO₂‑Ausstoßes führen könnte. Eine Anfang 2026 veröffentlichte Meta-Untersuchung zeigte allerdings, dass nur in vier von 154 untersuchten Modellrechnungen wirklich generative KI-Systeme betrachtet wurden. Dabei sind genau die es, die den derzeitigen KI-Boom antreiben.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 10.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: Science Corporation's brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post.
Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.
Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.
Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.
Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.
With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.
Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

articles.title: Maintainers don't need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
articles.text:
Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half.
AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.
AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?
GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH, Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on.
The process
Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked:
Find.Codename MDASH, an AI system from Microsoft Security, scanned each project using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model and suggested fixes for what it found.
Filter. An AI triage agent from the GitHub Security Lab, built on tailored Copilot skills, removed duplicates, checked validity, and focused on high-impact bugs, so maintainers never had to review raw scan results.
Report privately. Reports reached maintainers through GitHub private vulnerability reporting, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix.
Fix. Maintainers decided what to fix, how to fix it, and when.
Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work.
The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release.
What we learned
These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons.
1. Fixes matter more than findings
Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding.
The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes.
AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later.
Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers.
Netty maintainer
2. Codename MDASH, with researcher review, gave maintainers high-quality findings with fixes
Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy maintainers said they surfaced obscure bugs and filled gaps that earlier reports had missed. For FastMCP, the scan went beyond what AI scanners had given them before. ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, received 22 reports.
AI did the finding, researchers did the checking, and maintainers stayed in charge.
One ImageMagick report looked like a kind of issue the maintainers had seen before. Its summary showed it wasn’t and pointed to the exact lines of code. They were able to push a fix in 15 minutes.
Normally, a security advisory would take us around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand, and make a fix. It is a huge difference.
ImageMagick maintainer
Codename MDASH was able to find unknown, obscure security bugs in our project with succinct reports, and it filled in gaps from some prior reports that hadn’t been noticed.
Caddy maintainer
3. Open source still has gaps to close
The pilot worked because people did careful work at every step, and that work doesn’t scale yet. Seven researchers spent about two days per project checking findings by hand. Meanwhile, low-quality reports still reach maintainers every day.
For open source, fixes need to be delivered via private vulnerability reporting (PVR). Maintainers need to run CI/CD tests on private forks to verify those fixes. And to close the gap between defenders and attackers, maintainers need access to cyber-capable models to verify a proof of concept, before and after the fix.
The Codename MDASH scan provided unique insights into the security of our project above and beyond what AI scanners have provided us in the past
FastMCP maintainer
Why it matters
If you’re a maintainer, this approach changes what a security report costs you. A checked, private report that comes with a suggested fix takes less of your time. You shouldn’t have to triage a scanner’s output. That’s the sender’s job.
If you use AI to find vulnerabilities in open source, maintainers’ feedback points to this standard:
Check every finding before you send it, against what the project already knows and against its threat model and security policy.
Report it privately.
Include a suggested fix. Let maintainers set the pace.
Features are easier and easier to ship, but in the future maintaining software will probably come down to who cares enough to manage the security.
AutoGPT maintainer
Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports.
Express maintainer
What you can do today
If you maintain any open source project, turn on private vulnerability reporting so researchers can report security issues to you without making them public. If your project is on GitHub, turn on core security features in about two minutes with gh-secure.
If you build on open source, turn on Dependabot alerts so you know when a dependency you use needs a security update.
If you send AI-generated vulnerability reports to open source projects, hold them to the standard above before you send them.
Repositories using GitHub code security can use agentic autofix to help automatically remediate their alerts with Copilot
What happens next
Fixes, where maintainers already work. GitHub is bringing these lessons into private vulnerability reporting and security advisories, where GitHub Security Lab is already investing to reduce the burden of low-quality reports on maintainers.
MAI Cyber 2. Today Microsoft announced MAI Cyber 2. The Codename MDASH pilot ran on the earlier MAI Cyber model. GitHub and Microsoft will keep working together to help secure open source.
Closing the gaps, starting with the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund. We’re working with Microsoft to scale researcher review without cutting corners. GitHub will offer every alumni project AI security scans, with findings checked before they’re reported privately. Alumni also get GitHub Copilot Max. We’ll bring this support to future sessions of the Fund.
Everyone downstream benefits from this system. When a maintainer publishes a security advisory on GitHub and it’s reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert the repositories that depend on that package. That’s the idea behind the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: 216 projects so far, with more than 300 maintainers fixing more than 4,000 vulnerabilities in software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month.
Thank you
To the maintainers of AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty: thank you for your time, your trust, and your feedback. Thank you also to the Codename MDASH team at Microsoft Security, the MAI Cyber team, the researchers of Microsoft FORGE Lab, and GitHub Security Lab.
Maintainers do the fixing. Our job is to make sure they never do it alone.
Hear from maintainers about their experience with Codename MDASH. 👇
About the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund
All six projects in this pilot are alumni of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, which gives each project $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors, plus security training and a supportive alumni community.
The GitHub Secure Open Source Fund, powered by GitHub Sponsors, funds open source projects that underpin the digital supply chain, catalyze innovation, and are critical to the AI stack. Want your company to help secure the open source it depends on? Become a funding partner through the Fund page. Learn more about the Fund or apply.
Through the Fund, maintainers receive security training and Azure credits from Microsoft for Startups. That support sits alongside Microsoft’s European Security Program and its Secure Future Initiative, whose principle is security above all else. Most organizations are downstream in the same way. If your software depends on open source, do the same: back the maintainers you rely on.
I work on open source strategy and programs that support maintainers inside GitHub and across the ecosystem. I also serve on the Steering Committee for the TODO Group, where we help organizations use and sustain open source responsibly.
Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting recursive clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.
GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.

articles.title: JBL’s headphones that are great for in-flight entertainment are 67 percent off
articles.text:
If you’re looking to upgrade your headphones before the big wave of Black Friday deals arrives, you can buy JBL’s Tour One M3 for a new low price of $149 ($300 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and directly from JBL. The deal is so good that my colleague John Higgins, The Verge’s audio and TV reviewer, popped in on his day off to tell us just how much of a steal they are at this price.
JBL’s headphones that are great for in-flight entertainment are 67 percent off
They include a transmitter that let you listen to in-flight entertainment without plugging in your headphones.
JBL’s Tour One M3 stand out largely because they come with the Smart Tx wireless audio transmitter. Frequent fliers will likely appreciate the accessory, which plugs into a plane’s in-flight entertainment system via a 3.5mm cable, allowing you to listen to audio wirelessly. It also works with other devices that lack Bluetooth support but have a headphone jack. The small touchscreen-equipped transmitter also lets you easily adjust the headphones’ noise cancellation, EQ settings, and volume. It can be used to answer calls, too.
Fancy tricks aside, the headphones get the essentials right. According to John, they offer excellent passive noise isolation, and their active noise cancellation is good enough to block out low-frequency sounds, like airplane engines. He also praises their overall sound quality, though he notes that JBL’s default tuning slightly affects midrange clarity, something you can easily fix by adjusting the EQ. They also support high-resolution lossless audio over the included USB-C or 3.5mm cable, plus spatial audio with head tracking. JBL says they can last up to 70 hours on a single charge with noise cancellation off — enough to get you through multiple long-haul flights — while the USB-C-chargeable transmitter offers up to 18 hours of battery life.

articles.title: Kleinere Teams, weniger Freigaben, neue Rollen: Wie Unternehmen ihre Organisation für KI umbauen müssen
articles.text:
Kleinere Teams, weniger Freigaben, neue Rollen: Wie Unternehmen ihre Organisation für KI umbauen müssen
Ein Chatbot hier, ein Copilot dort: In den meisten Unternehmen gehört Künstliche Intelligenz zum Alltag, allerdings meist als Werkzeug für einzelne Aufgaben. Wie groß die Lücke zwischen Nutzung und echtem Umbau ist, zeigt eine Befragung der Technologieberatung Bearing Point. Demnach ist KI nur bei acht Prozent der deutschen Unternehmen tief in die meisten Geschäftsabläufe integriert und liefert messbare Erfolge. In China liegt der Anteil bei 20 Prozent, in den USA bei 18 Prozent.
Unser Cover bringt auf den Punkt, worum es jetzt geht: Aus der GmbH & Co. KG wird die GmbH & Co. KI. Solange KI nur ein Tool unter vielen ist, bleibt ihr Effekt begrenzt. Sie muss ein grundlegender Teil der Organisation werden. Der Organisationsforscher Kai Reinhardt von der HTW Berlin formuliert es so: „Viele betrachten KI fälschlicherweise als Softwaretool und nicht als Infrastruktur, die neue Prozesse und Entscheidungswege eröffnet.“
Wie das konkret aussehen kann, zeigen die Unternehmen in unserer Titelstrecke. Beim Auto-Abo-Anbieter Finn entsteht ein Großteil des Codes inzwischen automatisiert. Deshalb übernehmen die Product Engineers dort auch Produktverantwortung. Beim Fintech Pliant bauen Produktmanager:innen mit KI-Tools eigene Prototypen, bevor die Entwicklung überhaupt loslegt. Der gemeinsame Nenner: Arbeit wird domänenübergreifend. Dadurch schrumpft der Abstimmungsbedarf spürbar, und der ist einer der größten Zeitfresser in Unternehmen.
Das verändert die gesamte Organisation. Bei Lexware bestanden Projektteams bislang aus fünf Leuten, plus/minus zwei. Jetzt stellt die Marke mehr und mehr auf Zwei-Mensch-Teams mit KI um. Spezialist:innen braucht es weiterhin, aber eher als Leitplanke und Qualitätsinstanz denn als Station im Prozess. Und wer einzelnen Mitarbeiter:innen mit KI mehr zutraut, muss Entscheidungswege neu denken: Wann ist noch eine Freigabe nötig, wann reicht ein KI-Check?
Wie weit der Weg für die meisten noch ist, beschreibt Organisationsforscher Phanish Puranam im Interview mit dem Bild einer Pyramide. Fast alle nutzen KI für die individuelle Produktivität, also die unterste Stufe. Prozesse mit KI von Grund auf neu zu gestalten oder gar neue Geschäftsmodelle zu entwickeln, schafft bislang kaum jemand. Wer KI vor allem als Sparprogramm versteht, kommt dort auch nicht hin, warnt der Insead-Professor.
Je mehr Aufgaben KI-Agenten übernehmen, desto wichtiger wird zudem die Frage, was sie eigentlich dürfen. Sie sind derzeit die am schnellsten wachsende Klasse privilegierter Identitäten in Unternehmen und für Angreifer eine bequeme Hintertür. Eines ändert sich aber auch in der GmbH & Co. KI nicht: Entscheidungen lassen sich an Maschinen delegieren, die Verantwortung dafür nicht.
Der Titel im Überblick:
- GmbH & Co. KI: Unternehmen wollen KI-nativ werden und müssen sich dafür strukturell verändern
- „KI ist kein Sparprogramm“: Organisationsforscher Phanish Puranam über die kluge Balance zwischen Menschen und Agenten
- Bye-bye Big Tech?: Die Firmen-IT von morgen soll souveräner sein. Der Weg dahin ist kompliziert
- Zutritt nur mit Ausweis: Mehr KI bringt mehr Cyberrisiken. Ein sauberes Identitätsmanagement wird noch einmal wichtiger
- „Der technologische Wandel funktioniert auch wirtschaftlich“: Von der Agentur zur Plattform: Wie ein Gründer seine Firma auf neue Füße gestellt hat
- Software? Selbst gebaut!: Dayone zahlt viel weniger Lizenzkosten, seit die Agentur Anwendungen selbst erstellt. Ein Erfahrungsbericht
Jetzt bestellen!
Außerdem in der neuen Ausgabe:
„KI schließt die Lücke beim Kauferlebnis“
Vom Katalog zur KI: Etwa ein Prozent des Otto.de-Traffics kommt bereits über Chatbots. Im Interview verrät Otto-Chef Boris Ewenstein, wie er diesen Anteil steigern will, ohne den direkten Kontakt zur Kundschaft zu verlieren. Und wie die Shoppingplattform trotz neuer Checkout-Kanäle relevant bleiben soll.
Die fetten Jahre sind vorbei
Noch vor wenigen Jahren rissen sich Unternehmen um IT-Fachkräfte, heute tun sich viele Jobsuchende schwer. Warum Firmen so zögerlich einstellen und welche Profile im KI-Zeitalter gefragt bleiben.
Durstige Chatbots
Künstliche Intelligenz hat einen Bauboom bei Rechenzentren ausgelöst, auch in Deutschland. Zum Problem wird dabei nicht nur der steigende Energiehunger, sondern auch der immense Wasserverbrauch. Umweltschützer:innen blicken besorgt auf den KI-Boom.
Weitere starke Themen in der t3n 86:
- „KI hat in der Industrie den größten Hebel“: Sphere Intelligence digitalisiert Ingenieurs-Know-how und könnte damit dem Wirtschaftsstandort Europa den nötigen Push geben
- Passt schon: Der E-Commerce leidet unter der Retourenschwemme und setzt auf digitale Gegenmittel
- Lohnt sich das?: Die Kosten für KI explodieren in vielen Unternehmen. So schafft man Transparenz
- „Die meisten Unternehmen haben kein KI-Problem, sie sind nur vergesslich“: Johanna Heise und Andy Lenz diskutieren über das „Second Brain“
- Job ohne Jetlag: Chronoworking ermöglicht das Arbeiten nach der inneren Uhr. Ein Modell, das sich lohnen kann
- „Betriebe verschließen bewusst die Augen“: Rechtsanwalt Jens Ferner über die Risiken der Schatten-KI
- Ein Werkzeug für alle Fälle: Drei digitale Vordenker verraten, wie KI im Arbeitsalltag hilft
- Vergiftete Daten: Hacker versuchen, Sprachmodelle zu manipulieren. Wie sich Data-Poisoning verhindern lässt
- Maschinen lernen Moral: Forscher wollen der KI ein Gefühl für Gut und Böse geben. Ein riskantes Spiel
- Guten Morgen, Claude!: Unser Autor startet jeden Tag mit Kaffee und KI. Einblicke in einen erfolgreichen Selbstversuch
- Jetzt geht’s rund: Mit Loop-Engineering geht es oft schneller zum Ziel. Worauf es dabei ankommt
- Komm mit ins Abenteuerland: Vibe-Coding macht alle Menschen zu Entwicklern. Ein Plädoyer fürs Ausprobieren
- Context is King: Wer Wissen sauber auf seinem Rechner sortiert, erleichtert der KI die Arbeit und sich selbst auch
- Sichtbarkeit baut man gemeinsam: Damit die eigene Marke in KI-Antworten auftaucht, ist mehr nötig als gutes SEO
- So funktioniert Werbung bei ChatGPT: Der Ads-Manager von OpenAI wirkt vertraut. Doch an ein paar Stellen müssen Werber umdenken
- Wie kennzeichnet man KI-Inhalte richtig?: Die EU verschärft die Regeln. Worauf es in der Praxis ankommt

articles.title: Nvidia's first big move after Jensen Huang's exit targets national security | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia has formed a committee to oversee national security policies and export control compliance following the abrupt resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who had links to one of the company’s customers.
Nvidia said Tuesday that the new standing committee will give board-level oversight of national security policies, export control compliance, and global trade risks. The move comes amid increased scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Huang’s alleged ties to the suspected spy and his advocacy for easing restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China.
The Commerce Department said Monday it was planning to introduce new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside of the U.S. in an effort to prevent companies in China and elsewhere from circumventing existing rules by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries. The interim rule was made in direct response to the unfolding chip smuggling scandal at Nvidia.
The announcement comes just a few hours before Nvidia’s highly anticipated third-quarter earnings call. Analysts, the media, and shareholders expect the company to address the controversy and outline how it might affect operations. This is the first major action by the company under the leadership of Colette Kress, the company’s CFO who took over as interim CEO after Huang stepped down last week.
The committee, which will meet at least quarterly, will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include fellow directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members.
Nvidia already has a national security team and global trade compliance team. Those teams will now report to this board committee and Kress on day-to-day operations.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress later this month.

articles.title: A espera por GTA 6 já rendeu 620 milhões de visualizações no Kwai
articles.text:
Em 17 de novembro de 2026, a dois dias do lançamento de GTA 6, o jogo da Rockstar já soma mais de 620 milhões de visualizações e 240 mil publicações no Kwai, segundo dados da própria plataforma. O número aparece em um momento em que a expectativa deixou de ficar só nos trailers e virou conteúdo de fã, em vídeos curtos que passam por teoria, análise e saudade.
Não é exagero dizer que a espera virou um evento à parte. Nos vídeos, os usuários comparam o novo jogo com GTA V, discutem os protagonistas, reagem às prévias divulgadas pela Rockstar Games e especulam sobre o que vem por aí no mapa. Entre os criadores que alimentam essa conversa estão os perfis GTA6 Clipes, Alan Geek e Cenas Memoráveis, que misturam curiosidades, cenas dos jogos anteriores e debate sobre o novo título.
GTA 6 chega 13 anos depois de GTA V
O lançamento de GTA 6 está marcado para esta quinta-feira (19), no PlayStation 5 e no Xbox Series X|S. É o fim de uma espera de mais de 13 anos desde GTA V, que chegou em setembro de 2013. A história acompanha Jason e Lucia, dois protagonistas envolvidos em uma conspiração criminosa em Leonida, estado fictício que abriga Vice City, a cidade inspirada em Miami que os fãs da série já conhecem.
O tamanho da expectativa não aparece só nas redes. Em entrevista à CNBC, publicada em 10 de novembro, o CEO da Take-Two, Strauss Zelnick, disse que as pré-vendas de GTA 6 estão superando amplamente as expectativas da empresa, sem confirmar números. Já a Sensor Tower estimou que o jogo passou de US$ 1 bilhão em receita em 11 de novembro, oito dias antes do lançamento, com cerca de 10,3 milhões de unidades em pré-venda. São estimativas de mercado, e não números divulgados pela Take-Two.
Vídeos curtos como parte da espera por GTA 6
O caso do Kwai mostra como o formato mudou a forma de acompanhar lançamentos. Quem joga não só consome a novidade, mas também produz, opina e puxa a conversa. Para ver o que a comunidade está publicando, basta buscar pela hashtag #GTA6 no aplicativo, disponível para iOS e Android.
A contagem regressiva já aconteceu bem antes do dia 19, em milhões de telas de celular.
É técnica em audiovisual e community manager com 7 anos de experiência no universo gamer.

articles.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
articles.text:
Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud.
Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.
In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.
Why one integration per client stopped working
GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have.
At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity.
Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is.
Designing a protocol for agents on every client
The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients.
At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent behavior. Unlike the domains that produced the Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol, the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them.
You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal.
The result of these requirements is the Agent Host Protocol (AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example.
Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them. Clients and servers are straightforward to debug. And reducer-based state also plays nicely with popular UI frameworks like React.
Shipping five clients and two hosts
Adopting the Agent Host Protocol in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The Copilot Chat extension, which used to provide all of VS Code’s AI and agentic capabilities, had been growing for over three years, reaching over 400,000 lines of TypeScript, not counting tests. But, as a VS Code extension, it was structured around the lifecycle of a VS Code window and depended entirely on the VS Code extension API. Neither that lifetime nor those APIs would be available in a standalone agent host process.
As we started building the Agent Host Protocol in early 2026, the Copilot SDK was also being developed, and it made sense to leverage it as the foundation for the new agentic stack. This was a big transition. It’s easy to build a harness implementation that says hello and can edit files—we were using the agent host to develop the agent host after the first couple weeks—but it’s another thing to build one that covers the long tail of features developers had come to expect from Copilot Chat.
GitHub has had Copilot cloud agents for a couple of years, allowing developers to run tasks in the cloud from any device. While VS Code was quietly developing the Agent Host Protocol, GitHub was looking to expand that capability to coordinate sessions running on your own devices via the Copilot app, or in cloud sandboxes. This was exactly the N:M problem that AHP was built to solve, so adopting the same technology made perfect sense.
From the outset, the GitHub Agent Host had different requirements than VS Code’s implementation. VS Code runs the host locally and can drop its host on other compute over SSH, containers, WSL, or Dev Tunnels, and it is actually included as part of the VS Code Server bundle. The GitHub Agent Host needed to run in the cloud and across a much wider variety of infrastructure, environments, and security constraints.
Those differing requirements are why they’re separate implementations written in different languages: VS Code’s in TypeScript and GitHub’s in Rust. For now, having two agent hosts has been a good acid-test for the protocol itself. How well does it work when two entirely different teams and sets of agents implement the same protocol independently?
Pretty well, it turns out. Like MCP, the Agent Host Protocol provides escape hatches via custom methods and _metadata on objects that consumers can use for out-of-band signaling. After several months heads-down on our respective implementations, our first task as we worked toward unification was inventorying the ways each implementation had extended the protocol. Many of these extensions reasonably stay GitHub-specific, such as the GitHub Agent Host using metadata to link to project boards. In other cases, variance was a sign of a gap in the protocol; early versions, for example, could not accurately represent shell-type tool output that wasn’t backed by a PTY. And some were bad assumptions, like VS Code’s client assuming a particular structure for the session URIs it received from the agent host. A protocol with only one implementation isn’t truly portable; as we taught our clients and servers to talk to each other, AHP became portable in practice, not just in theory.
Today, the Agent Host Protocol provides that same continuity across all VS Code and GitHub surfaces. Agent sessions running locally in the GitHub Copilot app, in cloud sandboxes, and in VS Code all share the same underlying protocol. To see how it’s used, read about how you can work from anywhere with the new connected Copilot cloud experience.
Using the Agent Host Protocol
AHP was designed to be easy to use in clients and servers. Agent Host Protocol libraries are available in Rust, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, .NET, and Go, and agents are able to build clients and servers with little prompting. I have a macropad sitting on my desk that reflects my agent’s state in real time, and others have built everything from smart watch apps to Kanban-style task management tools against the protocol. Whether you want a companion app for your own agents, a way to bring agent sessions into your team’s tools, or AHP support in your own editor or agent, the protocol is open for you to build on.
You can connect to an agent host you implement in the Copilot app (enable Experimental > Direct Connections, then go to Environments > Add Agent Host Protocol Host) and in VS Code (via Add Remote Agent Host in the Agents window). You can spawn a standalone version of VS Code’s agent host by running code agent host in your terminal, or see the endpoints for the one in your editor by running code agent endpoints, and samples can help you and your agent get started.
The Agent Host Protocol is an open standard, and questions and suggestions are welcome on GitHub.
Happy coding!

articles.title: Voyager 1 atteint un jour-lumière de la Terre : à 26 milliards de km de la Terre, cela aurait pris 28 250 ans en voiture
articles.text:
Lorsque vient le moment d’appréhender les distances absolument colossales dans l’univers, la mesure de référence est l’année-lumière. C’est elle qui permet usuellement d’indiquer l’écart entre des objets incroyablement distants entre eux. Et c’est parfois presque insuffisant, à l’image de ce signal ayant franchi 10 milliards d’années-lumière avant de nous parvenir.
La notion d’année-lumière est en fait assez simple à comprendre : cette unité de longueur détermine la distance parcourue par la lumière dans le vide en un an. Du coup, on saisit facilement la logique d’un jour-lumière. C’est la même chose, mais en 24 heures. Mais concrètement, à quoi cela correspond-il ?
Cette question se pose avec force, car le jour-lumière est aujourd’hui au cœur de l’actualité : en effet, ce 18 novembre, vers 11h16 (heure de Paris), la sonde Voyager 1 de la NASA franchira cette barre d’un jour-lumière de distance avec la Terre. Aucun autre objet fabriqué par l’humanité n’est allé aussi loin : Voyager 1 détient ce record depuis février 1998, quand elle a dépassé la sonde Pioneer 10. Jusqu’ici, on comptait sa distance en heures-lumière.
En 24 heures, donc, la lumière traverse dans le vide la distance de 25,9 milliards de kilomètres. La conséquence ? Une instruction envoyée par radio depuis la Terre met une journée entière pour atteindre la sonde. Sa réponse met autant de temps à revenir. Un échange simple prend donc deux longues journées. Et ça ne va faire que s’aggraver.
Car la sonde, lancée le 5 septembre 1977, continue son odyssée sans retour dans le cosmos.
Mais pour rendre cette distance de jour-lumière plus parlante, la NASA a publié une infographie avec une série d’équivalences le 16 novembre. Pour qui le souhaite, l’agence spatiale américaine invite aussi le public, la veille du passage, à faire un « coucou » à la sonde en morse avec son smartphone. Une initiative surtout symbolique.
Plus de 67 000 trajets jusqu’à la Lune
Les équivalences donnent le tournis : 25,9 milliards de kilomètres, ça fait plus de 646 000 tours de la Terre au niveau de l’équateur. Une vie humaine moyenne compte environ 30 000 jours (en se basant sur une espérance de vie de l’ordre de 82 à 83 ans). Pour boucler ces 646 000 tours en une vie, il faudrait en faire presque 22 par jour.
C’est aussi environ 67 400 trajets entre la Terre et la Lune, les deux corps étant séparés d’environ 384 400 kilomètres. En filant à 299 792 km/s, la lumière fait presque 7 fois et demie le tour de la Terre, et cela en une seule seconde. Malgré cette vitesse, l’espace est si grand que la lumière met du temps à le traverser.
Pour prendre une comparaison plus terre à terre, la NASA propose aussi une version à l’échelle d’un terrain de football américain, long de 91,4 mètres. La Terre défend une zone d’en-but et Voyager 1 se trouve à l’autre bout du terrain, prête à marquer. Saturne, que la sonde a survolée en novembre 1980, serait à moins de 4,6 mètres de la Terre.
28 250 ans en voiture, 49 ans pour Voyager 1
Si la lumière est imbattable en termes de vitesse, Voyager 1 se défend bien. La sonde est même assez rapide : elle file à environ 61 155 kilomètres par heure, soit près de 1,47 million de kilomètres par jour (la lumière va encore près de 17 650 fois plus vite, en comparaison). En ramenant l’affaire à des km/h, on a plus de facilité à appréhender les choses.
Une voiture qui roulerait sans s’arrêter à environ 105 kilomètres par heure parcourrait quelque 2 510 kilomètres par jour. Il lui faudrait donc environ 28 250 ans pour couvrir un jour-lumière. Un avion de ligne lancé à 885 km/h mettrait encore environ 3 340 ans. Voyager 1 a mis presque un demi-siècle à y parvenir, à une vitesse élevée qui a varié au fil du voyage.
La sonde ne fonctionne plus qu’en partie : deux instruments scientifiques, un magnétomètre et un détecteur d’ondes de plasma, sont encore allumés ; les autres sont tombés en panne ou ont été coupés pour économiser l’énergie. Voyager 1 a permis de mieux comprendre l’environnement interstellaire, mais son héritage le plus marquant est peut-être symbolique.
Le 14 février 1990, Voyager 1 a pris la photo du « point bleu pâle », où la Terre n’est qu’un point minuscule. La sonde était alors à environ 6 milliards de kilomètres du Soleil, et le cliché a inspiré un très célèbre commentaire à l’astronome Carl Sagan, membre de l’équipe d’imagerie de Voyager et à l’origine de la photo. Dans son livre Pale Blue Dot (1994), il y voit le rappel de la place minuscule de l’humanité dans l’univers.
Le 25 août 2012, la sonde a traversé l’héliopause, la limite de la bulle de particules et de champ magnétique créée par le Soleil, à environ 18 milliards de kilomètres du Soleil. Voyager 1 est alors entrée dans l’espace interstellaire, qui reste, à l’échelle de l’univers, notre très proche voisinage.
À l’échelle des étoiles, un jour-lumière reste minuscule. Une année-lumière en contient un peu plus de 365, et Proxima du Centaure, l’étoile la plus proche du Soleil, est à 4,24 années-lumière. La NASA estime que Voyager 1 passera à 1,7 année-lumière de l’étoile Gliese 445 dans environ 40 000 ans. D’après l’infographie, la sonde sera alors à quelque 2,14 années-lumière de la Terre, soit environ 780 jours-lumière.

articles.title: Optimizely Vulnerability Exploited to Serve Malware on Major Websites
articles.text:
Digital experience platform Optimizely has patched a vulnerability that hackers exploited to inject malicious code into customer projects, causing the websites of many major organizations to serve malware to visitors.
The company confirmed the incident in a status page update posted early on November 17 and in a post on X, where it said some Web Experimentation customers were affected.
“Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects,” the company said on its status page. “We’ve fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects.”
Optimizely added that it has taken steps to secure affected user accounts and introduced additional protections, but it has not said how many customers were impacted.
Report URI, a security firm that investigated the attack, said it examined 1,611 Optimizely scripts and identified 188 infected ones, belonging to 178 organizations. Names on the list include the BBC, CNN, Zoom, GitLab, Salesforce, Equifax, HSBC and IKEA.
According to Report URI, the malicious code was placed in an optional field meant for a customer’s own JavaScript, which executes on every page. The tampered files came from Optimizely’s content delivery network, so the websites loading them treated them as trusted.
The first Optimizely injection in Report URI’s timeline is dated November 16, 04:21 UTC. By 21:52 UTC, only one of the infected scripts had yet to be cleaned.
The malware could swap cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s own and skim payment card details. It could also collect cookies and screenshots of the page. By Monday evening, roughly $7,000 in cryptocurrency had reached the attacker, Report URI said.
iPhone and iPad users were served the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits, according to Report URI. Hudson Rock confirmed links to the exploit-kit infrastructure, but noted that successful exploitation has not been demonstrated.
“The supported conclusion is a connection to exploit-kit delivery infrastructure. The current evidence does not establish a zero-day, successful device exploitation, or collection of specific device data by unseen downstream stages,” Hudson Rock said.
Hudson Rock’s report, which includes findings from a researcher at Ohey, shows that Optimizely was not the only delivery channel. Scripts from Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute-ly were seen serving a small loader that led to the same iOS-targeting infrastructure.
The earliest of these observations dates to November 13. It’s unclear how the code got into these providers’ scripts.
Hudson Rock also warned that blocking the attacker’s domain may not be enough. Some of the poisoned Optimizely scripts had a full version of the payload embedded in them, which could run if the remote file failed to load.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached,” Report URI’s Scott Helme said.
Optimizely disclosed a separate incident in February, when a threat actor accessed its systems through a voice-phishing attack.
